channel.title: Personal News Feed — Other
channel.description: Personally scored travel, food, and lifestyle articles curated by news-filter

item.title: Thousands of African birds are missing from sound libraries. A massive grassroots effort hopes to change that
item.description:
Source: Adventure Score: 4.32
Thousands of African bird species remain missing from the sound libraries that train AI-powered research and conservation tools. Now, the Cornell Lab of Ornithology and BirdLife South Africa are leading an ambitious continent-wide grassroots effort to fill in the gaps. Alexandra Owens reports.

item.title: Traditional gumbo, kettle-boiled bagels, Chelsea buns: What do ‘endangered dishes’ tell us about the world today?
item.description:
Source: Adventure Score: 3.79
Globalization, overtourism, climate crisis, and social change can all contribute to the loss of beloved cultural practices—including what we eat. But what does this mean for cultural and food heritage? And how can travelers help preserve the flavors that make our experiences so much richer?

item.title: This Indigenous-led tour in BC is part of a Canada-wide initiative to put First Nations tourism in the spotlight
item.description:
Source: Adventure Score: 2.58
Seven in 10 Canadians say they’d enjoy learning about Indigenous cultures on their travels, but many don’t know how or where to find a tour. Indigenous-owned Talaysay Tours and B Corp tour operator Intrepid Travel are hoping to fix that. “We are on the unceded territories of the Squamish and Lil’wat people,” says Talaysay Campo, whose name translates to ‘ocean breeze’, ‘wind blowing on the water’ or ‘whispering winds’. “There’s one thing I want to share, and that’s that the land is absolutely everything.” We’re just outside Whistler Village in British Columbia about to embark on a forest trail walk to Lost Lake (Sḵwiḵ), a critical stopping point for Indigenous communities to gather resources and fish when traveling between the coast and the interior. Today we’re on a preview of Campo’s new ‘We Are The Land’ tour. “The reason we chose this name for the tour is something my Aunty Talaysay would tell me when I was a little girl: ‘We are the land’. It means that we are the caretakers of the land,” she says. Campo is co-owner of Talaysay Tours, an Indigenous, women-owned tourism company offering Indigenous-led experiences across British Columbia. Founded by her mother Candace Campo, in 2002, the company is rooted in the traditions and knowledge of both the Shíshálh (Sechelt) and Sḵwx̱wú7mesh (Squamish) Nations, of which the women are members. Walking beneath a canopy of towering old-growth Western Hemlock trees, Campo points out the Devil’s club, a woody shrub used by her ancestors for pain relief. “It’s important to have Indigenous tourism so our local guests and out-of-town guests can build a stronger relationship with the land,” says Campo as we pause by a babbling brook, where glimmers of sunlight dance on the slow-moving creek. “There’s so much going on with logging, global warming—one thing I’ve realized is that if (people) don’t have a relationship with the land, how are they going to take care of it or know how to take care of it?” It’s a question that sits at the heart of a growing conversation about what responsible travel in Canada should look like. As part of this conversation, Talaysay Tours has partnered with B Corp tour operator Intrepid Travel on this new ‘We Are The Land’ experience. It’s aim is to help bring place-based learning, cultural ecology, stewardship and storytelling to Intrepid’s 10-day Grand Canadian Rockies itinerary beginning in 2027. “For us, it’s at the cornerstone of everything that has to do with responsible tourism. We think it’s also just an amazing experience for our customers to really understand the real Canada, and the only way to do that is to partner with an Indigenous-led company.” - Christian Wolters, Intrepid Travel Canada President The Talasay partnership is part of a broader initiative by Intrepid to include more Indigenous tourism across its Canadian itineraries, with the goal to have an Indigenous-led experience on 75 percent of Canada tours by the end of this year, and one on every Canadian itinerary by the end of 2031. According to new research from non-profit foundation Angus Reid, commissioned by Intrepid Travel in July this year and surveying a group of 1,507 Canadians, 57 percent say they are interested in participating in an Indigenous-led tourism experience within Canada, yet fewer than one in five have ever done so. Part of the problem may be visibility. Among Canadians who have never participated in an Indigenous-led experience, 42 percent say they have not encountered one while planning a trip, while another 30 percent say they don’t know where to find one. According to the survey, seven in 10 Canadians would enjoy learning about Indigenous cultures, while more than four in 10 would be more likely to choose a Canadian trip that includes an Indigenous-led tourism experience. The appetite is certainly there. For Intrepid Travel Canada President Christian Wolters, who has joined us on the walking trail, making these experiences easier to access is more than a business opportunity. “For us, it’s at the cornerstone of everything that has to do with responsible tourism,” he tells me, after stopping to taste a few reddish salmonberries, native to the Pacific Northwest. “We think it’s also just an amazing experience for our customers to really understand the real Canada, and the only way to do that is to partner with an Indigenous-led company.” Intrepid is also working closely with the Indigenous Tourism Association of Canada (ITAC) and has committed over USD$350,000 over five years to support the growth and promotion of Indigenous tourism in Canada. This includes adding Indigenous experiences to existing tours, as well as developing new, bespoke experiences alongside Indigenous tourism operators. “Partnerships like this create tangible opportunities and ensure communities gain direct economic and cultural benefits, while supporting our vision of Canada becoming a world leader in Indigenous tourism by 2030,” said Keith Henry, chief executive officer and president of ITAC in a press release. Coming up in 2027, a Huron-Wendat experience in Wendake, Quebec, will be added to Intrepid’s Eastern Canada by Rail itinerary, which will include a guided visit to the Huron-Wendat longhouse at the Huron Traditional Site. This addition will see Intrepid reach its goal of an Indigenous-led experience on 75 percent of their Canada itineraries—a significant milestone on the road to integrating Indigenous-led experiences across every Canada trip. “When it comes to Indigenous tourism in Canada, we only take up five percent of tourism and that’s such a small percentage,” says Campo, as we stand before the lovely Lost Lake with its mountainous backdrop. “So this partnership with Intrepid and other Indigenous companies throughout Turtle Island—these are the partners I wanna work with.” As she distributes traditional ‘hush’ tea made with soothing raspberry leaf, refreshing mint sweet licorice root and vibrant rose hips, we talk of the importance of stories. “When it comes to a lot of Indigenous history and our government, they try to write our story for us,” she says. “We’re redirecting that chapter so we can write and share our stories ourselves.” The writer was hosted by Intrepid Travel **** Adventure.com strives to be a low-emissions travel publication. We are powered by, but editorially independent of, Intrepid Travel, the world’s largest travel B Corp, who help ensure Adventure.com maintains high standards of sustainability in our work and activities. You can visit our sustainability page or read our Contributor Impact Guidelines for more information. Journalist and wanderluster Charmaine Noronha is a travel writer with a penchant for adventure, culture and chocolate. She started her career as a reporter with The Toronto Star before becoming the EIC of Vervegirl Magazine for five years then reported on Canadian news for The Associated Press for 11 years. Most recently, she was a Lifestyle reporter/editor at HuffPost Canada.

item.title: Dark sky camp-out one day, zebra migration the next. An alternative adventure in northeastern Botswana
item.description:
Source: Adventure Score: 2.12
Camping on cracked earth in the middle of one of the world’s largest salt pans followed by a zebra migration across a dried-up riverbed prove to be an unexpected safari combo in northeastern Botswana. “Makgadikgadi means ‘dry and thirsty place’,” our guide Metal Matmos tells us. No kidding. This is cracked earth indeed. We’ve arrived at one of the world’s largest salt pans to spend a night under one of the planet’s darkest skies. Bar our group and guides, there’s no-one around in this southern section of northeastern Botswana’s lunar-like Makgadikgadi Salt Pans. Here, southeast of the Okavango Delta in the Kalahari Basin where the ancient Lake Makgadikgadi (pronounced Mah-caddy-caddy) once stood, salt denies grass and trees cannot germinate. It is barren, vast and surreal. As we rock up to where Metal’s colleagues are setting up trestle tables and chairs, I spot our ‘rooms’ in the distance. Five cozy ‘bedrolls’ with a thick duvet inside bivvy bags—a tent-like covering we can crawl into—a couple of storage stands, and each bedroll a sizeable distance apart. Camping is not in my comfort zone—mostly down to an ick for shared bathrooms as opposed to sleeping outdoors, which is the good bit. But one thing travel does is test, and stretch, comfort zones. Perhaps falling asleep under a dark sky resplendent with stars on this flat, crater-like landscape with a 360-degree view of the horizon will do just that. An equally fair distance away in the opposite direction is the ‘bathroom’, a tented toilet with a washing bowl outside. Clean, far enough for privacy, close enough to (mostly) avoid middle-of-the-night Salt Pan Scaries. As Metal, full name Mathale Mosheti, gets the campfire going, I take a moment to take in this vastness. I’ve been to remote spots before: The Kalahari Desert in South Africa’s Northern Cape province; the salt desert of Kutch, Gujarat, northwestern India; Churchill, Canada, the polar bear capital of the world. But I’d never felt this distant from life, so off-grid, surrounded by a silence that’s both unsettling and soothing. Within minutes, I fall asleep. When I wake, it’s to the most exquisite sunrise, a soft orange glow rising from the flat horizon ahead. This Makgadikgadi Salt Pans sleep-out is a seasonal experience from Desert & Delta’s Leroo La Tau lodge, one of 11 lodges and camps in their Botswana portfolio. A four-hour drive from the salt pans, I’d already spent one night there, and would return for another, if I survived the camping. 100 percent-Botswana-owned, all properties are managed by local people with staff empowerment woven in; Chobe Game Lodge, further north, home to Botswana’s first all-female-led guiding team. “The Makgadikgadi Pans are visible from the Moon,” Metal says as he hands me a bottle of local St Louis lager to accompany sunset. It’s not hard to believe; Lake Makgadikgadi, long evaporated, once covered an area larger than Switzerland. During the wet season, water surrounds the edges of the pans, attracting zebra, wildebeest and antelope en route to greener pastures, and flamingoes to the saltwater lakes that spring up. Metal, who has worked for Desert & Delta Safaris for nearly 18 years, is also a walking encyclopedia, whether it’s about geology, birdlife or conservation. He’s one of those guides you just don’t forget; I feel lucky to have met a fair few on my travels and like many others, has a natural calling to share the joy of the landscapes, people and wildlife he works with and in. After cold beers at sunset and a barbecued meal under the southern skies, bed beckons. The bedroll is cozy, and the night sky sparkles above. I take out my phone, purely to bring up an offline stargazing app. I find the Southern Cross and a haze of stars that form the Milky Way. It’s utterly mesmerizing. While other constellations elude me, simply staring up at this twinkling sky with zero light pollution is satisfying enough. A cliché for a reason perhaps but sometimes we need such moments to remember how insignificant we are, when we live in our own heads for much of the day, and there are mysteries as yet unsolved. I don’t believe this inner conversation lasts long; I’m sure I fall asleep within minutes. When I wake, it’s to the most exquisite sunrise, a soft orange glow rising from the flat horizon ahead. At breakfast, we trade stories of our first salt pan camping experience. I admit, despite craving a hot shower, I leave the salt pans with a slight pang. When it’s a daily challenge to quieten the busy mind, this one night had done exactly that. Back on the road, a movement in the grasslands catches Metal’s attention. We all squint and ‘tune in’ with our eyes; I see something vaguely stripy scampering across the savannah. Metal’s eyes glint. “It’s an aardwolf.” It’s a rare sighting—it’s only the fourth time he’s seen one. “They’re from the same family as hyenas,” he tells us. I learn, despite their somewhat feral appearance, they’re actually insectivores. An aardwolf’s idea of a good feast is munching around quarter of a million termites in one night, using their signature long sticky tongue to catch them. It’s a joy to return to my room at Leroo La Tau, perched above the seasonal Boteti River, the main outflow of the Okavango Delta, and along the western boundary of Makgadikgadi Pans National Park. Its 11 thatched-roof chalets and one suite are glass-fronted, so wherever you sit, stand, lie down, or shower, there’s a Royal Circle view of the currently dry riverbed and watering holes. The river had began to recede in the mid-1980s, due to fewer flood waters from the delta and low rainfall. By the mid-1990s, it had dried up leaving just a few waterholes for crocodiles, hippos, zebras and wildebeest. In 2009, record rainfall arrived, reinstating this watercourse, albeit with a degree of unpredictability. Today, some 15,ooo zebras move 310 miles (510 kilometers) between the Okavango Delta/Moremi region and the Makgadikgadi Pans. We’re towards the end of the May-October dry season, the rainy season looming, and this river-turned-ravine, following a shift in tectonic plates, is teeming with herds of zebra, wildebeest, oryx, impala, elephants. Sat on the deck with views over Boteti River Valley, I enjoy the scene unfolding in front of me. A vulture flies past then swoops below. Moments later, a monkey appears on the railings. I eyeball him or her, while guarding my cookie and sipping my tea. “When you reach a herd of elephants, you should pass by when they’re behind you, so you can drive forward if you need to and not in reverse which is slower. If guests want to die, they can die somewhere else.” - 'Metal' Mathale Mosheti, Desert & Delta Safaris guide Later, I head to the lodge’s hide, past the campfire and pool, for a closer close-up. It’s extraordinary to see zebras, wildebeest and the gang this close, and in such numbers. Walking back to the restaurant, an impala wanders across the lawn. They pause, I pause. For urbanites like me, these moments are (almost) as enchanting as the mightier scenes below. It’s also a reminder you are on the edge of a national park. When darkness falls, staff escort you to the rooms, and we’re advised to be vigilant. A windstorm blows outside, an eerie combination of piercing shrieks and deep gusts. Later, what we’re convinced is a leopard, comes close to camp. It’s exciting when you’re inside four walls and cocooned under a duvet and mosquito net. It’s definitely not the time to step onto the balcony to test your camera’s ‘night mode’. No matter what ‘people’ say about the early-morning game drive, it’s the late afternoon one I love. The bleary eyes of the dawn safari are long gone, it’s still warm, wildlife mooches about, and golden hour is kicking in. As we drive through Makgadikgadi Pans National Park with our ranger Kets, Metal shares some of his road safety tips. “When you reach a herd of elephants, you should pass by when they’re behind you, so you can drive forward if you need to and not in reverse which is slower,” he tells us. “If guests want to die, they can die somewhere else.” It’s hard to argue with that. We all lodge this advice for the next time we’re driving and come across a herd of the largest living mammal on earth. As we head down to the riverbed itself, the scenes from our decks are magnified. African savanna elephants on the move, dazzles of zebras sipping at watering holes, a confusion of wildebeest join their stripy friends for a drink, and above, kori bustards, the largest flying bird native to Africa. From a ridge, we spot crocodiles lurking at the water’s edge and grunting hippos enjoying their late afternoon dip. Alongside elephant health and safety, Metal tells us why zebras and wildebeest can happily graze together; zebras like taller grass while wildebeest go for shorter grass. “And you see how the impalas have an M-shape on their back?” he asks. We nod, expecting some mystical interpretation. “We call it McDonald’s for the lions.” We know our chances of seeing lions are slim, due to human-wildlife conflicts. “Lions used to go beyond the gate and kill goats in the villages; then they’d be killed,” says Metal. The river is the boundary, with the national park on one side, and community land and the lodge’s private land on the other. Communities live close to and around national parks and reserves, and their livelihoods and food security is vital. It’s something Desert & Delta are acutely conscious of, and part of their work involves investing in local education, community empowerment, and research. I’m reminded of a talk I attended back in London: “When an animal destroys someone’s garden, that person doesn’t have a Waitrose at the end of their road.” On my final morning, I stand on the deck and watch the scene in front of me for the last time. Zebras yap like puppies reuniting at Doggy Daycare, elephants arrive majestically at the watering hole, giraffes stroll along the ravine, while wildebeest, who look like they picked up the last remaining body parts in a fancy dress shop, move en masse. Between this sensory overload and the quiet emptiness of the salt flats, I feel my senses have had the full workout. ** The writer’s trip was supported by Desert & Delta Safaris and African Pride who curate a variety of packages in their properties across Botswana including Leroo La Tau and the salt pans sleep-out (dry season/June to October). **** Adventure.com strives to be a low-emissions travel publication. We are powered by, but editorially independent of, Intrepid Travel, the world’s largest travel B Corp, who help ensure Adventure.com maintains high standards of sustainability in our work and activities. You can visit our sustainability page or read our Contributor Impact Guidelines for more information. London-born-and-bred with a Ugandan-Indian heritage, Meera Dattani is Adventure.com's executive editor and an award-winning freelance travel journalist. Her stories center on food and cultural heritage, wildlife and conservation, and soft adventure, often through a lens of decolonizing and modernizing travel writing. Her work has been published in National Geographic Traveller, BBC Travel, Condé Nast Traveller, Olive magazine and many others.

item.title: These 6 Gear Trends Took the Long Trails By Storm in 2026
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine Score: 5.46
(Photo: Zoe Gates) On long trails, gear and clothing trends can seem as fad-driven as they were in high school. Caps are out, bucket hats are in. Heavy boots are so 2005. And if you aren’t dressed in a hooded, collared shirt with donuts all over it, are you even a thru-hiker? Show up to the trailhead with the wrong setup, and just like when you were a teenager, you might feel like you risk being laughed all the way back to town for a resupply. Not that every trend exists across every trail, of course. Trail culture—and the gear that contributes to it—varies from place to place. For example, “Ultralight felt very ‘in’ out west in a way that it didn’t out east,” says thru-hiker Madelyn Dukart, who has trekked long trails across the country. When something is hot in the thru-hiker community, it’s only a matter of time before it trickles down to the rest of the backpacking world. And while some gear crazes only stay in vogue for a season or two, plenty of fresh gear and apparel becomes popular thanks to its practicality or innovation. Here are the trends that took the long trails by storm this past season. To say the ultralight material Alpha Direct swept the thru-hiking community off their feet may be an understatement. “Just a year or two ago [thru-hikers] were all about microgrid hoodies, but they definitely have moved on to Alphas,” notes Mary Pillsbury, owner of 2 Foot Adventures outdoor stores located along the PCT in Julian and Kennedy Meadows. It makes sense: Alpha Direct is lighter, more compact, breathes better, and still insulates well when layered under a windproof jacket. Hoodies made from the material have been popular for a few seasons, but this year’s hikers aren’t stopping there: pants, hats, socks, even gloves have been hot ticket items this year for their gram-consciousness and versatility. Head to any trail town and there’s one thing you’re practically guaranteed to find in every hiker box: a quarter-full IsoPro fuel canister or three. After all, no one wants to leave town with one day of fuel left in their canister then have to carry it empty to the next resupply. Enter fuel transfer devices. These pocket-sized wonders allow hikers to combine fuel from multiple partially empty containers into one. They aren’t new this year, but they were formerly built of hefty metal materials. But a 2.4-gram plastic version is becoming ubiquitous: “Almost every hiker carries a fuel transfer device thanks to Alpenglow Gear. They are so light and inexpensive; 3D printing is changing the market,” says Pillsbury. “This is the first year I’ve heard thru-hikers talk about microplastics,” says Pillsbury. Where Smartwater bottles were once the go-to, more hikers have made the swap this year to using reusable CNOC or M!Go bottles, she’s noticed. Smart, since studies have shown that reusing single-use plastic bottles results in ingesting more microplastics. Plus, reusable bottles are designed to last for years and are only marginally heavier. “Most people that get involved in outdoor recreation begin with their love for nature, and it can feel dissonant to preach respecting nature while relying on single-use plastics for such a crucial piece of gear. Seeing multiple brands with thru-hiker-friendly water bottles seems to alleviate some of that dissonance,” Dukart says. Long gone are the days of huffing and puffing into your inflatable sleeping pad every night thanks to the rise of ultralight pad pumps. In fact, the gadgets have gotten so small and light––thanks in part to the rise of 3D-printed gear and the cottage industry––that there’s little reason not to pack one. After all, there’s an option to suit every hiker, from the stupendously light Alpenblow that you plug into a power bank to the battery-powered Flextail Zero Pump. Wander into any thru-hiker camp this season, and you’re unlikely to see many people inflating their pad the old fashioned way. While Durston has enjoyed a loyal cult following for several years now, this past thru-hiking season brought an explosion in popularity. “It feels like you can hardly walk through a campsite without seeing an X-Mid,” says Amber Rae Hedman, a thru-hiker who completed the PCT in 2022 and 2025, among other trails. It makes sense: The unique offset design of the trekking pole tent offers a more spacious layout and for staggering low weight. Plus, while they were once difficult to get as limited batches were often released months apart, more regular production has allowed hundreds—if not thousands—more hikers to become instant die-hard fans. A more surprising piece of gear that’s made an appearance on long trails in the last year are standalone cameras. Be they digital, film, or disposable, more thru-hikers are ditching the photo capabilities of their phones for a dedicated image-capture experience. “Documenting the journey has become such a big part of the thru-hiking experience,” Hedman says. To do so, many modern hikers are turning away from their smartphones. Is it worth the weight? That’s a personal choice. But compact cameras take measurably better photos than phones (and without draining your battery).

item.title: Aspen Season Starts Now. See Peak Color On These 5 Trails
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine Score: 3.36
Fall foliage in Minnesota (Photo: Tammi Mild via Getty) For just a few precious weeks each year, the aspen forests of the West and Midwest flare into a golden wonderland. The trees flush from electric green to crayon-yellow, a color so vivid you could easily mistake the leaves for sunflower petals. River corridors become veins of ore. Mountainsides glow. Trails turn into vibrant tunnels carpeted in fallen gold. At high altitudes and latitudes, the color quickly blazes and fades. The narrow leaf-peeping window adds to the allure, but it also makes peak season easy to miss—especially if you don’t know where to go. These five trails are true autumn hot spots. Most wind through spectacular aspen groves, and a few offer sweeping vistas of golden forests far below. They make perfect places to hike this month and experience the spectacle of fall. If you let King Midas touch a forest, it might look something like this. While the nearby Maroon Bells are famed for their fall scenery, you’ll get a less crowded look at the golden goodness on the nearby Capitol Creek Trail. Target mid-September and hike 6 miles through dense aspen forest to the alpine lake beneath 14,137-foot Capitol Peak. Camp in one of the meadow’s secluded primitive sites to make a weekend of it, or return via the Capitol Peak Trail for a 12-mile lollipop loop. Capitol Creek Trail: Come mid-September, Wisconsin’s scattered aspens begin their fall transformation. For your best shot at concentrated color, head to Northern Highland-American Legion State Forest (NHAL), where a mix of wild and cultivated aspen groves keep the saturation dial turned all the way up. Our top picks: the Fallison Lake Trail, a 2.4-mile loop that wanders through glades and wetlands, and the Escanaba Loop, an 8.9-mile trek that winds past more than a dozen lakes and ponds. Whichever you choose, keep your eyes peeled for wildlife. Bald eagles and osprey soar over both trails, and beavers frequent the tree-fringed ponds. Fallison Lake Trail: Escanaba Loop: When fall starts in Michigan, the Porkies are one of the first places the tide of color touches. Aspens deepen their yellows around mid-September just as the forest’s famed hardwoods begin to blush orange and crimson. Lake of the Clouds is a local classic for color, but there’s no reason to stop at the parking-lot overlook; connect the North Mirror Lake and North Country National Scenic Trails for 13.2 miles and three summits over 1,500 feet. For regular foliage updates, check out West Michigan’s weekly fall color report. Lake of the Clouds Loop: Pando, a grove of interconnected clonal aspen trees, is widely considered to be one of the world’s largest single organisms. Its 47,000 genetically identical stems all share a single, interconnected root system. Most of the year, Pando blends into the surrounding foliage of Fishlake National Forest. But in late September, it goes up in a blaze of gold. To see it, park or camp at Doctor Creek Campground and wander the tangle of Forest Service roads southwest of the lake. For a longer trek, tackle the 16.4-mile Fishlake Loop, which offers nonstop views of the forest mirrored in the glassy water. Fishlake Loop: In the far north of the U.S., fall comes early. Take advantage by planning a mid- to late-September trip to the Boundary Waters, where lakeside vantage points unfurl expansive views of golden aspen forest. For top color, start at the Caribou Rock and Mossy Lake trailhead near the Canadian border. Tighten your laces and head north for a 13-mile linkup of Duncan, Rose, Patridge, Birch, and Moss Lakes. Be sure to leave enough time to linger on the cliffs overlooking Rose. When the timing’s right, the northern slopes turn into a riot of yellow, red, and peach. Rose and Duncan Lakes Loop: The hardest part of planning a fall foliage trip is hitting the colors as they’re peaking. Many factors affect how and when aspens (and other deciduous plants) turn color and shed their leaves. If you don’t time your hike right, you might arrive just before or after the colorful climax. There are tools that can help you, though. Check out Explore Fall’s interactive fall foliage map or the Farmer’s Almanac fall foliage map and leaf forecast. Both resources make it easy to time the best leaf-peeping experience.

item.title: Colorado Bear Euthanized With Trash in Intestines as Food Scarcity Drives Record Conflict
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine Score: 2.58
Unsecured garbage cans are a liability for both bears and humans. (Photo: CPW) Wildlife officials euthanized a black bear in Durango, Colorado, on September 9, after it was discovered moaning in pain in a residential yard. The bear had dug itself into a hole, and the homeowner who called Colorado Parks and Wildlife (CPW) said it was acting extremely lethargic and making strange noises. Arriving on scene, CPW Officer John Livingston and his colleagues immediately noticed the bear’s distended, bloated belly. They managed to get it to stand up, but couldn’t get it to move or leave the area. They tranquilized the animal, and as soon as they touched the bear’s stomach, Livingston says they realized something was very wrong. They made the tough call to euthanize and performed a field necropsy. “Immediately upon getting into the stomach, we just started pulling out cleaning wipes and full trash bags that still had the whole drawstring,” Livingston told Backpacker. “It was pretty rough stuff.” This incident comes as human-bear conflicts are peaking across the state. So far this year, Livingston says CPW has logged over 8,000 bear reports—the most they’ve ever dealt with. The agency has euthanized over 294 bears so far this year. In all of 2025, the number was just 98. “It’s definitely going to be a record year,” Livingston says. Between this year’s drought and a late Spring freeze that devastated natural food supplies, he expects human-bear conflicts to continue rising this fall. That’s why CPW is advocating extra caution among mountain residents—not just for their own safety, but for the bears’. Livingston is the CPW public information officer for southwest Colorado and the lead for the agency’s Statewide Bear Working Group. He says that CPW officers have been responding to bear incidents since June, working 18- to 20-hour days, often without weekends. Bear relocation incidents are up 3.5 times the 5-year average, and euthanizations are up 2.7 times, according to CPW. Livingston was preparing to head out on a bear call even as we spoke on the phone. “It’s been a busy year,” he says. “Across the state, we’re seeing more bears getting into homes and crossing lines that maybe, in most years, they’d be too timid or not quite bold enough to cross.” That’s largely due to two factors, he says: food scarcity and habituation. Livingston points to the record-low snowpack that has caused drought across the state and an early spring freeze in May that decimated natural food supplies in the southwest. That drove bears down into the towns early in the season. Now, Livingston says, they’re habituated to that food source. “As long as they are getting trash and human-provided food like bird seed, pet food, or whatever gets left outside, they don’t have the incentive to go back up and look for those natural foods,” he says. That creates a dangerous situation for these ursines. It’s much easier to make a fatal mistake, like breaking into homes or cars, or eating garbage that they can’t digest, when neighborhoods represent their main source of food. It can even mess with their biology. “Bears that get human-provided foods will continue to stay up looking to eat as much as they can for as long as they can,” Livingston explains. It isn’t cold weather that drives them into hibernation; it’s a lack of food. “In some places, there have been instances of a few bears never denning because they continued to access food year-round.” As winter draws nearer, CPW is asking residents across Colorado to exercise greater caution. Many towns and neighborhoods require bear-resistant trash containers, but Livingston points out that they do no good if they aren’t regularly cleaned, as bears will still be drawn to their scent. If they get broken, owners need to fix them, and make sure they’re secured every night. Failing to do so could result in a $100 fine for the first offense and a $200 fine for subsequent offenses. He also says that leaving windows or doors open, or your car unlocked at night, is asking for trouble. “It may not be a person you have to worry about coming into your house or trying to get into your car at night,” he says. “It might be a bear.” Finally, he says, don’t be afraid to haze bears who wander near your home. Livingston suggests yelling at them, sounding your car alarm, banging pots and pans, or using an airhorn. “If you’re going to take the time to take out your phone and record the bear, help send the right message and record it while you’re yelling,” Livingston says. “We shouldn’t want them being around our homes.” If there is any year to exercise greater bear caution, he says, it’s this one. The bears need our help.

item.title: What happens when a place has two different names?
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 5.93
Lake Ontario/Lake America: What happens when a place has two different names? Open the same map in the US and Canada and you may see two different names for the same lake. So, who decides what a place is really called? Open Google Maps in Toronto and you may see one name for a place. Open it in New York and you may see another. Increasingly, the map in your pocket can depend on where you're standing. That is what's happening with Lake Ontario, the smallest of the Great Lakes that lie on the US-Canadian border. After President Trump ordered the US government to rename it "Lake America" following failed trade talks between the two nations this summer, the lake began appearing under different names on different maps. But changing a name on a government database doesn't necessarily change what the rest of the world calls it. From digital maps to tourism organisations and local communities, the Lake Ontario dispute shows how complicated it can be to rename a place – and who ultimately decides which name sticks. Who decides what goes on a map? Unsurprisingly, Canada has not entertained a change. In the US, the modification began with the federal Geographic Names Information System (GNIS), the database used to standardise geographic names for federal use. Trump's executive order required "Lake America" to be added to the system and the former moniker removed. Google reflected the change in line with its long-standing policy of using official government naming sources, meaning US viewers now see "Lake America" while Canadian viewers continue to see "Lake Ontario". Apple Maps has also adopted the new name after pressure from Trump. But private mapping companies are not legally required to follow the federal designation. MapQuest, best known for being one of the earliest digital mapping tools, has refused to adopt the new name – and its refusal subsequently propelled MapQuest to number one overall on Apple's US App Store, with the company saying it had recorded more than 1.5 million installs across the US and Canada since the executive order was issued. "MapQuest focused on maintaining a name that people are familiar with," said Doug Berger, general manager at MapQuest. "When people need directions, they seek familiarity. It was an easy decision." What's in a name? The differing responses show how a federal name change can quickly produce multiple versions of the same geography. Oswego County in New York, which borders the lake, has chosen to retain Lake Ontario in its official and business materials, citing the historical significance of the name and expense to taxpayers and business owners for the cost of rebranding. "In our traditional Seneca language, its name is sga:nyodai:yoh, meaning 'beautiful lake'," said J Conrad Seneca, Seneca Nation President. "To us, Lake Ontario is not a political pawn. It does not separate the countries of the United States and Canada. It is all Indigenous land, which has been occupied by Indigenous people since time immemorial." When two names coexist But beyond the US and Canada, the impact of the name change may be limited. "The naming of bodies of water typically falls within national jurisdictions," explained Taufiq Rahim, senior fellow at non-partisan think tank New America and author of Trump 2.5: A Primer. "While there are international bodies like the IHO [International Hydrographic Organization], they do not have any authority to adjudicate disputes and typically when there is a dispute, two or multiple names can be used." A longstanding example is the dispute over "Persian Gulf" and "Arabian Gulf". Persian Gulf remains the standard name used by the UN, the IHO and most world atlases, while Arab states bordering the waterway – including Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain and Oman – generally use Arabian Gulf and have encouraged allies to do so as well since the 1960s. More like this: A more recent example is Trump's January 2025 decision to rename the Gulf of Mexico the "Gulf of America". The new name was adopted on US federal maps and by some digital mapping services, while Mexico and international users continued to encounter "Gulf of Mexico" or both names. In Mobile, Alabama, the National Maritime Museum of the Gulf of Mexico had only recently spent nearly $100,000 (£74,000) rebranding when the federal name changed, leaving it with a newly minted identity tied to a now-disputed place name. At the time, its director told BBC Travel that another name change would require "a complete redo of the entire museum" and that she would follow the lead of city officials. Its website now identifies it simply as the National Maritime Museum of the Gulf. A similar issue is now playing out on the US side of Lake Ontario. The Lake Ontario National Marine Sanctuary, a federally designated protected area covering 1,722 sq miles (4,460 sq km) of waters and lakebed along the eastern New York shoreline, is retaining its name. The National Oceanographic and Atmospheric Administration, which comanages the sanctuary with New York State, says in a statement that the executive order applies to federal references to the lake itself but did not change the sanctuary's separately designated name. The agency is updating its materials to refer to the lake as "Lake America", while the sanctuary remains the Lake Ontario National Marine Sanctuary. A diplomatic wedge The organisational and financial burden of the name change will likely fall on the United States and its taxpayers. "This adds another unnecessary line to US expenses which in total can exceed hundreds of millions of dollars annually," said Usha Haley, Barton Distinguished Chair in International Business at Wichita State University. "People have to divert time, another important resource, to manage these changes for different audiences." While the change will have practical impacts, it's the symbolic implications that will likely have the most lasting effects. "Geographic naming becomes a proxy for sovereignty and power. It's geopolitical signalling on who controls national and bi-lateral narratives," said Haley. "The downstream symbolic and diplomatic consequences of a name change such as this can be much larger than the immediate commercial calculations." The change is likely to continue the erosion of diplomatic trust between Canada and the US, says Haley, hindering a weakening trading relationship between the two nations. Canada has long been a top destination for US exports, and the third-largest source of US imports, following Mexico and China. She said that symbolic disputes like this can become proxies for larger conflicts. --

item.title: Six US drive-ins where you can stay the night
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 5.01
Six places in the US where you can sleep at a drive-in From retro 1950s properties to modern glamping sites, these places are reviving one of the US's most enduring pastimes – and offering travellers one last classic summer experience. At the Frontier Drive-Inn, there are no televisions in the guest rooms. Instead, as the property rather cheekily puts it, the biggest TV in southern Colorado is right outside your door. That would be the outdoor screen left over from the Frontier's first life as a drive-in cinema, which opened in 1955 and went dark three decades later. Today, the former cinema anchors a retro-inspired hotel where guests sleep in Quonset-style yurts and vintage trailers, then gather outside for films beneath the famously dark skies of the San Luis Valley. As Labor Day (7 September) approaches, the Frontier and other properties like it are providing a fresh take on one of the US's most enduring warm-weather pastimes – and offering one last classic summer experience before the season winds down. For generations of Americans, drive-ins have been inseparable from summer. The country's first drive-in opened in 1933, but they exploded after WWII, when rising car ownership, suburban expansion and the baby boom helped push their number to nearly 5,000 by the late 1950s, according to April Wright, a drive-in historian and director of Going Attractions: The Definitive Story of the American Drive-In Movie in which she visits roughly 500 open, abandoned or former drive-in sites. "Going to the drive-in was just something you did every summer," Wright said. Though their heyday may have passed, Wright says the appeal of drive-ins isn't purely nostalgic. Plenty of younger visitors are experiencing them for the first time, drawn to the fact that a night at the drive-in is as much about the ritual around the film as the film itself. "What it's always been about, and what it is still about today, is spending time with friends and family, and creating an experience," Wright said. Now, a handful of hotels, motels and campgrounds around the US are turning that experience into an overnight stay. Some have revived long-shuttered drive-ins, while others let guests sleep within sight of giant screens that have been showing films for decades. At these properties, film night doesn't end with the final credits. Frontier Drive-Inn – Center, Colorado Luke Falcone, co-owner of Frontier, said the screen had survived decades of the San Luis Valley's harsh weather and was too important to the site's history to lose. "When doing historic preservation projects, if you come across something that isn't broken, you've hit the jackpot," he said. Despite the name, the Frontier is no longer a traditional drive-in: guests don't pull up in their cars, but settle into lawn chairs or onto blankets to watch fan-favourite films under the stars. "By bringing folks out of their rooms (and cars), we provide an entirely different experience that we can all bond over," Falcone said. The programming leans into nostalgic cult classics, while the accommodation is decidedly modern. Best Western Movie Manor – Monte Vista, Colorado The motel was built beside The Star Drive-In Theatre, which opened in 1955 as drive-ins were booming across the US, and many rooms face one of its two screens through large picture windows, with the film's audio piped inside. Each room is named after a movie star, from Cary Grant to Robert De Niro, and guests can also head outside and watch from their cars. More than 70 years after The Star first lit up, it still shows films seasonally (generally from spring to the end of September). Sutherlin/Umpqua Valley KOA Holiday – Sutherlin, Oregon The Sutherlin/Umpqua Valley KOA Holiday campground occupies the former Cloverleaf Drive-In, where the original 100ft (30m) screen survived long after the cinema itself closed. When the current owner bought the property in 2006, they chose to keep the screen and eventually added a digital projector and FM transmitter, bringing films back to the site. Today, films are shown most weekends. Some RV sites sit directly in front of the screen (or have private patios angled towards it), allowing guests to watch from their rigs and tune into the film over their radios, much as they would at a traditional drive-in. Tent campers and guests in the rest of the RV sites can bring chairs or blankets to a grassy viewing area just in front of the screen, where the sound plays aloud. Hotel Caravana at Four Brothers Drive-In – Amenia, New York Unlike most of the places on this list, Four Brothers isn't a survivor from the golden age of the silver screen. The Hudson Valley theatre opened in 2013, reviving the format decades after thousands of its predecessors had disappeared. Since then, the family-run property has added mini-golf, fire pits and Hotel Caravana, where guests can sleep in vintage trailers within the drive-in grounds or even pitch their own tent. Ofland Escalante – Escalante, Utah Set along Scenic Byway 12 in southern Utah, Ofland Escalante occupies a former drive-in site within Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument. Guests spend the day hiking, exploring slot canyons or visiting nearby Bryce Canyon and Capitol Reef national parks, then return in time for the nightly film. "The movie starts just after dusk and it anchors the whole evening," said Noah Ellis, CEO of Ofland Hotels. "It's a key amenity, not an add-on." The old drive-in comes with its own fleet of vintage cars – including a 1957 Chevrolet and Ford Thunderbird – that are parked facing the screen. Guests grab complimentary popcorn and classic sweets from the concession stand, choose a car and settle in beneath the desert sky. "The site was a drive-in long before it was a hotel, so keeping actual cars in the mix mattered to us," Ellis said. "There's something about a row of vintage cars, climbing in with a bag of popcorn, that stays with people." Overnight options range from modernised vintage Airstreams to a variety of cabins. Tiger Drive-In – Tiger, Georgia Tucked into the mountains of north-eastern Georgia, the Tiger Drive-In first opened in 1954, went dark in the 1980s and then sat abandoned for roughly two decades. It returned to life in 2004, and today guests can stay after the movie in one of three vintage 1960s campervans parked on the drive-in grounds (each with a private deck facing the screen), or camp in a tent or RV. --

item.title: Vienna's great surprise: The Globe Museum
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 4.71
The museum charting how humans understand the world Beautiful, surreal and eerily empty, Vienna's Globe Museum the only public museum on Earth dedicated to globes, and it – quite literally – tells the story of our world. It's a chilly afternoon in Vienna, and the line for the Austrian National Library has already spilled out the door, curling like a ribbon around the grand Josefsplatz square. I'm not in the mood to wait – I've already struck out at several crowded nearby attractions where timed-entry tickets were sold out. Rather than join the queue, I walk down the street and stumble onto a smaller, somewhat hidden site: The Globe Museum. Tucked inside Vienna's 17th-Century Palais Mollard, it's the only public museum on Earth dedicated entirely to globes, and one of Vienna's greatest surprises. Different worlds I soon realise that I've wandered into another world – or more accurately, many of them. Just steps from some of the city's most celebrated, crowded attractions, Vienna's Globe Museum displays more than 220 rare and antique spheres, most created before 1850, ranging from towering Coronelli globes to tiny, foldable pocket orbs. Beautiful and surreal, the museum's extensive collection goes beyond geography to reveal how humanity has mapped and imagined the Earth and heavens above. It's a chronicle of human curiosity, and – quite literally – the story of our world. "Globes show the change in our imagination of our planet," says Nikolaus Schobesberger, the director of museum. "And this is the only place in the world where you can see so many of them at the same time." Visitors start by travelling through the Golden Cabinet, a lavish room with centuries-old frescoes depicting scenes from Greek mythology. It's the backdrop for a stunning array of globe-related instruments, like telluriums, which illustrate the Earth's orbit around the Sun, and armillary spheres, which use a framework of rings to visualise the movements of celestial bodies. As I reach the museum's four main galleries, I realise the whole place is pin-drop quiet. I shuffle slowly from one glass case to another, holding my breath to not disturb the stillness, even though I'm alone with centuries-old objects. I find myself marvelling at two spherical worlds suspended in time. One is terrestrial, with oceans awash in vivid blues and squiggly brown coastlines. The other is celestial, where mythological creatures and constellations spill across a tea stain-coloured backdrop. Barely bigger than beach balls, these two time capsules were made by the same craftsman 10 years apart in the mid-1500s and preserve a world as it was still coming into focus. In one, Europe, the Mediterranean and Africa's coasts are filled with place names, while North America fades into the uncharted Arctic. Asia is distorted, a hypothetical southern continent stands in for Australia and Antarctica and the Pacific is populated by sea monsters instead of islands. In the other, Renaissance astrological observations exist alongside Pegasus taking flight and Perseus brandishing Medusa's severed head. "They're some of the oldest globes we have in our collection," says Schobesberger. Moving from one globe to the next, I notice how these relics extend beyond geography and depict what people once believed. Many fill the space of unexplored oceans with dragons, while some confidently depict my home state of California as an island. Some pieces also preserve colonial-era prejudices with elaborately painted scenes depicting Indigenous people as cannibals. On one, African coastlines are dotted with Spanish and Portuguese flags, showing "ownership". "They're a part of this colonial thinking. And so, they're beautiful art, but you also have to think about the time they were created," Schobesberger says, explaining that every globe is as much a record of what people knew as what they didn't. That's why he believes the museum resonates with all types of people, not just historians or cartography enthusiasts. One of Schobesberger's favourite objects is a lunar globe from 1961. The front portion of the Moon is meticulously mapped. The back, however, is a stark white strip, intentionally left blank because the far side of the Moon had not yet been seen. An updated lunar globe made two years later, also on display, contains the missing portion. I can't help but circle back to a showstopper in the front hall, a replica of the Behaim Globe – completed by Martin Behaim in 1492, the year Christopher Columbus sailed west – which shows a world without the Americas. There's simply an expanse of ocean between Europe and Asia. "A globe is such a great thing because it's a small-scale model of our planet, so you can tell stories about the world on it," he says. "Climate, geology, topography, trade routes, everything." From curios to cultural cornerstones Walking through the museum, visitors can see the globe's own journey unfold. The earliest examples were luxury objects reserved for aristocrats and wealthy merchants. Over time, globes lost their exclusivity, shrunk in size and became more affordable and popular. They entered schools, appeared in living rooms and even became playthings for children. Today, they are so commonplace that my son even won his desktop globe in a classroom raffle. I entered the museum expecting to view globes as historic artefacts, but I'm surprised by how alive they still feel. Even with Google Earth at my fingertips, these tactile objects invite curiosity and imagination in a way that a screen doesn't. "It's not just that the globe is a scientific instrument. It's also an object which lets you dream of foreign countries," says Schobesberger. Globes in pop culture Beginning 24 September 2026, the museum's newest exhibition, Globes in Everyday Life, Art and Culture, will explore how globes evolved from a status symbol to a familiar fixture. It also showcases the globe's enduring place in pop culture, from architecture to art and film, like Charlie Chaplin's famous dance with an inflatable globe in The Great Dictator. "The main idea was to show that globes are almost everywhere as a part of everyday life," Schobesberger says. Schobesberger's own fascination began as a young child, when he became captivated by the ships, sea monsters and mythical creatures that filled the blank spaces of historical maps and globes. He began to draw his own world maps when he was just six years old. "You can think about what's possible on the other side of the world, even when you're sitting here in Europe," he says. "Nothing else can capture the imagination quite like it." More like this: That sentiment resonates with author JF Penn, who stumbled onto the Globe Museum while researching her novel Spear of Destiny, based on a relic housed in Vienna's Imperial Treasury. Like me, she ended up lingering far longer than planned. "I particularly loved the oversized antique globes with the patina of age and use," she says. "I considered how many fingertips have turned them over generations and wondered if they thought of travelling to these far-off places that I do." Even after visitors leave Palais Mollard, the search continues. Across Vienna, some 50 globes are perched on rooftops and facades, hidden in plain sight. The museum even charts them on a virtual map in its new exhibit, encouraging people to look upward as they wander the city. When I finally step back outside, the sky is dark and the streets are even more crowded. Earlier in the day, I had been seeking a quieter corner of Vienna. Instead, I was given a whole new way of seeing the world – a place that's constantly being redrawn and reimagined. --

item.title: The smoky plant goo that Finns can't stop eating
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 4.18
Pine tar: The surprising, smoky goo that Finns can't stop eating Once used to waterproof boats and treat infections, this smoky plant byproduct is now used to flavour everything from schnapps to bread. But how does it taste? I've been in the sub-Arctic city of Oulu, Finland for only a few hours when I'm caught under a torrent of late summer rain. I take refuge in a cafe and order a coffee and sugar-dusted pannukakku (a thick pancake). The waiter asks me, "What flavour? We have almond, tar, blueberry..." I'm certain I've misunderstood: "Did you say tar?" He nods nonchalantly. Welcome to Oulu, the northern Finnish city where terva (pine tar, usually translated in English simply as "tar") is on the menu. Produced by heating pine wood without oxygen, this thick, dark substance flavours everything from lager to ice cream, lending a distinct, rich smokiness. "It's an intense flavour, so a little goes a long way," says Matti Moller of the Arctic Food Lab, an initiative showcasing northern Finland's culinary culture. "But it's brilliant to experiment with in everything from fish to desserts." To Finns, pine tar's aroma has long been associated with wooden boats, summer cottages and sauna scents. So what's the recent culinary appeal? I've decided to find out. From sealant to meal Yet just two centuries ago, Oulu had a very different reputation. Encircled by dense pine forests and the winding channels of the Oulujoki delta, it was famed as the tar capital of the world. "Oulu has been a major trading hub since the 15th Century thanks to its position on the Oulu River," says local guide Sirpa Törmä. "By the 1860s, it had become the world's largest tar-exporting port." Essential for waterproofing wooden sailing ships, tar was produced by smouldering wood in tar pits across villages along the river, then transported in narrow boats to Oulu's harbour for global export. Thanks to its antibacterial properties, tar had also long been used as a natural wound treatment all over Finland. "As the well-known saying goes: 'If sauna, spirits and tar do not help, the disease is fatal,'" explains Ritva Kylli, a food historian at the University of Oulu. But how did it make its way to the Finnish palate? Tar-as-flavour made its debut on pharmacy shelves. Archives at the National Library of Finland reveal that tar-flavoured medicinal lozenges date back to the early 1900s, and Oulu's local papers advertised tervakaramellit ('tar sweets') as early as 1902. "These were medicinal lozenges sold in apothecary shops for coughs and respiratory diseases," says Kylli. Even if not every Finn enjoys the taste of tar, virtually everyone has tried the iconic black terva pastille. The nation's most famous brand is Terva Leijona (Tar Lion), sold to this day. Launched in 1933, the pastilles were created by Oulu pharmacist YW Jalander after watching locals inhale smoky tar fumes for their health. Facing low profits, he invented a tar essence (tervaessanssi) and infused it into liquorice pastilles, which he sold through his confectionary company, Merijal. Terva Leijona eventually changed hands, but it is still made using his recipe. As popular as they were, tar didn't make the leap from pastille to gourmet treat until the end of the 20th Century, says Kylli, as living standards rose and interest in regional heritage cuisine grew across the country: "[It] seems to be connected to a growing interest in the cultural memory of Oulu's tar economy, a trend spreading beyond northern historical trade routes to all of Finland," she says. "It was reimagined into a distinctive heritage flavour." 'It can be addictive' Matti tells me he buys tar chocolate and syrup a few times a year. "The taste is unique – sweet, smoky, medicinal and completely unmistakable," he says as we walk across the picturesque island of Pikisaari, connected to Oulu's city centre by a short bridge. "Why do we love it? Perhaps we're tasting our roots, the Finnish forest and our heritage." The Oulu region, as the historic heart of the pine tar culture, has also become the symbolic centre of pine tar cuisine, with a high concentration of restaurants, cafes and bakeries that produce terva foods. At Pekka Heikkinen, a family bakery in Kajaani founded in 1913, owner Kaisa Marin bakes traditional bread and pastries. "Tar boats used to sail right past our bakery to Oulu," she explains. "When pine tar food innovations emerged in the '90s, it was natural to start baking tar-flavoured bread." For Marin, the connection is deeply personal: "My grandmother washed my hair with tar shampoo in the sauna, and our cabin's boat was sealed with tar. To me, the scent is cosy, nostalgic and rooted in home. I love it!" She always keeps thinly sliced tar bread in the freezer, ready to fry in butter when guests arrive. Though not for everyone, she warns it can be addictive. "My uncle, a master confectioner, created a rich tar chocolate that we bake every Christmas. We've even made cakes with pine tar and spruce needles." Rina Hirviniemi, owner of the cosy Kahvila Kiikku, also bakes tar bread at least once a week, usually pairing it with gravlax. "In summer, I serve vanilla ice cream with tar syrup, and in winter, we grill with tar outside," she says. "I like keeping tar products on hand, though I don't put them on the menu – I have an eye for people I can recommend it to." So what does it taste like? Convinced, I decide to – literally – bite. According to Marin, ice cream is the best starting point for tar newcomers, so I head to Market Square's ice cream van. Cone in hand, I sit by Toripolliisi, the brawny bronze police statue keeping watch over the square, and take my first hesitant taste. A smoky-sweet aroma rushes from nose to palate – the unexpected whiff of bacon. Yet, it's surprisingly sweet. Intrigued, I can't stop eating. Bite by bite, it completely wins me over. Just as Marin predicted, I find myself becoming addicted. I head next to ChocoSomnia, an Oulu chocolate maker. "We make tar pralines, chocolate bars and tar coffee. We get curious first-timers, but also loyal regulars," says co-owner Mika Lähteenmäki. Sampling a square of dark chocolate infused with pine tar and cranberry, I'm struck by the balance of smoky depth, rich cocoa bitterness and soft berry sweetness; the very taste of a pine forest in midsummer. I can't stop there. My local friend leads me to a supermarket for Terva Leijona pastilles. Like impatient children, we tear open the box and pop the tiny black sweets. Instead of subtle sweetness, an intense, smoky rush clears my airways. My friend introduces me to two of his mates, and I discover that local usage varies widely: some drizzle tar syrup on bacon, others serve tar schnapps before nights out. For others still, tar candies reign supreme. While most Finns buy ready-made tar products, today's skilled chefs craft them from scratch. This is what brought me to Lasaretti, a restaurant tucked into the riverfront oasis of Oulu's Hupisaaret Park. Today, head chef Laurance Robinson is serving smoked whitefish pasta with tar pearls, pickled fennel and red onion. "I can't build a tar pit, so I buy flavouring from Kujala's farm to make my syrup for sweet and savoury dishes," he says. "Balancing its strong, pungent taste took time." Resembling caviar, the tar pearls burst in my mouth against the whitefish, sharp fennel, and sweet archipelago bread. It is pure umami with subtle smokiness. More like this: Originally from the Isle of Man, Robinson cooked across Europe before settling in Finland. "I'll never forget my first taste of tar in 2011 – a sauna soda from my future father-in-law. It tasted like an ashtray at first, but the smokiness mellowed. Later, when I had the freedom to experiment, I said, 'I want to be the tar chef.'" His tar pavlova recently won best dessert at an Oulu culinary contest. "I wonder how far I can push it." Watching passersby drift through the sunny park, I marvel at how tar shifted from a maritime necessity to the flavour of local identity. "You know what," says my friend. "I've had a horrible headache since morning, but after eating this dish, it's completely gone." I can't promise it cures headaches, but in every sense, tar remains a uniquely Finnish ingredient that still works its quiet magic. --

item.title: When Russia colonised California
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 3.70
'The forgotten empire': When Russia colonised California For nearly 30 years, part of Sonoma was ruled by Tsarist Russia, and it played a pivotal – if little-known – role in shaping the US. It's a pretty, two-hour drive north from San Francisco to Крѣпость Россъ. After slicing through the Golden Gate fog, I wound past sunburnt vineyards to Sonoma's remote coast and rolled down the windows. To my left, California plummeted into the Pacific and seals barked from boulders cropping out of the foamy surf. To my right, cliffs rose sharply and titanic redwoods shot up from the road's switchbacks. Suddenly, a lonely twin-domed chapel topped with Orthodox crosses appeared against the blue ocean. I got out and followed a footpath past a Cyrillic sign towards a wooden, frontier-like stronghold built 150ft (46m) atop a bluff hanging over the sea. Every year, millions of travellers set out on the Pacific Coast Highway to twist and turn their way along, one of the US's most stunning roads, as it hugs the entire California coastline. But chances are, few of these road-trippers realise that hidden here on a secluded headland 90 miles (145km) north of San Francisco lies a relic from the days when part of California was ruled by Tsarist Russia. I didn't, and judging by Fort Ross's eerie emptiness, it seems I'm not alone. "Even most Californians don't know Russia once had a colony in California," Kent Lightfoot, an anthropologist at the University of California, Berkeley, later told me. "They all know about the Spanish and the Mexicans, but almost no one knows anything about the Russians being here. It's kind of like the forgotten empire." While some Americans may recall that the US's largest state, Alaska, was part of Russia for nearly 70 years, the Russian Empire's only permanent overseas colony, known as Russian America, also extended into California from 1812-1842. In fact, Russians settled in California decades before newly independent Americans did. Innovative and surprisingly cosmopolitan, Fort Ross (short for Rossiya, meaning "Russia") was intended to be a breadbasket for Russia's struggling Alaskan settlements, but it also became the source of hotly debated plans for Russian expansion across North America. The beginning of Russian America As European powers expanded west in the 1500s and 1600s, Russia expanded east. By the 1640s, Russian fur traders and mercenaries had swept their way across Siberia to reach the Pacific coast. This rush led to permanent Russian settlements along Alaska's islands and coasts. In 1799, Tsar Paul I formalised the empire's Alaska claims by chartering the Russian-American Company. Modelled after the British East India Company, the for-profit venture didn't just control the fur trade; it now controlled all of Alaska as a corporate colony. But there was a problem: while the company was growing rich on sea otter pelts, the colonists were growing hungry because they couldn't farm in much of Alaska's frozen landscape. So, the Russian settlers sailed south in search of warmer climates and Spanish trading partners. California dreaming In April 1806, with his colony stalked by starvation and his crew decimated by scurvy, Russian-American Company director Nikolai Rezanov steered the prow of his ship, the Juno, into San Francisco Bay. As the brig limped towards Spain's northernmost California settlement, a Spanish soldier grabbed a megaphone and demanded the strange vessel identify itself. "Russia," a voice called back. It was a response the Spanish had been expecting for nearly 40 years. Though Spain claimed all of California starting in 1542, it didn't actually occupy it until 1769, after getting word that Russian fur traders were rapidly moving east across the Alaskan islands. To prevent Russian and British advancement, Spain created a chain of presidios (military outposts) along the coast, starting with San Diego. "The expansion of all of Alta [Upper] California, in many ways, was stimulated by the Russians," Lightfoot said. "The Spanish were nervous about the Russians coming south. So, the founding of San Diego, Santa Barbara, Monterey and San Francisco were a response to the Russians in Alaska." During Rezanov's six-week stay in San Francisco, the 42-year-old statesman secured enough food from the Spanish to save the starving Alaskan colonists by getting engaged to the 15-year-old daughter of San Francisco's Spanish commandant. As he sailed back through the Golden Gate, Rezanov realised that the entire northern coast of California was undefended and far sunnier than Siberia or Alaska, so he hatched a plan to extend Russian America into California. In 1812, after years of stealthily surveying the coast, 25 Russians and 80 Native Alaskan hunters settled on a shelf-like plateau overlooking the Pacific on what is now Sonoma County's rugged coast. Here, close enough to the area's abundant sea otter population but far enough from the Spanish Empire's sparsely guarded northern frontier, they lived in a Siberian-designed settlement hewn from California redwoods under the tsar's double-eagle flag. Exploring Russian California Today, Russia's far-flung California colony remains a solitary, surreal place. Set 12 miles (19km) from the nearest town or mobile phone service, the weathered wooden remnants of a once-bustling settlement open onto a 180-degree view of the sea. In two days at the 3,400-acre Fort Ross State Historic Park, I counted 14 other visitors, and except for the occasional chime from the St Nicholas chapel, the only noise breaking the stillness was the waves crashing below the bluff. "There's a magical feel to Fort Ross," said Robin Joy Wellman, who worked as an interpreter with California State Parks for nearly 30 years. "It's something of a mystery, but once people discover it, they say it's one of the most beautiful places they've ever visited." The site's dramatic setting straddles the San Andreas fault, and the same earthquake that flattened San Francisco in 1906 also levelled much of the original wooden outpost. But detailed displays of the partially reconstructed fortress paint a vivid picture of frontier life in Russia's wild, wild East. The heart of the colony was the fort-like stockade, where a handful of high-ranking Russian soldiers, officers and company officials lived in barracks enclosed by a 12ft (3.6m) palisade. I followed Kimsey up the steps of two blockhouses armed with enough cannons to command the coast. He explained that while the Russians chose this natural overlook to defend against Spanish attacks, the two empires never actually clashed, and even depended on each other for survival. "The Russians and the Spanish were at the very far edges of their overstretched empires. They both needed things the other side could provide, so they traded illicitly," Kimsey said. In the warehouse, drying sea otter pelts worth $100 each (a year's salary for a Pennsylvania farmer at the time) destined for China, Europe and Spanish California would have hung from the rafters. Under the bulbous dome of one of the oldest Orthodox churches in the Western hemisphere, the little settlement gradually grew into a cosmopolitan colony, complete with banyas, bakeries and some 60 buildings. "It was a bustling, pluralistic mercantile village, with lots of languages and people from different homelands living together," Lightfoot said. "The stockade was just the tip of the iceberg. The real action was outside." Beyond the fort As Kimsey and I walked out of the palisade, he explained that as the colony expanded to include nearly 400 people by the 1830s, it became one of the most diverse places in California – and virtually everyone there worked for the Russian-American Company. Here, where the sloboda (village) once stood at the edge of the cape, paid Aleutian and Kodiak hunters lived with Native California women, mixed-race Russian and European Creoles married local Kashaya Pomo and Coast Miwok workers and people were buried next to each other at the Old Russian Cemetery up the hillside. Compared to other European colonies, it was also largely tolerant. "The Russians didn't come here to 'civilise' like the Spanish," said Kimsey, who serves as the tribal liaison for the area's Native communities. We then followed a steep path down to a crescent-shaped beach where coopers, carpenters and blacksmiths brought in by the Russian-American Company from as far afield as Finland and Hawaii once worked side by side. "This is where the first ocean-going ships in California were built," he said. It's also where the first bricks, glass and windmills in California were made. As workers crafted longboats, forged iron, cast brass and made metal, Fort Ross became the centre of manufacturing in California. The Russians traded these highly coveted goods with their Spanish and (later) Mexican neighbours in exchange for further provisions for their Alaskan settlements – and in doing so, they unwittingly helped their rivals settle California. More like this: This shallow-water cove was also where cargo boats and kayak-bound hunters would set off for the colony's main deep-water port 20 miles (35km) south in Rumyantsev (present-day Bodega Bay) and its sealing station off the coast of San Francisco on the Farallon Islands. As Fort Ross' footprint grew, so did the calls from within the Russian-American Company to heed Rezanov's recommendation of annexing North America's west coast for Russia. In 1821, Tsar Alexander I issued an imperial decree claiming Russian control over modern-day Oregon through Alaska. The US's soon-to-be sixth president, John Quincy Adams, swiftly objected and his warning to Russia that the Americas "are no longer subjects for any new European colonial establishments" established one of the most fundamental principles of US foreign policy: the Monroe Doctrine, which opposes foreign interference in the Western hemisphere. From the beach, Kimsey and I climbed a steep hill past the stockade to the orchard the Russians started with a single peach tree in 1814 and pushed open the gate. Of the hundreds of citrus trees and crops the Russians planted, only a single branch of a 200-year-old Capulin cherry survives. Yet, the Russians actually left a far greater agricultural legacy here than most people realise. "It was the Russians who planted the first grapes in [what is now] Sonoma County in 1817," said Megan Jones, Sonoma's official wine librarian. As Jones explained, while Sonoma is now considered "the birthplace of the modern American wine movement", Russian traders introduced the now-rare Mission grape to Sonoma and produced small batches of light red wine. For all its innovations, however, Fort Ross never succeeded in its two main goals: turning a profit and feeding hungry Alaskans. By the early 1820s, the Russian-American Company's Native Alaskan hunters had speared so many sea otters they wiped out the local population, and a combination of heavy coastal fog and rampant rodents yielded just 13 tonnes of wheat annually between 1826 and 1833. When the British-run Hudson's Bay Company agreed to supply Russian Alaska with provisions from its Pacific Northwest settlements starting in 1839, it was the beginning of the end for Tsarist California. Two years later, a Swiss emigrant named John Sutter purchased Fort Ross' buildings and assets from the Russians for $30,000. He cannibalised parts of the structures to create his new settlement in Sacramento. Seven years after the Russians sailed back to Alaska, a chance discovery on Sutter's property ignited the California Gold Rush. Russia's California legacy Today, reminders of California's Tsarist past are still scattered across the Golden State as you drive north from San Francisco. One of the city's most famous neighbourhoods, Russian Hill, gets its name from the graves of Russian-American Company sailors discovered there during the Gold Rush (look for a plaque near 1120 Vallejo Street). A historical marker at Bodega Bay shows where Russians set sail for their Alaskan capital, Novo-Arkhangelsk (present-day Sitka). And more than a million people visit the Russian River Valley each year to splash, hike and taste some of the US's best wines. "The Russians called this river Slavyanka, and it's one of the main arteries they used to exploit the area," said Suki Waters, a Kashaya Pomo descendant and the owner of WaterTreks, which leads eco-tours along the Russian River. As we kayaked past harbour seals and migrating pelicans, she recounted stories from her great-great-grandmother, who was alive when the Russians sailed in. "Fort Ross was a seasonal fishing village called Metini for thousands of years," she said. "When the Russians first came, the Elders called them the 'Undersea People', because from high on the bluff, it looked like they rose out from under the ocean." Later that afternoon, I walked back through Fort Ross' Cyrillic signs, stockade and sloboda towards a lone bench at the edge of that bluff. Peering across the Pacific, I wondered how many days it would take to reach Russia. But as a distant chime from the chapel echoed in the air, I was reminded of something Wellman told me. "The fact that a little part of Russia was right here in California is amazing. Why would we ever want to forget that?" --

item.title: Inside the places that shaped Dolly Parton
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 3.05
'Everything about her was East Tennessee': The places that shaped Dolly Parton From her Appalachian childhood to Nashville and Dollywood, a journey through the Tennessee she loved – and transformed in return. On a sunny day on 24 June 2026, hundreds of travellers, locals and Dolly Parton fans from across the US gathered in the small rural community of Cornersville, less than an hour's drive south of Nashville, for the unveiling of her Tennessean Travel Stop. It was the country star's last public appearance before her death just two months later. Wearing her signature fringe and rhinestones and a grin as bright as that Tennessee morning, Parton cut the ribbon and welcomed travellers to the new roadside stop, complete with a Southern meat-and-three restaurant, live music and – of course – a Dolly-themed gift shop. It was a fitting final chapter for an artist whose life and career were inseparable from Tennessee. From crooning about the Smoky Mountains to investing in rural East Tennessee where she grew up, Parton spent decades sharing her home state with the world – and transforming it in return. Explore Parton's Tennessee mountain home In 1964, US President Lyndon B Johnson launched the War on Poverty, a federal effort to reduce poverty and expand economic opportunity across the United States. Southern Appalachia, one of the nation's poorest regions, was thrust into the national spotlight. Media portrayals often depicted its residents as backward and destitute, reinforcing the caricature of the "hillbilly", a stereotype that had persisted since the 19th Century. But when Dolly Rebecca Parton came into the spotlight, this daughter of Appalachia who grew up in a two-room cabin with 11 brothers and sisters offered the world a different view of her home: one of joy, dignity and talent. Follow Dolly Parton's story across Tennessee Sevierville: See the bronze statue of Parton outside the Sevier County Courthouse and The Pines, where she performed for a paying audience for the first time at just 10 years old. RCA Studio B, Nashville: Visit the legendary recording studio on Music Row where Dolly Parton and other iconic artists like Elvis Presley recorded some of their greatest hits. The Country Music Hall of Fame, Nashville: A must-visit Nashville institution that chronicles the history of country music through artefacts, exhibits and the stories of the artists who trailblazed the genre. Dollywood, Pigeon Forge: Set in the Smoky Mountains that Parton loved so dearly, Dollywood takes guests on a journey through the singer's roots, from an exact replica of her childhood two-room cabin to the Dolly Parton Experience, which displays childhood memorabilia.
