"Dolly Parton told a new story about Appalachia that was rooted in her very particular experience," said Dr Jessie Wilkerson, a history professor and Appalachian scholar at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville. "Yes, her family was poor, but they weren't desperate or hopeless, and they took care of one another. There was a lot of love and beauty in the place where she grew up, and so we get a different story about Appalachia through her." In the title track of her 1973 album, My Tennessee Mountain Home, Parton describes her Appalachian home as "peaceful as a baby's sigh". The landscape around her childhood home on the edge of the Great Smoky Mountains, along with Appalachia's storytelling traditions and bluegrass heritage, inspired much of Parton's music. In Great Smoky Mountains National Park, a blue-grey mist that gives the Smokies its name settles over the peaks and valleys and waterfalls tumble through the forest. The 522,000-acre expanse is threaded with hiking trails and scenic overlooks, with autumn bringing a canvas of brilliant jewel tones and spring a kaleidoscope of wildflowers to the lower slopes. The landscape was a reoccurring muse, from the mountain blooms that inspired her 1987 ballad Wildflowers to the fog-covered peaks evoked in Blue Smoke, the title track of her 2014 album, and the pastoral idyll captured in My Tennessee Mountain Home. In nearby Sevierville, the main town serving rural Locust Ridge, where Parton grew up, the region's pride in its local legend is evident. A bronze statue on the courthouse lawn depicts her as a young girl playing guitar. Down the street is the Wings of Wander mural, inspired by her hit song Love Is Like a Butterfly, and the Red's Cafe mural, another larger-than-life depiction of Parton as a child, this time getting a cheeseburger from her favourite childhood restaurant. "People in East Tennessee really, really adore her, and it's something that's been important for the region to have someone who's really proud of coming from there, and who's a positive representation of Appalachia, when historically the representations of the region are the opposite," Wilkerson said. Retracing Parton's path in Nashville On the day Parton graduated from high school in 1964, she boarded a Greyhound bus headed west for the neon lights of Nashville. In a letter home shortly after arriving, feeling homesick and uncertain, she wrote, "Nashville isn't what I thought it was gonna be, but I think I'll like it once I get used to it." "When she came to Nashville, she came with a very distinct East Tennessee identity and made that very clear in both her music and her accent," said Robert K Oermann, co-author of her memoir Dolly Parton: Songteller, My Life in Lyrics and a longtime collaborator. "Everything about her was East Tennessee and mountain, and I think that was the message she brought to Nashville." Nashville looks very different today from when Parton first stepped off that bus 62 years ago, but visitors can still trace Parton's path from her early days fresh out of Sevier County to her rise as a country music icon who never lost the Appalachian sound of home even as she became one of Nashville's biggest stars. On Music Row, the city's historic record-industry district, visitors can step inside RCA Studio B where a blue X marks "The Sweet Spot" where Parton recorded hits including Jolene and I Will Always Love You – both of which she wrote on the same day. Nearby, the Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum is featuring Dolly Parton: Journey of a Seeker, an exhibition spanning her career and featuring memorabilia like her Gibson five-string banjo and handwritten music drafts. A few blocks away, the historic Ryman Auditorium is where a 13-year-old Parton made her Grand Ole Opry debut in 1959 and earned three encores. Murals of Parton dot the city in her honour, museum exhibits display her stage costumes and in the wake of her passing, fans have left flowers on her star on the Music City Walk of Fame. Visiting Parton's Appalachia Nashville, however, was never the end of Parton's journey. The further her career carried her from the mountains to Nashville and eventually Hollywood, the more firmly she seemed to plant her roots at the centre of her story. In 1982, she told Barbara Walters in an interview about her dream of opening a "mountain Disneyland" in her Appalachian home region. More like this: Today, that "mountain Disneyland" is Dollywood, a major tourist destination in Sevier County that invites visitors into the version of Appalachia Parton spent her career sharing with the world. Beyond the thrill rides and water park are shows featuring Parton's music, some performed by members of her own family. But to Parton, Dollywood was also a way to give back to the mountains and the community that nurtured her. --

item.title: Why Swedes think standing out is embarrassing
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 2.84
'You're not to think you're anything special': Why Swedes hate standing out Swedes prize equality, dislike boasting and are famously reluctant to stand out – yet they're also fiercely individualistic and know how to celebrate. The century-old idea of Jantelagen helps explain these contradictions, and offers visitors a fascinating key to decoding Swedish culture. As an utlandssvensk – a Swede who grew up abroad – I've always been fascinated by the unwritten rules that shape Swedish social life. I once got to chatting with a fellow Swede at a party. It was 4 July, and we discussed why our country didn't celebrate its national day as fervently as Americans. No fireworks, no parades – how come? "Well, it would be fairly embarrassing wouldn't it?" she said. "All that self-celebration. It's a bit over-the-top," she added, lowering her voice, as if there was an American hovering inches away from our table. As she explained, setting off fireworks for your nation (and therefore yourself) smacks of back-patting and ostentatiousness – two things that are anathema to much of Scandinavia. When I complimented my companion on how well she'd outlined the issue, she looked askance and waved my praise away like a bad smell. "No, please. That's just my little opinion, of course." A modest code of conduct To understand this aversion to basking in even the smallest of spotlights, many Swedes point to Jantelagen, or the Law of Jante: an unwritten social code embedded across Scandinavia that prizes humility, equality and not placing yourself above others. The term comes from Danish-Norwegian author Aksel Sandemose's satirical 1933 novel A Fugitive Crosses His Tracks, set in the fictional town of Jante. Sandemose used Jante to skewer the conformism of small-town Scandinavian life, laying out 10 "laws" designed to put anyone who considered themselves exceptional firmly back in their place. Rules such as "you're not to think you're anything special" and "you're not to think you're smarter than [anyone else]" leave the reader with a deliberately bruised ego – and that's the point. Nearly a century on, Sandemose's laws remain memorable and highly quotable, helping Jantelagen endure as cultural shorthand. How to connect with Swedes Be proactive: Small talk with strangers isn't the norm, so don't mistake reserve for unfriendliness. "Swedes tend to be very loyal and trustworthy once a friendship is established," says Gossner. "I often advise newcomers to take the initiative. Don't wait for Swedes to come to you, as they appreciate when others make the first move." Suggest fika: The Swedish ritual of cake and coffee offers a low-pressure way to socialise. Meet over coffee and a modest but delicious kanelbulle (cinnamon bun) rather than trying to force conversation in the street. Be punctual: Swedes place a high value on being on time, particularly when you're invited to someone's home. Stefan Dahlberg, a professor of political science at Mid Sweden University, has written a paper on Jantelagen's modern legacy. He sees the rules less as firm laws governing Swedish behaviour. Instead, he explains, "they are better understood as a cultural shorthand for a set of familiar norms […] that you can recognise in everyday Swedish interaction. Status differences tend to be played down, social relations are relatively informal and conspicuous self-promotion can be viewed negatively." Visitors to Sweden will likely see this in action when chatting to locals. Compliment a Swede on their English, for example, and they may quickly play it down – switching to Swedish and muttering, "Äsch, det är ju inte flytande…" (Shucks, it's not like it's fluent…). Sandemose would be proud. The qualities can also be seen in everyday Swedish rituals, from Fredagsmys – unpretentious "cosy Fridays" with friends or family – to Lördagsgodis ("Saturday-candy") that's practiced by parents as the one day that kids can unleash their sweet tooth after a week of modest abstention. That doesn't mean that Jantelagen functions as a literal rulebook – or identically across Scandinavia. Dahlberg's study of Jantelagen in Norway, a geographical and cultural neighbour, found the average respondent tended to disagree with the Jante statements. After all, Dahlberg explains, Sandemose invented the list as a scathing takedown of conformity. "So there are really two things mixed together in the concept: an egalitarian idea that nobody is inherently better than anyone else, and a more negative pressure not to distinguish yourself too much." Jante's mirror image Jantelagen has another, less obvious side. In a culture where seeking the limelight is usually frowned upon, Swedish reserve can disappear at parties when a tradition of snappsvisor (increasingly risqué songs belted out while drinking heroic amounts of aquavit) and performative speeches create safe social spaces to open up. So, while Jantelagen is often used as a reasoning for Swedish reserve and diffidence, it can also reveal the inverse. More like this: As Dahlberg notes, "'Don't think you are better than anyone else' can be read in the opposite direction: don't assume that somebody is better than you simply because they are richer, more successful or have a more prestigious title." With so much bubbling under the surface, Sweden can feel deceptively complex. Luckily, there are classes designed to help mystified foreigners. Yvonne Gossner runs Learn Swedish Culture AB – and business is booming. "I realised there was a big demand for practical insights into Swedish culture, especially for foreigners trying to navigate life here," she says. "Many felt lost or misunderstood in everyday settings, or even when trying to make Swedish friends." Case in point: a South American client once arrived at a Swedish woman's party an hour late, carrying a big dish of food as a surprise. The hostess "was not pleased" as the guests had already eaten, and the immodestly large, late-coming dish was left untouched in a bedroom. Swedes, Gossner says, place a high value on punctuality and politeness; if you're invited to a Swede's house, she suggests sending a post-party message of thanks. "There is even a Swedish joke: 'Don't forget to send a thank-you note for the thank-you note'," she adds. An unasked-for dish can risk looking like a statement that "my food is better than yours", while failing to acknowledge someone's politeness can jar the sense of social balance. Cracking the Swedish ice Lola Akinmade Åkerström, a Nigerian-American author, travel writer and photographer who moved to Sweden more than 15 years ago, was initially "a bit floored by the unspoken ethos" of Jantelagen, as well as the contradictory layers of national character. "Sweden is the most open society, run by the most private people," she says. If you want to deeply discomfit a Swede, she advises, just make eye contact on a quiet train, and hit them with "Hi! How you doing?" Yet they're not being cold, just respectful of the idea that no one should impose themselves on a stranger's space. That preference for understatement extends beyond social interactions. Travel through the countryside and you can see it reflected in the nation's beloved summer houses. "I think Swedes hold the world record in the number of summer houses per capita – around half the population has access to one," says Orvar Löfgren, professor emeritus of ethnology at Lund University. Yet these are rarely flashy second homes; instead, they reflect rustic, rural values, even among wealthy owners. (Don't think your cabin is better than other cabins, Sandemose might say.) While in Sweden, visitors might also notice small Swedish flags on birthday cakes, supermarket products and during student celebrations. "Swedes who love to see themselves as non-nationalistic are actually good at waving the flag," says Löfgren. And despite their quiet reputation, "Swedes are great at celebrating," he adds. Christmas, Easter, Midsummer, birthdays, and student exams are celebrated "with more intensity than in most European countries". You could say these occasions showcase Swedes at their best – not that they'd put it so boastfully, of course. --

item.title: Glamping on Vermont's newest bikepacking trail
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 2.43
The US's newest bikepacking trail is pioneering a whole new way to see Vermont The Heart of the Greens trail threads through Vermont's stunning Green Mountain wilderness, and is the first part of an ambitious bikepacking adventure that will someday span the state. My mountain bike tyres thud over pebbles and roots as I whizz through the darkening path. Dusk has fallen over Vermont's Green Mountain National Forest and nearly 400,000 acres of woods extend in every direction. In the distance, I spot pinpricks of light. The campsite is finally near. In the last fleeting moments of light, I arrive at the Chittenden Brook campground. As I wheel my bike past the welcome sign, I spy a slick, modern hut with pine siding. I'd planned to simply pitch a tent – to this weary bikepacker, the hut's glass windows and wraparound porch seem like the lap of luxury. Next time, I thought, I'm staying there. This hut is part of the Heart of the Greens Loop, a 38-mile (61km) bike trail loop and the first completed segment of an ambitious, continuous bikepacking network that, when completed, will stretch 485 miles (780km) and span the entire state. Plan your trip When to do it: Spring and summer are ideal, but tackle the trail in autumn to appreciate its stunning changing leaves. Most riders can expect to complete the loop in one to three days. How to get there: Rochester has limited bus service, so it's easiest to drive to the trailhead. Alternatively, park in Pittsfield and start your ride from there. What to eat: Bring your own provisions. The two villages anchoring the trail have a handful of eateries, like Rochester's farm-to-table Maple Soul and Pittsfield's Clear River Inn & Tavern. Sample dishes made with Vermont's famous maple syrup, like the iconic Creemee ice cream. Pittsfield has two general stores. Blazing a path for bikepackers My journey began that morning in Rochester, a picturesque village nestled in Vermont's mountainous White River Valley. I've driven through it dozens of times without stopping, but since it became the official start and end point of The Heart of the Greens when it opened in 2024, the tiny town has become a magnet for bikepackers. Like me, many are eager to blend the escapism of camping with the thrill of cycling through Vermont's glacial-carved wilderness and explosion of autumnal colours. The loop is a closed-circuit preview of the forthcoming Velomont, a bikepacking route through Central Vermont with a twist: it will be connected by 30 cleverly spaced off-grid huts allowing tired pedallers to bed down in protected forest shelter. On track to finish the first 200 miles (321km) within the next 10 years, the project echoes a larger trend in bicycle travel: statewide bikepacking routes are in development in Utah, Massachusetts and along the entire West Coast. I grew up near Rochester and have dreamed of such a multi-day bikepacking route. For now, I'm thrilled to take on the Heart of the Greens. Two huts are already placed along the trail, roughly 19 miles (30km) apart: the Chittenden Brook Hut, featuring simple bunks and a self-service kitchen, and Spikehorn Yurt. The yurt doesn't have electricity, and neither accommodation has running water. The route's huts will straddle a curious middle ground between camping and traditional stays, allowing bikepackers to carry lighter gear and immerse themselves in the wilderness. The Heart of the Greens may be considerably shorter than the Velomont, but with a cumulative ascent of nearly 6,000ft (1,830m) on largely unpaved forest roads and trails, it's no less intense. "It's a big walk on the wild side," says Doon Hinderyckx, owner of Green Mountain Bikes in Rochester, when I stop by before shoving off. Hinderyckx encourages visitors to hire e-bikes for navigating the steeper grades: "You're mixing mountain biking and the adventure of the challenging terrain. You're on and off the seat a lot." It also requires a bike with thick tyres and suspension, a water filter and provisions, since the current route passes through only two small backcountry villages – Rochester and, 9 miles (14km) south, Pittsfield. Like the huts, eateries and general stores along the trail itself are still in development, so I've packed several meals, plus rain gear and insect repellent, despite the beautiful late summer weather. Hinderyckx checks the air pressure in my inner tubes and oils my chain. He's the last mechanic I'll see for the next two days. Next door to Green Mountain Bikes stands the Stable Inn, run by Hinderyckx's wife, Anni MacKay. This handsome two-story guesthouse opened in 2023, with a range of rooms, Nordic-chic decor and rooftop solar panels, converted from a timber-frame warehouse from the 1840s. While not an official hut on the trail, the Stable Inn has become a base for many Heart of the Greens riders to unwind, or bookend their bikepacking journey with jaunts to the village's quaint art centres and shops. "[The loop is] a very strategic, positive thing," says MacKay. "People always want to have access to the backcountry, in a safe way, with the benediction of the community that is providing services. It's a complete win-win." Ups and downs in the Green Mountains I know Vermont well and have bike-toured widely, but this is harder than I expected. On asphalt, a 38-mile ride makes for a pleasant afternoon. The Heart of the Greens is far more demanding – and adventurous. Rugged roads lead to mountain bike trails, which scissor their way up the alpine forest. The first day, I coast south along Route 100 and turn onto State Garage Road, into a residential area. Houses disappear beyond the canopy, and I huff up one shelf of road, then another. All at once, the road transforms into steep gravel. I grind past the Spikehorn Yurt, the Loop's first hut, a rounded fabric enclosure with bunkbeds, a futon, homey furniture and a spacious terrace with views of the mountains. The route then devolves into two dirt tyre trenches cutting through the grass – what mountain bikers call "double track". My temples pound as I climb. Summer mosquitoes drone in the sultry air. After a couple of gruelling miles, the road finally descends, and so do the conditions. Logging lorries have shredded the ground into potting soil, my wheels sink into a mire of turned earth and broken branches. As I struggle, another cyclist pulls up behind me. "This is crazy, isn't it?" he wheezes. "I don't think I'd have made it if I wasn't on an e-bike." I can't help but agree. The grades are tough on my middle-aged thighs, and I frequently dismount and push. I got a late start to begin with, and as I reach the third major trail section of the day – a mile of switchbacks cheekily named "Perspiration" – my legs boil with lactic acid, and the Sun melts beyond the ridge. This is how I come to arrive at Chittenden Brook Campground after nightfall. I pitch my tent onto the cold ground and gaze longingly at the modern hut before me. Riding high After a decent night's sleep, I finally hit my stride. I sail down the smooth pavement of Route 73 and pedal through the pastoral scenery of the quiet, unpaved Bingo Brook Road. Dense trees all around, I pass occasional farmhouses and cottages, but most of this land is national forest. Fog lifts over a pond, and the air is cool and quiet. I try to imagine what the Velomont will look like in future decades. The Heart of the Greens now passes through just two village centres with a loose string of businesses straddling Route 100. As the Velomont expands, it will tether together more towns and country shops, making it easier for cyclists to resupply and interact with locals. Bikepackers will traverse ever-more-varied terrain and, like me, stop in towns they might never notice by car. "You're camping, but you're not really camping," says Georgia Grzywacz, a Maine resident who rode the loop and stayed at the Chittenden Brook Hut in June. She appreciated the kitchen, electricity and bunk mattresses, as well as the nearby brook. "You're without running water, but you have these creature comforts." Even the booking process was easy: "The [Vermont Huts] website is so navigable." I veer off Bingo Brook Road to find a final trailhead. Two mountains remain, totalling 12 miles (19km) and more than 2,000ft (609m) of climbing, but this time, I'm prepared. Teeth clenched, I grind my way up the switchbacks of Swan's Mill Trail, fighting for every foot of elevation. More like this: At last, my reward: Tunnel Ridge is a five-mile-long (8km) flow trail that snakes its way back down to Rochester, for a total of 110 switchbacks. My tyres shudder over washboard terrain and swerve around S-curves. I choke the brakes, my saddlebags bounce noisily over my rear rack. The forest becomes a wash of brown and green. Gravity lures me downward, into the valley. Endorphins flood my brain as I drift into The Stable Inn's parking lot, back to my waiting car. I'm euphoric but exhausted. For now, I'm closing the loop. But in time, there should be many miles, and many huts, more. And I'll be ready. --

item.title: What Is Half-and-Half, Exactly?
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 5.77
Despite the promise of its name, the half-and-half you buy at the supermarket isn’t actually equal parts heavy cream and whole milk. While the dairy-aisle staple does fall somewhere between the two, and you can get away with substituting it for one part milk and one part cream in most cases, the truth is slightly more complex. By law, half-and-half must contain between 10.5% and 18% milkfat. Most commercial products land on the lower end of that spectrum, at around 11.5%. The result is dairy that’s richer and more luscious than whole milk, but more fluid than heavy cream. Whole milk, meanwhile, has a fat content of about 3.25%, and cream contains at least 36%. Mix the two in equal measure, and you’ll end up with something considerably richer than most store-bought half-and-half. For a closer substitute, combine two parts milk to one part cream (~14%) or three parts milk to one part cream (~11%). What about shelf-stable half-and-half? Your first interaction with half-and-half might have been those tiny cups that get tossed on the table at diners, fast food joints, and other less-than-fancy places. One or two of them does the trick to make even the cheapest, most burnt coffee taste better—or, at the very least, creamier. To keep these thimble-sized cups shelf-stable, manufacturers use ultra-high-temperature processing and may add stabilizers. Similar-looking cups labeled “creamer” may contain little to no actual dairy. What is fat-free half-and-half? Fat-free half-and-half is typically made from skim milk that’s been amended with thickeners and other stabilizers. While the cartons might look similar, the taste and texture aren’t quite the same (not creamy like melted ice cream, but creamy like melted shaving cream). Some manufacturers claim the cooking properties of their fat-free products are equal to those of regular half-and-half, but we generally don’t recommend swapping one for the other. How to cook with half-and-half Half-and-half is an ideal ingredient for soups, sauces, mashed potatoes, and custards when you want richness without the heft of heavy cream. Because it contains less fat, it’s more likely to curdle when added directly to high heat or acidic dishes (such as tomato sauce or lemon desserts). For added insurance, you can temper the cold half-and-half with some of the hot liquid, then add it back in. More often than not, though, you can add half-and-half straight to the saucepan, like in our creamy cauliflower soup, where the dairy is added to hot broth and vegetables and simmered before blending, or our coconut cream pie, where it’s added to reduced coconut milk and cooked. Half-and-half also works well in quiche and other egg bakes, chowders, panades for meatballs or meatloaf, and custardy desserts like our Caramelized Banana Pudding and panna cotta. How to store half-and-half Keep half-and-half refrigerated and generally follow the manufacturer’s guidance for how quickly to use it; recommendations vary by brand. Once opened, some cartons can last up to 10 days. Ultra-pasteurized dairy generally has a longer shelf life when unopened than conventionally pasteurized half-and-half. Unused half-and-half can be frozen for up to 2 months, but may separate upon thawing—shake well and blend into soups or mix into batters. You can also freeze half-and-half in an ice cube tray and add a few cubes straight to a pan sauce. What can you substitute for half-and-half? If you’re out of half-and-half, combine ¾ cup whole milk with ¼ cup heavy cream for a substitute similar to most supermarket half-and-half, or ⅔ cup whole milk with ⅓ cup heavy cream for a slightly richer version. Homemade half-and-half won’t behave exactly like the homogenized stuff you buy in stores and may separate a little. Just give it a shake or stir before adding it to your coffee, sauce, or stew. No heavy cream? Whole milk can stand in for half-and-half in many recipes, though the result will be less rich. For hot dishes, you can compensate by adding a few pats of butter. Going the other direction, heavy cream can generally replace half-and-half 1:1, though the result will be richer (you could also thin it somewhat with water, if desired). If dairy isn’t a requirement, a barista-style plant-based milk works well. Canned evaporated milk can also work in a pinch, but its richness falls somewhere between whole milk and half-and-half, and it has a cooked flavor that may not suit every application. And what if you have half-and-half but the recipe calls for milk or cream? Half-and-half can generally replace whole milk 1:1 in savory dishes like soups, sauces, and mashed potatoes; expect a richer result. It can also replace heavy cream when the cream is primarily there to add richness (like in chowder or custard), though the finished dish will be lighter. Just remember, unlike heavy cream, half-and-half doesn’t contain enough fat to whip, no matter how vigorously you agitate it. Editor’s note: This story was originally published in 2018; it has been updated for style with additional reporting by Anna Hezel and Joe Sevier.

item.title: Lemon Bars With Shortbread Crust
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 5.01
These lemon bars have everything we want from the classic dessert: buttery shortbread crust, smooth, puckery lemon filling, and a snowy dusting of powdered sugar. The filling gets extra citrusy flavor from rubbing fresh lemon zest into the sugar before whisking in the eggs and lemon juice. Better yet, there’s no stovetop curd to make—the filling goes straight on the baked crust. That simplicity comes with one important rule: Pack the shortbread crust firmly and evenly into the pan before baking. A flat-bottomed measuring cup, drinking glass, or large offset spatula works well for this. Once baked, let the crust cool for just 5 minutes, then pour in the lemon filling while the crust is still hot. The heat helps set the filling on contact, keeping the liquid custard from seeping beneath the crust. Chill the baked lemon bars at least 4 hours before slicing so the filling has time to set completely. Dust with powdered sugar just before serving—it will gradually dissolve into the moist lemon topping if added too far in advance. Lemon bars FAQ Why did my lemon bars turn out upside down? If the lemon filling seeps underneath the shortbread, the crust can essentially float to the top as the bars bake. To prevent this, pack the crust firmly and evenly into the pan before baking, ensuring it reaches all the way to the corners. Once the crust comes out of the oven, set a timer for 5 minutes. As soon as it goes off, pour in the filling and return the pan to the oven promptly. The crust should still be hot when the filling goes in. How do I know when lemon bars are done? The lemon filling should look set around the edges but still jiggle slightly in the center when you gently shake the pan, which should take 20–25 minutes. The filling will continue to firm up as the bars cool and chill. Refrigerate them for at least 4 hours before slicing. Do lemon bars need to be refrigerated? Yes. Once cooled, refrigerate the lemon bars until cold and keep leftovers chilled. They can be baked up to 2 days ahead; wait to dust them with powdered sugar until just before serving. Can I make lemon bars with Meyer lemons? Yes. Meyer lemons will work, though their juice is typically sweeter and less sharply acidic than that of conventional lemons, so the finished bars will have a softer, more floral lemon flavor. Can I make lemon bars in a 9x9" pan? Yes. An 8x8" pan gives these lemon bars their thick layers, but a 9x9" pan also works. Because the crust and filling will be slightly thinner, start checking for doneness toward the early end of the suggested baking times. Read more: Watch Kendra make lemon bars: Recipe information - Total Time 70 minutes (plus cooling and chilling) - Yield Makes 16 Ingredients 1¼ ¼ 1¼ 7 2 1 2 3 ⅔ ¼ Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Line an 8x8" baking pan with parchment paper, leaving overhang on all sides. Pulse 1¼ cups (156 g) all-purpose flour, ¼ cup (28 g) powdered sugar, and ¾ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a food processor to combine. Add 7 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and pulse until mixture is sandy with very small butter pieces. Add 1 large egg yolk and pulse until combined; mixture will be very dry looking and powdery but should hold together when squeezed in your hand. Step 2Transfer mixture to prepared pan and spread into an even layer to fill pan. Using a flat-bottomed measuring cup or glass, pack into a compressed layer (use your fingers to get into the corners). Bake crust until golden, 27–29 minutes. Let cool 5 minutes. (Set a timer; you don’t want to go longer. The crust needs to be warm when you add the lemon mixture.) Step 3While the crust is baking, place 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar and 2 tsp. finely grated lemon zest in a medium bowl. Using your fingers, massage zest into sugar until fragrant and lightly tinted yellow, about 1 minute. Add 3 large eggs, remaining 1 large egg yolk, and remaining 3 Tbsp. (23 g) all-purpose flour and gently whisk just until combined. Add ⅔ cup fresh lemon juice, ¼ cup whole milk, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt; stir to combine. Step 4As soon as the timer for the crust goes off, pour lemon mixture over (the hot crust will start to cook the filling and prevent the layers from inverting). Gently tap pan on counter to pop any air bubbles on surface and return pan to oven quickly. Bake until lemon mixture is set but still jiggles slightly when gently shaken, 20–25 minutes. Let lemon bar cool, then chill until cold, at least 4 hours. Step 5Using parchment paper overhang, lift lemon bar from pan and place on a cutting board. Cut into 16 squares. Step 6Dust lemon bars with powdered sugar just before serving. Do Ahead: Lemon bars (without powdered sugar topping) can be baked 2 days ahead. Cover and keep chilled. Editor’s note: This recipe was originally published on October 19, 2023. In response to reader feedback, we retested it in September 2026 and updated the instructions with additional guidance for keeping the shortbread crust and lemon filling in distinct layers. Head this way for more of our best lemon desserts →

item.title: A Really Big Chicken Parm
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 4.74
When Senior Test Kitchen Editor Jesse Szewczyk first came across Chef Skyler's giant chicken cutlet that went viral on TikTok, he knew he wanted to put his spin on it. His take? This supersized chicken Parmesan topped with marinara, melted mozzarella, and fresh basil. (Turns out Chef Skyler also had the same idea; check out her version here.) To make it, you’ll start by rolling out ground chicken between two sheets of parchment paper until it’s as thin as a ruler. You’ll coat the top of it with flour, eggs, breadcrumbs, and Parmesan—just like you would a typical cutlet. The next step is the only one that takes effort, and one that requires a burst of confidence to pull off: You’ll flip the entire disk in one swift move, exposing its undressed underbelly so you can bread the other side. If this process does not go as planned, don’t fret: A misshapen “cutlet” will bake up just as delicious (and hidden underneath all the toppings, no one will see its flaws). Serve it as is, tuck it between slices of crusty bread for a filling sandwich, or serve it alongside a simple salad for dinner. Check out more winning weeknight dinners here: Pad Kra Pao; Sheet-Pan Feta With Tomatoes and Chickpeas; and Spaghetti With So Much Zucchini. Recipe information - Total Time 1 hour - Yield 4 servings Ingredients 1 2 3 1 4 1½ 8 Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 425°. Place 1 lb. ground chicken in the center of a large sheet of parchment paper cut to fit a rimmed baking sheet. Place a second sheet of parchment paper (the same size) on top, then roll out chicken until very thin and it covers parchment, leaving 1"–2" border around sides. Carefully and slowly peel off top sheet of parchment; set aside. Step 2Whisk 2 large eggs in a small bowl with a fork to combine. Mix together 3 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (½ cup), 1 cup panko, a pinch of kosher salt, and a pinch of freshly ground pepper in another small bowl. Step 3Generously season top of chicken with salt and pepper. Scatter 2 Tbsp. all-purpose flour over and rub into an even layer to completely coat surface. (It’s easiest to use your hands for this.) Brush half of eggs on top with a pastry brush or your hands. Scatter about half of panko mixture over, pressing in with your hands to adhere. Generously coat entire surface with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Place reserved sheet of parchment on top of chicken, then hold both sheets together and turn over in a swift, confident motion. Peel away top layer of parchment and discard. Generously season top of chicken with salt and pepper. Scatter remaining 2 Tbsp. all-purpose flour over and rub into an even layer to completely coat surface. Brush half of egg on top. Scatter remaining panko mixture over, pressing in with your hands to adhere. Generously spray entire surface with nonstick spray. Step 4Transfer chicken with parchment paper onto a rimmed baking sheet. (It’s easiest to hold baking sheet flush against the counter and drag parchment paper with chicken onto it.) Bake chicken, rotating baking sheet front to back halfway through, until deep golden brown all over, 28–35 minutes. Remove from oven, turn cutlet over with tongs, and spread 1½ cups homemade or store-bought marinara sauce over. Scatter 8 oz. mozzarella, coarsely grated (1–1½ cups), on top, then bake just until cheese is melted and browned in spots, 14–18 minutes. Remove from oven and top with basil leaves and drizzle with extra-virgin olive oil if desired.

item.title: 19 Margarita Recipes for Any Season
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 4.71
A great margarita is hard to beat: tequila, fresh lime juice, orange liqueur, and salt in sweet-tart harmony. But the classic margarita recipe is also an excellent starting point for experimentation. Small tweaks—swapping triple sec for agave syrup, say, or tequila for mezcal—can create a whole new drink. Perhaps even more compelling is the margarita's ability to veer into maximalism. Blend yours with frozen mango, muddle in fresh blackberries, or infuse the tequila with chiles. Below you’ll find 19 of our best margarita recipes, including frozen margaritas, spicy margaritas, fruit-forward riffs, and a few less traditional variations. There’s a salted watermelon margarita for summer, a blood orange version for winter, and an avocado margarita that blends up remarkably creamy. Whether you like yours on the rocks, straight up, or frozen, there’s a margarita here for you.

item.title: Gochujang Yogurt Chicken
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 4.28
Don’t be surprised if this becomes your new go-to weeknight chicken dish. The marinade features a host of winning pantry ingredients you likely already have on hand: yogurt, gochujang, soy sauce, and maple syrup. A smack of freshly grated garlic joins in to make a delicious spicy-savory-sweet marinade you’ll find yourself using on everything. (Yes, in fact, you can reserve a small portion to thin out later to become a nice drizzling sauce over the cooked chicken. More on that below in the recipe instructions.) Yogurt is a powerful tenderizer, so even just 20 minutes of marinating time while you prep the rest of dinner is enough to imbue flavor into the meat. The yogurt also helps to temper the heat from smoky-spicy gochujang, the assertive and versatile Korean hot pepper paste. If you have the time, an overnight rest in the fridge is even better. Lean on my favorite go-to broiler for a quick cook with minimal cleanup. These chicken thighs take very well to batch-cooking at the start of the week and enjoying in the ensuing days. They are great with rice, over salad, in a wrap, or even just cold out of the fridge (who, me?). Save more weeknight dinner winners: Gorgeous Green Shrimp; Spicy Salmon Bowl; and Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry Recipe information - Total Time 30 minutes (plus marinating) - Yield 4–6 servings Ingredients 4–6 ½ ¼ 3 3 1 1½ ½ 2½–3 Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Whisk 4–6 garlic cloves, finely grated (about 1 Tbsp.), ½ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt, ¼ cup gochujang (Korean hot pepper paste), 3 Tbsp. pure maple syrup, 3 Tbsp. soy sauce, 1 Tbsp. vegetable oil, 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1 tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper in a small bowl until salt is mostly dissolved. (If you’d like to reserve ¼ cup marinade for dressing, now is the time; chill until ready to use.) Step 2Pour marinade into a large resealable plastic bag and add 2½–3 lb. skinless, boneless chicken thighs. Close bag and turn chicken to coat. Let sit at room temperature at least 20 minutes, or chill, turning occasionally, up to 12 hours. Step 3Heat broiler. Place a wire rack inside a foil-lined rimmed baking sheet. Coat or brush rack with nonstick vegetable oil spray or vegetable oil. Remove chicken from marinade, letting excess drip back into bag, and arrange, smoother side up, on rack. Broil, turning halfway through, until golden brown with some edges getting a deeper char, 15–18 minutes. Let chicken rest about 5 minutes, then slice if desired. Step 4If using reserved marinade as a sauce, add 1–2 Tbsp. water to reserved marinade to thin to desired consistency. Serve chicken with sauce drizzled over.

item.title: 3 Best Bread Knives, After Testing 36 Blades (2026)
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 3.00
Serrated bread knives may seem like specialized kitchen tools, but you’d be hard-pressed to slice that beautiful loaf of sourdough you brought home without one. Unlike standard kitchen knives, serrated knives have, well, serrations—a line of individually sharpened teeth along the edges that dig into whatever you’re cutting with each stroke. This sawing action easily cuts through a soft bread crumb without smooshing it, and it’s also helpful for slicing delicate tomato skin or peeling a watermelon. Our top picks - Best bread knife overall: Mac Superior Bread Knife - The best cheap bread knife: Mercer Culinary M23210 10" Bread Knife - A worthy splurge: Shun Classic 9" Bread Knife For years, the common thought was that a good serrated knife didn’t have to be expensive, and we generally agree—you can find an affordable bread knife that’ll do the job well and free up more of your knife budget to invest in the rest of your knife set. Some of that is because part of what makes a chef’s knife expensive, the high quality steel forged to hold a fine, sharp edge for a long time, isn’t as much of a thing for serrated knives. The design of the teeth makes it so that the blade can still function even if it isn’t that sharp; that’s not really the case for straight edge knives. And, because sharpening a serrated knife is a much more involved process than sharpening a straight edge knife, some people think it’s better to replace a serrated knife after several years rather than try to maintain it. However… After testing 36 bread knives over the past few years, I think it’s worth investing in a high-end bread knife that’ll stay sharper longer, with blade geometry that makes slicing as easy as possible. And so I recommend one of those along with a variety of more affordable picks below. Regardless, the best bread knives at any price point are sharp, long enough for large loaves of bread, and sturdy in the hand. The top picks below all aced that criteria even with long-term testing. New in this update: We replaced the top pick in this piece after long-term testing of our favorite knives, and because of pricing and availability issues with a longtime favorite brand Tojiro. We also updated additional reviews, including on knives from Made In, Winco, and Mac after more testing. Finally we added a section on serrated knife sharpening and tested a well-liked serrated knife sharpening rod. Best bread knife overall: Mac Superior Series 10.5" bread knife Pros and cons Pros: - Long blade makes slicing through wide bread loaves easy - Curved shape offers extra leverage Cons: - On the pricier end of the spectrum Specs Knife length: 15.38" Blade length: 10.75" Weight: 6.6 oz. What we love: Mac’s Superior Series bread knife features an extra-long curved blade that makes slicing bread a breeze. Even the crustiest, oversized miche loaves were no match for this knife. It features rounded teeth that cut easily into the crust without snagging, making each stroke smoother and more deliberate. It also sliced neatly through tomato skin and glide effortlessly through the pulp, delivering perfectly uniform tomato slices. The Mac is made from high-carbon stainless steel that will keep an edge longer—a plus because serrated knives are so labor-intensive to sharpen. The curve to the blade is another excellent design choice. That curve adds cutting force to the knife because the belly extends about half an inch beyond the handle, creating immediate leverage with each stroke. In long-term testing, I found that Mac’s Superior Series offered sustained performance that cheaper knives just couldn’t match, bumping this knife into our top-pick slot. What we’d leave: My biggest gripe about this knife is the price point and handle construction. While the blocky handle scales are comfortable, it seems reasonable to expect a $100 knife to have an integrated bolster and nicer finish. For those looking for a nicer handle and are willing to spend money, you can check out the Mac Professional Series below. NOTE: The Mac Superior series is sometimes listed as the Mac Professional series on Amazon and other large marketplaces. It is not! The Professional series has a metal bolster between the blade and the handle. No bolster, not Professional. The actual Professional series knife should also cost about 50% more than the Superior series model. The best cheap (but very good) bread knife: Mercer Culinary M23210 10" Bread Knife Pros and cons Pros: - Great value knife Cons: - Not full tang - Plastic handle Specs Knife length: 15.5" Blade length: 10" Weight: 5.9 oz. What we love: Premium bread knives have their perks, but a good one doesn’t have to break the bank. The Mercer Culinary Millennia 10" bread knife is less than $20, and it’s the one we use most frequently in the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen. “This bread knife came in the kit bag I got in culinary school, and I am still using it today,” food director Chris Morocco says. “It won’t split atoms, but it is dependable, and for this price, you will love it all the more.” It has deep, wide serrations, also known as a wavy edge, as opposed to the pointy teeth you see on the Wüsthof or Tojiro. Instead of a wooden handle, the ergonomic handle of the Mercer is made from a combination of rubber and plastic. While this knife isn’t full-tang (no knife at this price is), it still feels stable and comfortable to hold. Our editors have used this knife for every slicing task you can imagine: crusty bread, pineapple, ripe tomatoes, overstuffed BLTs—and it always gets the job done. What we’d leave: This knife performed admirably for its price point, but it was the least sharp of our other two winning bread knives, requiring a bit more effort to cut crustier loaves. Some people also didn’t like the Mercer’s plastic handle, which wasn’t as comfortable as our other picks. A worthy splurge: Shun Classic 9" Bread Knife Pros and cons Pros: - High carbon steel will stay sharper longer - Beautiful knife Cons: - Pricey Specs Knife length: 14" Blade length: 9" Weight: 6.8 oz. What we love: While chef’s knives are often praised for their steel quality and appearance, bread knives are typically prized for their functionality. While you don’t need to spend as much on a bread knife to get top-tier performance, we really loved the total package from Shun’s Classic line bread knife. It’s made from Damascus steel with a VG-MAX core, which is a much higher-carbon-content steel than most bread knives. This means that the serrated edge of the knife is less likely to dull over time—key for a knife that needs to be maintained professionally to keep sharp edges. In testing, it sliced tomatoes beautifully thin, and even the crustiest sourdough provided almost zero resistance. We also appreciated the height of the blade, which provided some extra heft and cutting force without adding extra weight. Finally, the Japanese wa-style handle was comfortable to grip when you needed a little extra leverage. Because there’s no palm swell or shape to the handle, it lets the user find the position that’s most comfortable for them. Shun’s bread knife might be pricier than our other top picks, but the price definitely matches the performance and knife quality. If you’re looking for a serrated knife that will stay sharper for longer, then this might be the right pick for you. What we’d leave: The 9" blade was plenty long for most loaves of bread, but wider boules were tricky to cut all the way across without having to angle the knife. It’s hard to ignore how expensive this knife is. While it does have the highest quality fit and finish of our winners, its performance boost over our two budget picks might not quite be enough for some people. Still, if you’re picky about the details of knife construction and steel quality, this knife justifies its price point. How we tested bread knives We spoke with our Test Kitchen editors to find out which blades they’ve relied on throughout their careers. Then we tested more than two dozen bread knives on crusty sourdough and winter vine tomatoes—ideal examples of that tricky firm-outside, soft-inside texture that serrated knives handle so well. We also conduct long-term testing on our top picks to evaluate how they hold up with daily use, noting whether the blades retain their sharpness and if the handles show any signs of cracking. What makes the best bread knife We focused on evaluating the following factors when it came to making our selections: How effectively it cuts The ideal knife practically does the work for you, creating clean cuts with minimal downward pressure. In our testing, we found that thin knives usually got the job done best. Weight Your knife should have enough heft to cut through foods that have a firm exterior and a delicate interior. A too-heavy knife, however, will be cumbersome to wield. Shape of teeth A serrated knife is defined by its toothlike edge, but there are a few variations on the design. A serrated knife can have rounded, scalloped teeth; pointy teeth; and even double serrations that feature a combination of the two. While scalloped teeth might seem like the least effective option, our testing proved that this is not always the case. In fact, knives with teeth that were too pointy risked snagging and tearing on bread interiors or tomato flesh. How it feels to hold We considered the knife as a whole—from the tip of its blade to the end of the handle. We looked for knives that had ergonomic handles that fit the natural contours of our hands and paid attention to the balance of weight between the handle and the blade. We wanted a knife that felt hefty enough to give us proper leverage when slicing hardier loaves, but not so heavy as to become unwieldy. The ones we picked above were the most stable and comfortable to hold, the easiest to work with, and they made the cleanest cuts. Other bread knives we like Dexter Russell Basics 10" Scalloped Bread Knife This knife from Dexter-Russell was a top contender for the best budget spot thanks to its super sharp scalloped blade, which made easy work of slicing through tough sourdough crusts and delicate tomato skin. In the end, the Mercer edged out the competition because of its grippy, more comfortable handle, slightly sturdier construction, and (just barely) lower price tag. That said, this would be a good option if the Mercer is ever out of stock. Hedley & Bennett 8.6" Bread Knife Senior test kitchen editor (and Bon Appétit’s resident baking expert) Shilpa Uskokovic loves this bread knife from Hedley & Bennett because it’s sleek and light. While it has a smaller 8.5" blade, its angled, serrated edge becomes more pointed at the tip, making it easier to maneuver and offering heightened precision for more fragile slicing tasks. It’s relatively affordable at $90 at the time of writing, and it comes in a variety of colors. However, for all those positives, the Hedley & Bennett doesn’t offer quite the force you get from a longer blade. MAC Professional Series 10.5" Bread Knife After long-term testing, this knife is a personal favorite of Bon Appétit writers and editors—but the price makes recommending it tricky. With nearly the exact same blade as MAC’s Superior series, MAC’s Professional Series bread knife is also a high performer. The slight curve on the spine gives you tons of leverage to get through crusty bread with little effort, and the sharpness of its rounded teeth lets it slice without snagging. The big thing that sets this knife apart is its fit and finish. With a full bolster that has enough room for a pinch grip, full tang construction, and three handle rivets, this knife is built to withstand heavy-duty wear and tear. Is it overkill for a bread knife? Absolutely. But for knife aficionados, the high price tag might be worth it. Performance-wise, the MAC Professional bread knife easily sliced through the crustiest loaves and glided through tomatoes. It also felt great in the hand, even if it was a little heavy. Overall, the price-to-performance ratio kept this bread knife from the top picks, but if you want an upgrade on our top pick, it is a great option to consider. Wüsthof Classic 9" Double Serrated Bread Knife This German-made knife is another pricey blade, but it justifies that price tag with its interesting and super-effective design. While this one has a shorter 9" blade, it’s double serrated, which means it has mini teeth within the larger, scalloped serrations. All those extra sharp points give it a better grip on waxy surfaces like the exterior of a tomato or watermelon and make for fast, easy slicing. It’s also a knife that asks very little of you—during testing, the double set of serrations cut through hard crust with very little exertion from the tester and produced such thin slices of tomato that we could see right through them. One final advantage of a double-serrated blade: because there are more of them, each individual serration will wear less, so the knife stays sharper for longer. The shorter blade did make it tricky to cut wider loaves straight across, though it was an adequate length for most batards and pan loaves. Mercer Culinary 8" Züm Bread Knife Sharp and with a comfortable handle, the Züm knife from Mercer Culinary excelled in our testing. It neatly sliced through the tomatoes, piercing the tough skin easily without smashing the delicate flesh. It also perfectly sliced through the sourdough crust and crumb without snagging. The only thing we didn’t like was the 8" blade length, which was a little short for bigger sourdough loaves, but for around $50, it’s an effective budget option with high-end handle construction and a full bolster. Not quite our favorite budget pick, but a good alternative, and a good option for people who want a very comfortable handle. Misen 8" Serrated Knife Misen’s bread knife was a mid-tier performer in our tests, cleanly cutting through tomatoes and bread without any notable issues. We also thought the handle was comfortable, and its overall build quality was high. The blade’s taller heel also meant it performed well slicing through larger sourdough loaves. However, its performance didn’t quite match our top picks, and our two budget models performed better at half the cost. We recommend either spending a little more for a nicer bread knife, or saving a bit of cash instead—unless you can find this knife on sale. Bread knives we don’t recommend A former top pick, I still stand behind this knife’s performance and build quality. What I don’t love, however, is its spotty availability and fluctuating price. At around $60, I thought this knife was a steal. Now that its price has rocketed up to match Mac’s Superior Series bread knife, I can’t recommend it when the Mac offers better build quality and consistency. Still, if you can catch this knife on a deal, go for it—it’s sharp and nimble, but sturdy enough to tackle most tasks. Like its sturdier cousin, this bread knife from Tojiro is sharp and swift. But when we originally picked this serrated knife, its price was around $40. For that price, this knife was a great pick. But its cheaper build quality, lack of a full tang, and slightly smaller wood handle mean we don’t see much value in recommending this knife now that it’s price has nearly doubled. Bob Kramer is a legendary knife maker, but the Bob Kramer Essential Bread Knife by Zwilling felt like overkill for a serrated knife. Its $400-plus price point is excessive for a tool with such a narrow set of uses (no matter how often you bake homemade bread), and because this knife is made from carbon steel, it'll be prone to corrosion and rust. Does it work well? Definitely; it was one of the better tomato knives we used. But is it worth the sky-high price? In our opinion, no. This knife has a nice weight to it—stable without being heavy—and it’s easy to control through longer cuts. However, it wasn’t as sharp or efficient as the top performers. Global’s great knives have won the hearts of many a BA staffer. That said, the brand’s metal handles are divisive—some people think they’re comfortable to hold and others find them too thin and slippery. While our testers say this knife is well-balanced and decently sharp, they ultimately disqualified it from our winners list due to its handle shape, short blade length (8.5"), and less-than-perfect performance in the tomato test, where its large teeth snagged just a bit on the tomato’s flesh. Ikea’s $25 bread knife handled bread and tomatoes competently without excelling at either. The serrations weren’t the sharpest we tested, but they cut cleanly enough for everyday use. We were impressed by the sharpness of Kuhn Rikon’s serrations, which allowed for precise cuts. Its limitation is its reach; at under 8", wide bread loaves demand more back-and-forth. But if you’re not into sourdough boules, this will be an impressive performer. This is a beautiful knife (just look at that gorgeously curved handle grip), but the Lamson’s teeth weren't sharp enough. The knife snagged on crusty sourdough boules and required a lot of force to make cuts. Its 8" blade was also too short to cut through entire loaves, and it snagged slightly on tomato skin. Lamson does offer complementary sharpening for life, but for this price ($90 at the time of writing), we feel the bread knife should be sharper out of the box. Sharp and well-made, we do like Mac’s Chef’s Series bread knife. But it’s only slightly cheaper than our top pick and doesn’t feature a curved belly. Again, the decision not to recommend it comes to value; you’ll get a much more better slicing experience if you drop an extra $10 on the Mac Superior. Though it was razor sharp, MAC’s offset knife was too short to effectively slice bread. At only 7.5", we had to maneuver it to make it through an entire sourdough loaf. We also didn’t like its offset blade, which made it hard to intuitively feel where the blade was compared to the handle. It did excel as a tomato slicer, but it would be hard to recommend it at this price point. The first time we tested Made In’s bread knife, we found it lacked sharpness. That’s no longer the case—their slightly updated model has sharper serrations and slices through bread and tomatoes with ease. The big issues are with the weight and the price—the heftier handle does balance well against the blade, but overall it’s a heavy knife. It’s also more expensive than our top pick while having a shorter, straighter blade. This knife is fine, but there are plenty of others that offer better value. A little too flimsy, this knife struggled to neatly slice through sourdough bread. Even though it was sharp, the blade tended to flex when cutting, creating uneven slices of bread. We also didn’t like the cheapness of the handle or the offset blade shape, but it did offer solid performance at a very affordable price. For how pricey this knife is, we were disappointed in how dull the blade appeared to be. Because it’s difficult to sharpen a serrated knife, initial sharpness is a key factor in picking out the best option for your kitchen. This knife snagged on tomato skin and tore apart the delicate sourdough bread crumb. Though the handle was beautiful and felt nice in the hand, this knife was the most expensive model we tested and had some of the worst performance. Considering it's one of the most expensive bread knives we tested, we were hoping for better performance out of the Miyabi Kaizen 9.5" Bread Knife. Instead, it crushed most loaves of bread instead of cutting them, and it got stuck on tomato cores. The Opinel Intempora fell short—in some cases, literally—in a few areas. Its 8" blade is shorter than we’d like, making it hard to cut through sourdough boules without changing the slicing angle. Its teeth weren't quite as sharp as we’d like either. It didn’t mangle the tomatoes (a win!), but we had difficulty keeping the blade straight—the knife typically snagged on the fruit’s core, creating wobbly, inconsistent tomato slices. We do like the round polyurethane handle and the high-quality high-carbon stainless steel, but we expect better performance from a knife of this price. The Shun Classic Master Serrated Knife has a unique wavy edge that adds to the overall serration pattern. It excelled at slicing paper-thin tomatoes and was comfortable to hold, but its edge shape didn't consistently cut through bread well. Its blade was also on the shorter side, making this knife less well-suited for large loaves. This knife has a lot going for it: The Shun Ultimate Utility looks almost like a toy shark and, accordingly, has plenty of bite—we loved how sharp its rounded teeth were. Its flat sides and curved tip mean that this knife is able to both slice your sandwich toppings and spread mayo on a piece of soft bread. It also sliced tomatoes perfectly and slid right through the crust of the sourdough boules. But its tiny 6" blade, which is more similar to a santoku than a typical bread knife, made it hard to cut even slices. And when you factor in the price ($140 at the time of writing), we just can’t recommend it. This model from Victorinox, the makers of one of our favorite budget-friendly chef’s knives, performed pretty well overall. Testers found that while the plastic handle looks flimsy, the knife cut really well and felt sturdy. However, this is an incredibly light knife—so much so that it verges on too light—and at more than double (or triple, at some stores) the cost of our affordable picks, it costs more than we think is worth spending. The Victorinox Swiss Army 8" knife sliced bread okay, but it required more effort than most other models; worse, it crushed tomatoes. It was also too lightweight to maneuver comfortably. Sharp, well-made, and great at cutting, there’s a lot to like about the Wüsthof Classic bread knife. It easily sliced through tomatoes, and it cut swiftly through crusty sourdough bread. But its 8" length struggled to span the entire loaf, and then there’s the price. As one of the most expensive bread knives we tested, we think there’s better performance for less money—or, you can upgrade to the double-serrated version, which was one of our top picks. The double serrations of this Ikon series knife performed as well on waxy surfaces as the Wüsthof Classic double serrated knife above, but struggled a bit against crusty bread. The bigger issue is that this knife regularly retails for about $200 (30% more than the regular Classic series knife). You’re paying for the Ikon finishes, which are lovely, but if you’re interested in double serration, we think the standard Classic offering (listed above) is a better bet at a slightly more affordable price. Although billed as a “13-inch” bread knife, Zulay’s blade is only 8 inches. The short blade struggled with thick, wide sourdough loaves. It was also hard to control; the blade wandered during cuts, making it difficult to produce straight, clean slices. Both bread and tomatoes eventually yielded, but the process felt imprecise compared to most knives we tested. We struggled to make clean cuts with Zwilling’s entry-level Gourmet series. While it sliced tomatoes just fine, its teeth often caught on crusty sourdough loaves, interrupting the sawing motion and requiring more force to power through. During testing, its handle scales felt clunky, making the knife awkward to hold and even more awkward to wield, and it failed to perform as well as our two budget picks—both of which are significantly less expensive. Zwilling’s double-serrated knife is a good slicer, and its double-serrated edge is similar to the Wüsthof model we recommend. It performed well in testing, yielding thinly sliced tomatoes and perfectly straight slices of bread, but ultimately, this knife’s overall weight and high price tag kept it from being a winner. A bit heavier than much of the competition, Zwilling’s bread knife was trickier to wield comfortably, and its longer handle made it hard to find a good balance point. Offset knives are awkward to cut with because they remove the leverage you can create with the handle. While this knife from Winco slices tomatoes nicely, it struggles with crustier bread and dulls more quickly than other serrated knives we tested. It does have a bargain price tag though, so there’s that. Serrated knives feature dozens of individually sharpened teeth, meaning that, if you do want to sharpen your bread knife, you need to sharpen dozens of edges instead of the single edge most kitchen knives have. While this process can be tricky and is generally best left to professionals, you can pick up a serrated knife sharpener that lets you add more bite to your blade. These sharpeners work best with pointy serrations that create neat half-circle teeth—simply run the diamond-coated rod in the interior of each curve until they’re sharper than they were before. The only issue? The rod is shaped to work best with pointy serrations, so rounded scalloped edges won’t easily sharpen with a tool like this. Also, even the finest diamond surface is still rougher than ceramic—you can sharpen each pointy tooth on a bread knife with this thing, but it won’t be as highly polished and smooth as a professionally sharpened bread knife. Overall, I recommend these tools for budget-tier bread knives that you want to breathe some life into. Since bread knives don’t smack against hard cutting boards the same way as chef’s knives do, they also don’t dull as quickly. And if you have a high-end bread knife made from harder steel, it’s likely your knife will hold an edge for a long time without any intervention from you. Fill out the rest of your knife block - The best chef’s knives to serve as your daily driver - A nakiri knife is a blade you didn’t know you needed - How much do you need to pay for a good knife anyway? Get to know the experts Jesse Raub: I’ve been a professional kitchen product tester since 2021, where I tested nearly everything: espresso machines, wooden spoons, bread proofing baskets, pizza stones, garlic presses, and more. My fascination with kitchen knives began in 2003 when the chef at the kitchen where I worked let me use his personal Wüsthof knives during prep work one day. Over the last two years, I’ve tested over 70 different knives for Bon Appétit and written about the best knife sharpeners and how to best sharpen your knives at home. If you’re ever on the phone with me and hear a light scraping noise in the background, just know that I’m likely touching up my kitchen knives on a whetstone and testing their sharpness by slicing sheets of paper. Additional reporting and testing by Alaina Chou and Jamie Thilman.

item.title: I've Tested 41 Rice Cookers and Swear By These 4 (2026)
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 2.04
In college, I was introduced to the world of rice cookers when my roommate bought one for our house. I didn't fully realize how spoiled I'd been until we graduated and she moved across the country, taking her rice cooker with her. I was left to make do with the finicky stovetop method that never turned out quite right. In the years since, I've never been without one. Having consistently fluffy, well-cooked rice means I can turn my attention to the other components of the meal, and that convenience is well worth the price tag and the extra storage space a rice cooker comes with. Besides, there's nothing as humbling as cooking a big pot of rice for company only to find it's turned into a pile of mush. Our top picks - Best rice cooker for most people: Hamilton Beach 7-Cup Digital Programmable Rice Cooker - The one that makes the best rice: Zojirushi 5.5-Cup Induction Rice Cooker (NP-HCC10) - Best small rice cooker (that's also PFAS-free): GreenPan Advanced 4-Cup Rice Cooker - A great stainless steel rice cooker: Tatung Electric 6-Cup Rice Cooker and Steamer The best rice cookers are like a kitchen cheat code, a helping hand that ensures at least one part of your meal goes off without a hitch. But they vary a lot in performance. I've tested 41 rice cookers and cooked over 120 cups of rice (and that's just in the Test Kitchen), so I'm here to give you the lowdown and help you choose the right one for your lifestyle, budget, and household size. I believe the best rice cooker for your money is the Hamilton Beach 7-Cup Digital Programmable Rice Cooker. It's the right size for most people (making up to 14 cups of cooked rice), and at $70 it's a great price. But I also have picks for PFAS-free options, small cookers for tiny spaces, and the Zojirushi NP-HCC10 that makes the absolute best rice, as long as you're willing to pay for it. We think it's worth it. New in this update: I tested the GreenPan Advanced 8-Cup (Cooked) Rice Cooker and found it to be a good option for those looking for a small rice cooker with a ceramic, PFAS-free nonstick inner pot. I also tested the new KitchenAid Compact Grain and Rice Cooker, but didn't think its performance merited its price tag. Best rice cooker for most people: Hamilton Beach Digital Programmable Rice Cooker Pros and cons Pros: - Consistently good rice - Affordable - Handy features Cons: - Rice can get scorched on the bottom - Brown rice may be too al dente for some Specs Capacity: 7 cups (uncooked rice) Dimensions: (W x D x H) 10.75" x 10.75" x 11" Weight: 4.8 lb. Warranty: One-year limited warranty Features: Delay cook, automatic keep-warm function Menu settings: white rice, quick rice, whole grain, hot cereals, steam cook, heat/simmer You don’t need to spend hundreds of dollars to make great rice. The Hamilton Beach Digital Programmable Rice Cooker has consistently impressed me throughout years of testing, and at under $70, I think it’s the best option for most home cooks. What I love: The Hamilton Beach ranked right behind the Zojirushi (our splurge pick below) in a side-by-side blind tasting of white rice. It excelled in the brown rice test, producing individual and intact grains that had a satisfying amount of bite to them (though if you prefer your brown rice on the softer side, I'd recommend adding a bit more water than the recommended amount). It also fared well with long-grain basmati, producing a pot of fluffy rice on par with (if not better than) some of the more expensive cookers I tested. It cooked each pot of rice significantly faster than the Zojirushi, too: 35 minutes for a pot of white rice as opposed to the Zojirushi’s 50, and an hour for brown rice as opposed to 90 minutes. But what I really loved about the Hamilton Beach is that despite its low price tag, it doesn't sacrifice some of the helpful features the more high-end cookers tend to have. Besides a standard Keep Warm function, there are also six presets to choose from (white rice, quick rice, whole grain, heat/simmer, steam cook, and hot cereals), a handy delayed start feature (great if you want to prep a pot of rice before work and have it ready by the time you get home in the evening), a cook time countdown, and an audible beep when the rice is done cooking—all things most other options at this price point lack. Its 7-cup (uncooked) capacity is also larger than that of many of the other rice cookers I tested, but the machine's footprint is comparably compact. It's also technically a multi-cooker thanks to the heat/simmer and steam cook settings, though I was primarily interested in its rice-making capabilities for this review and will not vouch for those other functions here. I named the Hamilton Beach our budget pick two years ago, but after continuing to test it against the previous overall winner and countless other new-to-me models over the past couple of years while watching the price of the Zojirushi climb closer to—and oftentimes above—$400, I can confidently say that it’s the best choice for most home cooks for its balance of performance, features, and affordability. What I'd leave: While I found the Hamilton Beach to be well-made for a $70-ish machine, it didn’t feel quite as sturdy as the higher-end models we tested. I also didn’t love the design of the lid: It requires you to press and hold a button while manually opening it, and it opens sideways rather than front to back. The inner pot is also relatively thin, which contributed to a scorched layer of rice at the bottom in some of my tests—something that wasn’t a deal-breaker for me in the end but is worth noting. And, unlike many other models we tested, there is no differentiation in the recommended amount of water for different types of rice. I didn’t find that this negatively impacted the resulting rice, though the brown rice, which had a nice bite to it, could be a tad al dente for some with the recommended amount of water. The one that makes the best rice: Zojirushi 5.5-Cup Induction Rice Cooker (NP-HCC10) Pros and cons Pros: - Consistent results - Wide range of capabilities Cons: - Expensive - Bulky cord is not retractable Specs Capacity: 5.5 cups (uncooked rice) Dimensions: (W x D x H) 10" x 14" x 8" Weight: 9 lb. Warranty: One-year limited warranty Features: Micom technology, induction heating, delay cook, automatic keep warm function Menu settings: white rice (regular, softer or harder), jasmine rice, mixed rice, sushi rice, porridge/congee, sweet rice, brown rice, GABA brown rice and quick-cooking, rice paddle and measuring cup, nonstick pot. Zojirushi is to rice cookers what Vitamix is to blenders, and KitchenAid is to stand mixers. That is to say, it's the brand everyone knows to buy if you want the best. We've tested seven of Zojirushi's 19 models, and I've been most impressed by the NP-HCC10, which has won our blind taste tests every time. If you're serious about your rice and willing to invest in a perfectly fluffy pot, this is the model for you. What I love: BA staffers have crowned this machine the winner time and time again in blind taste tests, noting the way it produced grains that were not too soft, not too hard, and never mushy. In my own testing, it turned out evenly cooked, perfectly fluffy rice every time. That comes down to two technologies working together. Micom (short for microcomputerized) technology, found in many of Zojirushi's cookers, uses built-in sensors that adjust temperature and cook time according to real-time feedback, acting as a safeguard against imprecise water-to-rice ratios. Induction heating, more specific to this tier of Zojirushis, lets the cooker maintain a precise temperature and conduct heat evenly across the whole pot, rather than from the bottom only, as non-induction cookers do. Rice quality was my number one criterion in evaluating these cookers, but I also gave points for design and features. The NP-HCC10 has a 5.5-cup (uncooked) capacity, enough to feed six people. Its nonstick pot is a breeze to clean, and the interior is clearly marked in white with the water levels for various types of rice. I loved that this model counts down the total cook time, a surprising rarity among the rice cookers I've tested, though the Hamilton Beach does it too. Its extended Keep Warm setting, on top of the standard automatic one, prevents rice from yellowing or drying out when it's left to sit. A delayed start setting lets you set your rice to be done cooking at a certain time. And nine programmed settings cover several types of rice, including jasmine, brown, and sushi (the White Rice setting on a Zojirushi refers to short-grain white rice). For other grains like quinoa or oats, Zojirushi has a guide here. What I’d leave: The main downside to the NP-HCC10, and the reason it's no longer my top pick, is the price. This model has gotten steadily more expensive over the years and now sits around $400, which makes it a definite investment piece. Still, our testers could tell the difference in rice quality during every blind tasting, so if rice is something you care about, that's what you're paying for. Zojirushi also tends to fall short on brown rice across the board. I found the brown rice this model produced to be a touch soft for my liking, though using a bit less water than the recommended amount fixes it. There's also no retractable cord, which makes storage more of a hassle. Another thing to know if you’re new to the world of precision rice cookers, is that it takes a very long time to make a pot of rice. Depending on the volume, white rice can take up to an hour and brown rice up to two. That's not a shortcoming. It's part of the reason they work so well. Get in the habit of starting the cooker before you begin the rest of your cooking and you won't notice. On weeknights when you're tight on time, the timer function guarantees your rice will be done when you need it. For more information about Zojirushi’s line of rice cookers, read our guide. Instagram content The best small rice cooker: GreenPan Advanced 8-Cup Rice Cooker Pros and cons Pros: - Easy to use - Decent rice - PFAS-free ceramic nonstick inner pot Cons: - White rice was a touch unevenly cooked - Brown rice may be too al dente for some Specs Capacity: 4 cups (uncooked rice) Dimensions: (W x D x H) 9.8" x 7.5" x 8.7" Weight: 5.2 lb. Warranty: Lifetime limited warranty Features: Delay cook, automatic keep-warm function Menu settings: white rice, quick rice, brown rice This sleek little rice cooker makes a good pot of rice and takes up less counter space than the other models on this list—plus it's got a PFAS-free ceramic nonstick-coated inner pot that makes cleanup a breeze. What I loved: This new rice cooker from GreenPan is lightweight, relatively compact, and quite sleek, with a straightforward interface that’s intuitive to use. It made serviceable white and basmati rice in testing and excelled in the brown rice test, producing extremely individualized grains with a satisfying amount of bite, similar in texture to the batch made in the Hamilton Beach. While the GreenPan doesn’t offer a ton of presets, it’s got everything you need if your main use case for it is cooking rice: dedicated white and brown rice settings, a Quick Cook setting, an automatic Keep Warm function, and a Delay Timer. The ceramic nonstick-coated inner pot cleaned up easily with a sponge during testing, but it’s also dishwasher-safe. What I’d leave: While the GreenPan made acceptable rice, it wasn’t perfect—the white rice was a bit unevenly cooked according to some blind taste testers, and the brown rice was too firm for some tasters’ preferences (though others disagreed). Unlike the Hamilton Beach and the Zojirushi, the GreenPan is limited when it comes to settings. I also wish it had a carrying handle, though it’s so lightweight that it’s relatively easy to move around anyway. The best PFAS-free rice cooker: Tatung Electric Rice Cooker and Steamer Pros and cons Pros: - PFAS-free - Makes great rice Cons: - Stainless-steel pot is hard to clean - Lid gets very hot - Lid rattles around when rice is cooking - Pricey given lack of features Specs Capacity: 6 cups (uncooked rice) Dimensions: (W x D x H) 12" x 9.8" x 9.8" Weight: 7.1 lb. Warranty: One-year limited warranty Features: Automatic keep warm function Menu settings: None Tatung has been a leading manufacturer of rice cookers and steamers in Taiwan for over 60 years. With its straightforward on/off switch and cook/warm lever, the company's signature rice cooker looks like some of the simpler Zojirushi models, but it features a unique inner and outer pot system that steams the rice as it cooks. What I loved: In my testing, the Tatung produced fluffy pots of rice that earned praise from blind taste testers. The white rice had a nice amount of bite to it and a pleasant, slightly sticky texture. The brown rice was a good middle ground, al dente but not as dry as the rice from the Hamilton Beach.
