And the basmati was fluffy, the delicate grains all relatively intact. One major plus? Each pot of rice was done in about half the amount of time as the Zojirushi NP-HCC10. The Tatung is all stainless steel, with an inner pot that fits inside the appliance like a nesting doll. That nesting design is what makes it work differently from most rice cookers. Rice and water go into the inner pot as usual, then you add more water to the outer pot, which heats up and steams the rice from the outside in. The Tatung features an all-stainless-steel construction, with an inner pot that fits inside the appliance like a nesting doll. To make a pot of rice, you'll add rice and water to the inner pot as per usual, and then add more water to the outer pot before covering with the lid and setting to cook. What I'd leave: Because it's made of stainless steel, the Tatung can get quite hot while cooking—especially the lid, which I burned my hands on a few times during testing. The lightweight lid and addition of water surrounding the inner pot also meant that this model rattled quite a bit as it cooked, and water occasionally bubbled up over the edge when making large batches of rice. The stainless-steel inner pot is, as expected, much harder to clean than a nonstick pot, and required some soaking and serious elbow grease in order to scrub clean. The other thing to note is that at $210 at the time of writing, this is not a cheap appliance, but it doesn't come with the kinds of features (like delayed start or multiple settings) you might expect from a rice cooker at this price. How we tested rice cookers Many rice cookers these days try to position themselves as do-it-all appliances (the Instant Pot-ification of the category), but we were here to see how each model performed at one all-important function: making rice. We’ve spent years testing over two dozen models and have held numerous taste tests among Bon Appétit staffers, abiding by the following testing process each time: Each rice cooker was first put through a white rice test. We used Nishiki Japanese medium-grain white rice, cooking two cups worth in each full-size cooker and one cup in the mini cookers (models with 4-cup uncooked capacities or less). Models that performed adequately in this test then moved onto short-grain brown rice, and finally to long-grain basmati rice. Our tasters were on the lookout for fluffy pots of rice made up of nicely individualized grains that had just enough bite and didn’t mush together. Cookers that fared well in our initial testing were then given to several different editors to use in their own homes. Those editors have and will continue to provide feedback on how these models perform in the long-term. What we looked for in the best rice cookers Let’s start with the obvious: How was the rice? While we evaluated rice cookers based on several factors, no amount of fancy features or high-tech claims mattered if the resulting rice wasn’t up to par. Our testers and tasters scored models on the quality of all three kinds of rice, and they were looking for evenly cooked grains that were neither over- nor undercooked, not too wet and not too dry, and fluffy rather than gummy or mushy. How’s the user experience? The whole point of having a rice cooker is to make your life easier, so we were looking for rice cookers that were straightforward and intuitive to use. We valued clear instructions on how to wash and measure rice, guidance on water ratios and selecting settings, and automatic Keep Warm functionality. A timer function was an added bonus that we appreciated in some of the more advanced models. We also looked at the accessories each model came with. Every rice cooker comes with a few necessities, which usually include a rice paddle and a measuring cup. Every model we tested, save for the Cuckoos, came with a built-in paddle holder, and many came with an additional steamer basket insert. While we didn’t test out steamer or synchro cooking functionality in our initial tests, our long-term testers were encouraged to report back on how such functions performed. How easy is it to clean? Nearly every model we tested had a nonstick coating on its inner pot, and the few that didn’t were a bit of a nightmare to clean. We wanted to be able to cleanly scoop rice out of the cooker without leaving any residue behind, and looked for pots that were easily washed with a soapy sponge and some warm water (if you are really trying to avoid PFAS coatings, note that most rice cooker pots are not dishwasher-safe). Some models have removable, cleanable lids, something we appreciated and noted where applicable. How easy is it to store? We took note of the footprint of each model, but found that most full-size options were around the same size. Is it worth the price? The rice cookers we tested ranged in price from $25–$750. While we think a great model like our winning Zojirushi is worth its $300 price tag, we awarded points to models like the Hamilton Beach that provide a great value, performing better than their cost might suggest. Other rice cookers we tested and liked Cuckoo 6-Cup Rice Cooker and Warmer CR-0655F This model from Cuckoo is a great rice cooker for the price. Tasters ranked the rice it made nearly as highly as our winning Zojirushi, which is a feat considering the Cuckoo is a third of the price. It’s also much faster than the Zojirushi, finishing in 15 minutes less, and a bit larger, with a 6-cup capacity. Why didn’t it take the top spot, you might ask? A couple of reasons: The lid jerks open with so much force that it can knock the whole appliance off the counter (as well as any objects surrounding it), and it doesn’t have a countdown for the total cook time. Tiger Micom Rice Cooker JBV-A10U This former best budget pick is made by Tiger, another Japan-based company with over 100 years of history making many of the same kinds of products Zojirushi does. It’s one of the most affordable Micom models out there, ringing in at $99 (at the time of writing). And while it doesn’t have all the fancy bells and whistles of our winning Zojirushi, it still makes consistently great rice. In our blind taste tests, staffers picked the Tiger over several more expensive models. We also loved this cooker’s generous 5.5-cup (uncooked) capacity, the fact that it’s easy to clean, and that it offers something a step above a simple one-button, non-Micom model. This is still a dead-simple, no-frills rice cooker though. You get what you pay for: There is no alarm, timer, or digital interface, and fewer settings than you’ll get on something like our winning Zojirushi or some of the fancier Tiger models. In our most recent round of testing, the Hamilton Beach model edged it out by producing slightly better rice and having more helpful features, all while ringing in at practically half the price. Zojirushi Pressure Induction Heating Rice Cooker & Warmer NW-JEC10 The Zojirushi NW-JEC10 is like if Apple made a rice cooker: It’s sleek, high-tech, and expensive. It’s the most expensive home rice cooker in the brand’s lineup, as a matter of fact. Of its host of features, the one that sets it apart from the other high-end models Zojirushi offers is the My Rice setting, which uses artificial intelligence to learn your preferred rice texture based on inputs you give it after cooking through each batch of rice. Commerce writer Wilder Davies has been testing the NW-JEC10 for over a year and has come around to the view that the My Rice functionality is no gimmick. He found that his batches of rice evolved for the better over time as he gave the machine more feedback (specifically, it will ask you to input whether the stickiness and firmness of the previous batch you made was “not enough,” “okay,” or “too much”). What’s more, this rice won its initial taste test with our staffers. But the difference in rice quality was not enough to merit the $750 price tag, hence our recommendation for the average rice eater remains the (nearly $450 cheaper) NP-HCC10. Zojirushi Micom Rice Cooker & Warmer NS-TSC10A This model is similar to our top pick in design and functionality, but rings in at about $100 cheaper. The main reason for that is likely that it lacks the induction heating capabilities of the NP-HCC10. While it produced good rice across all of our tests, it never quite achieved as perfectly textured results as our winner. Our testers found the rice to be a bit too soft across the board (though this could be remedied by adding a bit less water than the recommended amount). We did, however, appreciate the retractable cord—plus the silver-and-light gray design is rather chic. Toshiba TRCS01 Rice Cooker This model performed exceedingly well in our initial blind taste test, producing fluffy grains that won over our testers. We also loved its suite of programmable features, the way it gave us a timer countdown from the start of cooking as well as the option to delay cooking until later, its audible alarm, and its use of fuzzy logic to make minute temperature and time adjustments according to real time sensor feedback (something more typically seen in higher priced models). We found it easy to use, with helpful presets for a range of rice types and a Quick Rice function that worked well for grains like quinoa, farro, and polenta, and an included steamer basket. But our long-term testing of this product revealed a major flaw: We found that the timer would repeatedly freeze (sometimes for 20 minutes or longer) while the machine continued to cook. This issue was particularly prevalent when using the Mixed Rice and Quick Rice settings. It’s worth noting that the timer function on a rice cooker is typically more of an approximation, and it’s not uncommon for it to change or stall momentarily—but not to this extent. It resulted in overcooked or even burned rice. It was not a consistent problem, but a problem nonetheless, and a big enough one to give us pause about recommending this model as our top budget pick. Zojirushi Neuro Fuzzy Rice Cooker and Warmer NS-ZCC10 The Zojirushi NS-ZCC10 didn’t make as nicely textured and fluffy rice as our winning pick. It does include many of the features we loved in our winner at a lower price point, like the intuitive interface, sturdy inner pot, Keep Warm function, and array of presets. It also had some additional features our winner lacked, like a retractable cord and handles on the sides of the pot that allow you to lift it out from the cooker while it’s still hot. However, at over $240 at the time of publication, we just don’t think this cooker produced rice that merited the still-high price tag. Toshiba TRSH01 Low-Carb Digital Programmable Multi-Functional Rice Cooker This sleek model from Toshiba has an intuitive digital interface and eight different settings, including one for “low-carb” rice that uses a colander-like insert to drain away starchy water as the rice cooks (which Toshiba claims “can remove unhealthy digestive starch by up to 37% and increase healthy resistant starch by up to 34%”). We aren't going to vouch for the low-carb claims, but we can tell you that this model fared relatively well in testing. We found the white and jasmine rice to be a tad soft for our liking, which ultimately kept it out of our top picks (though this could be remedied by using a touch less water than recommended). It excelled in the brown rice test, producing rice with just enough bite—the Goldilocks of brown rice, as one of our taste testers put it. If you’re a brown rice fiend, this may be the model for you. Tiger 5.5-Cup IH Rice Cooker JKT-D10U This model performed similarly to our winning pick from Zojirushi, scoring just a few points below it in our taste test. It has a 5.5-cup uncooked capacity, a sturdy nonstick inner pot with handles for safely lifting it out of the machine while hot, and all the other features we’d expect from a rice cooker with its price tag: A bevy of settings (12 to be exact), automatic logic technology, an audible chime, and an automatic Keep Warm functionality. It produced beautifully cooked white rice that was nearly on par with the Zojirushi NP-HCC10, but fell a bit short in the brown rice test, where the grains were on the mushier side. All in all, it’s a great rice cooker that any home cook would be happy to use, but for just a few dollars more, we’d recommend you go with our winning pick from Zojirushi. Zojirushi Induction Heating Rice Cooker & Warmer NW-QAC10 This model is part of Zojirushi’s newest line of rice cookers, and it looks similar to the pricey NW-JEC10 model we mentioned above. It is similar to our winner in terms of functionality, but it couldn’t match up to the NP-HCC10’s results in the white rice test. Our tasters found the rice this model produced to be soft and less intact than they’d have liked. That said, the NW-QAC10 features quinoa and oatmeal settings, which makes it a good rice cooker for anyone with a particular affinity for either of those grains. Zojirushi Pressure Induction Heating Rice Cooker & Warmer NP-NWC10 With Micom technology and induction heating, this model is very similar to our top pick. If you’re wondering why it’s over $100 more expensive, that’s because, unlike our winner, it uses pressure when cooking rice. While intended to produce a more tender grain, our testers preferred the rice the NP-HCC10 churned out, deeming the NP-NWC10’s rice a bit soft for their liking when cooked on a standard setting. It’s worth noting that this model allows you to adjust texture and consistency with relative ease, which worked well in our long-term testing, but we cannot recommend you shell out an additional $100-plus for it based on its overall performance. Rice cookers we don’t recommend Whether because of how they fared in our taste test or because of their design, these are the rice cookers that we don't recommend buying. - Aroma Digital Rice Cooker ARC-914SBD: This affordable 4-cup model performed well in the white rice test, but failed with brown rice. It leaked starchy water onto the lid that would have spilled everywhere had we not mopped it up. The rice itself was wet and oh-so-mushy. - Aroma 2.5-Cup Rice Cooker ARC-753SG: This model from Aroma has a stainless-steel inner pot that we found difficult to clean. It made white rice in near record time (20 minutes or so), but it tended to be a bit underdone. The same can be said for the brown rice test—the rice was good, but certainly not great. This model also exhibited some leakage through the steam vent even when just cooking one cup of rice, which we imagine would only get worse if you filled it to capacity. - Beautiful by Drew Barrymore 14-Cup Rice and Grain Cooker: I’ve generally been impressed by Drew Barrymore’s line of appliances, but this rice cooker was disappointing. It produced mushy, gummy white rice and didn't make it past the first round of testing. - Cosori 5-Cup Rice Cooker: Standard settings on this model produced rice that was a bit undercooked, according to most of our testers. This machine does have a whopping 18 settings, including a range of different grains, so it could be a decent option for anyone who frequently cooks steel-cut oats, barley, farro, and the like. - Cuckoo 6-Cup Heating Pressure Rice Cooker CRP-P0609S: The rice this Cuckoo made was incredibly sticky. It also suffered some design flaws: the lid snaps open aggressively, the control panel is unintuitive, and there's no countdown timer. - Cuckoo 6-Cup Micom Rice Cooker CR-0675F: This model made great rice. However, unresponsive buttons, a confusing interface, and a poorly translated manual made it frustrating to use. So while this cooker checks the "Makes Great Rice" box, the same cannot be said for the "Is a Joy to Use" box. - Cuckoo 6-Cup HP Twin Pressure Rice Cooker CRP-ST0609F: Like the other Cuckoos, this model made decent rice. However, its control panel was irritatingly unresponsive. It also talks, and in a voice that can only be described as Barbie DreamHouse-core—which may be amusing to some, but aggravating to others. - Cuisinart 4-Cup Rice Cooker: This mini model didn't move past the white rice test–the rice it produced looked very wet and undercooked at the time it finished cooking and switched to the Keep Warm function, and it tasted too firm in the middle. - Dash Mini Rice Cooker: This one-button model has a lid that is too light to stay sealed, allowing steam and heat to escape during cooking. - Imusa GAU-00011 Electric Nonstick Rice Cooker: This is one of the cheapest rice cookers you can get these days. Was the rice edible? Totally. But we found the white rice to be undercooked, and the brown rice it made was sort of wet, as if not enough water had been cooked off. - Instant Pot Duo: The beloved Instant Pot Duo is a multi-cooker that claims to do it all—including make rice. It was one of the fastest models to do so, but the grains it produced were gummy and decidedly un-fluffable. - KitchenAid Rice and Grain Cooker: This model from KitchenAid has a unique design that comprises an integrated scale and attached water tank. It uses that scale and whichever of the 21 preset functions you've chosen to determine how much water to add, eliminating the need to futz around with measuring cups and ratios. While it's an interesting concept, we weren't impressed enough by this model's performance to recommend it. The first batch of white rice we made was painfully dry, though the second batch we made using the Softer setting was an improvement. The brown rice was serviceable, nicely textured if still a touch dry. We spent time in 2025 testing its other capabilities as well and found them hit or miss. You can check out our complete KitchenAid rice cooker review here. - KitchenAid Compact Rice and Grain Cooker: This new version of the KitchenAid model above eliminates the attached water tank for a more compact footprint. While it made decent rice, we found the workflow of pouring water into the inner pot while it was attached to its base (rather than filling it to a designated line at the sink) somewhat annoying, and ultimately weren't impressed enough by the quality of the rice to justify the somewhat steep price tag. - Nutribullet EveryGrain Cooker: This cooker has settings for specific grains like white rice, quinoa, and oats, plus other nice-to-have features like a Delay Start button and Steam option. While we can't comment on how this cooker performs with other grains, we can say that it did not fare well with rice. The white rice we made was wildly inconsistent, even within the same batch. - Our Place Rice Cooker: This rice cooker is cute as can be. It's intuitive to use and looks nice on a countertop—an attribute most rice cookers lack; however, the appliance is bulky and pricey considering the small, 3-cup uncooked capacity. After some long-term testing, we found that the rice cooked inconsistently, either too mushy one time or too dry another, despite the fuzzy logic, so ultimately we don't think it's worth the price tag. - Tiger Microcomputer Controlled Rice Cooker JAX-T10U: Despite its promising features, this model produced white rice that was a bit wet and soft for our testers' liking. The brown rice had a nice bite to it, but its exterior was a tad mushy. We found that the less expensive Tiger JBV-A10U outperformed this pricier model. - Tiger 10-Cup (Uncooked) Rice Cooker JNP-1800-FL: This is a straightforward, single-button rice cooker that makes enough rice for the whole family (and a large one at that). Unfortunately, the rice it produced proved some of the softest of the bunch. With few features and lackluster performance, it's hard to recommend. - Toshiba TRCS02: This 3-cup model from Toshiba fared relatively well in the white rice portion of our taste test, but produced overcooked brown rice that kept it from earning a top spot. - Yum Asia Panda: This cooker is a bestseller on Amazon, so we wanted to see what all the fuss was about. It remained a promising contender through the first round of taste testing, in which it produced excellent white rice. However, the brown rice this model made was overcooked and mushy. But if brown rice isn't your thing, you might still consider this model. - Zojirushi 3-Cup Rice Cooker: This dead-simple mini model from Zojirushi uses a single button to start cooking. Unlike some competitors we tested, it didn't leak starchy water, but it produced inconsistent results. It also lacks a Keep Warm function, and we found it didn't handle brown rice well. - Zojirushi Micom Rice Cooker & Warmer NS-LGC05: This 3-cup version of one of Zojirushi's micom models ultimately failed to impress us—especially compared to the other mini models we tested, which performed much better even despite being lower tech. The white rice made in this model was quite sticky and mushy, as was the brown rice. Because of that micom technology, it also took longer to cook than the other small models. - Zojirushi NL-EAC10: This newest model in Zojirushi's lineup is cute, but it lacked the helpful carrying handle that most other Zojirushis have, took longer to cook rice than our winner, and produced white rice that was overcooked and a touch mushy. FAQs Should you rinse your rice? To make a long story short, you probably should. Washing rice strips the grains of their starchy coating and keeps them from sticking together and becoming a gummy mess when cooked—something you want for most types of rice (exceptions to this rule include arborio rice used for risotto, where the excess starch is necessary to create that creamy texture). In testing these cookers, we followed each model’s instructions with regard to rinsing rice. In general, you’ll want to swish your measured rice around in some water, pour that water out, and repeat until the water runs clear. Do you need a rice cooker? What about stovetop rice? You don’t need a rice cooker, but there’s no denying that having one makes getting weeknight dinners on the table or cooking rice for a crowd infinitely easier. That said, making great stovetop rice is a skill worth mastering—and the food editors in our test kitchen can help you with that. How much rice can a rice cooker make? You’ll notice that many of the rice cookers on this list have cup capacities in their names. That number refers to the amount of uncooked rice a given cooker can make at a time, measured in 180-ml rice cooker cups rather than standard US cups (which are 237 ml). Rice approximately doubles in size after cooking, so a 5.5-cup rice cooker like the winning Zojirushi will make a maximum of about 11 cups of cooked rice (which is enough to feed around 5–6 people). If you’re cooking for just yourself, note that the minimum amount of rice most rice cookers can make is one rice cooker cup’s worth. This will likely be more rice that you need for a single serving meal, but we’d advise against trying to make less rice than the cooker is designed for. And besides, the leftovers will make for excellent fried rice the next day.

item.title: TSA’s New PreCheck Perk Allows Non-Ticketed Visitors to Accompany Friends and Family at the Gate
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 5.44
TSA’s newest PreCheck perk is intended for people who aren’t flying at all. Gateside by TSA PreCheck, which began rolling out this month at 13 US airports, allows eligible non-ticketed visitors to pass through security after receiving advance approval. That means they can accompany someone to a departure gate, meet an arriving traveler airside, visit a friend or relative during a layover, or access the restaurants and shops beyond the checkpoint. The program marks an expansion of an idea that several individual airports have experimented with in recent years: allowing some people without boarding passes back into the secure side of the terminal. But Gateside also raises a more practical question—who actually wants to go through airport security on their own volition when they don’t have a flight to catch? Jennifer Yellin, managing editor at travel rewards platform Points Path, expects the answer to be mostly people helping or meeting someone they know. “I think families will be the ones to use this the most,” Yellin says “I foresee this being the most beneficial for parents accompanying their child for an outbound flight as well as welcoming home family members.” She also sees potential for older travelers, nervous or infrequent fliers, and people navigating unfamiliar airports with the help of a friend or relative. In those cases, Gateside could make it possible for someone to stay alongside a traveler all the way to the gate, rather than saying goodbye before security. “If you have a child, parent, spouse, or even friend who is a nervous flier, being able to walk them to their gate and see them off could help put their nerves to ease,” Yellin says. “It can also be useful to help the same younger or older family member navigate an airport, which might otherwise be challenging. For some travelers, having someone there with you to the very end can put them at ease.” That doesn’t mean Gateside will replace existing assistance available to travelers who need it. Airlines already issue escort or gate passes in certain circumstances, including unaccompanied minors, and airports and airlines offer assistance for travelers with disabilities. Gateside is broader: A visitor doesn’t need to be escorting someone who qualifies for one of those services. Instead, access is based primarily on the visitor’s eligibility for TSA PreCheck screening and approval for Gateside. How Gateside by TSA PreCheck works Gateside is currently being offered as an “operational assessment” at 13 airports, including major hubs such as Dallas Fort Worth International Airport, Los Angeles International Airport, and Salt Lake City International Airport. To use it, visitors need to be eligible for TSA PreCheck screening and have a Known Traveler Number. That includes TSA PreCheck members as well as eligible members of trusted traveler programs such as Global Entry, NEXUS, and SENTRI. The pass itself is free, but visitors have to apply online one to three days before their intended airport visit and select the participating airport they plan to enter. Those who are approved bring an acceptable form of identification to the airport and go through a TSA PreCheck checkpoint; they are still subject to normal security screening and restrictions. An approval is valid for the designated calendar day and allows the visitor to leave and re-enter the secure area that day. Gateside isn’t the first way for a non-ticketed visitor to get beyond airport security. Airports including Seattle, New Orleans, Orlando, Tampa, Palm Springs, and Tulsa already operate their own visitor-pass programs, each with its own rules. Detroit and San Diego have existing visitor programs in addition to being among the first Gateside airports. The distinction with the new TSA program is that Gateside is tied to PreCheck eligibility and gives approved visitors access through the PreCheck screening lane. For the average traveler, Yellin says, the program is still likely to remain fairly niche. “While it's a meaningful change, it's only beneficial for a small group of travelers,” she says. “For the average traveler, it won't change the airport experience since this is limited to a very small subset of airports and advance approval is required.” Seeing off a family member is perhaps the most obvious use for the program, but Gateside could also make it easier to spend time with someone who isn’t beginning or ending their trip in your city. “If you have a friend or family member traveling with a long layover in your home airport, meeting them during their connection is the perfect situation,” Yellin says. “This allows the traveler to stay near their gate without having to leave security.” Currently, meeting a connecting passenger generally requires the traveler to leave the secure area of the airport, then go through security again before continuing their trip. That may not be practical on a shorter connection, particularly at a large airport where getting between the gate and terminal exit can itself take time. With Gateside, the local visitor goes through security instead. Still, Yellin doesn’t expect non-ticketed visitors to start heading to airports simply because they now can. “The airport experience today is tiring for many and extremely different than what it once was,” she says. “Because of that, I do not believe too many people are going to choose to park their car and navigate their way through security, without actually traveling that day, unless they have a very real reason.” The program’s arrival also comes 25 years after the September 11 attacks transformed who could access US airport gate areas. Before 9/11, people without tickets could generally accompany passengers through security; afterward, access to the secure side of terminals became largely limited to ticketed passengers and those with specific authorization. However, Yellin doesn't believe Gateside is a signal that TSA is returning to the old airport model. “Now that it's been 25 years, TSA is experimenting to see how the overall experience can be better for travelers, while still keeping safety in mind,” she says. Airports offering Gateside by TSA PreCheck - Mesa Gateway Airport (AZA) in Arizona - John Glenn Columbus International Airport (CMH) in Ohio - Dallas Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) in Texas - Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport (DTW) in Michigan - Wichita Dwight D. Eisenhower National Airport (ICT) in Kansas - Indianapolis International Airport (IND) in Indiana - Harry Reid International Airport (LAS) in Nevada - Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) in California - Bill and Hillary Clinton National Airport (LIT) in Arkansas - Will Rogers International Airport (OKC) in Oklahoma - Eppley Airfield (OMA) in Nebraska - San Diego International Airport (SAN) in California - Salt Lake City International Airport (SLC) in Utah

item.title: A New Museum, Cruise Haute Couture, and Gorgeous Glassware: Here's What's Exciting Us in Travel Right Now
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 5.40
Whether you're on land or at sea, in a bar or in Bahrain, there are myriad reasons for design lovers to get excited about travel right now. In the September/October 2026 issue of Condé Nast Traveler, we went long on a number of these stories—how Como's enduring craft traditions help make it one of the planet's most luxurious destinations, why Fort Worth is the sartorial epicenter of the rise of ranchcore in fashion. But we also collected a few juicy morsels worth sharing in brief. There's a new museum in the Middle East to earmark if you're interested in the intersection of craft and history, and a French cruise line has launched a new itinerary that will bring haute couture to the high seas. Read on for all we think you should know. A gem of a new museum on Bahrain's pearling path “Inside an elegant home formerly owned by a wealthy merchant family in Bahrain's coastal city of Muharraq sits the two-year-old Siyadi Pearl Museum. The space is the latest addition to the Pearling Path, which connects important structures from the city's pearling history. Along its two miles are 17 significant sites; public squares shaded by flame trees; and a pedestrian bridge that reconnects Muharraq with its original shoreline, which has been mostly lost to development. Terrazzo lampposts topped by pearl-shaped light bulbs double as trail markers. Tales of wealth are told in the grand living quarters of merchants and traders; those of hardship in the display of the simple tools pearl divers relied on (nose clips, stone weights, leather finger covers) during arduous months aboard dhows at sea.” —Nicola Chilton High fashion comes to the high seas “In September 2027, French line Ponant will sail a commonly traveled route along Italy's coast with an entirely unique agenda: placing the country's fashion maisons at the center of the passenger experience. Sailing down the coast from Tuscany and then up to Venice, guests on board the intimate Le Boréal will experience five major haute labels. They will chat with a Brioni tailor about making the perfect alterations; observe a master craftsperson cut precious gemstones at iconic jeweler Pomellato; and explore two historic sites in Florence tied to Gucci via the Palazzo Gucci and the 15th-century Palazzo Settimanni, home to the Gucci archives. Think of this as high fashion on the high seas.” —Erin Florio Drinks wear designer around the globe “Striking, artisanal glassware that upstages the concoction it holds is the coolest thing in cocktail culture these days. Here, bars around the world and the gorgeously unique vessels you may just encounter while there.” —Michelle Tchea This article appeared in the September/October 2026 issue of Condé Nast Traveler. Subscribe to the magazine here.

item.title: Everyone Seems to Be Taking a “Fallcation” This Year—What Does That Mean for Travel
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 5.18
Fall was always my favorite time to travel. It’s when the crowds have loosened their grip on Paris, the weather is better in Italy, and the hotel rates are lower in Marrakech. But over the last few years, I’ve noticed more and more travelers at airports near and far in September, October, and November. Indicating demand, plane tickets haven’t been dipping in the same way that they used to when the leaves turned. Open any news app, and you’ll see the headlines shouting from the rooftops: We are in the era of the “fallcation.” “Savvy travelers are establishing autumn as the new peak season for global trips,” says John Clifford, a Condé Nast Traveler Top Travel Specialist and founder of International Travel Management. He attributes this to the fact that more people are traveling than ever in the summertime, leading to crowded destinations. On top of that, summers are only getting hotter. All this, Clifford says, leads to people looking to take their big annual vacation outside of the summer season. The data backs it up: According to Virtuoso, the global network of luxury travel agencies and advisors, bookings for fall travel this year have increased by 59% compared to last year; the network’s agents report a 77% increase in September sales, making it a peak month for travel. October and November sales are up 54% and 71%, respectively. Fall travel is increasing even to destinations in Asia, where the window between September and November is already the peak season. Catherine Heald, another CNT Top Travel Specialist and founder of Asia-focused Remote Lands, says her company has been seeing around 15% more fall bookings in the last few years. But nowhere is it more pronounced than in universally loved Italy, where September and October have become the height of the season, when it’s still “summer-like” in Southern Europe, says Gary Portuesi, a CNT Top Travel Specialist and a co-managing partner of Authentic Explorations. To Portuesi, fall in Italy now means November and December—and yes, they’re seeing a surge in bookings for those months too, when temperatures are cooler, crowds have dwindled, and hotel rates tend to drop. As he puts it, “It’s the new shoulder season.” To learn more about the rise of the fallcation, I tapped a host of Condé Nast Traveler Top Travel Specialists to weigh in: Who’s actually traveling in the fall? Where are people going? And will we eventually have to avoid traveling in the fall, too? In a few years, will we be craving “summercations”? Here’s what the experts had to say. What is leading to more “fallcations”? At this point, it’s conventional wisdom that September, October, and November are more comfortable times to travel because, in most destinations, you get more temperate weather and fewer crowds in the fall. “Autumn has outperformed summer for at least the past two years,” says Tom Barber of UK-based Original Travel. For Barber, September and October departures are up by 53% and 45%, respectively, compared to August departures. He explains, “People still want the classic summer destinations—Greece, Italy, Spain, Egypt, Morocco—but they increasingly want to experience them without the intense heat.” September is now one of the busiest months for travel company Red Savannah, says Camilla Davidson, its head of destination management for the UK, France, and Ireland. The relentless summer news cycle is also playing a part in this behavioral shift. “It’s all dominated by headlines around European wildfires, unlivable temperatures, endless lines on arrival at airports, overtourism, and elevated prices,” Davidson says. “Many savvy travelers are looking to shoulder seasons to avoid these pitfalls, with the fall seen as a more ‘reliable option’ than the spring.” On the other hand, Cari Gray of Gray & Co., which focuses on private active trips, says that fall has always been her clients’ preferred travel period over the summer season. “So many folks have well-established summer routines like going to their cabins and annual visits to favorite lodges,” Gray says. “They break free in the fall when kids are in school—both in grade school and college—and the weather is perfect for outdoor activities.” Who are the people actually taking “fallcations”? Travelers with kids in school are often tied to the academic calendar—back to school in the autumn, big vacation periods in the summer. So fall travel has historically been the domain of empty-nesters, young couples without dependents, parents bringing along adult children (or vice versa), friend groups, and solo adventurers. This has largely remained the case in our current era of the fallcation. “Couples and adults traveling without children have the most flexibility,” says Jonathan Alder of Jonathan’s Travels. But he notes that a good chunk of parents aren’t opposed to their kids missing class for the right family trip. “It really depends on the age. Pulling a child out of kindergarten for a week is very different from pulling an older child out during an important academic period,” Alder says. Rather than simply recreating a summer itinerary at a different time of year, fallcation travelers are looking for activities and experiences that are better suited to the autumn season, says Mark Bonte of France-based French Side Travel. Foodies in particular love to travel in September and October to catch various harvests, Bonte says: “Wine aficionados enjoy the mid-October fête des vendanges in Bordeaux’s Saint-Émilion. Champagne is another popular fall destination. Although the exact date varies annually, harvest typically begins in late summer and lasts several weeks.” More broadly speaking, Bonte says travelers who choose the fall tend to be keen on moving “more deeply” through a destination, “whether that means focusing on wine, gastronomy, culture, or a specific region rather than trying to see all of a country in one trip.” Are travelers swapping out summer for fall? The rise of the fallcation doesn’t necessarily spell the doom of the summercation. “Rather than give up the traditional summer vacation, travelers are adding a second vacation later in the year,” says Julie Durso, a private travel manager at Scott Dunn. “We’re seeing an increase in both summer and fall travel,” says Red Savannah’s managing director for villas Nick Westwood. The company’s villa bookings in June this year were up 24%, compared to the same month in 2025; July and August were up by 65%. Other travel advisors agree that summer travel is not going extinct, but have indeed noticed shifts in terms of where—and when—people are going. “There’s definitely some substitution happening,” says Barber of Original Travel. He observes that the UK market is increasingly staying closer to home during the summer, and their big international trips are instead happening in October or even the Easter season. Alder of Jonathan’s Travels says clients from the United States are saving places like Europe for later in the year: “Europe is fading as a summer destination for our clients, as it should be. When you have the flexibility, there’s little reason to fight the extreme heat and enormous summer crowds when you can experience many of the same destinations beautifully in September or October.” Authentic Explorations is seeing the same trend, says Portuesi; a wine tour in late October was sold out quickly, and past summer trips were more difficult to fill up with travelers who were largely staying in the US. Where are people going for “fallcations”? The short answer: People are going everywhere. Some fall trips, though, are certainly trending among the travel specialists I consulted. Going to Japan for the autumn is big right now, where the fall colors are just as spectacular as the cherry blossoms in spring. Of course Italy and Greece are big, especially for non-beach trips: the Peloponnese and Tuscany in the fall, Athens and Venice in winter. But for travelers insisting on jumping into the Mediterranean, October is still a good time to go. Overall the conventional wisdom holds: weather is better, crowds are fewer, and costs are more manageable outside of the summer season. Whether that pattern will hold as more people eye autumn remains to be seen. As for domestic travel, Clifford of International Travel Management says his clients are “focused on places where you can easily escape the crowds: the historic coastal estates of Newport, Rhode Island, the open spaces and private ranches of Big Sky, Montana, and the high-desert mountains of Santa Fe, New Mexico.” How is the travel industry meeting the moment? Now that September is squarely part of the summer travel schedule, “shoulder season” and “off season” are being pushed later into the year. This means some seasonal destinations and hotels are staying open longer. Gray of Gray & Co. name checks popular destinations that used to shutter at summer’s close, like the Amalfi Coast in Italy, where hotels like Palazzo Avino in Ravello welcome guests until late October, and Le Sirenuse in Positano until November 1. Gray says that the task of hoteliers and restaurateurs extending their seasons is to keep up the level of service and energy as one would expect in the summertime. The cruise industry, too, is investing in fall and winter travel. Cruise lines like Regent Seven Seas and Explora Journeys are operating their first full winter seasons in the Mediterranean this year. Cruises expert Mary Jean Tully of Tully Luxury Travel sailed with Explora in November last year and says, “It was fabulous. No crowds. The weather was fresh but not cold. It’s a great time to go.” Additionally, airlines are making moves for the fall and even the winter, extending seasonal flight routes beyond their usual September cutoffs. For example, United Airlines will operate its thrice-weekly flight between Newark International Airport and Palermo, Sicily, until mid-December this year. Delta is operating flights from New York-JFK to Catania in Sicily and Porto in Portugal through January 2027. What are the potential repercussions of the “fallcation”? The fallcation began as an escape from the heat and crowds of high summer, but its longer-term effect may be to redraw the entire travel calendar. Barber expects that seasons will shift: “September and October will stop being the ‘shoulder season.’ In the most popular parts of southern Europe, they’ll increasingly become part of the main season, with higher hotel rates, tighter availability, and fuller flights. Destinations will stay open longer. Hotels, beach clubs, restaurants, guides, and seasonal flight routes have a commercial reason to extend their seasons.” We’re already seeing this happening, though the adjustments currently seem like temporary novelties. There’s a world in which fall becomes a high-traffic season too. “That could be hugely positive for local employment, making tourism less dependent on an eight-week summer bonanza,” Barber says. “If fall travel continues to grow, certain destinations could eventually face some of the same pressures we're seeing in peak summer,” says Bonte of French Side Travel. He makes the case for cultivating travel programming that does not simply repeat its old mistakes—“reshuffling by destination” rather than the creation of “a single new peak season.” Regions could start reverting to the seasons that actually suit them, Bonte says, rather than times of year into which they’ve been pigeonholed. As opposed to a summer spree, the French Riviera could become hot for winter again, as it historically had been; the Alps could pick up as a summer destination. “Each region in France has a season where it truly shines, and the opportunity is to match travelers to that, rather than pushing everyone into the same few months,” he says. It’s work that falls on travel specialists to accomplish as well, to spread the travel traffic around—to bring it not only to the destinations that need it, but the parts of the calendar that do too. Is there still an off season in the age of the “fallcation”? Every part of the calendar is largely claimed by a good reason—and a good place—to travel. Put another way, one place’s “off season” may be another destination’s perfect window. Portuesi says the dead-of-winter months of January and February are still considered the low season in Europe, save for ski destinations like the Dolomites. Meanwhile, that’s one of the best times to go to the Caribbean because hurricane season is usually over by Christmas. For other places, what we might traditionally assume to be peak season is actually low season. Take Asia, for example. “Rainy periods in Southeast Asia and Japan also generally coincide with the summer months,” says Heald of Remote Lands. “But even then, some travelers will visit because it is the only time their schedules allow. In Japan, summers can be extremely hot and humid, yet travelers continue to go.” “I really don't think there is such a thing as an off-season anymore,” Alder says, adamant that the idea of everyone going to the same place at the same time of year is not sustainable or desirable. Besides, there’s a whole world out there and an entire calendar to consider. As Alder puts it, “There's almost always a great place to go, and increasingly we're helping clients identify when a destination is at its best for them, rather than simply when it's traditionally considered peak season.”

item.title: Where Was 'Practical Magic 2' Filmed? Coastal Massachusetts Moves Over for Southern England
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.97
On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favorite films, television shows, and more. This time, we take a look at Practical Magic 2. In 1998, Hollywood starlets Nicole Kidman and Sandra Bullock played Gillian and Sally Owens, two sisters in possession of special powers in Practical Magic, a film adapted from the eponymous Alice Hoffman novel. Set in the witch-rich state of Massachusetts, the outcasted siblings attempt to lift their ancestral curse, which strikes dead any man who falls in love with an Owens woman. As they embark on this harrowing journey, spells are cast, midnight margaritas are made, and matriarchy reigns supreme. At the time, the film’s reception was middling at best—with a New York Times review describing it as “Barbie Joins a Coven”—and its performance at the box office not much better. With a little room to breathe and bask in nostalgia’s rose-colored glow, the movie has transformed into a feminist cult classic with Gen X and Gen Z fans alike. From 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple to The Devil Wears Prada 2, the past year has been a boon for follow-up films. In that same vein, Kidman and Bullock have reunited in Practical Magic 2, a sequel directed by Susanne Bier that promises to delight fans and take us across the pond to a whole new continent of spooky locales. Another generation of the coven-loving lives on in Practical Magic 2, which picks up after a sizable time jump but with more of the same kooky hijinks. A generous interpretation of time—and a little movie magic—lands Sally’s daughters Antonia (Maisie Williams) and Kylie (Joey King) in their early 20s. Up until now, they have lived their lives ignorant to their powers, which their mother has deliberately shielded them from. Medical student Antonia most closely resembles her mother, while Kylie, now a Harvard student, is a bit more of a free spirit. When Kylie falls for sweet Gideon (Xolo Maridueña) and then he falls into a coma, she follows her mother’s path of attempting to right things. Counseled by the recently uncovered Book of the Raven, Kylie sets off to her family’s ancestral home of England, bringing much of the story to English territory. While the original movie used Washington State's Whidbey Island as a stand-in for New England, production for the sequel moved to the United Kingdom. Here are all the places where Practical Magic 2 was filmed. Leavesden Studios – Hertfordshire, England The Owens women remain the main characters in this film, and fans of the original film will recall the outstanding Victorian-style Owens family home. The house itself has reached a cult status with its cutesy cottage core aesthetic, and its recreation was crucial to the making of the sequel. Practical Magic 2’s production notes explain the importance of the revival of the house. Producer Denise De Novi felt that bringing the house back to life was one of the most rewarding components of making this movie. “The house in this movie is just a phenomenon,” she noted. In the first film, the exterior of the house was built on San Juan Island in Washington state, and the interiors were created on a soundstage in Los Angeles. Those structures no longer exist so this time around, production designer Tom Burton determined that the most economical option was to build the house from scratch on the back lot at Leavesden Studios. Great care was taken to ensure that the replica was consistent with the original home, including establishing the same positioning to the sun so that the sun would set in the same position as it did in the original film. Once the house’s construction was almost complete, the greens team descended upon the set to bring the renowned garden to life, with over 4,000 plants brought in. While about half of the 55 shooting days were spent at Leavesden Studios, the remainder were shot at several notable locations in and around the London area. Village of Hambleden The quaint village of Hambleden, just west of London, served as the town Thornfield. The center of the village is filled with old, picturesque brick and flint cottages, all with the signature dormer windows. The Royal Standard of England, Beaconsfield British viewers might take notice of this historic pub, which serves at the exterior of the fictional Thornfield Inn just northwest of London. The Royal Standard, which has been around for over 900 years, claims to be the oldest pub in Great Britain. Located in the Chiltern Hills, the scenic old pub is filled with charm and has been featured in numerous films and television shows, including The Theory of Everything, Hot Fuzz, and Too Much. Oysters, fish and chips, and a robust beer list are on offer, and Quiz Night is every Tuesday. Langleybury Mansion in Hertfordshire Langlebury is a vacant 18th-century period house that has served as a backdrop for several notable productions including Downton Abbey, The Crown, and Paddington. The crew utilized this mansion to stand in for rooms at Harvard University as well as some of the UK lodgings. Wormsley Estate in Buckinghamshire The private 2,700-acre estate boasting an opera pavilion, cricket grounds, and a walled garden served as the backdrop for the cottage of Tom Lockland (Solly McLeod), a longtime magic student at Thornfield. Black Park Country Park Practical Magic 2 features sweeping views of the British rolling hills and conifer forests. Black Park, a large park with woodland trails, horse riding, and a lake, was filmed as the forest surrounding Thornfield. The Royal Chelsea Hospital The historic Royal Hospital Chelsea in London is a retirement and nursing home for British Army veterans who have reached the state pension age. The hospital was founded by Charles II in 1692, and it has maintained its grand property while modernizing to fit the present-day needs of its inhabitants. The impressive grounds with brick buildings and Roman columns were used in the film for a flower market and shots meant to be Harvard University exteriors. The Victorian flats of Cromwell Buildings The tattoo-covered Professor Ian Wright (Lee Pace), who quickly becomes Sally’s love interest, is one of the more charming updates in this sequel. His apartment was shot in these flats.

item.title: An Ode to Gander Airport, 25 Years After 9/11
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.79
Twenty-five years ago, the remote Newfoundland town of Gander found itself becoming an unlikely haven at the edge of the North Atlantic. In the wake of 9/11, more than 4,000 airborne flights were forced to divert when the Federal Aviation Administration closed American airspace—and 38 of those aircraft landed in Gander, bringing nearly 7,000 passengers and crew to a town of just 10,000 people. Brian Mosher, a Gander resident and TV reporter, filmed practically non-stop in the days following September 11, in an attempt to share what was happening on the ground with the world. “There were 7,000 different reasons why people had to get home,” says Mosher. “We were their shoulders to cry on.” The “come from aways,” the Newfoundland term for out-of-towners, were welcomed into the community with warmth, love, food, and anything else their hosts could provide. Buffet tables were set up to feed the new arrivals, and accommodation arranged in homes, schools, and churches. “We thought we’d give them a bite to eat before we put them back on their planes, not realizing they were going to have to stay here five days,” he says. The events of these confusing, confounding days went on to inspire a hit Broadway musical, Come From Away, with Ganderites immortalized in song. Today, Gander International Airport feels smaller and sleepier than its reputation might suggest. Most travelers who find themselves here are on brief stopovers en route to or from other destinations in Newfoundland and Labrador. Others have made a special visit, drawn by the extraordinary architecture and design of the former International Departures Terminal, a Modernist time capsule dating back to 1959. Gander Airport’s legacy actually far predates the events of 9/11–in fact, going all the way back to a time when global aviation was, literally, just taking off. It was the late 1930s, just three decades after Orville and Wilbur Wright’s first flight took off from Kitty Hawk beach in North Carolina. With long-haul air travel underway, and Newfoundland’s location on the Great Circle Route—930 miles closer to Europe than anywhere else in North America—positioned Gander as the perfect staging point for refueling, maintenance, and emergencies at a time when flying was far more unpredictable and potentially unreliable than we know it to be today The first plane to land in Gander touched down on a snow-packed runway in 1938. By 1940, it was already the world’s largest airport, and in World War II served as the main maintenance point for Allied aircraft flying to Europe. Eventually, Gander would go on to welcome commercial flights from Europe and the Soviet Union for refueling stops, but it couldn’t throw off its military past. Until 1959, arriving travelers still found themselves disembarking into a hangar designed for WWII. The opening of the Gander Airport International Departures Terminal by Queen Elizabeth II in June that year changed everything. The new terminal was a showcase for an ambitious, modernizing, young nation featuring Canadian Modernist art and design, as well as stylish furniture by some of the design world’s greatest names like Charles and Ray Eames and Arne Jacobsen. Gander was now ready to welcome world leaders, celebrities, royalty, and rock stars to this little outpost in remote eastern Newfoundland, and was determined to put on a show. Major stars of the day passed through—Marilyn Monroe, Albert Einstein, and Elizabeth Taylor—and could be seen drinking martinis at the Big Dipper, Newfoundland’s only 24-hour bar. As the Jet Age advanced and aircraft became more powerful with increased ranges, trans-Atlantic flights no longer needed to make refueling stops. Arrivals into what was once the “crossroads of the world” began to slow, and Gander’s fortunes declined. The glamorous international terminal and lounge, no longer a necessity, was at risk of being lost to a newer, smaller, more economical option. Eventually, an outpouring of support led to its rescue, and in 2022 it reopened as a museum space with a small movie theater, gastropub, and souvenir shop. Today, it is preserved largely as it was in its heyday. The Mondrian-esque terrazzo floor in shades of salmon, slate, and jade still carries the sheen of 1950s glamour. Clocks on the wall still tell the time in London, Montreal, New York, and Moscow. Stylized bird sculptures by Arthur Price welcoming arriving passengers to Canada still gather in a flock. But the most dramatic feature is the 72-foot Flight and Its Allegories mural by Canadian artist Kenneth Lochhead, featuring a dynamic scene of activity and abundance. A matronly figure stands with arms outstretched. A bearded man feeds airplane-shaped bluebirds. A boy peers through binoculars. Stylized birds burst into the air, some Concorde-like in form, predating the iconic supersonic aircraft by over a decade. Gander-born Todd Saunders, the celebrated architect behind Newfoundland modern icon Fogo Island Inn, credits the International Departure Terminal as being his first exposure to contemporary architecture. “The Canadian government invested in architecture because this was the first face of Canada, and that first impression was really important,” he says. But the airport’s pull went beyond architecture alone. Saunders still recalls the smell of Cuban cigars that lingered after flights stopped in en route between Havana and Moscow. “In a way, it was like Penn Station in New York, but for the world,” he says. The international terminal used to be open to the public at the time, and in doing so, held a cosmopolitan allure for the people of Gander. “My dad worked there as an airplane mechanic and he would call me and say, ‘The [Rolling] Stones are here’, and I’d get on my BMX and head down. You’d be looking at Mick Jagger because they’d had to stop for gas," he recalls. For local textile artist and designer Janet Langdon, whose father worked as an aircraft refueler in Gander in the 1950s and 60s, the airport offered an opportunity to see the world come to town. “I was making my own clothes at the time, and through my young eyes it was super exciting to see worldly fashions.” As a teenager, she would hitchhike to the airport to see the exotic arrivals, including off the many Aeroflot flights that touched down in the early 1970s. “A passenger once gave me a small container of yoghurt,” Langdon says. “It was my first time enjoying it.” Today, flights use the more modern, but less romantic, building next door to the original, but for aviation geeks and history lovers, the museum space is still worth the flight to Gander, not least of all for the history it documents. One display highlights all the most unusual cargo to have moved through the airport, including an aircraft load of ping-pong balls en route to Moscow, a Boeing 747 full of toothpicks, and a shipment of live alligators. Another features episodes like the rescue of George Bush Sr. when he got stuck in a local bog, and Frank Sinatra being admonished for jumping the bar queue and being told to wait his turn. My favorite display is the photo of Fidel Castro sledding in Gander in December 1976: a cadre of heavy-coated officials looking on with concern as a giddy Castro is about to topple off into a heap of snow. But it’s not all about the history. The airport is still a vital part of the Gander community. “An economic impact study concluded last year shows that one in five jobs in the town of Gander are associated with the airport,” Reg Wright, President and CEO of Gander International Airport, says. “It’s nice to see Gander and its guests gather in the lounge again.” For Langdon, the airport is synonymous with what it means to be from this small aviation town in Newfoundland. “Originally it brought people together from all over for employment, and during 9/11 it brought the world to our town,” she says. “Today, people come for the history, some because of Come From Away, and of course the aviation geeks. I just met a retired Lufthansa flight dispatcher who was going to spend time at the lounge before heading back to Luxembourg.” Langdon is hopeful that the airport and departures lounge will remain thriving community spaces. “To quote Reg Wright, we as Ganderites have jet fuel in our veins.” For the town and its people, the airport will never be just a place people pass through; it is woven into their identity and history—and, despite the changing tides of aviation, will remain part of their future. And if there is ever another time when they must heed the call of the world's travelers again, the airport and the community will no doubt stand ready.

item.title: Shoulder Season on Paros: Ceramicist Christiane Smit Finds Inspiration at a Slower Pace
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.51
This is part of Off-Season Greece, a collection of guides highlighting the year-round appeal of Greece's most popular destinations, courtesy of our favorite local tastemakers. In this edition, we speak to ceramic artist and owner of Moonhouse, Christiane Smit. For Netherlander and artist Christiane Smit, a holiday on Paros in 2008 rerouted the course of her life. “It wasn’t a carefully planned life decision, it was something I felt instinctively,” she says of her unplanned move to the Cycladic island. “I listened to that feeling, stayed, and started building a completely new life on the island.” Having lived all over the island since then, she now operates a ceramics atelier in the village of Lefkes and owns the stunningly minimalist clifftop villa rental Moonhouse—both of which are open to visitors. She is currently completing the restoration of a nearly 100-year-old stone house in the village of Kostos. Here, the now-local shares the shoulder-season delights that keep her on-island year-round as well as her favorite hotel-slash-taverna for a warming meal and stay. What would you say is the sweet-spot time of the year to visit—when the travelers have not yet arrived, but local life is buzzing? For me, the sweetest time in Paros is late spring or early autumn. The island feels wonderfully balanced: Everything is open, but life is still unhurried. I love walking through the villages in the morning, when the streets are still quiet. The air smells of jasmine, fresh bread from the bakery, and the sea. You hear church bells, neighbors greeting each other, and the wind moving through the olive trees. The light is what inspires me most. It changes constantly, making the whitewashed houses glow and bringing out every texture in the stone. As a ceramic artist, I find myself collecting those colors, textures, and moments every day. They’re as much a part of my work as the clay itself. What do you love most about being there during this season? The season allows me to slow down and notice everything. The colors of the landscape, the textures of old stone walls, the shifting light on the sea—those details naturally find their way into my ceramics. I don’t have to look for inspiration here; I simply have to pay attention. Who’s around this time of year? Is it all locals? Greek domestic visitors? Are there any travelers at all? It’s mostly locals. The cafés are filled with familiar faces, fishermen are heading out in the morning, and shop owners have time to stop and chat. You also meet a small number of travelers: The people who aren’t looking for the typical summer vacation, but who want to experience the island more slowly and authentically. There are also Greek visitors escaping the city for a long weekend or visiting family. It’s a lovely mix, but the locals set the rhythm, and that’s what gives Paros its real character. What’s notable about the locals in Paros; do they have any of their own unique traditions or a reputation amongst Greeks for anything in particular? What I’ve come to appreciate most about the people of Paros is their warmth and sense of community. Even though it’s a popular island in summer, life outside the season is very local. People know one another, and there’s a genuine willingness to help each other. As someone who lives here year-round, that’s something I’ve really come to value. There’s also a deep respect for craftsmanship—from marble carving, for which the Cyclades are famous, to fishing, farming, and handmade work. Where would we find you eating during this time? One of my favorite places is the family-run taverna at Hotel Julia in Drios. I love it because it feels authentic and unchanged—a place where generations have welcomed people with simple, honest food and genuine hospitality. My perfect day always starts with a swim in the crystal-clear waters just below the taverna. Afterwards, I walk up for a long, leisurely lunch. There’s something so special about sitting there, the sound of the waves below and nowhere else to be. What’s the seasonal dish to order at this time of year? Winter on Paros is the season for revithada (slow-baked chickpea stew), hearty bean soups, and goat or lamb braised with local wine—dishes that are more like daily specials rather than menu staples. But if there’s one meal that defines the island’s quieter months, it’s whatever is cooking in the pot that day (mageirefta). That’s what locals order, and every taverna has its own depending on the day. Are there any areas of the island that really come alive during the off-season? I wouldn’t say any one area suddenly comes alive in the off-season; it feels more like the island returns to its natural rhythm. While Parikia is the social hub for year-round residents, it’s the villages—Lefkes, Marpissa, Prodromos, Kostos, and Dryos—that reveal the character of Paros through seasonal festivals, religious celebrations, and community events. How does the weather change the destination during this time of year, and what are the (dis)advantages of that? You get cooler temperatures; crisp, sunny days; and the occasional rainstorm, which turns the landscape unexpectedly green. The island feels softer and more vibrant. For me, one of the greatest advantages is the sense of calm. Of course, there are a few trade-offs. Stronger winter weather systems can occasionally disrupt ferry schedules, and many seasonal businesses close until spring. But these are minor inconveniences. What does a perfect Saturday in the off-season look like to you? My perfect Saturday begins slowly with a coffee in my house, catching the first sunlight. From there, I’ll often wander through Lefkes, Marpissa, or Prodromos before a long lunch at a traditional taverna. In the afternoon, I usually head back to my ceramic studio. The quieter months are when I’m most creative. Without the intensity of the summer season, there’s space to observe, reflect, and create. At sunset, I love taking a walk along one of the beaches or coastal paths. Even in winter, there are many clear, sunny days, and the light over the Aegean is extraordinary. I usually end the day with friends over a simple meal and a glass of wine. Do you have any favorite activities during this time of year? I love walking the ancient Byzantine paths that weave between villages. With few people on the trails, the silence becomes part of the journey. This winter is especially meaningful, as I’ll be putting the finishing touches on a small renovation project in the village of Kostos, a space I’ve been shaping with the same care and intention that I bring to my ceramics. Creating a home is, in many ways, another form of making, and I find great joy in both! This article was originally published in Condé Nast Traveller UK.

item.title: The Best Hotels in Berlin at Every Price Point
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.51
More than three decades after the wall came down, Berlin remains a city in constant flux, where the past and present intertwine in wildly innovative ways. A booming capital brimming with youthful energy and creative ideas, it is reinventing itself brick by brick—and nowhere is this more evident than in its dynamic hotel scene. New life has been breathed into landmark properties, and dilapidated buildings have been rescued and refashioned into chic boutique stays. Famed global brands such as Rocco Forte and The Hoxton have arrived on the scene, joining timeless classics that have stood for the past century. From the splashy west to the grittier east, property choices in every style and at every price point span the city. Here are the best hotels in Berlin that are open for check-in now, as chosen by our local editors. Our top picks: - Best for luxury: Waldorf Astoria Berlin - Best for a central location: Telegraphenamt - Best for families: Michelberger Hotel - Read Full ReviewHoused in a late 19th-century building, Irish lifestyle hotel brand The Dean brings its “vibe first” philosophy to the German capital, pairing bold design with cultural connectivity and a food concept that draws in more than just overnight guests. Interiors channel Berlin’s creative energy and avant-garde spirit from the moment you step inside. Historic architectural details sit alongside saturated colors, sculptural lighting, and a confident, contemporary design language. Room numbers are handwritten on the doors rather than printed—an intentionally imperfect detail that nods to Berlin’s slightly rough-around-the-edges character. In the bathrooms, original black-and-white tiles have been preserved, punctuated by red shower frames and boldly framed mirrors. Toiletries are by D.S. & Durga, lending a subtle spa feel. For food, Benedict is the heart of the hotel—a bakery, restaurant, and bar combined in one lively, open space. Breakfast is served until 4 p.m. on weekdays and all day on weekends. The focus is, naturally, on eggs Benedict in multiple variations: with ham and cheese, avocado, or pulled beef, served on brioche or a buttery croissant. The brand’s Irish roots are also present in the drinks offering: whiskey in every minibar, the Irish cocktail “Ól,” and even a dedicated Guinness tap behind the bar—a small but unmistakable nod to its heritage. —Susanna Gunst - Read Full ReviewThis sophisticated hotel in Mitte’s bustling center, steps from the Brandenburg Gate, features one-of-a-kind guest rooms decorated by local and international artists. The prominent neon sign on the façade is strategically placed above a self-portrait done in bronze by artist Alicja Kwade, and once inside, you’re transported into a moodily lit living room reminiscent of an art patron’s salon. Refined couples, having just finished their cocktails, chat quietly while on their way out to the Staatsoper (German State Opera). It all feels very calm and grown up, like an idealized version of Berlin’s past artistic glories, updated with a buzzy sense of creative present. Bed down in a room with hand-painted wallpaper or a hand-carved folding screen; each is uniquely decorated and may have a one-of-a-kind large-scale painting on the wall, or even a funky video installation. Bathrooms are lined in glazed subway-style tiles and have heated floors and large walk-in showers. The property is an easy to walk to the Reichstag; if you’ve come to shop, Friedrichstrasse is a block away; to run or bike, the large green expanse of Tiergarten is a hop and a skip. —Liz Humphreys - Read Full ReviewWith an exceptional location on Monbijoupark in the Mitte district, this grand neo-Baroque building once housed the city’s vast telegraph office—built between 1910 and 1916, and at one time the most sophisticated postal building in Germany. It has since been meticulously restored and transformed into a posh destination for discerning travelers looking to stay close to a huge selection of trendy restaurants, bars, and shops, as well as beloved Hackesche Höfe's old courtyards-turned-commercial spaces. The 97 guest rooms all have an industrial look, with brick-barrel vaulted ceilings divided by metal beams and exposed brick walls. Art Deco design elements like illuminated glass capsules, which display the room numbers, nod toward the building’s history, and hanging lamps adorn each side of the bed like a movie star’s chandelier earrings. Though occupied by digital nomads during the day, the bar at ROOT buzzes after dark, and a DJ spins techno beats nightly starting at 8 p.m.—this is Berlin, after all. —L.H. - Read Full ReviewFans of the flagship Waldorf Astoria New York will feel right at home in this Berlin outpost, set in an elegant skyscraper in City West and just around the corner from the exclusive shopping boulevard Kurfürstendamm (Ku’damm). Rooms are seriously big—starting at 452 square feet—and designed in a contemporary style, with neutral gray velour furnishings, swirl-patterned rugs, and a statement-making gold wall behind the beds. Large marble bathrooms have separate tubs and showers in every category, and the in-mirror televisions and Aesop toiletries add a luxurious touch. Reached by a separate elevator, the Tower Suites (floors 22 to 31) are worth it for the views—of the city, the Kaiser Wilhelm Memorial Church, or the neighboring Tiergarten park and Berlin Zoo. For a true splurge, the massive 30th-floor Astor Suite (with floor-to-ceiling windows, a balcony, and a separate dining room and kitchen) or the 31st-floor Presidential Suite (complete with a grand piano, open fireplace, and two balconies) boast sweeping city views. —Jennifer Ceaser - Read Full ReviewA neoclassical 19th-century bank houses this five-star Rocco Forte property, which enjoys an unrivaled location on Bebelplatz, right in the historic heart of East Berlin. Many of the building’s original details—graceful marble columns, skylights, an intricate iron staircase—have been retained, most notably down below in the pool area, formerly the bank’s jewel vault. A contemporary design streak runs throughout the lobby, which is dotted with oversized black velvet sofas, towering red-lacquer vases, and dangling globe lights, plus a playful pink neon birdcage as the centerpiece. Book one of the higher-end suites and get perks galore, including personalized concierge service, luggage unpacking, free pressing of one garment, and in-house movies. There's a standard minibar in all rooms, but you can request a bespoke Rocco Forte Nourish minibar in advance, stocked with a selection of healthy snacks and drinks. —J.C. - Read Full ReviewBuilt in 1891 as a private residence and converted into a hotel in 1911, Hotel Zoo has been one of West Berlin’s poshest stays for more than a century. In the 1950s, it served as the VIP hotel for the Berlin International Film Festival and was a haunt for A-listers like Grace Kelly and Sophia Loren. So it’s fitting that the hotel’s glamorous history has been reinterpreted by two Hollywood designers, Dayna Lee and Ted Berner. The cool design aesthetic and location on Ku'damm, Berlin's best shopping street, make it a covetable stay for anyone. —J.C. - Read Full ReviewToday, there’s that sense that Hotel Adlon Kempinski Berlin—having withstood the vicissitudes of a tumultuous century—is armor-plated, as unassailable as the bulletproof floor-to-ceiling windows of the presidential suites. Under the Kempinski aegis since the 1990s, it bottles that sense of timelessness and offers a feeling of security and tradition as something that is as precious as it is soothing. The past is present here, exuding patrician-style grandeur and elegance: the Art Deco floor gauges in the elevators, an old-fashioned bicycle that the bellboys use, the panels of walnut wood in the Michelin-starred Lorenz Adlon Esszimmer restaurant, acres of marble for a grand staircase, and gold flakes even on the lobby lounge’s currywurst. Old-school perfectionism calls for the three types of caviar and Champagne at breakfast, as well as butler-ironed newspapers brought to the table. It all contributes to that illusion that you are in a cocoon, away from the travails of the world. —Catherine Fairweather - Read Full ReviewKPM is the vision of Berlin banker Jörg Woltmann, who helped save the 18th-century Royal Porcelain Manufactory Berlin complex on which the hotel has stood since 2019. The ultra-modern, cube-like building has picked up multiple design and architecture prizes and was nominated as Europe’s Leading Design Hotel by the 2021 World Travel Awards. Rooms are minimalist, chic, and smartly designed, with functional desks, high-tech wall control panels, and clever built-ins that make the spaces seem larger than they are—aided by the floor-to-ceiling windows. If weather permits, take advantage of the rooftop terrace with great views over Berlin—just remember to bring your own drinks, as there is no bar. Major sites like Tiergarten and the Berlin Zoo are 10 and 15 minutes by foot, respectively. —J.C. - Read Full ReviewSet in a restored 1913 Art Nouveau building along leafy Oranienplatz, Orania is one of the few hotels—and the only upscale option—in the edgy, nightlife-filled Kreuzberg. A large, open-plan "Living Room," which functions as a restaurant-bar-lounge, is bookended by two roaring fireplaces (in winter) and surrounded by enormous windows; a raised corner stage sports a Steinway piano (there's classical or jazz most nights). The rooms and suites vary in size and layout, but all are similarly designed: lots of rich woods, deep red textiles featuring the hotel’s signature gold elephant, handmade Persian carpets, and curvaceous lamps from Catellani. If you're a frequent visitor to Berlin and love nightlife, this hotel is ideal for you. —J.C. - Read Full ReviewA renovated 1950s high-rise is home to the Berlin outpost of this hip German hotel chain, which is sandwiched between the Berlin Zoo and the trendy concept mall Bikini Berlin. There's a fun energy as soon as you walk into the third-floor reception area, dubbed Bikini Island, which sports a playful jungle-themed design, with tropical plants, stuffed monkeys, and hammocks perfectly positioned to look out over the zoo’s monkey and bird cages. All rooms, even the ones called XL, are on the smaller side, but the funky Jungle Rooms, many with their own hammocks overlooking the zoo, offer an escape different from others you can find in the city. The hotel is also home to the Monkey Bar, one of Berlin's most popular cocktail spots, and guests can cut the line by taking a private elevator straight to the door. —J.C. - Read Full ReviewThis five-star property, long known for its impeccable white-glove service, has a sophisticated look that nods to 1920s Berlin. Entry-level Deluxe Rooms are plenty spacious, measuring a generous 430 square feet, but it’s worth trading up to a Deluxe View Room for fantastic views overlooking Potsdamer Platz. For even more exclusivity, the 42 Club Level rooms and suites on the 10th and 11th floors offer 24-hour access to a lounge with panoramic city vistas, complimentary food and drink, and a private concierge.
