The elegant sandstone tower fits right in with the neighboring skyscrapers on bustling Potsdamer Platz, and guests are a short stroll from the Holocaust Memorial, the Brandenburg Gate, and Tiergarten park's 519 acres of tree-lined paths and flowering gardens. —J.C. - Read Full ReviewFrom the outside, the circa-1970s building housing The Hoxton doesn’t look like anything special. But step into the oversized lobby chock-full of comfy places to sit (with your choice of chairs and sectionals arranged around tables of various shapes and sizes, along with one long communal coworking table), and you see why the young (and young at heart) could spend all day here. When the mood strikes for a drink, the sophisticated bar lies right behind the lobby, separated by staggered shelves displaying artfully arranged vases, jars, books, and other design knickknacks. And since the Hoxton also has its own coffee shop (technically a teahouse) and Indian restaurant, it’s truly a place that invites lingering. Each of the 234 guest rooms has a similar look, with scalloped headboards in muted pink and green, speckled terrazzo side tables, Art Nouveau lamps, and hardwood floors. —L.H. - Read Full ReviewBuilt in 1914 in the style of a French palace, this magnificent villa has served as a private residence, embassy, naval officers’ club, and later, a luxury hotel, hosting notable guests such as Romy Schneider and Paul McCartney. In 2014, late Berlin fashion designer Patrick Hellmann acquired the property and began renovations, restoring its glorious historical details while bringing much of the design—previously done by Karl Lagerfeld in the 1990s—firmly into the 21st century. The 43 rooms and 9 suites feature particularly impressive details: A dual-bedroom Kaiser Suite boasts an antique library with original frescoes, and the first-floor Karl Lagerfeld Suite has lovely Art Deco touches and a stone balcony overlooking the gardens. —J.C. - Read Full ReviewVladimir Nabokov, Brigitte Bardot, and Alain Delon have all stayed at this luxury hotel at some point in its history. It opened in 1913 on a quiet, leafy square in posh Charlottenburg and was renovated a century later as part of Marriott’s Autograph Collection. It was just spruced up again in 2025 after its takeover by the Germany-based, design-focused Roomers brand. The boutique property retains its alluring Art Nouveau flourishes, including a sinuous canopy above the entrance, Moorish arched windows, and exquisite stucco work throughout. The flawless redesign integrates historic decorative elements with contemporary touches. The luxurious boutique vibe and ideal location—just a short walk to the shops along Kurfürstendamm and the Berlin Zoo—make it an enduring draw, even after the redo. —J.C. FAQ: What is the best area to stay in when visiting Berlin? For first-timers who want to get a true feel for the city, Mitte is the beating creative heart of Berlin, and where you'll find some of our favorite locally-grown hotels, including Telegraphenamt and Chateau Royal Berlin. Another ideal option is Charlottenburg, in western Berlin, which is home to upscale shopping, the grand Charlottenburg Palace, and hotels like The Hoxton. How do we choose the best hotels in Berlin? Every hotel on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider properties across price points that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination, keeping design, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind. This gallery has been updated with new information since its original publish date. It was originally published on Condé Nast Traveller UK. Recommended

item.title: On California's Central Coast, an Indoor-Outdoor Museum Connects Visitors With Centuries of Chumash Heritage
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.36
The Chumash Heritage Marine Sanctuary was featured on Condé Nast Traveler's Bright Ideas in Travel 2025. Read the full list of winners here. I am greeted by cast iron doors, engraved with spiraling pictographs and cool to the touch, even in the morning heat of June. I grip the handle—shaped, I'll learn, like a clapper stick, a traditional Chumash percussion instrument—and push it open. The sounds of birdsong, layered and ambient, rise toward a curved ceiling where light moves like cloud shadow. Here, what lies indoors simulates the beauty of the natural world. I have entered an 'Ap, the Chumash word for home, reimagined at monumental scale. The traditional version would have been made of willow branches and tule reeds, but this one is steel and stone with the same circular, embracing shape: This is the 14,000-square-foot Santa Ynez Chumash Museum and Cultural Center, which opened on May 15, 2025, after 20 years in the making. Every detail has been designed with intention by Native American architect Johnpaul Jones. The ancestral home of the Chumash, the Indigenous Native American people who have lived along California's central coast for more than 13,000 years, spans from Malibu to Paso Robles, including the Northern Channel Islands. In 2024, Chumash stewardship of more than 4,500 square miles of sea and coast in this region was formalized on the federal level as part of the Chumash Heritage National Marine Sanctuary, the first-ever Indigenous-led marine sanctuary in the US. The new museum is the most visible piece of a broader, sustained effort to connect visitors to California's central coast with Chumash culture. The tribe's Culture Department runs a state-credentialed language program—two of its teachers hold the specialized credential that California created in 2008 for Native language instruction—alongside basket weaving classes, an archery club, a youth camp, and a cultural resource management team that protects tribal sites and artifacts. "The circular shapes of the buildings, the model of the oak tree where the coyote lives in the Maria Solares Discovery Center, and the west-facing direction of the buildings represent important symbolism to our people," says Kenneth Kahn, Chairman of the Santa Ynez Band of Chumash Indians. The museum faces the Western Gates, or Point Conception—a spot on the cliffs overlooking the Pacific Ocean, which tribal beliefs describe as the place one departs this world and enters the spirit realm. Felicia Cogorno, Education Programs & Volunteer Manager and tribal member, tells me that if I stand in exactly the right place in the center of the museum's main room, I'll hear my own voice come back to me. I find the spot—a subtle seam in the floor's inlaid pattern—and say something small and ordinary. For a moment, my voice and the birdsong, and the fire and the Sʰamala (Santa Ynez Band native language) words floating from a nearby speaker, are all one sound, indistinguishable from each other. Cogorno grew up on the reservation, on whose lands the center now stands, and manages its education programs and volunteers. She points to the ring of painted figures along the upper walls, each mid-movement, each representing a different animal, each placed at a different ancestral village along the central California coast. "If you were being welcomed to our village," she says, "you would be welcomed with singing and dancing." I wave my hand near the fire. The movement activates the walls where animals light up—deer, bear, condor—each one accompanied by a voice pronouncing its name in Sʰamala, the language of the Santa Ynez Band. The polished stone floor, meanwhile, is inlaid with a seasonal round: concentric rings mapping harvests and hunts and gathering times, labeled in Sʰamala and English, with a bit of Spanish woven in. As Cogorno explains, the arrival of the Gregorian calendar required new words for things that hadn't needed naming before. Before going further into the museum, I stop at a photograph of a woman hanging on the wall. I continue to see her image, reappearing throughout the galleries like a thread you keep finding in the weave. Her name is Maria Solares, I learn. In the early 1900s, she was one of the last fluent speakers of Sʰamala. Between 1914 and 1915, she worked with linguist John Peabody Harrington, sitting for sessions that produced wax cylinder recordings of the languages and more than 100,000 pages of notes. The language survived because she sat in that room and spoke. "She's my five-times great-grandmother," Cogorno says, matter-of-factly. "Many of our volunteers are also descendants of Maria." The permanent galleries are accessed off the ‘ap lobby area through a set of iron doors whose design, Cogorno mentions, was made by her aunt. Inside, the ceiling rises and the light changes, cooler, darker. The exhibit moves through the Chumash cosmology of three worlds—Upper, Middle, and Lower—stacked like basket trays. Most of what surrounds me is the Middle World, the et ya shoop ("here world") display. Cases hold stone tools, hunting materials, and abalone ceremony regalia. Paintings that line the walls show figures fishing, gathering, and paddling. The objects in the cases mirror what the figures carry. I stop at a case of abalone shells, cut into jewelry and adornments, and polished to a high shine, almost iridescent under the gallery lights. "My cousin made those," Cogorno says. Nearby, there's a swordfish headdress with intricate shell work—her aunt, who cast the door handles at the entrance, made that, too. In the Upper World gallery, a taxidermied California condor has her own case, her own story. In 1986, when only 27 California condors remained on earth, she was the last wild female of her species before she was captured, then put into a breeding program. Because of this, she raised the next generation and was released with them, teaching the young birds, somehow, to be condors in a world that had nearly erased them. Nearby, a painting depicts the Condor dance, one of the newer dances in the Chumash tradition. "To me, [the condor return] represents a cultural resurgence," Cogorno says. "We're still here. We're still thriving. We're not static." Outside, the Culture Park opens wide across the landscape. Native plantings—dogbane, yerba mansa—border brooks and pools that are fed by greywater, which the tribe recycles on-site. The limestone underfoot came from a quarry twenty minutes away. Further down the path stands the Tomol House, an open-slatted building that holds its namesake: a 950-pound plank canoe known as a tomol. It is not a relic, but a vessel that regularly hits the water. This very tomol has made what is known as “the crossing”—a culturally significant journey across 26 miles of open Pacific water from Ventura to the Channel Islands—multiple times. The crossing takes 10-13 hours, with 6 people sitting on their knees to paddle. Moving by feel and tradition toward an island they could reach in twenty minutes by motorboat. Jennifer, one of the museum's volunteers and one of the only women to captain a tomol, joins me inside. She talks about the crossing the way any athlete talks about a journey that changed them. "You really connect with past ancestors," she says. I continue on, following an audio narration, drawn from the voices of tribal leaders, that guides me through the middle of the museum, chronicling the mission period—a traumatic era that involved the boarding schools, the forced silencing of language, and the cutting of hair. A time when children were taken away and conditioned into believing their heritage shameful. But as I walk further, the room shifts to contemporary photographs. Ceremonies, children, laughter, a tomol coming into shore. A collection of moments that show the Chumash thriving. On my way out, I pass the seasonal round again—the acorns of fall, the fishing of summer—and I grip the clapper stick door handle one more time. The birds still sing overhead. I push through into the heat and the light, back into the valley the Chumash never left. The Santa Ynez Chumash Museum and Cultural Center is located in Santa Ynez, California, and is open Thursday through Sunday from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.

item.title: 'The Gentlemen' Season 2 Takes Us From English Country Estates to Italian Palazzos in Mob Territory
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.28
On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favourite films, television shows, and more. This time, we ask: where was The Gentlemen Season 2 filmed? The second season of Guy Ritchie’s hit Netflix series, The Gentleman, is here. The first series introduced us to Eddie Horniman (Theo James), a young British aristocrat who had inherited his father’s grand country estate, only to discover that behind the family money was a secret cannabis empire. In Season 2, Horniman, now the Duke of Halstead, is keen to expand the operation, alongside his business partner, Susie Glass (Kaya Scodelario). This will take them out of the English countryside and subterranean criminal worlds of the East End and Liverpool, and thrust them instead into the world of the Mafia, as they attempt to go international and do business with the dangerous Capo dei Capi, Marco Moretti (Sergio Castellito). “The madness of Italy’s beauty, its culture, its history and its traditions was something I felt would fit perfectly into our show,” says Ritchie. “I had wanted to expand the canvas of The Gentlemen in this season. Italy was just an obvious choice. British gangsters colliding with the Italian Mafia just feels so right for our world. Some fruit hangs low and looks so tasty you just can’t resist for very long.” Here are some of the key locations used in the filming of The Gentleman Seasons 1 and 2, from Ritchie’s Ashcombe Estate to Lake Maggiore in Italy. Is The Gentlemen based on a real-life story? Both the film of the same name and the two seasons of The Gentlemen are not based on a true story, though of course, they borrow elements from the criminal underworld and its cast of characters. The situation that Eddie Horniman and his family find themselves in – of having to find new ways to monetise their vast aristocratic estates – is a reality, however. There are no real life examples of aristocrats running cannabis empires that we know of though. The main thrust of the action in Season 2 of The Gentlemen takes place in Lake Maggiore, connecting Horniman and his business partner Katie Glass to Italy’s criminal gangs – the mafia. Historically, the area has not been known as a mafia heartland – unlike regions like Sicily, for example – but it does have a relationship with organised crime. In particular, the ’Ndrangheta, the Calabrian mafia, have reportedly used the area for cocaine and weapons trafficking, thanks to its close proximity to the Swiss border. Where was The Gentlemen Season 2 filmed? The Badminton Estate, Gloucestershire While some scenes of The Gentleman were filmed on stage sets at Alperton Studios in Wembley, London, the exterior of Halstead Manor, the fictional home of the Horniman family, is The Badminton Estate. The real-life home of the Duke and Duchess of Beaufort is a popular filming location and wedding venue in the south Gloucestershire countryside. Viewers with a keen eye may recognise the property from Netflix favourite Bridgerton and movies including Pearl Harbour and 28 Days Later. The sprawling estate has been occupied for thousands of years, and the remains of several Roman villas surround the main home. The medieval property was owned by the Boteler family before Edward Somerset, fourth Earl of Worcester, purchased the manors of Great and Little Badminton in 1612. It’s his son, Sir Thomas Somerset, who made significant alterations to the original house, and the property has captured the imagination of high society and even the royal family over the centuries – Charles II stayed in the house, and the late Queen Elizabeth II was a regular visitor to the annual Horse Trials. “Badminton felt immediately right for Halstead,” says supervising location Manager Iggy Ellis, “because it’s a proper, lived-in home rather than a National Trust museum. So inside, there’d be some walking sticks by the door or a few shotgun rounds from where they’d been out shooting. There were cracks and tired bits, as you’d get in every family home. But there was also oil painting and history and majesty. It felt perfect for our story.” Ashcombe Estate, Wiltshire In episode one, Ritchie made his own country estate, Ashcombe Park, available for filming a shooting party scene. “That was a lot of fun but tricky at times too,” says production designer Martyn John. “You’re in the middle of nowhere with no phone signal or internet. We had to take everything in; so, flowers, food, dogs, guns and also… frozen partridges.” Ashcombe is a working farm set in 1,100 acres of rolling chalk land, and is named after the ash trees and the valleys (‘combes’) that monopolise much of it. It has been the family home of Ritchie since 2001 (when he bought it with ex-wife Madonna for £9 million), and was previously the home of photographer Cecil Beaton. Loseley Park, Surrey Much like in season one, some of the exterior and interior scenes at Halstead Manor were filmed at Loseley Park, a historic home just outside of Guildford that is now used as a wedding venue. “Where possible we tried to maximise every location because when you move around it costs money that could be on the screen,” explains supervising locations manager Iggy Ellis. “So we used a cottage in the grounds of Loseley for the exteriors of gamekeeper Geoff’s cottage and built the interior in the studio because we needed lots of camera space and somewhere for Geoff’s menagerie of animals.” Swakeleys House, Ickenham Another multi-purpose location was Swakeleys House, a 17th-century mansion in Ickenham. “It was a great find because we were able to use it for so many things,” explains Ellis. “From the rehab centre where Freddie is recovering from the cocaine habit he acquired in the first series to the interior of the prison where Bobby Glass is meant to be serving time.” Built in 1638, it is an excellent example of the ‘Artisan Mannerism’ architectural style, a form of Jacobean architecture that features decorative classical flourishes such as gable ends. It was the home of Sir Edmund Wright, Lord Mayor of London, and was visited twice by the famed diarist Samuel Pepys. The Adelphi Building, London The Adelphi Building off The Strand was transformed into an auction house for a scene in which Susie Glass bids millions for a Botticelli painting, which is later snatched by a gang on e-bikes outside. “I wanted to use that network of streets around the Savoy Hotel, including a secret little tunnel that cuts between John Adam Street and the riverside,” explains Ellis of the chase. “It takes at least three months’ notice to get London streets closed for filming, and there were some careful negotiations with everyone from Westminster Council to building owners and the Savoy Hotel itself. But that amazing chase really is one of the things I’m most proud of.” The Grade II-listed Adelphi has retained many of its original 1930s Art Deco features, including its impressive stone facade, classic columns and Gilbert Ledwood sculptures. Today it is predominantly used as an office space, and houses the publisher Condé Nast, whose titles include not only Condé Nast Traveler, but also Vogue, Tatler and GQ. Villa Rusconi Clerici, Lake Maggiore Villa Rusconi Clerici became the glamorous palazzo home of Mafia heiress (and Eddie’s love interest) Contessa Isabella Savanza de Parme, known as Bella. “We spent three full days looking at several amazing palazzos, including one on Lake Como,” shares John. “But as soon as I saw the one at Lake Maggiore, I knew this was the one. It was in a much less touristy area and it had such great light and glittering water. You could point the camera anywhere and it just looked beautiful.” The interiors too were perfect for Bella’s home. “I wanted a house or a villa which reflected the taste – if not the scale – of Eddie’s country estate, Halstead Manor” says Ellis. “I wanted these two aristocratic families to merge, stylistically. So, you have all the antiques and the paintings that reflect tradition and ancestry, but also modern pieces because, despite the centuries-old history of both families, there’s a new generation in charge now.” Villa Rusconi Clerici is a beautifully preserved 19th-century palazzo on the Piedmont shore of Lake Maggiore, and unsurprisingly is popular as a wedding venue. The villa that exists today was built for a Hungarian colonel and revolutionary, Stefano Türr, who was married to one of Emperor Napoleon’s cousins and became intrinsic to the unification of Italy. The interiors are Art Nouveau in style, including a grand staircase featuring a wrought iron balustrade. Grand Hotel Majestic, Lake Maggiore The Grand Hotel Majestic stood in for the fictional The Grand Hotel, where a wedding takes place later in the series. First built in 1870, it was one of the finest examples of luxury hospitality in the area, and was immediately popular with the international elite. Unsurprisingly, considering its location on the shores of Lake Maggiore, it is often chosen as a wedding venue for modern couples, much like in the show. One of its chief assets is the view across the lake to Borromeo Island, with actor Theo James pictured standing on one of the balconies looking out across the water in one scene. While the interiors are French in style, with parquet flooring and chandeliers, the grounds are also particularly lavish, with centuries-old trees and flowers, and there’s even a small private beach. Chiesa San Leonardo, Lake Maggiore The 16th-century church Chiesa San Leonardo also features in the new season. Located in the lakeside village of Pallanza, the church features striking columns of pink Baveno granite, as well as 17th-century wooden sculptures and altars. There’s also a 65-metre high bell tower, as well as access to the lake from a dramatic staircase. Where was The Gentleman Season 1 filmed? Stoke Court, Buckinghamshire The Badminton Estate gets much of the credit for appearing as the exterior of the fictional Halstead Manor, but some of the interior scenes used Stoke Court in Buckinghamshire. Stoke Court is home to the study, where Freddie shoots Liverpudlian drug dealer Tommy after a memorable scene featuring a chicken costume, Halstead Manor’s boot room, drawing room and orangery. The real-life property is best known for its association with mid-18th-century poet Thomas Gray, who holidayed there during his childhood. Wrotham Park, Hertfordshire Wrotham Park in Hertfordshire plays the part of the home of extravagantly wealthy drug lord Stanley Johnson, aka Bridgewater House. The neo-Palladian English country house was designed by Isaac Ware in 1754, and it’s where we see Susie Glass and Stanley engage in a polite-ish war of words over his desire to take over her father’s empire. London The Gentleman’sfilming locations depict two sides of the coin: lavish country houses owned by the landed gentry and hideouts used by the criminal underworld. For the latter, the locations team looked to London. Locations used across the capital include The Reform Club in Pall Mall, which doubled up for Pinky’s Club, and Billingsgate Market, which is mentioned by name in the series as the headquarters of the Liverpudlian drug group. The exterior shots of the Croydon Tower Block were taken at Brandon Estate, while the boxing ring is the now-closed party venue Printworks in Rotherhithe.

item.title: Off-Season Greece: Fall in Santorini Through the Eyes of Winemaker Michael Kouloglou
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.01
This is part of Off-Season Greece, a collection of guides highlighting the year-round appeal of Greece's most popular destinations, courtesy of our favorite local tastemakers. In this edition, we speak to winemaker Michael Kouloglou. For winemaker Michael Kouloglou, the decision to move from the mainland to Santorini 11 years ago was a simple one. “It is the mecca of Greek white wine,” he says. Since relocating here from the Athenian Riviera town of Piraeus, he’s worked with a number of local wineries before launching Orycton, his small-batch Assyrtiko featuring grapes grown on old vines from all over the island. It was a winner at the 2023 Decanter World Wine Awards. On top of the siren’s song of Santorini’s prized volcanic terroir, however, Kouloglou says he appreciates that the region’s windy conditions allow him to pursue his other passions: surfing and kitesurfing. He’s currently settled in Monolithos, a quiet seaside village in the east—but has historically lived all over Santorini, which has offered him great insight into the rhythm of the island. “Each village has its own unique character,” he says, “far beyond the image [of Santorini] that most visitors see.” Here, the longtime Santorini local shares why autumn is his favorite time of year—and all the treasures of the off-season. What would you say is the sweet-spot time of the year to visit—when the travelers have not yet arrived, but local life is buzzing? If I had to choose the best time to visit, I would choose the entire off-season, from late September until around May. Every part of [offseason] has its own personality: Autumn brings relief after harvest, winter offers complete peace, and spring fills the island with optimism as nature comes back to life, just before the new season begins. What do you love most about being there during the off-season? Santorini has two completely different lives. One is the island that millions of visitors experience during summer. The other begins in October and lasts until spring. That is the Santorini only the people who live here truly get to know. By the end of harvest [in September], both the vineyard and I are exhausted. After weeks of living on adrenaline, my body is desperately asking for rest. Around the end of September, the evenings become cooler; you need a sweater after sunset, the days grow shorter, and the strong summer meltemi (the Aegean wind) gives way to a gentler, northern wind. Everything feels softer. All the locals are tired after another demanding [tourism] season, but at the same time, there is a feeling of optimism. Restaurants and bars begin to close for the season, and that's when the closing parties begin. Friends you haven't seen for months suddenly reappear. You don't even need to make plans; you know you'll see them somewhere during a closing party. Who’s around this time of year? Is it all locals? Greek domestic visitors? Are there any travelers at all? During autumn, you'll still find some travelers, but they are completely different from the summer crowds. They usually come looking for a quieter side of Santorini. They enjoy walking, hiking, discovering wineries and small villages, instead of rushing from one attraction to the next. By the end of November, even the last seasonal workers have left the island. We have a saying here that the last boat has sailed. From that moment on, Santorini belongs almost entirely to its locals. Conversations become longer, people have time for each other again, and everyday life feels calmer. I think that's the Santorini most visitors never get the chance to experience. What’s notable about the locals in Santorini? Do they have any of their own unique traditions or a reputation amongst Greeks for anything in particular? One thing that has always impressed me about the locals is how deeply everyday life is connected to the Orthodox Church and its traditions. Almost every small chapel on the island has its own patron saint, and every saint's feast day is celebrated with a panigiri, a traditional village festival. During the summer, many of these celebrations continue late into the night with traditional music, dancing, and plenty of local wine. What I also find fascinating is that many of the locals still organize their year around the feast days of the saints. They won't say, "I'll start pruning in late November." They'll say, "I'll start after Saint Philip's Day and I have to finish before Saint Alexius's Day." That's how they measure time. It's a tradition that has been passed down from generation to generation, and it's still very much alive today. Where would we find you eating during this time? During the off-season, you will most likely find me at Pentozali, a traditional taverna that serves authentic mezze from both Santorini and Crete. I absolutely love it for its relaxed atmosphere, its genuine food, and its people. What I appreciate most during this time of year is that it becomes a gathering spot almost exclusively for locals. It is very common for me to run into someone who has just finished a hard day's work in the vineyards. We’ll sit down together for a glass of wine and a little chat, with absolutely no rushing around. What’s the seasonal dish to order at this time of year? If you are lucky and the spring timing is right, the dish to order is definitely an omelette with wild asparagus. It’s a rare treat because you can't just find it every day; it completely depends on whether someone woke up early in the morning and gathered the wild asparagus fresh from the countryside. Another staple that is almost always on the table is our traditional Santorini fava topped with sautéed onions. It is incredibly simple, but when cooked properly, you truly don't need anything more. Are there any areas of the island that really come alive during the off season? As the summer venues close, the life of the island doesn't disappear; it just shifts to the places where people actually live year-round. Areas like Karterados and Messaria become the real hubs. They are central points on the island that stay busy and full of life all year. The local closing parties of fall range from wild gatherings by the beach bars to more laid-back evenings in traditional cafés and small local hangouts. Later, in the winter, as people begin gathering more at homes, these central areas remain the heart of our social life. But if you want to talk about a completely hidden side of Santorini that comes alive in a very quiet, spiritual way, it’s the Askitaria. These are old stone monk lodgings perched right on the edge of the cliff on the mountain between Perissa and Kamari. In the spring, you will find many locals sitting there for hours, doing nothing in particular but gazing out at the endless blue, the passing ships, and distant islands like Anafi, Ios, and Anydro. How does the weather change the destination during this time of year, and what are the (dis)advantages of that? Autumn and winter are much warmer and sunnier than most people expect. They bring a rare, beautiful peace. For us winemakers, even the rain is a blessing, not bad weather. It’s a relief to see the vines finally get a drink after months of summer drought. The main disadvantage—if you can call it that—is the unpredictability. March, for instance, is a strange and stubborn month with strong winds, cold snaps, and constant weather shifts. What does a perfect Saturday in the off-season look like to you? My perfect off-season Saturday starts slowly, without checking my watch—perhaps walking through the narrow paths of the caldera in Fira or Oia. Later, I would meet up with friends. There is always an excuse for an impromptu barbecue, either with meat or, even better, fresh seafood; almost every group of friends here has at least one good fisherman. We would share a coffee or wine, talk without any rush, and if we are lucky, someone might randomly pick up a lute, a tsampouna, or a violin. No big plans or appointments needed, just letting the night unfold naturally. Do you have any favorite activities during this time of year? My favorite activities are tied to the water. The Aegean is ideal for kitesurfing due to its consistent winds, and as paradoxical as it may sound, specific weather systems often generate great surf here during the winter. We have a small but tight-knit community of surfers on the island, and when the conditions are right, we all head out into the water. Even though the water is still cold, the feeling is incredible. Sometimes you might even catch people paddleboarding inside the Caldera with absolutely no sea traffic, no cruise ships or catamarans, just you traveling parallel to the old quarries and rusty iron piers that hold the island’s history. This article was originally published in Condé Nast Traveller UK.

item.title: How to Make the Most of Greece’s Shoulder Season, According to Condé Nast Traveler Specialists
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.17
This is part of Off Season Greece, a collection of guides highlighting the year-round appeal of Greece's most popular destinations, courtesy of our favorite local tastemakers. In this edition, we speak to Condé Nast Traveler's Top Travel Specialists about how to decide which off-season destination in Greece for you. As we continue to spread the good word of traveling outside of summer—peak season for most destinations, but most of all European—let us convince you that this advice is especially prescient for Greece, which is also magical in late fall, winter (skiing, anyone?), and early spring. But you might ask, how do you even travel to Greece in the off season? This country of many island groups, from Aegean to Ionian, is not just to be experienced at its peak in the summer, when ferries are run to and fro, and your social feed becomes awash with selfies from white-plastered Mykonos. Nay—Όχι! For reasons climate- and crowd-related, certain sides of Greece shine brighter when the brutal Grecian sun lets up and Zeus’s calming clouds roll in, when you actually have breathing room at the Parthenon and can even potentially commune with Athena herself in the soft winter light of Athens. Or, hey, why not just take advantage of the cheaper hotel rates and airfare while most families are wrapped up at school? For these reasons and more, locals and in-the-know visitors know that, in Hellas, “off season” truly means “game on.” To learn what it takes to make the most out of the off season, we tapped some of our favorite Condé Nast Traveler Top Travel Specialists who are experts on visiting Greece: Julie Durso of Scott Dunn, Lisa Kusak of Kusak & Co., Emily Rister of Original Travel, and Laura Plansky of Audley Travel. Here they tell us the pros of visiting outside of summer, where to take a city break, and what to pack so that you’re prepared for your own off-season odyssey to Greece. Why you should visit Greece in the off season After an entirely too-hot Eurosummer this year (every year now, it seems), the pros of visiting Greece in the cooler off season have never been more evident. “Visiting off season is perfect for avoiding crowds and the heat,” says Rister of Original Travel. “Generally, Greece can be quite mild, even in winter, so it’s still pleasant to visit and be out and about exploring. Cultural sites are much quieter and you don’t have to book restaurants weeks in advance.” Rister also says that hotel rates massively drop at this time of year, outside of the peak summer travel months, so the off season is a chance to experience luxurious properties for a fraction of the cost. Beyond the weather and value-for-money factor, Kusak of Kusak & Co. says there’s a human element too: “In the off season you find a certain authenticity. With fewer people present, you can get a real connection with the local community—the pace is gentler for everyone.” To top it off, the off season is perhaps the best time for foodie travelers, given the bounty of the winter harvest. “The olive harvest runs from November into December, and some estates will welcome visitors to watch or take part,” Kusak explains. “Citrus season follows in the Peloponnese and Crete, when the orange and lemon groves are at their most vibrant." Of course, no rose is without its thorns: many establishments in Greece do close for the winter, and it’s not exactly prime time for beachgoers—so be sure to calibrate your expectations to cultural and culinary adventures. “It's not the peak season for swimming and boating, if guests have that as a priority,” says Durso of Scott Dunn. While there are locales where restaurants remain open year-round thanks to universities and locals (Athens, Corfu, and Crete among them) it depends where you are: “Many restaurants will also begin closing for the season, so I tend to recommend resorts with restaurants on property, so guests don't feel like they're missing out” if the small tavernas, cafés, and bakeries are shuttered until the spring. The cultural and culinary prowess of Greece in the off season First, the culture and history buffs will greatly appreciate Greece in the off season, Planksy says, because fewer people crowd the main tourist sites and the sun isn’t beating down on travelers as aggressively. Lines are shorter, and there’s more room to breathe in museums and at archaeological locations like the Acropolis or the Agora in Athens. Plus you’ll be able to relish the hike up to the Parthenon without melting in the heat. Of course don’t just waltz in anywhere without tickets or reservations—traveling in the off season still requires the usual due diligence as a traveler. You’ll just have less competition for tables at the best restaurants in Athens. “This time of year is also great for guests who are excited to interact more with locals in the small towns,” Durso says, “those who prefer a relaxed pace rather than enduring crowded tourist areas during high season.” Whether you go to romantic Nafplio in the Peloponnese with its neoclassical mansions or seaside Galaxidi with its cobblestoned alleys, locals will be pleasantly surprised to see out-of-towners passing through, happy for your business and company in the off-season. As Kusak puts it, the off season in Greece is for “someone who wants authenticity and a genuine connection to the place, rather than just boat days and beaches.” There’s no shame in wanting boat days and beaches, of course—we at Traveler love partying and seaside time when we go to Greece too. But just know that if that’s what you’re looking for, summer really is your best bet, Durso says, when all the restaurants and beach clubs are open. How to do it: practical tips When visiting Greece in the off season, one of the first things we need to talk about is the climate. “As the weather starts to shift, you get more wind and cooler evenings,” says Durso. “So it’s important to pack layers,” like lightweight sweaters, linen that you can wear on top of each other, a rain jacket, maybe a little bit of cashmere while you’re at it. Take it from me: Even in May of this year on Corfu, I found myself reaching for my denim jacket more than once, even on a beach day. The next thing to be mindful of is the country’s schedule, from the timetables for ferries to the opening hours of restaurants, tourist and archaeological sites, and even whole islands. “Ferry schedules are reduced in the off season and the weather is more likely to impact those journeys,” says Plansky. Don’t go to Greece in the off-season hoping for the typical island-hopping style vacation, because many of the smaller islands close between November to April. “So it’s better to explore the mainland of Greece and some of the bigger islands like Crete, Corfu, and Santorini during that time,” she says. And double check with your hotel if they’ll be open during your visit. Chances are that a hotel won’t accept your booking if they see that you’re in town when they’re not, but it never hurts to be sure. “It is worth planning around what is genuinely open rather than where you want to go on the map,” Kusak says. “This is where I lean on my team in Greece. They know which properties are running, which restaurants stay open through the winter, and where a January afternoon is best spent. It isn't information you can always find online, and it changes from year to year.” Are you, conveniently enough, hoping to spend a January afternoon in Greece? “A January afternoon in Athens is best spent on foot,” Kusak asserts. “I’d wander a few of the neighborhoods—Plaka, Monastiraki, Thisio, Kolonaki—just to get a feel for how the city lives, pausing at a small shop for a warm koulouri or a slice of spanakopita along the way. Then the Acropolis, which in the off-season is blissfully unhurried. With the crowds thinned, there's room to take it in properly.” Where (else) to go in Greece in the off season In the off season, while many places in some smaller islands and destinations may “shut down,” Greece does not close uniformly. Athens, the rest of the mainland, and many of the larger islands carry on much as usual. In addition to Athens, Corfu, Crete, Santorini, and Paros—as recommended by locals we admire and trust—our Top Travel Specialists also gave their own additional recommendations for where to go in Greece in the off season: Thessaloniki and the Peloponnese. Thessaloniki: Culinary heritage on the Thermaic Gulf Waterfront Thessaloniki is designated a UNESCO City of Gastronomy, with a dining scene informed by a long history as a crossroads of ancient and modern trade. Given its position in Northern Greece, Thessaloniki has played host to Greeks, Ottoman Turks, Sephardic Jews, Armenians, and Slavs for centuries, resulting in meals and dishes that pull influences from all over the continent. And because Thessaliniki is also the second largest city in Greece, it has more in common with Athens schedule-wise and stays open even after the summer is over. Kusak has two restaurant recommendations: “For something traditional, I suggest The Rouga. It’s a good place to share meze and a few Greek classics. For a quieter, more polished evening, there’s Olympos Naoussa inside the ON Residence, a Small Luxury Hotels of the World hotel. It sits in a restored heritage building overlooking the Thermaic Gulf, and suits a special occasion or a last-night-before-we-go-home dinner.” As for where to stay, Rister often books clients at The Modernist Thessaloniki set in a 1920s heritage building; The Excelsior, just a block away from the harbor; and Electra Palace Thessaloniki, a grande dame on Aristotelous Square. When it comes to cultural excursions, Rister recommends a walking tour of the city with a private guide—“Great for fans of Alexander the Great.” and a day trip to Vergina, home to the tomb of Philip II of Macedon, Alexander the Great’s father. Rister at Original Travel can help put these offerings together for those who are keen. The Peloponnese: Homeric outdoor adventure In lieu of the typical Greek islands vacay, a road trip that traces the coast of the rugged and mountainous Peloponnese peninsula could scratch that itch to be near some water, as long as you’re okay with the fact that it may be too cold to go in. Kusak recommends a few seaside towns in the Peloponnese: “On a rocky islet just off the coast, Monemvasia is a medieval town you reach almost by surprise, where you can wander the cobbled streets and stay in one of the restored stone houses,” she says. “And Pylos gathers around a waterfront square and an old natural harbor. It’s the way into the Costa Navarino resort area, with its beaches, golf, and resorts, though Pylos holds its own quiet history and lends itself to a slower coastal stay.” Kusak also recommends Nafplio for its proximity to Athens—under two hours apart by car—and the beautiful Venetian architecture in the area, souvenirs from when Venice held trading posts in Greece. Plansky also loves to send travelers to Nafplio: “It has a little bit of everything—history, culture, coastal beauty, plenty of food and wine. And there are some fantastic sites nearby including Mycenae, Epidavros, Ancient Corinth, and the Nemea wineries that are easy day trips.” Where to stay If you’re a fiend for a good hotel, Durso recommends Amanzoe, considered by Aman junkies to be one of the brand’s very best properties. “Plus it stays open through the second week of November, offering a luxurious option at sometimes less than half its peak-season rates,” Durso says. Conveniently it’s also close to villages like Nafplio and historic sites like Mycenae. “Another lovely property is Kinsterna in Monemvasia, a boutique hotel with fantastic farm-to-table cuisine,” Durso says. And for those seeking quiet, Rister suggests an easy-going stay in some of the most relaxing spa hotels in the Peloponnese for some true rest—Euphoria Retreat in Mystras and Manna Arcadia. The former is a wellness retreat located near epic Sparta and the UNESCO-listed Archaeological Site of Mystras, or castro (fortress), for those who like their relaxation with a side of historic adventure; the latter is surrounded by moody fir forests ideal for hiking, giving it the feel of a remote getaway. “They can be easily combined with a city break in Athens at any time of the year,” Rister says.

item.title: RF Kuang's New Novel Takes On the Angst of a Diaspora Kid on a Study-Abroad Trip to Taipei
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.13
In RF Kuang’s latest book Taipei Story, the genre of the campus novel outgrows its name. The novel follows Chinese-American college freshman Lily Chen, who leaves the pale, male, and Yale environs of New Haven, Connecticut, for an intensive Mandarin-language program in Taipei for the summer. While her own family has never stepped foot in Taiwan, Lily holds onto the belief that perfecting her Mandarin will finally reconcile the shortcomings of being a diaspora kid. And when it came to choosing a place to study the language, traveling to Taiwan conveniently didn’t require her to apply for a visa. But on this quixotic mission to achieve total fluency, she finds that the gulf between her and her complicated family history won’t simply mend itself through diligent study. Her presumptions quickly unravel as she seeks answers in the gaps between economy seats on the flight from Boston to Taipei; in the uncertain, stilting words of Chinese heritage speakers; and in arthouse cinemas and concert halls she’s drawn to for the promise of blending in. From the seasonally inappropriate hot springs of Beitou to the glossy, souvenir-flogging halls of Taipei Taoyuan International Airport, the plot of this coming-of-age story doesn’t shy away from the uncomfortable realities of traveling abroad. Compounded by the sudden passing of Lily’s grandfather—which renders her initial motivation to study Mandarin moot—these follies only deepen beneath a veil of complicated mourning. And yet, they are also softened and forgiven with a grace that comes uniquely from allowing ourselves to be vulnerable in foreign places. Condé Nast Traveler recently spoke with Kuang about how home, identity, and being split between two places inspired Taipei Story, which is available in bookstores now. This interview has been edited and condensed for length and clarity. Walk us through your research itinerary for Taipei Story. The first place I looked was personal experience. When I started jotting down notes for what would become this book, I didn't know what it was going to be. I was just trying to make legible a tough time in my life when my Gong Gong passed away and I was in Taiwan. I was also in an intensive language program where I was wandering aimlessly around Taipei, meditating on [concepts of] home and cultural alienation. I wasn't walking around with a research agenda. I was just following crowds into places to see what they were seeing. If a long line of people was swarming, I would just join it. I would end up at screenings of movies I'd never heard of, or bookstores that I didn't know existed because I felt so blank, confused, and empty. I wanted somebody else to show me the answer to, “what is your city?” and if I became a ghost in its wake, was there a way I could totally erase myself? A lot of the descriptions in the novel where Lily ends up going to a place by accident, like the National Concert Hall, are places I also encountered by accident. Then, I started thinking about turning all those notes into an exaggerated, fictionalized version of what this experience would be—like if I were even younger and more dim-witted about how the world works. I read a lot of the major modern Taiwanese authors [like Kaori Li, Bai Xianyong, Chen Yingzhen, Wu Ming-yi, and Yang Shaung-zi—all mentioned in the author’s note and available in English translation] and wondered how they were thinking about home, identity, and being split between their mainland cultural heritage, and what it meant to be Taiwanese. How does this novel interface with—the sometimes impossible—expectations of homecoming? I'm fascinated with fantasies of homecoming and the narratives we buy into about how certain cultural experiences can return you to the fold. A lot of Chinese heritage speakers end up getting these flattened experiences in the US that feel like touch points, but are actually silly ways to reconnect—distilled cultural simulations such as Lunar New Year, red envelope parties, and film screenings. I say this not to mock diasporic kids; it makes total sense. You get so little, so you take whatever you can have, even if it's not region-specific or what your parents experienced. In Lily's case, I'm fascinated by the promises of heritage speaker-study abroad programs (editor’s note: these are linguistic immersion programs designed for students who grew up in households speaking a second language) because they hold so much promise and meaning for many people attending them. With Taiwan in particular, if you think about it just on the logical level, every step of this premise that you could, as a Chinese-American, go to Taiwan, to study Mandarin, to feel closer to your family on the mainland—is crazy. Lily's family has never been to Taiwan. She's the only person who's ever stepped foot there until her mom has a layover. When she finally gets there, she starts learning all the ways in which she is so wrong and how her experiences of Chineseness and the trajectory of her family history has absolutely nothing to do with Taiwan. In the end, she is a little more aware of this complexity and moves towards a more genuine, honest encounter of a strange place. She's like, I'm a foreigner, this is a weird summer, and maybe that's okay. In what ways does foreignness, or a lack of fluency, act as a source of fuel for travel and exploration in this novel? I definitely think [feeling out of place] is generative because I’ve felt like an outsider culturally for most of my life. My family immigrated [to the US from Guangzhou when Kuang was four-years-old], and I never felt like I quite belonged in the world of Dallas, Texas. I was a pretty happy kid, but when you're on the periphery, observing how people behave, I think you just get more perceptive. When I go back to China, that’s also not home, which is not a unique perspective. I think almost every immigrant kid feels this way. When I'm in China, I am looking at my family, and I observe cultural codes that they're following, and I have to figure out how these rules work because I didn't grow up understanding them innately. Being reflective about all of this makes you a good writer. In Lily's case I don't think she perceives her bumbling and ignorance as virtues. For her, it’s a barrier between her and the rest of the world. Because she's so afraid of getting things wrong, she never asks for help and never willing to embarrass herself. The ethical argument that the book is making is that embarrassment is really good for you. To admit, “I don't know what's going on,” and also “somebody helped me,” is an attitude I wish we all embraced more, not just when we're traveling, but in our entire lives. I find it a strength, and Lily finds it a weakness, and by the end of the book, she's at least accepted that she's gonna mess up, and she might as well own it. From the Poppy War trilogy to your last novel Katabasis, you often take on the perspective of being a student. Why return to the eyes of an undergraduate for this story? This book was very different because it's the first book of mine where the protagonists weren't growing up with me. When I was working on the Poppy War trilogy, I was a teenager, and they're teenagers, then they're undergrads, grad students, and in their late-20s. I was writing very reflexively to try to understand the world from my vantage point in life, but I had a couple of life changes in the past few years that made me more interested in going back. With the maturity of turning 30, I have more comfort in making fun of the person I used to be. When I was writing Taipei Story, it was like, I could write a memoir of what I experienced, or I could make things even more ridiculous, even more embarrassing, and reach back to the person I was when I was 18 going to Beijing for the first time and overwhelmed with everything I didn't know. The key to writing from the point-of-view of adolescence is not from this position of condescension that the youths are so silly, but to be kind to your younger self and recognize that all of your insecurities, all the things that you were failing at, everything that you got wrong, are deeply hilarious and also a really shared experience. There's a lot of humanity in cringe. By setting a story in modern-day Taipei, the narrative acknowledges Taiwanese-Chinese geopolitics, and beyond that, the country’s past with Japanese colonialism, the Chinese Civil War. How did you want to depict Taipei as a city with those layered histories? I wanted to be really cautious here, because I'm not Taiwanese. I'm not an expert in Taiwanese history or literature. As I pointed out in the author's note, this is not a voice from the inside but the very filtered perception of an American teenager who’s learning about all of this for the first time. I did want to poke gentle fun at the way that people generally take Western ideological frameworks that are very binary and project them onto local histories with no attention to what locals are actually saying. There's the first chapter where her little cohort of friends are running around the city, and there’s a pecking order based on assumptions about race. People would ask her where should we go? What should we eat? And she’d always pretend to know the answers and go Google them in the bathroom. They do the same thing when they're at Chiang Kai-Shek Memorial Hall trying to understand, is he a good guy or a bad guy? Is he like George Washington? Should we be taking selfies with him? I wanted to give the experience of somebody who feels like they ought to be an expert by virtue of the ethnicity that they were born into, but who’s actually totally detached from genuine knowledge of the place or history. How did grief form your characterization of Taipei? [When Lily’s grandfather passed] it was a snapping moment for her. Up until that point, she is trying to slot all of her experiences into this predetermined narrative that this is getting her closer to the person she could have been if her family had never left China. After her grandfather passes, she is thrown into this weird grief and confusion, and she gives up on that goal altogether. She recognizes the futility of trying to go back and becoming a version of herself that never existed. Paradoxically, this frees her up to take in the things she closed her mind off to before. Now, she's okay with being a tourist. She goes on these Klook experiences [to Pinglin Tea Museum and Yehliu Geopark]. She’s on a bus with American families from Philly doing all the canned, predetermined activities just thinking, “oh, this is fun,” and learning a lot. Despite all the complex grief that is in this novel, it’s also very funny. Is Taipei a place that is particularly funny to you or has its own language of humor that you wanted to capture here? I think every place has surprising, inexplicable quirks if you know how to pay attention to them. One in particular I'm obsessed with is Taiwan English. I was inspired by a blog post by Tao Lin, an author who also wrote a novel called Taipei. It was just a series of pictures that he took walking around of ridiculous translations, and some of them are accurate on a very literal, character-by-character level, and some of them, I can't believe you would get this result if you ran it through any translation app. But it's not just in Taiwan either. You see it on the mainland. For instance, my mom was wearing a shirt, that just said, “GO FUCK” in repeating block letters. She bought it at a clothes market with her sister when she was in China, and she was only paying attention to the fabric, and she was like, “Oh, it's so lovely. Does this color look good on me?” and didn't register the text at all. I said, “Mom, do you know what that says?” She turned it inside out and wore it that way for the rest of the day.

item.title: Ready for a Euro Fall? Travel Experts Weigh In on the Best Destinations for 2026
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.81
Lower the beach club umbrellas and check on Dua Lipa: Euro summer is coming to an end. Maybe you, like Dua, went all in, losing track of days as you plunged in and out of the Mediterranean Sea. Or perhaps you didn’t get a chance to partake in Europe’s sunniest season, and the last few months have involved lots of envious scrolls on Instagram. Whether you still have room for more, or are making up for lost time, hold on to that last bit of PTO, because we’re entering what’s arguably an even more rewarding travel moment. Fall in Europe brings with it brisk temperatures that make sightseeing an utter joy, thinner crowds that leave room for locals, and an opportunity to experience cities in their most authentic light. You might find yourself falling in love with the version of Vienna that’s settling down after the tourist rush, or chasing new destinations entirely, whether that’s Denmark’s North Zealand coast or Italy’s “green heart” of Umbria. “I’m seeing people looking far more off the beaten path this season,” says Kimberly Davis of Trouvaille Travel. “Even if they want to travel to major European cities, it’s places like Copenhagen rather than the typical London, Paris, or Rome.” To help you plan your autumnal sojourn, we gathered expert-suggested itineraries, from the food haven that is the Basque Country to the moody Irish countryside. Below, the seven best places to travel to in Europe this fall. Copenhagen and the Danish Riviera, Denmark “Copenhagen just makes sense to me in the fall,” says Christine Andraus of Partenza Travel. “The food, the bakeries, candles everywhere, beautiful design, people actually embracing being cozy instead of trying to pretend it’s still summer.” Andraus is right: There’s no better place to embrace hygge than Denmark’s capital, where afternoons might look like strolling through golden-hued Assistens Cemetery or bundling up in a fisherman’s sweater at a harborside food hall like Reffen or Broens. Davis says she’s seeing clients opt for more design-forward hotels—think Hotel Sanders instead of Hotel D’Angleterre—to better lean into the city’s artsy edge. For a more comprehensive trip, Andraus suggests adding a couple of nights in North Zealand, otherwise known as the Danish Riviera, where historic palaces like Shakespeare-famous Kronborg Castle collide with vast forests and wild coastlines—plus, of course, the seaside stunner that is the Louisiana Museum of Modern Art. Where to stay in Copenhagen and the Danish Riviera: Vienna, Austria Things are changing in Vienna, the old-world city Nadine Fedorenko at Fora Travel cites as a top destination this fall. For the past few years, the capital has been welcoming a new crop of contemporary museums and galleries, restaurants moving beyond the farm-to-fork template, and a few luxury hotels, including a Mandarin Oriental and Rosewood. While Viennese gardens are lovely to stroll around any time of year, there’s added romance with a little chill in the air. This is the ideal time to visit vineyards just outside the city limits for glasses of biodynamic wine, house a schnitzel at an old-fashioned café, or catch a screening of The Third Man at the cozy Burg Kino movie theater. And while the city might be embracing change, Fedorenko points out that its cultural and artistic history forever looms: “Hotel Sacher turned 150 this year, the Albertina Museum turned 250, and even Mozart celebrated a big birthday [his 270th]!” Where to stay in Vienna: San Sebastian, Spain For travelers intent on planning their trips around food, there’s no better time to visit San Sebastian, a city with one of the highest numbers of Michelin-starred restaurants per square mile and a rich bar culture. In the fall, temperatures hover comfortably in the 60s, and quick spurts of rain lend the city an atmospheric mist. “San Sebastian in October gives you pintxos, the coast, Rioja nearby, and temperatures where you actually want to walk around all day,” Andraus says. This fall also marks the 50th anniversary of New Basque Cuisine—it’s being celebrated at San Sebastián Gastronomika (October 5–7), which will host the legendary chefs who pioneered avant-garde Basque cooking in the ‘70s as they engage attendees in masterclasses and tastings. As for where to stay, Andraus points travelers to Hotel Maria Cristina if you want to be right in town, or Akelarre for its world-renowned restaurant. Where to stay in San Sebastian: Midland Region, Ireland If you’re into the occult, there’s a certain draw to fall in the Irish countryside, where Samhain, the earliest version of Halloween, was first celebrated. Serious spooksters might visit the sacred sites of County Meath, including the ancient Hill of Ward and Hill of Tara, where ancient Celts first lit fires over 2,000 years ago to scare off spirits, or stick around for the holiday’s biggest celebration, the annual Púca Festival (October 29–November 1). Perhaps carrying a copy of Bram Stoker’s Dracula in your pocket while taking in the moody landscapes is more your vibe: “Ireland is one of those places where a little bit of weather almost makes the trip better,” Andraus says. “Give me a gorgeous country house, boots, a long walk, a fire, a great dinner, and maybe a little rain, and I’ll be very happy.” She recommends checking in at Ballyfin Demesne for a romantic, old-school stay, as well as combining the countryside with a few days exploring the island’s remote western region, from the counties of Clare and Mayo to the Connemara Coast, where you’ll encounter dramatic limestone formations and glacial lakes. Where to stay in the Midland and western region: Paris, France There’s something to be said about traveling to a familiar favorite in the off-season. When you visit Paris in the fall, you’ll be treated to temperatures that sit between the mid-50s and low-60s, shorter museum lines, and a few more vacant pistachio-green chairs at your favorite public parks. Known as the “rentreé,” the French version of back to school, this is when residents return to the city after their summer holidays, and everything comes alive again, from local shops to museum exhibits—including recent favorites like “Auguste Bartholdi and Mary Cassatt" at the Musée d’Orsay and “Cézanne and Us” at the Grand Palais. “Paris is always a hit, especially now with Celine Dion singing there this season,” Fedorenko says, referencing the star’s residency at the Paris La Défense Arena (running until October 17). There’s no shortage of excellent hotels to stay in either—like the affordable Hotel Rochechouart, which starts at around $300 per night—but for a trip you’ll simply never forget, consider renting an apartment with a view of the Eiffel Tower. Where to stay in Paris: The Dolomites, Italy “Everyone thinks of the Dolomites for skiing or summer hiking, but fall there is spectacular,” Andraus says. “The larches turn this crazy golden color, the air is crisp, the summer crowds are gone, and you can still spend your days outside before coming back to an amazing spa and a long dinner.” Be sure to plan your trip around mid-to-late October, when autumnal foliage is at its peak, and hit hiking trails that come alive with color, like the Croda da Lago Circuit and its reflective alpine lake, Lago di Federa. Or, visit the famous emerald-green waters of Lago di Braies when it’s not overrun with summer crowds. When it comes to where to stay, there’s an abundance of spa-forward hotels specializing in hydrotherapy and treatments that take inspiration from the surrounding nature. “I love Hotel Hubertus here—it’s dramatic and incredibly beautiful, but still has that cozy Alpine feeling,” Andraus says. “This is one I recommend to clients who want nature and wellness but still want a real five-star experience.” Where to stay in the Dolomites: Umbria, Italy Andraus believes Italy’s “green heart” is finally having its moment. Umbria, the underrated, landlocked region in central Italy, is famous for its lush landscapes, medieval palaces, and rustic trattorias. “I plan so much Italy, and I’m definitely seeing more clients who have either already done Tuscany or just want something a little quieter and less ‘on the circuit,’” she says. “Fall is when Umbria really shines—truffles, wine, olive harvests, tiny medieval towns, fireplaces, and amazing food.” Spend your days visiting museums, from the National Gallery of Umbria to the contemporary Fondazione Burri; visit the famous basilica in Assisi; or hike in the National Park of Montecucco. The region has also seen a growing interest in estates-turned-hotels: “Castello di Reschio is the dream here,” Andraus says. “It’s obviously a splurge, but it’s one of those rare hotels where I could happily send someone for four nights and almost tell them not to make plans.” Where to stay in Umbria:

item.title: The World’s Most Beautiful Libraries Worth Traveling For
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.61
The most beautiful libraries have long been more than places to check out books, though some make a particularly compelling case for lingering. As a demand for third places to gather outside of home or work continues to grow, libraries are having a moment as prime spots for idling, browsing, and simply taking a break from the bustle beyond their opulent doors. Libraries have taken on an array of forms around the world, as reading rooms that have been tucked into former monasteries, designed as futuristic cultural hubs, and constructed in the heart of the California redwoods. While the books are still the main attraction, it certainly doesn’t hurt to be surrounded by ornate frescoes or unexpected nooks that make you want to stay a while longer. From Colombia to Qatar, these 11 libraries are worth building into your next trip, whether you are architecture-obsessed or longing to sit down in a picturesque setting with a new read. This article has been updated with new information since its original publish date.

item.title: The Quiet Magic of Greece in the Off Season
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.58
Few eras of Greek history compare to the ancient times that the country has become so synonymous with—the cinematic fables of Odysseus, comic-book lore of Leonidas, and philosophic creeds of Socrates are ever-present in pop culture. But anyone who’s been to Hellas in the past few years can tell you that something new is brewing here—current-day Greece is coming close to a similar precipice, one that could be nearly as definitive as the Bronze Age, as visitors arrive in droves higher than ever before. Arrivals to the nation of 10 million people were up by 38% in the first few months of 2026, the highest increase on the continent for that period by far (Italy was second, with a 21% rise). Now, more than ever, it feels like everyone is planning a seafaring escape or mountain adventure to Athens and the islands—or, if you’re in-the-know, to the serene coastal towns of the Peloponnese peninsula or the northern Aegean’s sparkling Thermaic Gulf. One decade after the country’s financial crisis peaked, and a half decade since the pandemic-era halt in tourism that had so many here pleading for the long-despised cruise ships to return, you would think this is good news for a state as tourism-dependent as Greece. And you could be right—but the unfortunate reality, according to the Bank of Greece, is that the crescendo coincides with mounting climate disasters that threaten the infrastructure of a nation still in the throes of recovery; a particularly harrowing warning ahead of this year’s El Niño; not to mention during their Mediterranean neighbors' unprecedented fire seasons. The seasonal pressure has become a balancing act. The good news, though, is that summer is far from the only time to visit. Outside the grip of sweltering summer heat lies some of Greece’s most delicious adventures: tasting early spring’s olive oils straight from the groves right after harvest; fall parties with small-island locals celebrating another season of panigiria wrapped; perusing the treasures of Athens’ open-air ruins in the soft, pre-winter light. There is so much more to Greece than the postcard islands—and the packed ferries to get to them—and with the mainland about to have its moment in the sun (we’re looking at you, Christopher Nolan), there’s no better time than the off-season to uncover every corner’s most spectacular self—the one without the heaving crowds. To prove it, we’ve tapped the best local creators to share how they do it, and how you can, too, siga siga (more slowly). —Shannon McMahon, senior destinations editor Over the last 30 years, Nikos Tsepetis has made Ammos Hotel (and its beloved on-site Red Jane Bakery) one of Crete’s most talked-about hotels. Born and raised in Chania, the owner’s joyful, design-led approach to hospitality is rooted in his hometown, with 80% of his staff also locals. From its high-quality cuisine to its warm, home-away-from-home atmosphere, Ammos reflects Tsepetis’s deep connection to Chania. Here, he shares why spring is his favorite time to experience the city. For Dutch artist Christiane Smit, a vacation on Paros in 2008 changed the course of her life. Drawn instinctively to the Cycladic island, she stayed and has lived in villages across Paros ever since. Today, she runs a ceramics atelier in Lefkes and owns minimalist clifftop villa Moonhouse, while restoring a century-old stone house in Kostos. Here, Smit shares the shoulder-season pleasures that keep her on the island year-round, and where to eat and stay. For winemaker Michael Kouloglou, moving to Santorini from Greece's mainland 11 years ago was an easy choice: “It is the mecca of Greek white wine.” Since then, he has worked across the island’s wineries before launching Orycton, a small-batch Assyrtiko made with grapes from old vines. Now based in quiet Monolithos, Kouloglou has lived throughout Santorini, gaining an intimate understanding of its villages, landscapes, and rhythms. Here, he shares why autumn is his favorite season to explore the island. Greek family recipes are often passed down by instinct rather than instruction—a pinch here, a glug there, learned at the kitchen table. Food writer Anastasia Miari has spent nearly a decade documenting these dishes and the older generations and remote villages that have kept them alive. Her cooking celebrates Greece’s culinary traditions, while her latest book, Mediterranea, expands the journey across the region, from Moroccan tagines and Turkish breakfasts to Sicilian pasta. “Alive. That’s how Athens feels to me,” says Agapi Sbokou, co-owner and CEO of Greek hotel brand Phāea. Having lived in the capital since she was 18, Sbokou has watched the city continually evolve, while retaining its irresistible energy. For her, the joy of visiting somewhere lies in understanding its local rhythm. Here, she shares why autumn is so magical in Athens, alongside some of her favorite places to explore in the city. Lead editors: Sarah Allard, Shannon McMahon, Arati Menon, Lisa Riehl Writers: Shannon McMahon, Chadner Navarro, Noo Saro-Wiwa, Olivia Morelli Visuals and social media: Sophie Knight, Mercedes Bleth, Lucy Bruton Syndication editors: Kat Chen, Skyli Alvarez This article was originally published in Condé Nast Traveller UK.

item.title: From Kendall Jenner to the Clooneys: This is Where the A-list Stays for the Venice Film Festival
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.40
For over 80 years now the Venice International Film Festival has attracted the world's most glamorous and famous crowd. In the 1950s, it saw Brigitte Bardot pose for paparazzi while sitting on grass, and Elizabeth Taylor take a dip in the lido at Hotel Excelsior Venice. Fast forward to today and it's just as star-studded, with the 83rd Venice International Film Festival hosting an array of actors, supermodels and musicians, from Laura Dern to Robert Pattinson, Irina Shayk and Liam Gallagher. Much of the red carpet action takes place at Hotel Excelsior Venice, which has hosted the main event since 1932. Notably, following a three-year closure, the hotel reopened last year (2025), to reveal a grand renovation and thus many of this year's attendees – Kate Mara, Claire Foy, Maggie Gyllenhaal – have also chosen to stay in the boldly striped suites. It's not the only top hotel in Venice that is known to host film festival attendees. The A-listers that prefer something more private often book into one of the 24 opulent rooms within Aman Venice – not only do the Clooneys love to stay here, they also married in the Palazzo Papadopoli location in 2014. To be even further removed and escape the flashes of paparazzi, Hotel Cipriani, A Belmond Hotel, Venice sits on the eastern tip of the Giudecca island. Its peaceful location has been a long- time favourite for the world's most famous stars, with previous guests including Sophia Loren, Cary Grant, and more recently Jennifer Lawrence and Lady Gaga.

item.title: Off-Season Greece: To Avoid the Crowds on Crete, Hike and Ski in Early Spring
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.25
This is part of Off-Season Greece, a collection of guides highlighting the year-round appeal of Greece's most popular destinations, courtesy of our favorite local tastemakers. In this edition, we speak to hotel owner Nikos Tsepetis. For 30 years, Nikos Tsepetis has run Ammos, one of the most talked-about hotels in Greece. The seaside boutique hotel in Chania, northwest Crete, is a manifestation of the man himself: joyful and design-focused with a commitment to high-quality cuisine (including his Red Jane Bakery) and local roots. Tsepetis’s improvisational approach to hospitality creates a home-away-from-home warmth that keeps many of his guests returning, year after year. Born and raised in Chania, Tsepetis is deeply connected to his hometown, which he believes is different from other towns in Crete, because “we are more international and welcoming to foreigners, and it's a multi-layered city." Yet, 80 percent of his staff are locals, he says. “It adds to the experience, because you always meet people who were born here, who remember the past, so there is this continuity." Here, Tsepetis tells us why spring is his favorite time of year in Chania. What would you say is the sweet spot time of the year to visit? Just before high season. April and early May are my favorite time of year because the climate is amazing. Chania is on the western end of Crete and is the prettiest part of the island because it's greener, and we still normally have snow on the Lefka Ori [White Mountains]—you can see them from the sea while swimming. In spring, everything is very fresh, everything is well painted; you can go to the villages and monasteries, and all the flowers are out. Also, spring often coincides with Easter, which is important in the Greek Orthodox religion. I don't care at all about religion, but it's still very spiritual and beautiful. What do you love most about being there during this season? It's less busy. The rain cleans everything and the snow melts, so we are greener than other parts of the island. Everything's fresh and new; you can feel the rejuvenation, so spring is a very sweet time. Who’s around this time of year? Traditionally, Chania benefited from the presence of foreigners, even before it became touristy. It’s very urban, with more than 100,000 permanent residents, so you have everyone from hipsters and freaks to lefties living here—not the expected Greek island crowd. It's always very lively, and what sets it apart from some other towns in Crete is that the locals are a driving force with a very loud voice. They are not here to serve the foreigners. Where would we find you eating during this time? My all-time favorite local is Evgonia Tavern. Only a very simple tavern, it has fish and meat in a non-fish environment. I love Periplous Restaurant for its unbeatable location at the beautiful Tanneries Hotel. It’s one of the old buildings by the water where they used to process leather. In spring we go to the villages, because it's still very mild and there aren’t too many people. I always go to Ntounias, a very old, well-known rural taverna in the middle of nowhere near Drakona in the mountains. There's a crazy guy there, Stelios Trilyrakis, who has been involved with slow food for 30 years. You don't know what you’ll eat or when you’ll eat it. It's very inexpensive, and he cultivates everything himself. In Greece, we love French fries. And Stelios makes amazing chips by cooking them in olive oil in a ceramic pot. What’s the seasonal dish to order at this time of year? We're famous for doing a traditional Tsoureki Easter brioche, a kind of braided bread that's sweet but not too sweet. Once a year we also eat a special soup called magiritsa made from lamb intestines, lungs, and liver. We normally eat it at home—it’s not so much a restaurant dish—but we do a very good one at Ammos. Also, Nyketerida is famous for it. Spring is about beans and greens—we have beautiful asparagus and the best artichokes—and goat roasted in the oven with potatoes, zucchini, and tomatoes. We also have a very famous dish called dakos, a barley rusk with tomato sauce and this amazing goat’s cheese called mizithra. One of the best places to eat it is Costas Cafeneion, a family-run cafe in village Maza, which is between Chania and Rethymnon. Are there any areas of the island that really come alive during the off-season? In January and February, people from around the world come here for the mountains and skiing, including the annual Pierra Creta ski mountaineering race. How does the weather change the destination during this time of year, and what are the (dis)advantages of that? Summer is very hot and can be dry, and then we have the winter, which is rainy. But in spring, the weather is cooler and you can hike, ski, and swim. The sea is actually colder in spring than in winter because of the snowmelt. What does a perfect Saturday in the off-season look like to you? I’m biased, but Saturday is a great day to hang out at my Red Jane Bakery early in the day. I think it's very pretty. At around 2:00 p.m., I’ll visit my small wine shop next to Red Jane, and I always have one cigarette per day with one glass of wine. On Saturdays, it gets busy and the crowd is very interesting. They’ll have wine with a sandwich in our beautiful, small yard. I also love hanging out at a small, humble taverna called Kafeneio Fix in the old Turkish neighborhood, or I’ll go to Tamam, an amazing taverna inside a beautiful Turkish hammam dating back to 1645.
