Spring is also the beginning of the open cinema season. My favorite open-air theater is Attikon. Another one, Kipos, shows mostly old Hitchcock-style films in a public garden created during the Ottoman era. If I want to have a final drink before going home, I’ll go to Fagotto, a jazz bar that has been there for 40 years. Do you have any favorite activities during this time of year? I love hiking all the way down to Chora Sfakion, a small coastal town in the south. From there, you can either take a boat or walk for an hour along a very steep and narrow path—not for the faint-hearted—to Sweetwater Beach, a tiny cove made up of very tiny pebbles. If you dig your hand in it, sweet water from the mountains comes out. This article was originally published in Condé Nast Traveller UK.

item.title: How a Homecoming to Jamaica Helped Author Marlon James Write 'The Disappearers'
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.21
This is Write Here, a column where authors and literary luminaries tell us about the travels they took to find inspiration and create their latest books. In this installment, Booker Prize-winning author Marlon James describes returning to his hometown of Kingston to write his new novel The Disappearers. In it, a group of queer men gathered to rehearse a play experience an anti-gay hate crime, and the story follows the survivors as they navigate the 1980s and ’90s in Jamaica. The riotous 640-page door stopper grapples with homophobia then and now, the lingering specter of colonialism, the tumult of the AIDS crisis, and frameworks of power that demand dominance or submission. To develop the Booker Prize-nominated book, James conducted research in Jamaica to better understand a queer history and heritage he had refused before coming out. Below, he describes how his travels across the Caribbean nation shaped his most personal work to date. “I went to Kingston in 2023 and 2024 to do research for The Disappearers. For my books, I like to interview dozens of people, especially when I'm writing about something I don't know a lot about. I grew up in Jamaica in the 1980s, but I didn’t experience queer life there—I was in the church, praying away the gay. So I looked into those years, but also from the early 2000s all the way back to the 1940s. I get curious about my characters’ lives before the novel even begins. Most of what I uncover in research never makes it directly into the book, but I just need to know for myself. To meet Jamaicans who could share their experiences in those eras, I spoke to local queer friends, and word just got around that I was looking. Because it’s a novel and not a documentary, a lot of people wanted to talk to me. They were very forthcoming about their lives. I even spoke to Jamaicans in New Orleans, Toronto, and Montreal who helped fill in the blanks, recalling what I never knew about Jamaica. For example, given the country’s reputation as homophobic, I was shocked that, at one point, there were five gay bars in Kingston at the same time. They had wonderful names like Fanny Hill. There was Marshall’s—and then another Marshall’s because the co-owners had a falling out and they both refused to give up the name. There was The Closet, but then the people there also had a falling out, so some of them went to form their own club The Interim Closet. And there was Andante. Andante was a jazz bar, but everybody knew that by 9 p.m. the drag queens would perform. Celebrities and the brother of the prime minister would go to see the shows. But by the late ’80s and ’90s they were all gone. With the AIDS crisis, homophobia really exploded in Jamaica. As a religious country, we believe what preachers tell us, and they said AIDS was God’s punishment. The gay nightlife went underground, there were still parties, but the bars and clubs never lasted very long. Talking to the older gays, I learned they’re just trying to get back to where Jamaica already was in 1972. I wanted to interview this guy who I think is 90, which would make him the oldest gay in Jamaica right now. He owns this artists’ retreat called Mountambrin, about an hour from Montego Bay. He started it as a hotel primarily for queer people, but he opened it up because he needed more guests and money. It’s still around and it’s for everyone, but you walk in and he has a lot of phallic art and statues of naked men, as one does. Gays are actually staying in Jamaica, which tells me there’s now a sort of hopefulness. In the past so many queer and trans people had to leave just to survive. With the kids, I find there’s more ease. I visited my alma mater the University of the West Indies and talked to their queer students’ association, which I was shocked existed. I started to give them my whole “it gets better” speech, and they were like, “We don’t want to hear that shit. Do you know Beyoncé?” I loved it. They reserve the right to be 19, to have their crisis be “Beyoncé or Rihanna?” and not “will I be shot today?” One of the guys I interviewed for The Disappearers showed up in pink hair extensions and a pink jumpsuit. I asked, “Where are you going dressed like this?” and he replied, “I just got off the bus.” All right, girl. But I don’t want to paint too rosy a picture. I also spoke to lesbians who said men threaten to rape them every week. Shit’s still going on. We have the Jamaica Forum for Lesbians, All-Sexuals and Gays [now Equality for All] for a reason—it’s an uphill battle. To live in Jamaica is to confront history, which is all around you. But also it's hard tracking down that history. I've been trying for years to find just one piece of footage showing a drag ball in Jamaica. It has to exist. I haven't given up. But I get it because part of how past generations tried to stay safe was by destroying the evidence—actually, maybe the guy who owns Mountambrin has a massive trove. The Disappearers is loosely based on a gay bashing that I knew happened in the late ’80s, but I didn’t have material proof. I kept asking Jamaicans if they remembered it, until finally someone in my interviews corroborated my memory of it. Again, I just needed to know for myself. So my characters are fictional—composites of people I’ve met or heard of and whatever’s in my imagination—but some of them could have existed. There are Jamaicans who will read The Disappearers and recognize these characters, maybe even know people just like them. This is the most personal book I’ve written. I do want it to serve as a record. That’s what fiction can do: fill in the blanks that history can’t or doesn’t want to. History books, to an extent, are only the story of famous people and politicians. You don’t always see how regular people get through their lives, how extraordinary ordinary people are. This is the first time I traveled specifically for a book project, but some travels have inspired other stories. Traveling naturally makes me more curious. To feel like I’m really experiencing a place, the first thing I do is unpack my bags completely, everywhere I go. It makes me feel less like a tourist, I guess. When I settle in, I find that I’m more prepared to take a country on its own terms.” —As told to Matt Ortile

item.title: How to Make the Most of the Venice Film Festival, According to a Critic Who Goes Every Year
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.18
When one thinks of the Venice Film Festival, a few indelible, almost impossibly exotic images spring to mind. The most recent may be Lady Gaga with her legs coyly crossed over the side of a water taxi as she announced her arrival to town for the premiere of A Star Is Born. (Or, I suppose, Harry Styles maybe spitting on his Don’t Worry Darling co-star Chris Pine.) But there has been a wealth of such moments for many decades: Venice is the oldest event of its kind, first held in 1932 and running near continuously since then—minus a few gaps during the Second World War and during some severe political strife that rocked Italy in the 1970s. The festival’s origins are, well, not great: it was founded by fascists loyal to Mussolini and, eventually, Axis powers. But in the many decades since, the festival has evolved into one of the so-called “Big Three” festivals of Europe, alongside winter’s Berlin Film Festival and the mid-spring glitz and madness of Cannes. It is a premier showcase for art-house international fare and, on a good year, glossy Oscar bait sent across the Atlantic by American studios debuting their latest prestige fare. Compared to Cannes, Venice is more relaxed—its screening schedule not so densely packed, its staff not quite as snooty, its dress codes more lax. The climate may often be punishing—high temperatures in baking sun, 100% humidity, mosquitoes suddenly filling the air at dusk—but Venice is nonetheless regarded by many people on the festival circuit as the jewel in the crown, one of high programming quality and easy glamour. Lido v. San Marco: The Eternal War It’s not hard to be glamorous when your event is held in one of the world’s most beautiful cities, that floating tangle of red buildings and snaking canals. Well, that’s where a lot of the nighttime events are, anyway. All of the screenings, meanwhile, are held on the Lido, a barrier island dotted with low-key beach clubs (and one decidedly high-key one, at the ritzy Excelsior Hotel, where cabanas can go for hundreds of Euros per day). A small town center with a few restaurants and lots of retirees is home to the festival headquarters. Some people—industry professionals, veteran critics, publicists, and awards strategists—are near-religiously committed to staying on the Lido, where you can walk (or bike, or e-scooter) to screenings without having to deal with the vaporetti, the lurching water buses that ferry people around Venice’s many islands. Me, I figure that if I’m going to be in Venice, I want to be in actual Venice. In the years that I’ve been going to the festival (as the chief critic of Vanity Fair until last year), I’ve always stayed on San Marco island, the center of the city’s tourism industry and the host of its most iconic images: the eponymous Piazza with its tall brick tower and ornate palace, the Bridge of Sighs, that cute gondolier you keep seeing as he poles his boat under the Rialto Bridge. Traveling between San Marco and the Lido is one of the more grumbled-about aspects of the festival, though I’ve mostly found it easy enough over the years. One simply hops on the number 20 vaporetto at San Zaccaria (just a tiny bit south and east of Piazza San Marco) and, maybe 20 minutes later, the boat drops you off on the festival grounds. Lines can get long if you don’t time things right—a crush of people all trying to make the same movie in 45 minutes can be a harrowing mess—but if you give yourself a wider berth, the boats are calm and manageable and then you can while away your extra time on the Lido by having a bite at one of the festival’s snack bars or a drink on the charming terrace of the old-school Albergo Quattro Fontane, right across the street. (Hopefully in the shade; again, that sun is brutal.) Carb City Staying on San Marco can be way less expensive, due to the abundance of hotels and rental apartments, and it affords you far more opportunities to eat not only well but also surprisingly diversely. Seafood, pasta, and pizza still dominate most menus, but there are other kinds of cuisines to be found, like Chinese and Indian and North African—I even had a complex vegan tasting menu at the highly rated Bistro de Venise, located in a tiny alleyway off of an only slightly less narrow street that leads pilgrims on the well-trod path between the Rialto and Piazza San Marco. If one is busy covering the festival, one may not always have time for a long sit-down meal, preferring instead to grab a few cicchetti (little tapas-like crostinis that are a staple of Venetian cuisine) or a sandwich. The best place that I’ve found to do the latter is L’ Bacaro de’ Bischeri, tucked into one of the market stalls right across from the Rialto, on the island of San Polo. The most popular item on the large menu seems to be the Don’t Tell William, two massive squares of focaccia with a generous heaping of stracciatella, mortadella, and pistachios piled in between. Eat it on the street outside, or do what I did and take it back to your little garret apartment in Campo San Luca (right near the H&M!) so no one will see you make a mess. But if you do want to sit down, one classic option is Al Covo, just to the east of San Zaccaria, in a slightly quieter neighborhood. It’s a Michelin-recommended, seafood-heavy favorite among festivalgoers looking for a more elevated but affordable meal than they might get on the Lido. I know several journalists who make a point of going there every year, and have been doing so for decades. If you want something fancier, that’s both old and new, the Four Seasons has just reopened the iconic Hotel Danieli after a years-long remodel, and you can enjoy a posh lunch or dinner on the well-shaded fifth-floor terrace overlooking the lagoon. Just be careful that when you order the pinot grigio, the waiter knows you don’t mean the glass that costs €80. I made that unfortunately delicious mistake this year, on a placid afternoon when I’d had enough movies for the day. But again, most people attending the film festival have little time for such a luxury. It’s mostly foraging for food between screenings and writing assignments, scarfing down that same sandwich over and over again, or darting back to your apartment to eat the groceries you bought at Supermercato Punto, a nearly American-sized market that also has a lovely little cocktail bar off to one side. (Where I stopped before my big shop to enjoy my go-to Venice drink, a Cynar spritz, on the tiny balcony perched over a canal.) Where to Party If You Can Get In, or If You Can’t There is certainly elegant fun to be had, though, if you knock on the right doors. (Or email the right publicists.) American studios often hold pre-premiere parties in the garden of the Excelsior, steps away from the Pala Grande, where celebrities walk the red carpet and scores of onlookers—from matinee idol-crazed teens to elderly looky-loos—gather to gawp and take pictures. This year, I journeyed to the Excelsior garden to brush shoulders with Oscar-winning filmmaker Martin McDonagh, who has followed up his lauded film The Banshees of Inisherin with a dark comedy about CIA spooks called Wild Horse Nine. His life partner, the actor and writer Phoebe Waller-Bridge of Fleabag fame, was with him, as were several members of his cast, including Steve Buscemi, who looked perhaps a little perplexed to be there among the Euro swells and various influencer-type hangers-on. Those afternoon events are brief amuse-bouches compared to what comes later in the evening, when Italian and French fashion houses flex their resources and throw exclusive dinners or parties at palazzos around the city, or at revered Grand Canal-side hotels like the Gritti Palace and the St. Regis. At the former, two friends convinced hotel security to let me into the tail end of a dinner for Cartier, where I sat a stone’s throw from a pleased-looking Orlando Bloom in the hotel’s lavishly appointed bar and chatted with Kate Mara about the wild, weird Bucking Fastard, the Werner Herzog movie that she and her sister, Rooney, debuted at the festival. At the St. Regis, on another night, I sat one couch over from Robert Pattinson, who seemed relaxed and no doubt happy with the rave reviews for his award-worthy performance in A24’s big Venice premiere Primetime, in which Pattinson plays To Catch a Predator host Chris Hansen. The party was jam-packed and the bar lines were long, but one barely minds such things when one has a view of the canal and of Edward Cullen himself, dapper in a white dinner jacket. That said, Venice is not quite the party-hopping, champagne-guzzling bacchanal that Cannes tends to devolve into. It’s a more restrained affair, partly because the city of Venice shuts down pretty early—unless, of course, a local points you in the direction of the good late-night spots. At least one of those places, one that’s a staple of many attendees’ film festival experience, is easy to find on your own: Ai Do Leoni, a compact and jovial bar right off of Piazza San Marco that stays open until 1:30, friends and potential lovers and a few awkward critics spilling out into the square (or, near the square) to talk and carouse and flirt while the rest of the city goes to sleep. You’ll be hungover on a boat the next day, but hey, you’re still in Venice.

item.title: Off-Season Greece: Athens Comes Alive in Fall, According to Hotelier Agapi Sbokou
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.13
This is part of Off-Season Greece, a collection of guides highlighting the year-round appeal of Greece's most popular destinations, courtesy of our favorite local tastemakers. In this edition, we speak to Agapi Sbokou, co-owner and CEO of Greek hotel brand Phāea. “Alive. That's how Athens feels to me,” says Agapi Sbokou, co-owner and CEO of the Greek hotel brand Phāea. Sbokou grew up in Crete but has lived in Athens since she was 18. “There was never really a debate about where to live. We go back and forth between Athens and Crete, but the city just feels so buzzy. It’s a place that is constantly transforming.” Sbokou knows a thing or two about why people are drawn to a particular destination. “When you go to a place, it should be about understanding the local rhythm,” she tells me. “I'm in love with Athens. It’s a place that you can continue exploring your whole life.” Here, Agapi explains why autumn is so magical in the Greek capital, and lets us in on some of her favorite places to visit at this time of year. Tell me what you love most about Athens. Walking around and exploring. The city transforms with the seasons, and it feels completely connected with nature. For example, my neighborhood is full of these beautiful trees called jacarandas, which have very small, lilac flowers. They completely transform the whole neighborhood when they bloom. Elsewhere in the city, some areas are filled with bitter orange trees, which also have a strong scent when they bloom. There are a lot of young people here, and recently a lot of young travelers are coming to stay and live in Athens. They all come with a very open heart and the desire to explore as we, the locals, do. Athens is not about what’s cool and what’s not—it’s about discovering new things, revisiting old places, and watching the city transform over time. That’s what I love. When is the best time to come to Athens? When it’s not too busy, but local life is buzzing. I would say April and October or November. I've always been a summer person, but to be honest in Athens spring and autumn are the most beautiful seasons. In April, the blooms are starting to appear. There are beautiful scents around the city. But autumn is great because the weather is very mellow. There's still the warmth from the summer, and there is very little rain, so it's very pleasant and you can walk around all day. What makes autumn so special in Athens? There's a different light about the city, which is not that classic Greek light that you see during summer. It's more yellow and soft. The city starts preparing for winter, so there is a kind of excitement with the locals—people are returning from the islands, they still go swimming in the sea, and still it's quite warm. It's the perfect season because it combines it all. Who’s around this time of year? There are travelers year-round. But in autumn, it's a different kind of traveler. People who come during this season have a slower appreciation of the city, which I love. I think that's what tourism should be. We should spend more time exploring a place and really getting a sense of it to understand its rhythm, rather than going in and out, just ticking off things. Do as the locals do. Maybe spend two hours in a coffee shop. Get to know the person sitting at the next table and start a conversation. Spend three hours in a museum, not one. There are so many museums here, and not just the big ones. The Benizelos Mansion is the oldest house in Athens, or, of course, the Benaki Museum with the Nema Collection. There are so many things to discover, and it shouldn't all be packed into one trip. The kind of travelers who appreciate this tend to come off-season. What’s notable about the locals in Athens? Do they have any of their own unique traditions or a reputation amongst Greeks for anything in particular? An appreciation for a slower way of life, I guess. Athens is very much about its neighborhoods, which is characteristic of the city and its people. You start your day at your local coffee shop, then visit your local barber, grocery store, and dry cleaner. You stop for a few minutes, you exchange a few words. That's very typical of people here. You have a sense of community. Sometimes you buy things and you don't need to pay—they know you, and write it in a notebook and you pay at the end of the month. Athens feels like a village, even though it's a city of four million. Where would we find you eating in autumn? I love exploring new places, but I also love going to the same places again and again, because then you begin to know the people. There is a new generation of fantastic restaurants that embrace Greek cuisine, but I’d rather visit the ones that have been around for 20, 30, or even 50 years. I go to Manári Taverna a lot, which is in the city center. It's right by a Byzantine church, and it has very traditional cuisine with strong Cretan influence. There is Pharaoh, a very cool restaurant where everything is slow-cooked over a wood-fired grill. It has the best music and the coolest bar, so it's really fun to visit. Plus, it belongs to a friend, so it's always fun to see him and catch up. There’s a place called Dourambeis where I've been going with my dad since I was a kid. It's very traditional, and it has the most delicious fish. In autumn, these places are perfect because they are traditional and laid-back, but have really good food. They all use excellent, seasonal ingredients. Speaking of seasonal ingredients, what is the most traditional dish that people should eat when they come in autumn? That's a good question. It's hard to say, because the weather in Greece stays warm into autumn, so we tend to drag summer dishes into the year. For example, one very traditional dish we continue to eat in autumn is gemista. It’s often made with very ripe tomatoes—you empty them, and fill them with rice, mince meat, and other ingredients like herbs and nuts. You could replace tomatoes with zucchini, or eggplant, or peppers. It is very, very Greek and very traditional. And then, of course, in autumn, we eat a lot of pastries and pies. The most typical one is spanakopita, a cheese-and-spinach pie. Those are more home-cooked recipes, though. Athens is like the melting pot of the whole of Greece, so a lot of wider Greek traditions are incorporated in the restaurants. Skioufichta is a specific thick pasta dish, made by hand. You boil it in a broth, and then it's sprinkled with cheese. And it's the most delicious dish, very soothing, very appropriate for autumn—perfect with a glass of red wine. Order this at Manári—it's one of my favorite dishes there. Are there any areas of Athens that really come alive in autumn? I've always lived in and around Kolonaki. It's an area that's quite buzzing and quite well-known, but I love the streets that are purely residential. There are a couple that are quite high, with amazing views, because Kolonaki is at the bottom of Lycabettus Hill. From those streets, you can see straight down to the Acropolis, in between buildings. In the autumn, when the light is right, it just feels amazing and very Athenian. It's almost like a secret—you know that if you turn down a specific street, you’ll suddenly get this view. That feeling always makes me feel very lucky to be there. In autumn, it’s easier to be more spontaneous in Athens, because it’s not as busy. It feels like normal life is back, so you can access museums, galleries, exhibitions, and restaurants more easily. Us Greeks are very welcoming. We want to share the best of what we have. It’s the perfect time to do that.

item.title: Where was Pressure filmed? Behind the scenes of the war epic starring Andrew Scott
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 5.52
On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favourite films, television shows, and more. This time, we ask: where was Pressure filmed? On 6 June 1944, the largest seaborne invasion in history took place on the shores of Normandy, France. After years of global conflict, the Normandy Landings – now known as D-Day – paved the way for the Allied victory on the western front. But the build-up to the operation was nothing short of monumental. Behind the scenes of the deployment of more than 150,000 troops was an intricate web of logistics. Despite meticulous planning, the landings largely depended on the weather – if a storm had rolled in, the results could have been very different. This is where Scottish meteorologist James Stagg (played by Andrew Scott) comes in. With millions of lives at stake, General Dwight D. Eisenhower enlists Stagg to set a timeline for the landings. In doing so, Stagg faces opposition from fellow meteorologist Irving P. Krick and Eisenhower, putting him under immense pressure to deliver an accurate forecast that supports the war effort. This is the tale playing out on the big screen right now, as a stellar cast enacts a crucial but forgotten wartime story that ultimately saved countless lives. But filming a war epic isn’t plain sailing. Here, we take a look at the locations across England used to bring the story to life. Rand Bros Farm Founded in the 1930s by a trio of brothers, Rand Bros Farm, on the edge of Royston, was transformed into the London-to-Portsmouth route seen in the movie’s early scenes. Mentmore Towers Director Anthony Maras scouted more than 100 buildings for the Allied Headquarters – the centrepiece of the movie. While Southwick House, the real-life war headquarters, was considered, its status as an active military base, surrounded by post-war buildings, made it an unsuitable candidate. Mentmore Towers was deemed the best fit – a 19th-century country house built for the Rothschild family. RAF Halton Airfield The airfield featured in the film is one of the oldest and largest in the UK, founded in the First World War and an active training base to this day. St Mary's Church, Mentmore The church featured in the movie sits just beyond the gates of Mentmore Towers. Mentioned in the Domesday Book, it’s likely a wooden structure stood here before the charming medieval structure that stands today. The Historic Dockyard Chatham This historic dockyard stands in for the port of the D-Day embarkation, as troops and submarines headed towards the coast of France.

item.title: Behind the scenes with Condé Nast Traveller on its latest fashion shoot in Salzburg, Austria
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.97
A team from the UK, France, Italy, the Czech Republic and Germany travelled to the beautiful lakes, soaring Alpine peaks and historical towns of the Salzkammergut region in Austria to shoot the new Fall/Winter collections. The varied weather, where you can experience all seasons in one day, inspired a rich palette of outfits from faux furs to gossamer silk. Soft leather and chunky knitwear, paired with diamonds and pearls, fit in perfectly with the elegant Salzburg crowd, who didn’t seem surprised to see our model, Ustyna, treat the cobbled street as her catwalk in a full look from Maria Grazia Chiuri’s first collection for Fendi. Here we share a behind-the-scenes peek at the locations and looks. Traunkirchen, Lake Traunsee The village of Traunkirchen lies on the western edge of Lake Traunsee in the Salzkammergut, directly across from Traunstein, an imposing peak that rises dramatically above the water. The dramatic scene is unsurprisingly a favourite spot among Instagrammers and was a shoo-in for the UK cover and a bright Chanel coat. The best view of the mountain is from the dock at Das Traunsee – Das Hotel zum See, whose owner Wolfgang Gröller has a considered collection of vintage boats. From time to time, he enjoys taking lucky guests out onto the water – our model Ustyna being one of them! First on the traditional boat in a national-inspired denim look and then again on the more modern motor boat wearing a very smart Stella McCartney Moire silk suit. Along with its charming shops and old boathouses, Traunkirchen’s town centre draws people with its stone walls and boathouses set amid green meadows. Other attractions include the Belétage restaurant and bar at the Hotel Post am See, a second property from the Gröller family. We recommended the basil cocktail for a refreshing start to an evening of traditional Austrian food. Feuerkogel Not far from Traunkirchen, the Feuerkogel is a must-hike mountain (if you’d rather, you can opt to take a cable car to the top). When there is still snow on the ground at the 5,200-foot summit, conditions can shift within minutes from crystal-clear sunlight to thick fog, a dynamic shoot location to say the least. If the visibility is good, stay on the northern side of the crest where several terraces offer the best views of the region, and a hot drink. If clouds roll in, a short hike takes you to Alberfeldkogel mountain less than a mile west of the Feuerkogel. Fir trees, cliffs and a mist-shrouded icy terrain create a mystical atmosphere like something out of a fantasy film. This was the perfect place to re-enact that twirling scene from The Sound of Music and to Yodel into the void. Our hairdresser Paulo was inspired by Heidi’s twin plaits, and they looked so chic against the snowy vista in a Louis Vuitton jumper dress complete with hood. Konditorei Zauner, Bad Ischl In the spa town of Bad Ischl, around 30 minutes by car from Traunkirchen, you’ll find the Konditorei Zauner, a patisserie with a glorious display case filled with exquisitely decorated cakes. Zauner has been in business since 1832, and to this day lovingly preserves traditional Austrian coffee culture, serving drinks from a milky melange to an indulgent double mocha. Ustyna, dressed exquisitely in Prada, fit right in. They also offer the country’s largest selection of cakes with some 250 creations as well as about 60 varieties of truffles, pralines and chocolates. The Zaunerstollen, a hazelnut and chocolate wafer, and the Ischler Törtchen, a fruity shortbread, are not to be missed. Lake Fuschl Located on the shores of Lake Fuschl, the Rosewood Schloss Fuschl Hotel is truly straight out of a movie… scenes from the famous Sissi trilogy of films starring Austrian-born Romy Schneider were shot here, and there is a small museum on-site. Today it is the hotel, inside and out, that is the star. The bar is one of the most beautiful in the country with dark wood panelling and hand-painted murals, while the clear lake is strikingly blue. It’s also decidedly more peaceful than other nearby lakes as motorboats are strictly prohibited. Every swim (or paddle) in its waters and every stroll through the nearby green meadows and forests feels like a meditative moment. When the weather might tempt you indoors, the oil paintings on display, whisky menu and board games on offer are extensive. Salzburg The most important city in this part of Austria, Salzburg is famous for its cultural highlights – it’s a destination for everyone who loves art, music and cuisine. The Hotel Goldener Hirsch, a Luxury Collection Hotel, is the place to enjoy a morning coffee with the dailies in a gemütlich historic setting – the hotel was first mentioned in a document from 1407. Or head straight to dinner, where backhendl, a traditional Austrian breaded fried chicken, is a delicious treat. A must on every Salzburg itinerary is a visit to the Kirchtag factory in the old Getreidegasse lane where Mozart was born. There you can watch craftsmen make umbrellas by hand. If you ask nicely, you may be able to take in the city views from the rooftop terrace, wearing Burberry, optional of course. It could be one of the most memorable moments of your Austrian holiday.

item.title: The world's busiest airport is no longer Dubai
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.92
The world's aviation landscape looks a little different this year, with South Korea's Incheon International Airport outranking Dubai International as the world's busiest for international passengers. According to preliminary data from the Airports Council International (ACI), released by Incheon, the South Korean airport served 38.4 million international passengers during the first six months of 2026. Once confirmed by the ACI in its World Airport Traffic Report (to be released next month), the airport will now rank as the world's busiest for the first time since opening in 2001. Dubai International Airport is expected to place outside the top five this year, despite ranking first for international traffic for the past 12 years. The decline in international footfall follows the outbreak of the US-Iran war, which reconfigured the globe's skies when it began on 28 February, with ACI data showing the UAE travel hub fell from 7.4 million passengers in February to just 2.5 million in March. Incheon also reported an 18 per cent increase in transfer passengers this year, as many who previously transferred in the Gulf on their way to Europe had to rethink their route amid airspace closures. This year, London Heathrow is set to rank in second place, recording 37.79 million passengers in the first half of the year, followed by Singapore's Changi Airport, which has seen 34.53 million international passengers pass through its terminals during this period. It's not just the war that's contributed to Incheon's sharp rise in numbers. According to the airport, an infrastructure expansion (which was completed in 2024) has enabled it to handle a larger traffic load – now serving 101 airlines flying to 158 international destinations. And with a growing global interest in Korean culture, from its TV shows to its music, food, beauty and fashion, it's little wonder the airport has continued to climb the ranks, placing fifth in 2018 to being named third busiest in 2024 and 2025, and now reaching the top spot. Before the conflict, Dubai's global status as a tourism hotspot and destination for transfers was increasing year on year. In April, it was named the world's busiest airport for international passengers in 2025, with 95.2 million international passengers landing in the city over the course of 12 months. The figure marked an increase of 3.1 per cent from 2024, and a 10.3 per cent rise from pre-pandemic numbers in 2019. In February, the emirate was also named the world's best-connected city by Mozio, which compared the journey time from arrivals to a central landmark in 50 of the world's most-visited cities. With tensions continuing and the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) extending its conflict zone advisory for the Gulf until 31 August, it remains unclear when air traffic in the region will return to its pre-war levels.

item.title: Where was Practical Magic 2 filmed? An insider's guide to the long-awaited sequel
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.62
On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favourite films, television shows, and more. This time, we ask: where was Practical Magic 2 filmed? In 1998, burgeoning Hollywood starlets Nicole Kidman and Sandra Bullock played Gillian and Sally Owens, two sisters in possession of special powers in Practical Magic, a film adapted from Alice Hoffman’s novel by the same name. Set in the witch (history) rich state of Massachusetts, the ingenue outcasts attempt to lift the ancestral curse that strikes dead any man who falls in love with an Owens woman. As they embark on this harrowing journey, spells are cast, “midnight margaritas” are made, and matriarchy reigns supreme. At the time, the film’s reception was middling at best – with a New York Times review describing it as “Barbie Joins a Coven” – and its performance at the box office not much better. With a little room to breathe and bask in nostalgia’s rose-colored glow, the movie has transformed into a feminist cult classic with Gen X and Gen Z fans alike. From 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple to The Devil Wears Prada 2, 2026 has been a year of follow-up films. In that same vein, Kidman and Bullock have reunited in Practical Magic 2, a sequel directed by Susanne Bier that promises to delight fans and take us across the pond to a whole new continent of spooky locales. Another generation of coven-loving will live on in Practical Magic 2, which picks up after a sizeable time jump but with more of the same kooky hijinks. A generous interpretation of time – and a little movie magic – lands Sally’s daughters Antonia (Maisie Williams) and Kylie (Joey King) in their early twenties. Up until now, they have lived their lives ignorant of their powers, which their mother has deliberately shielded them from. Antonia, a medical student, most closely resembles her mother, while Kylie, now a Harvard student, is a bit more of a free spirit. When Kylie falls for sweet Gideon (Xolo Maridueña), and then he falls into a coma, she follows her mother’s path of attempting to right things. Counselled by the recently uncovered Book of the Raven, Kylie sets off to her family’s ancestral home of England, bringing much of the story to English territory. While the original movie was shot in Coupeville, Washington, on Whidbey Island, as a New England stand-in, the sequel's production moved to the UK. Here are all the places where Practical Magic 2 was filmed. Leavesden Studios, Hertfordshire, England The Owens women remain the main characters in this film, but fans of the original film will recall the outstanding Victorian-style Owens family home. The house itself has reached cult status with its cutesy cottagecore aesthetic, and its recreation was crucial to making the sequel. Practical Magic 2’s production notes explain the importance of the house's revival. Producer Denise De Novi felt that bringing the house back to life was one of the most rewarding components of making this movie, “The house in this movie is just a phenomenon,” she noted. In the first film, the exterior of the house was built on San Juan Island in Washington, and the interiors were created on a soundstage in Los Angeles. Those structures no longer exist, so this time around, production designer Tom Burton determined that the most economical option was to build the house from scratch on the back lot at Leavesden Studios. Great care was taken to ensure that the replica was consistent with the original home, including establishing the same sun position so that the sun would set in the same place as it did in the original film. Once the house’s construction was almost complete, the greens team descended upon the set to bring the renowned garden to life, with over 4,000 plants brought in. While about half of the 55 shooting days were spent at Leavesden Studios, the remainder were shot at several notable locations in and around London. Village of Hambleden The quaint village of Hambleden, just west of London, served as the town of Thornfield. The centre of the village is filled with old picturesque brick and flint cottages, all with the signature dormer windows. The Royal Standard of England, Beaconsfield British viewers might take notice of this historic pub, which serves as the exterior of the fictional Thornfield Inn just northwest of London. The Royal Standard, which has been around for over 900 years, claims to be the oldest pub in Great Britain. Located in the Chiltern Hills, the scenic old pub is filled with charm and has been featured in numerous films and television shows including The Theory of Everything, Hot Fuzz, and Too Much. Oysters, fish and chips, and a robust beer list are on offer and quiz night is every Tuesday. Langleybury Mansion in Hertfordshire Langleybury is a vacant 18th-century period house that has served as a backdrop for several notable productions including Downton Abbey, The Crown, and Paddington. The crew utilised this mansion to stand in for rooms at Harvard University as well as some of the UK lodgings. Wormsley Estate in Buckinghamshire The private 2,700-acre estate boasting an opera pavilion, cricket grounds, and a walled garden served as the backdrop for the cottage of Tom Lockland (Solly McLeod), the longtime magic student of Thornfield. Black Park Country Park Practical Magic 2 features sweeping views of the British rolling hills and conifer forests. Black Park, a large park with woodland trails, horse riding, and a lake, was filmed as the forest surrounding Thornfield. The Royal Chelsea Hospital The historic Royal Hospital Chelsea in London is a retirement and nursing home for British Army veterans who have reached the state pension age. The hospital was founded by Charles II in 1692, and it has maintained its grand estate while modernising to meet the present-day needs of its inhabitants. The impressive grounds, with brick buildings and Roman columns, were used in the film for a flower market and for shots meant to be Harvard University exteriors. The Victorian flats of Cromwell Buildings The tattoo-covered Professor Ian Wright (Lee Pace), who quickly becomes Sally’s love interest, is one of the more charming updates in this sequel. His apartment, was shot at these flats.

item.title: UK airport latest: thousands of flights delayed and cancelled at UK airports
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.28
Tens of thousands of passengers are unlikely to be entitled to compensation for delays following a technical failure in air traffic control that caused widespread chaos this week. The Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) has told those impacted that the “disruption caused by the Nats outage is likely to be considered the result of ‘extraordinary circumstances’ under passenger rights rules”. That advice means passengers are “unlikely to be entitled to compensation for delays or cancellations that were directly caused by the incident.” On Tuesday 8 and Wednesday 9 September, more than 2,000 flights were cancelled. Inbound and outbound UK flights were impacted, with London airports including Heathrow and Gatwick, as well as regional airports such as Manchester, most affected. As of the morning of Thursday 10 September, flights are largely operating as normal, and stranded passengers have been able to journey home. What was the air traffic control failure? Several major UK airports experienced delays and cancellations following a technical failure in air traffic control on Tuesday 8 September. The National Air Traffic Services (NATS) has now resolved the issue, which affected its flight processing system, but the disruption continued into Wednesday as airlines and airports worked through the backlog. NATs boss Martin Rolfe apologised for the disruption, telling the BBC there would be a full investigation into what had gone wrong, after the firm said resolving the issue had taken "longer than hoped". An official statement on the NATs website reads: “This has been a very complex recovery and has created difficulties for the whole aviation network, from which it will take time to recover.” The failure caused widespread disruption across the UK on Tuesday, with FlightRadar24 reporting around 1,300 cancellations to and from UK airports. Heathrow, Gatwick, Manchester and Stansted were among the airports affected, while the disruption also had knock-on effects at airports across Europe. Heathrow was particularly impacted. Arrivals were suspended for the remainder of Tuesday, while departures resumed later in the day. The airport has warned that disruption will continue and is advising passengers to check directly with their airline before travelling. A statement on the airport's X account on Wednesday morning reads: “Following yesterday's NATS technical issue, flights are operating today, but some disruption may continue as airlines reposition aircraft and crew. Please check your flight status with your airline before travelling to the airport and only travel if your flight is confirmed to be operating.” UK airports that reported disruption include: - London Heathrow Airport - London Gatwick Airport - London Luton Airport - London Stansted Airport - Manchester Airport - Birmingham Airport - Belfast City Airport - Edinburgh Airport - East Midlands Airport - Jersey Airport

item.title: 11 most beautiful autumn train journeys in Europe that encourage slow travel
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.02
Summer is a gorgeous time to enjoy train-hopping on France’s Mediterranean coast (the Train de la Côte Bleue is a journey you must add to your summer 2027 bucket list) or southern Italy on a regional train from Naples to Reggio Calabria – but autumn is arguably the best time to visit Europe by train. While summer sees hordes of tourists travelling from around the world, putting pressure on rail networks and often making a train trip feel like a sauna, autumn – as well as spring – allows you to visit even some of the continent’s most popular destinations with a little more ease and comfort. While Switzerland and Italy may be the ultimate destinations for scenic train travel, there are routes across Europe that combine fabulous scenery with interesting sights and activities at both ends of the journey. We have gathered some of the best train rides across Europe to give you some ideas for your next train adventure. Italy Train line: Vigezzina Centovalli Railway Italians love to complain about their railway system, but the truth is Italy has one of the best – if not the best – train travel offerings in Europe. Simple regional trains often offer fabulous views over the Italian countryside and coastlines – my yearly train from Naples to Paola is one of my favourite summer activities – but there are some specific routes that deserve the detour. The Vigezzina-Centovalli Railway connects Domodossola in Italy to Locarno in Switzerland in around two hours, passing through the striking Vigezzo Valley and the Centovalli (Hundred Valleys) and allows travellers to stop and visit charming villages such as Santa Maria Maggiore or impressive sites like the Sanctuary of the Madonna del Sangue in Re. In autumn, the service becomes known as the ‘Foliage Train’. Just note that the special foliage ticket allows one intermediate stop on either the outward or return journey, rather than unlimited hopping on and off, so choose wisely. Switzerland Train line: GoldenPass Belle Époque (from Montreux to Zweisimmen) When it comes to scenic train routes, Switzerland always makes it to the top of the list. Out of the many famous routes, the Bernina Express is probably the most popular, but I think that is a route that can wait for winter. Instead, autumn is the perfect time of year to book a GoldenPass Belle Époque train and admire some truly stunning Swiss foliage while sitting in vintage 1930s-style carriages. This route takes travellers from Montreux to Zweisimmen in around two hours through the Gruyère district and the Pays-d’Enhaut. The carriages have panoramic windows, offering uninterrupted views of lakes, mountain peaks and forests along the way.T Greece Train line: Odontotos Rack Railway (Diakopto to Kalavryta) Greece is more popular for boat-powered island hopping than for train travel, but the country has a few gorgeous routes up its sleeve. If finding an unspoiled Greek island is becoming more and more difficult, the Peloponnese region is still fairly under the radar and has a lot to offer year-round. The Odontotos Rack Railway from Diakopto to Kalavryta takes around one hour and shows you a different side of Greece, following the Vouraikos River through its dramatic gorge. Take this opportunity to enjoy a few days in Diakopto, a lovely seaside town usually still sunny and warm in autumn, before getting a complete change of scenery when arriving in the mountain town of Kalavryta. France Train line: Strasbourg to Sélestat via Molsheim, Obernai and Barr (following the Route des Vins d'Alsace) If there is one event that defines autumn in Europe, it is the wine harvest, and France has a fabulous train route to celebrate this time of year by rail. The Route des Vins d’Alsace winds through eastern France and offers a wonderful introduction to the Alsace wine region. There are a few itineraries that can be created following this route but, if it’s your first time in the region, starting from the beautiful city of Strasbourg seems like a good option. From there, take the Strasbourg-Sélestat line that runs through vineyards and allows you to stop in some charming towns such as Molsheim, Obernai and Barr. From early August to mid-October, wine villages across the region host a packed calendar of harvest festivals and events, so make sure you check the calendar and organise your visit to coincide with an event that catches your eye. Portugal Train line: Douro Valley Line (Linha do Douro) The Linha do Douro is a 160-kilometre historic line that connects the city of Porto to the village of Pocinho, running alongside the Douro River, and crossing 35 bridges along the way. The one-way trip is three hours and twenty minutes, but the full journey can still be tackled as a day trip, returning to Porto the same evening. If you don’t feel like committing to a seven-hour train journey in a day, you could stop in the charming town of Pinhão for a wine tasting at Quinta do Bomfim or Quinta das Carvalhas. It cuts one hour off the journey each way and you can still do it in one day if you take the morning train from Porto and make sure you are back in time to take the last train back to the city from Pinhão station. Serbia and Montenegro Train line: Belgrade to Bar If you thought that the Balkans didn’t have great train routes, the trip from Belgrade to Bar will change your mind. With its eleven hours and 476 kilometres, this is a very long train journey that takes travellers from the green hills of Serbia to the rugged mountains of Montenegro. The journey can be made on an overnight service year-round, while a daytime train operates seasonally. In 2026, it runs until 30 September, although it’s worth checking the operator’s website before travelling as timetables can change. Of course, the morning train is the one to take to be able to fully enjoy the views through the Dinaric Alps. The railway crosses 435 bridges – the most spectacular being the 498-metre-long Mala Rijeka Viaduct, which rises almost 200 metres above the valley floor. This is neither the quickest nor the most comfortable train ride you can take in Europe, but it’s definitely worth it if you are passionate about train travel. Norway Train line: Flåm Railway Not only is this one of the most beautiful train journeys in Europe year-round, but in good Norwegian fashion, the route is extremely well organised for tourists who want to enjoy everything that the area has to offer. You can simply book your train tickets and enjoy the ride, or choose a package that includes excursions and accommodation through Norway in a Nutshell. The train journey is twenty kilometres long and lasts around one hour one way, taking you through peaks, valleys, waterfalls and rivers. From cycling, hiking and swimming to ziplining, there is a lot to do along the way so you can spend one day or a full week exploring. Austria Train line: The Arlberg Railway This train route connects the Austrian cities of Innsbruck and Bludenz and is 136 kilometres long, with direct trains completing the journey in around one hour and 45 minutes. During this time, you will speed through charming Alpine villages, rivers and steep-sided valleys framed by mountain peaks. If you are travelling from Innsbruck, this is only one of the many stunning train routes you can take around Austria, to Switzerland or through South Tyrol all the way to Italy, but it’s an ideal option if you want maximum scenery without committing to a full day on the rails. Germany Train line: West Rhine Railway If you are looking for a train journey that will immerse you in nature but want a less obvious alternative to the Alpine railways of Switzerland and Italy, consider Germany’s West Rhine Railway. The route stretches for 185 km, starting from Cologne and arriving at Mainz via Bonn, Koblenz, and Bingen. Cologne makes an excellent starting point, with its Gothic cathedral and lively riverside neighbourhoods worth exploring before you board. The two-hour journey is stunning from beginning to end, but the highlight is the Rhine Gorge, a UNESCO World Heritage Site visible from the train. Bulgaria Train line: Rhodope Narrow Gauge Railway This train from Septemvri to Dobrinishte runs four times a day year-round, takes about five hours for the one-way trip, and costs only a few euros. This route is the closest thing in the Balkans to an Alpine train ride, winding through the valleys and gorges of the Rila, Pirin and Rhodope mountains and stopping at Avramovo, the highest railway station in the Balkans. If you want to stop anywhere during your trip, make it the town of Velingrad, the country’s most popular thermal spa destination.

item.title: Craft x Tech: Shining a light on Japan’s Tokai region at London Design Festival
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.99
What happens when centuries-old Japanese craft techniques meet the imagination of some of the world’s most experimental designers? At this year’s London Design Festival, the answer can be found inside the V&A in South Kensington, where six artisans from Japan’s Tokai region have joined forces with internationally acclaimed designers and artists to create a new generation of objects. The resulting works span ceramics, washi paper, textiles, cloisonné enamel, and braided cord, but share a common starting point: a desire to view tradition as something alive rather than fixed. For Craft x Tech Tokai Project, founded by designer and engineer Dr Hideki Yoshimoto of design studio Tangent, each designer was paired with a specialist maker from one of the region’s long-established craft communities, bringing contemporary perspectives to techniques passed down through generations. It forms one of the key shows at this year’s festival. “Japan has accumulated an extraordinary amount of knowledge through craft – knowledge about materials, processes, nature and making – much of it developed over hundreds of years,” says Yoshimoto. “I wanted to take that knowledge outside the context in which it is normally understood, and see what new relevance it might have when it encounters very different minds.” Tokai, which encompasses the prefectures of Aichi, Gifu, Mie and Shizuoka, has a rich history of making. Its abundant water, natural resources, high-quality clay and position along historic trade routes have fostered a diverse craft culture, while traditional knowledge and industrial innovation have developed alongside one another. Speaking of visitors to the show, Yoshimoto says: “I hope they see that Japanese craft is not one homogeneous culture, but an accumulation of very specific knowledge developed in different places over a very long time. Tokai is particularly rich in this respect, and if the project can bring some of that knowledge into a wider contemporary context, I think that is more important than simply introducing Japanese craft to a new audience.” Here, we speak to the designers behind the collaborations about the makers they worked with, the techniques they encountered, and what happened when their own creative languages met centuries of Japanese craft knowledge. Fushi: David Caon × Yohei Ito For Fushi, Australian industrial designer David Caon collaborated with Yohei Ito of pottery manufacturer Fudogama to explore the possibilities of Mino Yaki ceramics. Together they created a console and lighting piece from modular ceramic elements. “The material drove most of the decisions in the design, especially in terms of form and scale,” says Caon, who embraced the randomness of the glazing process in favour of its “deeply beautiful and emotive” surface. In Tokai, he was surprised to discover that the craftsmen surrounding the process were “young and energetic”, rather than the older, more serious group he had expected. The collaboration reinforced Caon’s belief in putting more faith in a fabricator's advice and not trying to control every detail. The precision lies in the form and structure of the modules, while the Oribe glaze is deliberately left unconstrained. “I hope people get a little lost looking at all the different ways the glaze has reacted across the individual modules,” he says. Websites: @caondesignoffice, fudogama.com Chair in Japanese Nuki and Dami style, The Everyday at the Atelier: Eugene Kangawa x Mayuki Kato Japanese contemporary artist Eugene Kangawa worked with Mayuki Kato of pottery manufacturer Shingama, drawing on the brushwork and tonal variation of the Japanese underglazed porcelain craft Seto Sometsuke Yaki. “The diversity of expression that comes from clay, the handwork of the brush, and the variations created by heat were especially compelling,” says Kangawa. “In particular, the variations within the deep indigo blue were fascinating.” The collaboration evolved through experimentation, with the kiln undertaking tests it had never tried before, while deliberately retaining “a diversity of forms and moments.” For Kangawa, the process reinforced his belief that craft is intrinsically connected to the geology, history and everyday life of a place. “New discoveries often seem to lie within the process of trial and error,” he explains. He hopes the finished work encourages people to recognise that even techniques passed down for generations can still leave room for new findings. Websites: the-eugene-studio.com, store.singama.jp Kasane: Philippe Malouin × Shigeyuki Ando Shigeyuki Ando of Ando Cloisonne and British-Canadian designer Philippe Malouin joined forces to explore the architectural potential of Owari Shippo cloisonné (a type of enamelware). “The first thing that struck me was the precision of the work and the depth of the enamel,” says Malouin. “It somehow feels very precise and technical, but also obviously handmade.” The project took shape around a practical limitation: the kiln's maximum size. Rather than work against it, Malouin designed a series of boxes that could be stacked to form a larger, totem-like object. The pattern began as “very casual marks” drawn randomly with a felt marker, which Ando and his team translated into silver wire and black enamel. Visiting the Tokai region gave Malouin a deeper appreciation of its craft traditions: “I already had a huge amount of respect for Japanese craft, but being in the Tokai region made me understand how closely these techniques are connected to a particular place and to the people who practise them.” Of the finished piece, he says: “I hope that, at first, people see something quite simple and calm. Then, when they get closer, they start to understand how complicated it actually is.” Websites: philippemalouin.com, ando-shippo.co.jp Grid Unwoven: Lanzavecchia + Wai × Takanori Senda Grid Unwoven brings together Takanori Senda of Warabi Paper Company with designers Francesca Lanzavecchia and Hunn Wai of Lanzavecchia + Wai. They have reinterpreted the traditional Japanese shōji – a lightweight sliding screen traditionally made with a wooden lattice and translucent paper – through the material qualities of Mino Washi, a handmade Japanese paper. “We came to see washi not as a surface, but as a living material that holds light within itself,” say Lanzavecchia + Wai. Working with Senda revealed how its fibres, density, and translucency could become architectural qualities. “We were interested in imagining what would happen if that order were touched by nature, as if a ripple or a raindrop had disturbed the grid. The wooden structure begins to bend and soften, while the washi and light amplify this sense of movement,” they explain. Their experience of Tokai also reinforced the connection between Japanese craft and its landscape: “The rivers, the kozo, the workshops, the people all shape the final work. We loved seeing how craft is not separated from everyday life there. It is embedded in homes, architecture, and the landscape itself.” The turning point in their creative process came at a visit to Senda's workshop: “We realised washi could extend far beyond the traditional sheet, into architecture and interiors. That understanding shifted our ambition, from designing a screen to creating a quiet spatial experience.” Website: lanzavecchia-wai.com, warabipapercompany.com Kataginu: Bethan Laura Wood x Hiroyuki Murase British designer Bethan Laura Wood collaborated with Hiroyuki Murase of Suzusan, transforming the colour and texture of Arimatsu Narumi Shibori – a traditional Japanese textile technique that creates patterns by folding, stitching, binding or clamping fabric before dyeing – into illuminated sculptural works. After researching textile shades and volumes, Wood was intrigued to create a family of lighting that retained elements normally removed during the process. She worked with Suzusan to develop colours that would respond to light: “I discovered that the soft, gentle pastel pink transforms into an almost neon colour when lit.” She was particularly drawn to the interplay between control and chance in the technique, from the delicacy of traditional threadwork to the organic effects of reactive dyes. Working directly with Suzusan allowed the project to evolve through testing and experimentation. “It was very important for me to get to visit the company in Tokai to see how they make their work and be able to discuss different directions and possibilities,” she says. “I really enjoyed seeing the crafts in the flesh and getting to have a go…and of course the yummy food.” Websites: bethanlaurawood.com, suzusan.com Yamollo: Atang Tshikare x Tomoyuki Matsuda Created by South African designer Atang Tshikare and Tomoyuki Matsuda of Itogo, Yamollo is a sculptural lighting work informed by the structure and colour of Iga Kumihimo braided cords. “The braiding process made me think about sculpture as a living line rather than a fixed object. I became interested in how repeated strands could create volume, movement and shadow, allowing light to become an active material within the form,” says Tshikare. The precision of the Kumihimo art form also reminded him of African hair-braiding and craft traditions, “where repetition and rhythm are used to create meaning and structure.” A trip to Tokai deepened his appreciation of the patience, discipline, and intergenerational knowledge embedded in Japanese craft, while showing him how preservation and innovation can coexist. The collaboration ultimately became a cross-cultural exchange, with Tshikare preserving the integrity of the Kumihimo technique while exploring it in a new sculptural context. “For me, respect comes from understanding rather than imitation,” he says. “The work is ultimately about finding common threads between different cultures, histories and ways of making, and recognising how craft can become a bridge between them for a brighter future.” Websites: atangtshikare.com, itogo.co.jp Find Craft x Tech at Medieval & Renaissance, Room 64b, The Simon Sainsbury Gallery, V&A South Kensington, as part of London Design Festival 2026. Exhibition runs 12 - 30 September 2026. Free entry. Find out more at craft-x-tech.com and londondesignfestival.com.

item.title: Off Season Greece: Winemaker Michael Kouloglou on Santorini's flavours, viticulture and seaside peace
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.90
This is part of Off Season Greece, a collection of guides highlighting the year-round appeal of Greece's most popular destinations, courtesy of our favourite local tastemakers. In this edition, we speak to winemaker Michael Kouloglou. For winemaker Michael Kouloglou, the decision to move from the mainland to Santorini 11 years ago was a simple one. “It is the mecca of Greek white wine,” he says. Since relocating here from the Athenian Riviera town of Piraeus, he’s worked with a number of local wineries before launching Orycton, his small-batch Assyrtiko featuring grapes grown on old vines from all over the island. It was a winner at the 2023 Decanter World Wine Awards. On top of the siren’s song of Santorini’s prized volcanic terroir, however, Kouloglou says he appreciates that the region’s windy conditions allow him to pursue his other passions: surfing and kitesurfing. He’s currently settled in Monolithos, a quiet seaside village in the east – but has historically lived all over Santorini, which has offered him great insight into the rhythm of the island. “Each village has its own unique character,” he says, “far beyond the image [of Santorini] that most visitors see.” Here, the longtime Santorini local shares why autumn is his favourite time of year – and all the treasures of the off-season. What would you say is the sweet-spot time of the year to visit – when the travellers have not yet arrived, but local life is buzzing? If I had to choose the best time to visit, I would choose the entire off-season, from late September until around May. Every part of [offseason] has its own personality: Autumn brings relief after harvest, winter offers complete peace, and spring fills the island with optimism as nature comes back to life, just before the new season begins. What do you love most about being there during the off-season? Santorini has two completely different lives. One is the island that millions of visitors experience during summer. The other begins in October and lasts until spring. That is the Santorini only the people who live here truly get to know. By the end of harvest [in September], both the vineyard and I are exhausted. After weeks of living on adrenaline, my body is desperately asking for rest. Around the end of September, the evenings become cooler; you need a sweater after sunset, the days grow shorter, and the strong summer Meltemi (the Aegean wind) gives way to a gentler, northern wind. Everything feels softer. All the locals are tired after another demanding [tourism] season, but at the same time there is a feeling of optimism. Restaurants and bars begin to close for the season, and that's when the closing parties begin; friends you haven't seen for months suddenly reappear. You don't even need to make plans; you know you'll see them somewhere during a closing party. Who’s around this time of year? Is it all locals? Greek domestic visitors? Are there any travellers at all? During autumn you'll still find some travellers, but they are completely different from the summer crowds. They usually come looking for a quieter side of Santorini; they enjoy walking, hiking, discovering wineries and small villages, instead of rushing from one attraction to the next. By the end of November, even the last seasonal workers have left the island. We have a saying here that "the last boat has sailed." From that moment on, Santorini belongs almost entirely to its locals. Conversations become longer, people have time for each other again, and everyday life feels calmer. I think that's the Santorini most visitors never get the chance to experience. What’s notable about the locals in Santorini: do they have any of their own unique traditions or a reputation amongst Greeks for anything in particular? One thing that has always impressed me about the locals is how deeply everyday life is connected to the Orthodox Church and its traditions. Almost every small chapel on the island has its own patron saint, and every saint's feast day is celebrated with a panigyri, a traditional village festival. During the summer, many of these celebrations continue late into the night with traditional music, dancing and plenty of local wine. What I also find fascinating is that many of the locals still organise their year around the feast days of the saints. They won't say, "I'll start pruning in late November." They'll say, "I'll start after Saint Philip's Day and I have to finish before Saint Alexios' Day." That's how they measure time. It's a tradition that has been passed down from generation to generation, and it's still very much alive today. Where would we find you eating during this time? During the off-season, you will most likely find me at Pentozali, a traditional taverna that serves authentic meze from both Santorini and Crete. I absolutely love it for its relaxed atmosphere, its genuine food, and its people. What I appreciate most during this time of year is that it becomes a gathering spot almost exclusively for locals. It is very common for me to run into someone who has just finished a hard day's work in the vineyards. We’ll sit down together for a glass of wine and a little chat, with absolutely no rushing around. What’s the seasonal dish to order at this time of year? If you are lucky and the spring timing is right, the dish to order is definitely an omelette with wild asparagus. It’s a rare treat because you can't just find it every day; it completely depends on whether someone woke up early in the morning and gathered the wild asparagus fresh from the countryside. Another staple that is almost always on the table is our traditional Santorini fava topped with sautéed onions. It is incredibly simple, but when cooked properly, you truly don't need anything more. Are there any areas of the island that really come alive during the off season? As the summer venues close, the life of the island doesn't disappear; it just shifts to the places where people actually live year-round. Areas like Karterados and Messaria become the real hubs. They are central points on the island that stay busy and full of life all year. The the local closing parties of fall range from wild gatherings by the beach bars to more laid-back evenings in traditional cafés and small local hangouts. Later, in the winter, as people begin gathering more at homes, these central areas remain the heart of our social life. But if you want to talk about a completely hidden side of Santorini that comes alive in a very quiet, spiritual way, it’s the Askitaria. These are old stone monk lodgings perched right on the edge of the cliff on the mountain between Perissa and Kamari. In the spring, you will find many locals sitting there for hours, doing nothing in particular but gazing out at the endless blue, the passing ships, and distant islands like Anafi, Ios, and Anydro. How does the weather change the destination during this time of year, and what are the (dis)advantages of that? Autumn and winter are much warmer and sunnier than most people expect. They bring a rare, beautiful peace. For us winemakers, even the rain is a blessing, not “bad weather” – it’s a relief to see the vines finally get a drink after months of summer drought. The main disadvantage, if you can call it that, is the unpredictability: March, for instance, is a strange and stubborn month with strong winds, cold snaps, and constant weather shifts. What does a perfect Saturday in the off-season look like to you? My perfect off-season Saturday starts slowly, without checking my watch – perhaps walking through the narrow paths of the caldera in Fira or Oia. Later, I would meet up with friends. There is always an excuse for an impromptu barbecue, either with meat or, even better, fresh seafood; almost every group of friends here has at least one good fisherman. We would share a coffee or wine, talk without any rush, and if we are lucky, someone might randomly pick up a lute, a tsampouna, or a violin. No big plans or appointments needed, just letting the night unfold naturally. Do you have any favourite activities during this time of year? My favourite activities are tied to the water. The Aegean is ideal for kitesurfing due to its consistent winds, and as paradoxical as it may sound, specific weather systems often generate great surf here during the winter. We have a small but tight-knit community of surfers on the island, and when the conditions are right, we all head out into the water. Even though the water is still cold, the feeling is incredible. Sometimes you might even catch people paddleboarding inside the Caldera with absolutely no sea traffic, no cruise ships or catamarans, just you travelling parallel to the old quarries and rusty iron piers that hold the island’s history.

item.title: “I think every place has surprising, inexplicable quirks if you know how to pay attention to them.” RF Kuang takes us to Taipei in her new novel, Taipei Story
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.70
In RF Kuang’s latest book Taipei Story, the genre of the campus novel outgrows its name. The novel follows Chinese-American college freshman Lily Chen, who leaves the pale, male, and Yale environs of New Haven, Connecticut, for an intensive Mandarin-language program in Taipei for the summer. While her own family has never set foot in Taiwan, Lily holds on to the belief that perfecting her Mandarin will finally reconcile the shortcomings of being a diaspora kid. And when it came to choosing a place to study the language, travelling to Taiwan conveniently didn’t require her to apply for a visa. But on this quixotic mission to achieve total fluency, she finds that the gulf between her and her complicated family history won’t simply mend itself through diligent study. Her presumptions quickly unravel as she seeks answers in the gaps between economy seats on the flight from Boston to Taipei; in the uncertain, stilted words of Chinese heritage speakers; and in arthouse cinemas and concert halls she’s drawn to for the promise of blending in. From the seasonally inappropriate hot springs of Beitou to the glossy, souvenir-flogging halls of Taipei Taoyuan International Airport, the plot of this coming-of-age story doesn’t shy away from the uncomfortable realities of travelling abroad. Compounded by the sudden passing of Lily’s grandfather – which renders her initial motivation to study Mandarin moot – these follies only deepen beneath a veil of complicated mourning. And yet, they are also softened and forgiven with a grace that comes uniquely from allowing ourselves to be vulnerable in foreign places. Condé Nast Traveller spoke with Kuang about how home, identity, and the split between two places inspired Taipei Story, which is now available in bookstores. Walk us through your research itinerary for Taipei Story. The first place I looked was personal experience. When I started jotting down notes for what would become this book, I didn't know what it was going to be. I was just trying to make legible a tough time in my life when my Gong Gong passed away and I was in Taiwan. I was also in an intensive language program where I was wandering aimlessly around Taipei, meditating on [concepts of] home and cultural alienation. I wasn't walking around with a research agenda. I was just following crowds into places to see what they were seeing. If a long line of people was swarming, I would just join it. I would end up at screenings of movies I'd never heard of, or bookstores that I didn't know existed because I felt so blank, confused, and empty. I wanted somebody else to show me the answer to, “what is your city?” and if I became a ghost in its wake, was there a way I could totally erase myself? A lot of the descriptions in the novel where Lily ends up going to a place by accident, like the National Concert Hall, are places I also encountered by accident. Then, I started thinking about turning all those notes into an exaggerated, fictionalised version of what this experience would be – like if I were even younger and more dim-witted about how the world works. I read a lot of the major modern Taiwanese authors [like Kaori Li, Bai Xianyong, Chen Yingzhen, Wu Ming-yi, and Yang Shaung-zi – all mentioned in the author’s note and available in English translation] and wondered how they were thinking about home, identity, and being split between their mainland cultural heritage, and what it meant to be Taiwanese. How does this novel interface with – the sometimes impossible – expectations of homecoming? I'm fascinated with fantasies of homecoming and the narratives we buy into about how certain cultural experiences can return you to the fold. A lot of Chinese heritage speakers end up getting these flattened experiences in the US that feel like touch points, but are actually silly ways to reconnect – distilled cultural simulations such as Lunar New Year, red envelope parties, and film screenings. I say this not to mock diasporic kids; it makes total sense. You get so little, so you take whatever you can have, even if it's not region-specific or what your parents experienced. In Lily's case, I'm fascinated by the promises of heritage speaker-study abroad programs (editor’s note: these are linguistic immersion programs designed for students who grew up in households speaking a second language) because they hold so much promise and meaning for many people attending them. With Taiwan in particular, if you think about it just on the logical level, every step of this premise that you could, as a Chinese-American, go to Taiwan, to study Mandarin, to feel closer to your family on the mainland – is crazy. Lily's family has never been to Taiwan. She's the only person who's ever stepped foot there until her mom has a layover. When she finally gets there, she starts learning all the ways in which she is so wrong and how her experiences of Chineseness and the trajectory of her family history has absolutely nothing to do with Taiwan. In the end, she is a little more aware of this complexity and moves towards a more genuine, honest encounter of a strange place. She's like, I'm a foreigner, this is a weird summer, and maybe that's okay. In what ways does foreignness, or a lack of fluency, act as a source of fuel for travel and exploration in this novel? I definitely think [feeling out of place] is generative because I’ve felt like an outsider culturally for most of my life. My family immigrated [to the US from Guangzhou when Kuang was four-years-old], and I never felt like I quite belonged in the world of Dallas, Texas. I was a pretty happy kid, but when you're on the periphery, observing how people behave, I think you just get more perceptive. When I go back to China, that’s also not home, which is not a unique perspective. I think almost every immigrant kid feels this way. When I'm in China, I am looking at my family, and I observe cultural codes that they're following, and I have to figure out how these rules work because I didn't grow up understanding them innately. Being reflective about all of this makes you a good writer. In Lily's case, I don't think she perceives her bumbling and ignorance as virtues. For her, it’s a barrier between her and the rest of the world. Because she's so afraid of getting things wrong, she never asks for help and is never willing to embarrass herself. The ethical argument that the book is making is that embarrassment is really good for you. To admit, “I don't know what's going on,” and also “somebody helped me,” is an attitude I wish we all embraced more, not just when we're travelling, but in our entire lives.
