I find it a strength, and Lily finds it a weakness, and by the end of the book, she's at least accepted that she's gonna mess up, and she might as well own it. From the Poppy War trilogy to your last novel Katabasis, you often take on the perspective of being a student. Why return to the eyes of an undergraduate for this story? This book was very different because it's the first book of mine where the protagonists weren't growing up with me. When I was working on the Poppy War trilogy, I was a teenager, and they're teenagers, then they're undergrads, grad students, and in their late-20s. I was writing very reflexively to try to understand the world from my vantage point in life, but I had a couple of life changes in the past few years that made me more interested in going back. With the maturity of turning 30, I have more comfort in making fun of the person I used to be. When I was writing Taipei Story, it was like, I could write a memoir of what I experienced, or I could make things even more ridiculous, even more embarrassing, and reach back to the person I was when I was 18 going to Beijing for the first time and overwhelmed with everything I didn't know. The key to writing from the point-of-view of adolescence is not from this position of condescension that the youths are so silly, but to be kind to your younger self and recognise that all of your insecurities, all the things that you were failing at, everything that you got wrong, are deeply hilarious and also a really shared experience. There's a lot of humanity in cringe. By setting a story in modern-day Taipei, the narrative acknowledges Taiwanese-Chinese geopolitics, and beyond that, the country’s past with Japanese colonialism, the Chinese Civil War. How did you want to depict Taipei as a city with those layered histories? I wanted to be really cautious here, because I'm not Taiwanese. I'm not an expert in Taiwanese history or literature. As I pointed out in the author's note, this is not a voice from the inside but the very filtered perception of an American teenager who’s learning about all of this for the first time. I did want to poke gentle fun at the way that people generally take Western ideological frameworks that are very binary and project them onto local histories with no attention to what locals are actually saying. There's the first chapter where her little cohort of friends are running around the city, and there’s a pecking order based on assumptions about race. People would ask her where should we go? What should we eat? And she’d always pretend to know the answers and go Google them in the bathroom. They do the same thing when they're at Chiang Kai-Shek Memorial Hall trying to understand, is he a good guy or a bad guy? Is he like George Washington? Should we be taking selfies with him? I wanted to give the experience of somebody who feels like they ought to be an expert by virtue of the ethnicity that they were born into, but who’s actually totally detached from genuine knowledge of the place or history. How did grief form your characterisation of Taipei? [When Lily’s grandfather passed] it was a snapping moment for her. Up until that point, she is trying to slot all of her experiences into this predetermined narrative that this is getting her closer to the person she could have been if her family had never left China. After her grandfather passes, she is thrown into this weird grief and confusion, and she gives up on that goal altogether. She recognises the futility of trying to go back and becoming a version of herself that never existed. Paradoxically, this frees her up to take in the things she closed her mind off to before. Now, she's okay with being a tourist. She goes on these Klook experiences [to Pinglin Tea Museum and Yehliu Geopark]. She’s on a bus with American families from Philly doing all the canned, predetermined activities just thinking, “oh, this is fun,” and learning a lot. Despite all the complex grief that is in this novel, it’s also very funny. Is Taipei a place that is particularly funny to you or has its own language of humour that you wanted to capture here? I think every place has surprising, inexplicable quirks if you know how to pay attention to them. One in particular I'm obsessed with is Taiwan English. I was inspired by a blog post by Tao Lin, an author who also wrote a novel called Taipei. It was just a series of pictures that he took walking around of ridiculous translations, and some of them are accurate on a very literal, character-by-character level, and some of them, I can't believe you would get this result if you ran it through any translation app. But it's not just in Taiwan either. You see it on the mainland. For instance, my mom was wearing a shirt, that just said, “GO FUCK” in repeating block letters. She bought it at a clothes market with her sister when she was in China, and she was only paying attention to the fabric, and she was like, “Oh, it's so lovely. Does this colour look good on me?” and didn't register the text at all. I said, “Mom, do you know what that says?” She turned it inside out and wore it that way for the rest of the day. This article was originally published on Condé Nast Traveler.

item.title: UK cities could soon be allowed to implement a tourist tax – here's everything you need to know
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.16
Regions and cities across the country are set to benefit from extra funds following the latest announcements regarding the UK tourist tax – officially known as the overnight visitor levy. In a statement published by the UK Government on 10 September, it was announced that mayors and local leaders would soon be handed the power to introduce the overnight visitor levy to maximise the benefits of tourism to the country. The new fee on overnight stays may then be invested to boost tourism and drive growth, supporting local communities. Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government Angela Rayner said: “Our amazing towns and cities, and our picturesque rural and coastal communities welcome millions of visitors every year – local leaders should have the power to make the most of that popularity.” “This measure will give mayors the choice to raise and reinvest funding where it’s needed most. It’ll help support the local services, public spaces and attractions that both residents and visitors rely on, with decisions taken by people who know their area best.” While early reports suggested that the UK tourist tax, as it has since been dubbed, would be uncapped, the statement released on 10 September made it clear that budget staycations would be protected. Rather than a flat fee or rate, the levy will be charged as a percentage of the cost of the accommodation – but UK citizens won’t be exempt from paying the fee in other UK regions or cities. This is just the latest in a growing number of fiscal devolution reforms that see local authorities have more power over their areas following the appointment of Andy Burnham as Prime Minister. Steve Rotheram, Mayor of the Liverpool City Region, said, “This is something I’ve been calling for over many years, so I’m really pleased the government is taking forward plans to give Mayors the power to introduce a visitor levy locally. “Our visitor economy is already worth more than £6.8bn a year and supports more than 55,000 jobs across the Liverpool City Region. A modest levy on overnight stays could potentially raise up to £18m a year – money that would stay here and be reinvested directly into the events, culture, experiences and infrastructure that bring millions of visitors to our region. “Visitor levy mechanisms are often used in many great cities across the globe to improve the visitor offer and attract even more people to enjoy the experience. It would give us more money to support the things that make our visitor economy such a success, while helping our businesses and communities to benefit from its continued growth.” Will there be a London tourist tax? While plans are yet to be confirmed, including how much visitors will need to pay on arrival in the capital, it’s expected that there will be some form of London tourist tax. In the 10 September statement, the Mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, said: “I strongly welcome the Government giving London the power to introduce an Overnight Visitor Levy. This needs to happen sooner rather than later. London’s visitor economy is a huge success story, supporting jobs, businesses and investment across the capital and the wider country, and I have long argued that London should have the same flexibility as other major global cities to raise and invest funding locally. “A well-designed, modest levy has the potential to provide an important additional source of funding to support growth, strengthen London’s offer to visitors and help us remain globally competitive. It would allow us to reinvest in the places, infrastructure, culture and experiences that make London one of the world’s greatest cities to visit, while helping manage the pressures that come with welcoming tens of millions of visitors every year. “I will work closely with London’s boroughs, accommodation providers, hospitality and tourism businesses and other partners, before final decisions are taken.”

item.title: Crackling fires, frost-dusted fells, and English fizz: 9 best UK Airbnbs to book for Christmas 2026
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.08
Whether you need more space to host the whole gang, or want to escape to pretty village for a change of scenery, taking over a UK Airbnb at Christmas is an ideal way to celebrate the festive season. For inspiration, we’ve rounded up the loveliest Airbnbs to book during the festive period – from seaside escapes for two to countryside hangouts big enough for the whole crew. item.title: Off Season Greece: Ceramist Christiane Smit on the joy of Paros at its most pure and peaceful
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.46
This is part of Off Season Greece, a collection of guides highlighting the year-round appeal of Greece's most popular destinations, courtesy of our favourite local tastemakers. In this edition, we speak to ceramic artist and owner of Moonhouse, Christiane Smit. For Netherlander and artist Christiane Smit, a holiday on Paros in 2008 rerouted the course of her life. “It wasn’t a carefully planned life decision; it was something I felt instinctively,” she says of her sudden move to the Cycladic island. “I listened to that feeling, stayed, and started building a completely new life on the island.” Having lived all over the island since then, she now operates a ceramics atelier in the village of Lefkes, and owns the stunningly minimalist clifftop villa rental Moonhouse – both of which are open to visitors. She is currently completing the restoration of a nearly 100-year-old stone house in the village of Kostos. Here, the now-local shares the shoulder-season delights that keep her on-island year-round, and her favourite hotel-slash-taverna for a warming meal and stay. What would you say is the sweet-spot time of the year to visit – when the travellers have not yet arrived, but local life is buzzing? For me, the sweetest time in Paros is late spring or early autumn. The island feels wonderfully balanced: Everything is open, but life is still unhurried. I love walking through the villages in the morning, when the streets are still quiet. The air smells of jasmine, fresh bread from the bakery and the sea. You hear church bells, neighbours greeting each other, and the wind moving through the olive trees. The light is what inspires me most; it changes constantly, making the whitewashed houses glow and bringing out every texture in the stone. As a ceramic artist, I find myself collecting those colours, textures and moments every day. They’re as much a part of my work as the clay itself. What do you love most about being there during this season? The season allows me to slow down and notice everything. The colours of the landscape, the textures of old stone walls, the shifting light on the sea – those details naturally find their way into my ceramics. I don’t have to look for inspiration here; I simply have to pay attention. Who’s around this time of year? Is it all locals? Greek domestic visitors? Are there any travellers at all? It’s mostly locals. The cafés are filled with familiar faces, fishermen are heading out in the morning, and shop owners have time to stop and chat. You also meet a small number of travellers: The people who aren’t looking for the typical summer holiday, but who want to experience the island more slowly and authentically. There are also Greek visitors escaping the city for a long weekend or visiting family. It’s a lovely mix, but the locals set the rhythm, and that’s what gives Paros its real character. What’s notable about the locals in Paros; do they have any of their own unique traditions or a reputation amongst Greeks for anything in particular? What I’ve come to appreciate most about the people of Paros is their warmth and sense of community. Even though it’s a popular island in summer, life outside the season is very local. People know one another, and there’s a genuine willingness to help each other. As someone who lives here year-round, that’s something I’ve really come to value. There’s also a deep respect for craftsmanship – from marble carving, for which the Cyclades are famous, to fishing, farming and handmade work. Where would we find you eating during this time? One of my favourite places is the family-run taverna at Hotel Julia in Drios. I love it because it feels authentic and unchanged – a place where generations have welcomed people with simple, honest food and genuine hospitality. My perfect day always starts with a swim in the crystal-clear waters just below the taverna. Afterwards, I walk up for a long, leisurely lunch. There’s something so special about sitting there, the sound of the waves below and nowhere else to be. What’s the seasonal dish to order at this time of year? Winter on Paros is the season for revithada (slow-baked chickpea stew), hearty bean soups, and goat or lamb braised with local wine – dishes that are more like daily specials rather than menu staples. But if there’s one meal that defines the island’s quieter months, it’s whatever is cooking in the pot that day (mageirefta). That’s what locals order, and every taverna has its own depending on the day. Are there any areas of the island that really come alive during the off-season? I wouldn’t say any one area suddenly comes alive in the off-season; it feels more like the island returns to its natural rhythm. While Parikia is the social hub for year-round residents, it’s the villages – Lefkes, Marpissa, Prodromos, Kostos, and Dryos – that reveal the character of Paros through seasonal festivals, religious celebrations, and community events. How does the weather change the destination during this time of year, and what are the (dis)advantages of that? You get cooler temperatures, crisp, sunny days, and the occasional rainstorm, which turns the landscape unexpectedly green. The island feels softer and more vibrant. For me, one of the greatest advantages is the sense of calm. Of course, there are a few trade-offs. Stronger winter weather systems can occasionally disrupt ferry schedules, and many seasonal businesses close until spring. But these are minor inconveniences. What does a perfect Saturday in the off-season look like to you? My perfect Saturday begins slowly with a coffee in my house, catching the first sunlight. From there, I’ll often wander through Lefkes, Marpissa, or Prodromos before a long lunch at a traditional taverna. In the afternoon, I usually head back to my ceramic studio. The quieter months are when I’m most creative. Without the intensity of the summer season, there’s space to observe, reflect, and create. At sunset, I love taking a walk along one of the beaches or coastal paths. Even in winter, there are many clear, sunny days, and the light over the Aegean is extraordinary. I usually end the day with friends over a simple meal and a glass of wine. Do you have any favourite activities during this time of year? I love walking the ancient Byzantine paths that weave between villages. With few people on the trails, the silence becomes part of the journey. This winter is especially meaningful, as I’ll be putting the finishing touches on a small renovation project in the village of Kostos, a space I’ve been shaping with the same care and intention that I bring to my ceramics. Creating a home is, in many ways, another form of making, and I find great joy in both!

item.title: We’re calling it: this autumn is the witchiest yet. Here’s why
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.44
Witches are stepping out of the shadows. They’re lighting up the big screen and casting their spells all over your social media feed. They’re frolicking in Welsh woodland at witchy retreats. They’re buying medicinal herbs at quaint boutiques. They're getting tarot readings and manifesting under the full moon. So come closer, my pretties, because the mystical has officially gone mainstream, just in time for autumn’s spooky season. Perhaps there’s something in the stars. In the wake of the solar eclipse, we’re looking to the universe and opening ourselves up to its infinite possibilities, magic included. Hollywood is giving witchcraft its moment in the moonlight, too. September sees the release of Practical Magic 2, the long-awaited sequel starring Nicole Kidman and Sandra Bullock, reprising their roles as the Owens sisters. Then in November, Hexed hits our cinema screens, Disney’s animated tale of a teenage girl who discovers she has secret magical abilities. That same month, the first UK flagship Harry Potter store will open in central London, a vast two-floor emporium for budding witches and wizards. TikTok is also bringing this once hush-hush world to a new audience, with 9 million posts using the hashtag #WitchTok. The online community showcases everything from tarot readings and spell tutorials to crystals and manifestation, making the occult more accessible to curious newcomers than ever before. For those ready to swap scrolling for something more immersive, Britain’s witches are gathering in person. On 24 October, Witch Festival arrives in Cornwall with more workshops and ceremonies than you can shake a wand at. Visitors can make oracle cards and herbal blends for yoni steams, delve into Cornish and Celtic folklore and, as darkness falls, gather for a collective fire ritual. Then on 14 November, Witchfest Market makes its debut in Lewes, with stalls piled high with cosmic wares and spell supplies, alongside a programme of esoteric talks. Offering a deeper dive, The Dreaming is an arts and crafts country house, once owned by interior designer Laura Ashley. Set within the leafy, ancient landscape of the Elan Valley in mid-Wales, it’s since been transformed into an enchanting healing centre by singer and activist Charlotte Church. Dust off your broomstick as The Dreaming’s witch retreats, held a handful of times a year, have proved so popular they sell out at lightning speed. “The response has been pretty extraordinary,” says Church, who created the course with High Priestess Tree Carr. “We’re adding as many dates as we realistically can, because the appetite for it is clearly there.” For Church, this surge of interest in her witchcraft retreats taps into a larger collective shift. “We live in a culture that has become incredibly disconnected, from the natural world, from community, from our bodies and, in many ways, from a sense of ritual and meaning,” she says. “There’s something very beautiful about returning to practices that remind us of the power incarnate in life.” That sense of reconnection is cultivated over five days, as guests use releasing rituals to banish negative thought patterns, dip into herbal baths, cast spells and listen to stories around the flickering campfire. Dream weaving, a practice involving dream incubation, takes place nightly, before participants retire to rooms decked out in flowing white fabrics, tatami flooring and lunar imagery. The archetype of the cackling wicked witch, once feared and mocked in equal measure, is being reconsidered, says Church. “The figure of the witch has historically been associated with people, especially women, whose knowledge, independence or power sat outside accepted structures. I think reclaiming the witch now can be about reclaiming intuition, creativity, community, our relationship with the earth and our own agency.” Nowhere understands this reckoning quite like Salem, the coastal Massachusetts city across the pond. It was here that the notorious witch trials took place in 1692, when 20 innocent people accused of witchcraft met a particularly gruesome end. In a curious twist, today Salem is a glorious witchy wonderland, filled with female-owned metaphysical businesses. More than a million tourists swoop into Salem for Halloween, and 2026 looks set to be a bumper year as the city also celebrates its 400th anniversary. The trick-or-treat season kicks off in early October with the Haunted Happenings parade through the cobbled streets. A month of celebrations and events follows, including a Ghostbusters gathering, gothic horror storytelling at the atmospheric House of the Seven Gables and a comedy night in Salem’s Witch Village. New for this year, The Witchery, a creative studio where practising witches teach their craft, has expanded to a second location in Salem’s wharf area. Alongside their beloved broom-making classes, The Witchery has added spell jar workshops, recreating the vessels that people once hid beneath their homes to ward off malevolent forces. Yours will be filled with twinkling crystal chips and good intentions, ready to take home and manifest positive change. The coven is growing in Los Angeles too, with the recent opening of the Witch’s Cottage. The two-floor café, restaurant, bar and event space harnesses its Hollywood location, with interiors that wouldn’t look out of place on a movie set. The fantasyland was created by Danielle Ozymandias and Celina Lee Surniak, two queer witches, as an ultra-inclusive space. “You do not need to be a practising witch to visit us,” says Lee Surniak. “When we built this place, we had the intention for people to come in from the urban, hyper-industrialised world to seek solace and comfort in our little forest.” Witch’s brew coffee is served beneath lights shaped like pointy black hats in the bakery, while the bar resembles an enchanted woodland. A highlight of the devilishly good cocktail list is the protection spell cocktail, made with agave and smoked black foam to ward off negative vibes. There’s also a calendar of regular metaphysical happenings, such as bewitched burlesque, magic mic nights, sound baths and sessions exploring the shadow self. Ozymandias says it’s not surprising that witchcraft is moving into the mainstream. “We’re seeking ways to belong, to feel safe, to feel cared for, because the current systems of capitalism, consumerism and patriarchy aren’t helping people.” “We are not meant to live and work ourselves to death,” Ozymandias adds. “Matriarchy, the turning of the seasonal wheel and witchcraft are much more rewarding.” Perhaps, amid the breakneck pace of modern life, there’s a certain allure in slowing down, following the moon rather than the clock and finding a coven of kindred spirits.

item.title: Off Season Greece: Hotelier Agapi Sbokou says Athens comes alive in the autumn
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.40
This is part of Off Season Greece, a collection of guides highlighting the year-round appeal of Greece's most popular destinations, courtesy of our favourite local tastemakers. In this edition, we speak to Agapi Sbokou, co-owner and CEO of Greek hotel brand Phāea. “Alive. That's how Athens feels to me,” says Agapi Sbokou, co-owner and CEO of the Greek hotel brand Phāea. Sbokou grew up in Crete but has lived in Athens since she was 18. “There was never really a debate about where to live. We go back and forth between Athens and Crete, but the city just feels so buzzy. It’s a place that is constantly transforming.” Sbokou knows a thing or two about why people are drawn to a particular destination. “When you go to a place, it should be about understanding the local rhythm,” she tells me. “I'm in love with Athens. It’s a place that you can continue exploring your whole life.” Here, Agapi explains why autumn is so magical in the Greek capital, and lets us in on some of her favourite places to visit at this time of year. Tell me what you love most about Athens. Walking around and exploring. The city transforms with the seasons, and it feels completely connected with nature. For example, my neighbourhood is full of these beautiful trees called jacarandas, which have very small, lilac flowers. It completely transforms the whole neighbourhood when they bloom. Elsewhere in the city, some areas are filled with bitter orange trees, which smell strongly when they bloom. There are a lot of young people here, and recently a lot of young travellers are coming to stay and live in Athens. They all come with a very open heart and the desire to explore as we, the locals, do. Athens is not about what’s cool and what’s not – it’s about discovering new things, revisiting old places, and watching the city transform over time. That’s what I love. When is the best time to come to Athens? When it’s not too busy, but local life is buzzing? I would say April and October or November. I've always been a summer person, but to be honest in Athens spring and autumn are the most beautiful seasons. In April, the blooms are starting to appear. There are beautiful smells around the city. But autumn is great because the weather is very mellow. There's still the warmth from the summer, and there is very little rain, so it's very pleasant and you can walk around all day. What makes autumn so special in Athens? There's a different light about the city, which is not that classic Greek light that you see during summer. It's more yellow and soft. The city starts preparing for winter, so there is a kind of excitement with the locals – people are returning from the islands, they still go swimming in the sea and still it's quite warm. It's the perfect season because it combines it all. Who’s around this time of year? There are travellers year-round. But in autumn, it's a different kind of traveller. People who come during this season have a slower appreciation of the city, which I love. I think that's what tourism should be. We should spend more time exploring a place and really getting a sense of it to understand its rhythm, rather than going in and out, just ticking off things. Do as the locals do. Maybe spend two hours in a coffee shop. Get to know the person sitting at the next table and start a conversation. Spend three hours in a museum, not one. There are so many museums here, and not just the big ones. The Benizelos Mansion is the oldest house in Athens, or, of course, the Benaki Museum with the Nema Collection. There are so many things to discover, and it shouldn't all be packed into one trip. The kind of travellers who appreciate this tend to come off-season. What’s notable about the locals in Athens; do they have any of their own unique traditions or a reputation amongst Greeks for anything in particular? An appreciation for a slower way of life, I guess. Athens is very much about its neighbourhoods, which is characteristic of the city and its people. You start your day at your local coffee shop, then visit your local barber, grocery store and dry cleaner. You stop for a few minutes, you exchange a few words. That's very typical of people here. You have a sense of community. Sometimes you buy things and you don't need to pay – they know you, and write it in a notebook and you pay at the end of the month. Athens feels like a village, even though it's a city of four million. Where would we find you eating in autumn? I love exploring new places, but I also love going to the same places again and again, because then you begin to know the people. There is a new generation of fantastic restaurants that embrace Greek cuisine, but I’d rather visit the ones that have been around for 20, 30 or even 50 years. I go to Manári Taverna a lot, which is in the city centre. It's right by a Byzantine church, and it has very traditional cuisine with strong Cretan influence. There is Pharaoh, a very cool restaurant where everything is slow-cooked over a wood-fired grill. It has the best music and the coolest bar, so it's really fun to visit. Plus, it belongs to a friend, so it's always fun to see him and to catch up. There’s a place called Dourambeis where I've been going with my dad since I was a kid. It's very traditional, and it has the most delicious fish. In autumn, these places are perfect because they are traditional and laid back, but really good food. They all use excellent, seasonal ingredients. Speaking of seasonal ingredients, what is the most traditional dish that people should eat when they come in autumn? That's a good question. It's hard to say, because the weather in Greece stays warm into autumn, so we tend to drag summer dishes into the year. For example, one very traditional dish we continue to eat in autumn is gemista. It’s often made with very ripe tomatoes – you empty them, and fill them with rice, mince meat, and other ingredients like herbs and nuts. You could replace tomatoes with courgettes, or aubergines, or peppers. It is very, very Greek and very traditional. And then, of course, in autumn, we eat a lot of pastries and pies. The most typical one is spanakopita, a cheese-and-spinach pie. Those are more home-cooked recipes, though. Athens is like the melting pot of the whole of Greece, so a lot of wider Greek traditions are incorporated in the restaurants. Skioufichta is a specific thick pasta dish, made by hand. You boil it in a broth, and then it's sprinkled with cheese. And it's the most delicious dish, very soothing, very appropriate for autumn – perfect with a glass of red wine. Order this at Manári; it's one of my favourite dishes there. Are there any areas of Athens that really come alive in autumn? I've always lived in and around Kolonaki. It's an area that's quite buzzing and quite well known, but I love the streets that are purely residential. There are a couple that are quite high, with amazing views, because Kolonaki is at the bottom of Lycabettus Hill. From those streets, you can see straight down to the Acropolis, in between buildings. In the autumn, when the light is right, it just feels amazing and very Athenian. It's almost like a secret – you know that if you turn down a specific street, you’ll suddenly get this view. That feeling always makes me feel very lucky to be there. In autumn, it’s easier to be more spontaneous in Athens, because it’s not as busy. It feels like normal life is back, so you can access museums, galleries, exhibitions and restaurants more easily. We Greeks are very welcoming. We want to share the best of what we have. It’s the perfect time to do that.

item.title: Off Season Greece: Hotelier Nikos Tsepetis on how to explore Crete's green heart during spring, without the crowds
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.35
This is part of Off Season Greece, a collection of guides highlighting the year-round appeal of Greece's most popular destinations, courtesy of our favourite local tastemakers. In this edition, we speak to hotel owner Nikos Tsepetis. For 30 years, Nikos Tsepetis has run Ammos, one of the most talked-about hotels in Greece. The seaside boutique hotel in Chania, northwest Crete, is a manifestation of the man himself: joyful and design-focused with a commitment to high-quality cuisine (including his Red Jane Bakery) and local roots. Tsepetis’ improvisational approach to hospitality creates a home-away-from-home warmth that keeps many of his guests returning year after year. Born and raised in Chania, Tsepetis is deeply connected to his hometown, which he believes is different from other towns in Crete, because “we are more international and welcoming to foreigners, and it's a multi-layered city”. Yet 80 per cent of his staff are locals, he says. “It adds to the experience because you always meet people who were born here, who remember the past, so there is this continuity”. Here, Tsepetis tells us why spring is his favourite time of year in Chania. What would you say is the sweet-spot time of the year to visit? Just before high season. April and early May are my favourite time of year because the climate is amazing. Chania is on the western end of Crete and is the prettiest part of the island because it's greener, and we still normally have snow on the Lefka Ori [White Mountains] – you can see them from the sea while swimming. In spring, everything is very fresh, everything is well painted; you can go to the villages and monasteries, and all the flowers are out. Also, spring often coincides with Easter, which is important in the Greek Orthodox religion. I don't care at all about religion, but it's still very spiritual and beautiful. What do you love most about being there during this season? It's less busy. The rain cleans everything and the snow melts, so we are greener than other parts of the island. Everything's fresh and new; you can feel the rejuvenation. So spring is a very sweet time. Who’s around this time of year? Traditionally, Chania benefited from the presence of foreigners, even before it became touristy. It’s very urban, with more than 100,000 permanent residents, so you have everyone from hipsters and freaks to lefties living here – not the expected Greek island crowd. It's always very lively, and what sets it apart from some other towns in Crete is that the locals are a driving force with a very loud voice. They are not here to serve the foreigners. Where would we find you eating during this time? My all-time favourite local is Evgonia Tavern. Only a very simple tavern; it has fish and meat in a non-fish environment. I love Periplous restaurant for its unbeatable location at the beautiful Tanneries Hotel. It’s one of the old buildings by the water where they used to process leather. In spring we go to the villages because it's still very mild and there aren’t too many people. I always go to Ntounias, a very old, well-known rural taverna in the middle of nowhere near Drakona in the mountains. There's a crazy guy there, Stelios Trilyrakis, who has been involved with slow food for 30 years. You don't know what you’ll eat or when you’ll eat it. It's very inexpensive, and he cultivates everything himself. In Greece, we love French fries. And Stelios makes amazing chips by cooking them in olive oil in a ceramic pot. What’s the seasonal dish to order at this time of year? We're famous for doing a traditional Tsoureki Easter brioche, a kind of braided bread that's sweet but not too sweet. Once a year we also eat a special soup called magiritsa made from lamb intestines, lungs and liver. We normally eat it at home – it’s not so much a restaurant dish – but we do a very good one at Ammos. Also, Nyketerida is famous for it. Spring is about beans and greens – we have beautiful asparagus and the best artichokes – and goat roasted in the oven with potatoes, zucchini and tomatoes. We also have a very famous dish called ‘dakos’, a barley rusk, with tomato sauce and this amazing goat’s cheese called mizithra. One of the best places to eat it is Costas Cafeneion, a family-run cafe in Maza village, which is between Chania and Rethymnon. Are there any areas of the island that really come alive during the off-season? In January and February, people from around the world come here for the mountains and skiing, including the annual Pierra Creta ski mountaineering race. How does the weather change the destination during this time of year, and what are the (dis)advantages of that? Summer is very hot and can be dry, and then we have the winter, which is rainy. But in spring the weather is cooler and you can hike, ski and swim. The sea is actually colder in spring than in winter because of the snowmelt. What does a perfect Saturday in the off-season look like to you? I’m biased but Saturday is a great day to hang out at my Red Jane Bakery early in the day. I think it's very pretty. At around 2pm I’ll visit my small wine shop next to Red Jane and I always have one cigarette per day with one glass of wine. On Saturdays it gets busy and the crowd is very interesting. They’ll have wine with a sandwich in our beautiful, small yard. I also love hanging out at a small, humble taverna called Kafeneio Fix in the old Turkish neighbourhood, or I’ll go to Tamam, an amazing taverna inside a beautiful Turkish hammam dating back to 1645. Spring is also the beginning of the open cinema season. My favourite open-air theatre is Attikon. Another one, Kipos, shows mostly old Hitchcock-style films in a public garden created during the Ottoman era. If I want to have a final drink before going home, I’ll go to Fagotto, a jazz bar that has been there for 40 years. Do you have any favourite activities during this time of year? I love hiking all the way down to Chora Sfakion, a small coastal town in the south. From there you can either take a boat or walk for an hour along a very steep and narrow path – not for the faint-hearted – to Sweetwater Beach, a tiny cove made up of very tiny pebbles. If you dig your hand in it, sweet water from the mountains comes out.

item.title: Off Season Greece: Author Anastasia Miari on Corfu's thriving food scene and why spring is the best time to savour the isle
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.30
This is part of Off Season Greece, a collection of guides highlighting the year-round appeal of Greece's most popular destinations, courtesy of our favourite local tastemakers. In this edition, we speak to food writer and author Anastasia Miari. Whenever I’m feeling disconnected from myself or from Greece – the place my mother’s family is from, and whose traditions I grew up with – I muster up the energy to make a comforting Greek meal. But whether it’s my yia yia’s old-school-style avgolemono soup, my mom’s traditional pastitsio, or my thea’s Americanised spanakopita, the recipe is rarely ever already written down. As with so many other cultures’ time-tested family dishes, they’re usually passed on by doing; surmising how many box grater’s-worth of tomatoes you'll need, or eyeballing the number of glugs of olive oil to add. Enter Anastasia Miari, a food writer and author who has spent the better part of a decade travelling all over the Mediterranean to document not only Greek recipes, but create an extensive, photographic encyclopedia of the many octo- and septuagenarians (and their often-remote villages) who passed those very dishes – and their way of life – to younger generations. Nowadays, when I want to try a new or lighter Greek dish than the handful of rib-sticking ones I know, I crack open my stained copy of ‘Yia Yia,’ Miari’s first cookbook. Better yet, when I want to explore the cuisine of the broader region – Moroccan tajin, Turkish breakfast, Sicilian pasta – there’s now also her newer iteration, ‘Mediterranea.’ To say Anastasia is an expert in all things Greek would be an understatement – she was born and raised on the Ionian island of Corfu in Greece’s northwest, and is currently renovating a historic cottage on the Cycladic island of Tinos to enjoy with her family in the summers (and filming a web series about it all). Here, the British-Greek Corfiot shares her guide to the Italian-leaning island’s Venetian traditions, natural splendour, and seasonal dishes – all of which are best experienced in the off-season. What would you say is the sweet-spot time of the year to visit – when the travellers have not yet arrived, but local life is buzzing? I would say May, springtime. Because of all this rain that we get then, the island is fully in bloom in May – it's stunning. It's like being in a Disney movie here. What do you love most about being there during this season? If you have in mind to do the Corfu Trail, which is a hiking trail that runs all the way from the south of the island to the north of the island, the month of May is a particularly incredible month to come in because you tend to have the best weather, but it's also not incredibly hot. You're still able to hike, especially in the morning and evening hours. Who’s around this time of year? Is it all locals? Greek domestic visitors? Are there any travellers at all? Corfu is really interesting because it doesn't have this sort of off-season, on-season vibe as much as the Cycladic islands do. What I mean by that is the island doesn't shut down when it isn't summertime. We have a university and we have a music school on the island, and because it is very cosmopolitan and because it's so big, we tend to retain our residents. People don't tend to move to Athens or to Saloniki as much as they might in more remote Cycladic islands. So of course, there are a few travellers, but it's not as many as you'll find in July and August. And I think it's usually people who love to hike and people who like to be in nature, so it's a different kind of traveller. What’s notable about the locals; do they have any of their own unique traditions or a reputation amongst Greeks for anything in particular? What's notable about the locals in Corfu is that, supposedly, we're the craziest in all of Greece? [Laughs] Other Greeks tend to say that Cretans and the Corfiots are the crazies of the nation. But I do think we are quite distinct in Corfu because we have this incredible heritage that comes from Italy, and we love to align ourselves with the Italians. The Venetians came and colonised 500 years ago, and many vestiges of our Venetian past are still visible, not just in the architecture and in our food. Where would we find you eating? The places that eat in the summer tend to also be open in the winter, and I think that's great because you are always able to rub shoulders with local clientele. One of my favourite places to eat is Marina's Tavern in Corfu Town because they do all of the classic yia yia home-cooked dishes in a really great home-cooked style – eating a pastitsada or a stifado at my léas table. So I love Marina's Tavern for all of the traditional home-cooked dishes that they serve. What’s the seasonal dish to order at this time of year? The dish to order is tsigarelia, which are like wild greens that you find at that time of year. And here in Greece, we sauté them with lots of spices. Again, this is a sort of vestige of the Venetians, and [a result of] our being put on the spice trail by the Venetians. So it includes lots of spices like cinnamon, cloves, and cayenne pepper. So cigarella, that's a great dish to have. Are there any areas of the island that really come alive during the off season? In the off-season, I think Corfu Town is the place to be because even everyone else from the rest of the [surrounding] island tends to sort of congregate in Corfu Town. It’s really popping off, especially because of the universities there: there's a high concentration of people hanging out in town; it's very much alive. Any coffee shop you go into will be full of people. Again, Corfu isn't one of those sort of Disneyland islands that shuts down in the winter and opens up this sort of like fake display of life in the summer. It's very much alive all year round. How does the weather change the destination during this time of year, and what are the (dis)advantages of that? Corfu is one of the wettest islands in Greece, so if you try and come in May you’ll have the occasional rain shower. But generally, it's just a very pleasant temperature and really great to experience the best of the island, which is its nature. September or October can be the trickiest months. What does a perfect Saturday in the off-season look like to you? It's fantastic to go into the mountains and visit mountain villages on weekends because I think much of the coastline has been marred by mass tourism. The real secret and beauty of this island is actually inland, in the mountains. Do you have any favourite activities during this time of year? It absolutely has to be hiking. And I think the most incredible way to live and experience this island is by doing the 112-mile Corfu trail. You don't have to do the whole of it, of course. You could just pick one part of the whole trail because it takes like seven days to hike it in full. It took me a bit longer, but you can pick a section of the trail and do just that. It's unmissable, really. Where to stay: Snugly in a pine-studded cleft beneath Mount Pantokrator, the island's tallest mountain, The Merchant's House has six guestrooms carved out of the stunningly renovated stone-walled shell of a 14th-century Venetian building. High ceiling rooms with chunky stone walls are far from mediaeval, however: there are Coco-Mat mattresses and large balconies with spectacular views over to the Albanian coast opposite.

item.title: From the Andes to the Arctic: 9 extraordinary group expeditions to book
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.30
It’s official: all across the globe, routine sightseeing is out, and immersive, adrenaline-fuelled exploration is firmly in. Truly, it seems our collective wanderlust has never been higher. Recent reports show the adventure travel sector is moving towards an eye-watering trillion-pound valuation, thanks to our collective desire to get firmly under the skin of a place while we’re away. Some studies suggest that over seven in 10 Gen Z and millennial travellers now choose active holidays over conventional fly-and-flop resorts, and there’s been a distinct rise in solo trippers joining small-group expeditions, starting the week as strangers, and ending as friends. Importantly, you do not need to be an athlete to get stuck in. "Soft adventure" itineraries – where physical effort is rewarded with comfortable lodging afterwards and the best local expert guides – now make up roughly two-thirds of all bookings. Everything is taken care of, from where you sleep to what you eat, and most itineraries can be altered to suit your own tastes. Whether rafting through deep European canyons, scaling iconic summits, or tracking rare wildlife in India, these handpicked bucket list group trips represent some of the very best landscape and experiences across the globe.

item.title: Elinor Dashwood's guide to Devon: wild moors, rickety antiques and historic pubs for the ultimate Jane Austen escape
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.29
There are few places in the world I know and love quite as much as Devon. I spent much of my youth growing up in the county that’s sandwiched between Dorset and Cornwall, exploring its woods, rolling hills and beaches, as well as its creaking old pubs and other assorted watering holes. With ancient lore baked into its bones, it’s little wonder this corner of the West Country has captured the imaginations of writers for centuries. Among all that verdant countryside, there really is magic at every turn. Jane Austen knew it. She spent time in Devon with her family in the early 19th century and, later, set much of Sense and Sensibility there. After leaving behind the grandeur of Norland, the Dashwoods move to Barton Cottage, on a fictional estate a few miles from Exeter. Their new abode may be considerably more modest than the home they have left behind, but its surroundings are thoroughly romantic: nestled in a valley, backing out onto high hills, and winding lanes, bucolic downs, woods, knolls and streams all around. It is nothing if not idyllic. With a new adaptation of Sense and Sensibility heading to cinemas this September, I decided to explore my hometown through the eyes of the book's heroine, Elinor Dashwood (played by Daisy Edgar-Jones in the upcoming film). From windswept walks to antique hunting, these are the places I think a modern-day Dashwood would frequent – and possibly fall in love along the way. Explore Dartmoor National Park Much of the Devon landscape you’ll see in this year’s adaptation is filmed in Dartmoor National Park, where vast stretches of open moorland are punctuated by granite tors, swirling rivers and plenty of wildlife – birds of prey, otters and, yes, Dartmoor ponies. Much of the production was based around Princetown, Tavistock and Gutter Tor near Yelverton, with Edgar-Jones knowingly referring to filming on “stormy Dartmoor” in a recent interview. There are countless walks through the national park, whether you want a gentle ramble or something more dramatic. AllTrails is particularly useful for finding routes on the go, but whichever direction you head in, expect sweeping views and the kind of wild landscape that feels made for an Austen heroine. Follow the antiques trail in Ashburton For furniture, art, books, trinkets and beyond, there is nowhere quite like Ashburton, home to more than 10 antique shops clustered together on the informally named Ashburton Antiques Trail. One can easily imagine Elinor Dashwood picking up a neat walnut writing desk, a stack of books or a pair of candlesticks here, alongside any number of other treasures she happened upon. Start along North Street, stopping at The Shambles, The Globe, Catherine Waters Antiques and Denis Perry Antiques and Interiors, where you’ll find everything from sizeable pieces of furniture to smaller decorative treasures. Continue along East Street for East Street Antiques and Alchemy Antiques, before ducking into the tiny shops on St Lawrence Lane, where rummaging is very much part of the fun. You’ll find pieces spanning the centuries – the 19th included – and at all manner of price points. Eat at Emilia Once the antiques have been acquired, there’s no better place to refuel than Emilia, a tiny Italian restaurant and wine bar on Ashburton’s East Street. The menu is designed for sharing, with plates spanning pappardelle with duck ragu and braised pork to pickled fennel and plenty of good bread to mop up olive oil, all eaten on chunky wooden tables. While it’s true that Elinor probably wouldn’t have been particularly au fait with Italian cuisine, it’s a lovely, rustic, cosy visit for anyone in the area – somewhere I'm fairly certain a modern-day Dashwood would surely adore. Wander around RHS Garden Rosemoor If you were to picture the perfect Austen-worthy garden, RHS Garden Rosemoor might be it. Like Barton Cottage, it sits in a valley, and encompasses everything from carefully designed formal gardens to sprawling woodland filled with ancient trees. It’s an ideal place to wander, lost in thought – a pastime of which any Dashwood sister would surely approve. Thanks to clever planting, there is something to see in every season, although late spring and summer are particularly lovely. Don’t miss the two rose gardens, home to more than 2,000 roses, both old and modern, which provide as much fragrance as they do colour. The cottage garden, complete with thatched summer house, is similarly enchanting. Together, they make for a very pretty way to while away a few hours. Go horse riding When in Rome, do as the Romans do – and in Devon, many would consider horse riding a crucial part of country life. In the novel, the Dashwood sisters sadly have to give up their horses when they leave Norland for Devon, but with a little artistic licence – and given that Elinor is depicted on horseback in Ang Lee’s 1995 adaptation – it seems safe to assume she’d take the opportunity to ride across the moor if she could. Close to Widecombe-in-the-Moor is Shilstone Rocks, a family-run riding centre where I learned to ride way back when. As well as mastering the basics in its – mercifully sandy-floored – arena, you can head out on hacks across the surrounding moorland. Few things make you feel more immersed in the Dartmoor landscape. Have lunch at Riverford Field Kitchen While we don’t know Elinor Dashwood’s modern culinary preferences, I’m willing to bet she’d be a farm-to-table kind of woman, preferring local produce for its taste and health benefits. Riverford Field Kitchen, on Riverford’s organic farm near Buckfastleigh, feels like an obvious choice. Here, organic vegetables take centre stage in generous, seasonal dishes, which are brought out to the whole restaurant at the same time. With dried flowers punctuating wood-clad walls and much of what’s on the plate grown just outside, it’s an excellent – and delicious – way to get your five a day. Stay at Glebe House Once a vicarage, Glebe House is now a Georgian guest house set within 15 acres of beautiful East Devon countryside overlooking the Coly Valley. There’s a kitchen garden, where produce is grown before making its way onto guests’ plates, an outdoor swimming pool and the sort of pastoral views Elinor could happily lose herself in. Inside is just as charming. With interiors that nod to Charleston, the rooms are layered with pattern, paintings, wooden armoires, antique furniture and inviting fireside spots made for reading. It’s colourful and characterful rather than overly polished – exactly the sort of country house one imagines a Dashwood sister settling happily into. Have a pint at the Pilchard Inn Given Elinor’s fondness for walking and the outdoors, she’d be impressed by the enormous beach at Bigbury-on-Sea, particularly at low tide, when great stretches of sand and rock are exposed for exploring. It’s then that you can walk across to Burgh Island, the island famously associated with another female writer, Agatha Christie, who used it as inspiration and a setting for some of her novels. Perched on the island overlooking the sea is the tiny Pilchard Inn. Dating back to 1336, it’s an atmospheric, slightly ramshackle pub that has welcomed fishermen, smugglers and countless other characters over the centuries. Today, it makes an excellent stopping point for a pint and a bowl of chips before heading back across the sand. Browse the Devon and Exeter Institution As an avid reader, Elinor would have loved the Devon and Exeter Institution, a historic independent library on Exeter’s Cathedral Green. Founded in 1813, just two years after Sense and Sensibility was published, it is home to two spectacular Georgian library rooms, lined with books and topped by cupolas. Today, visitors can buy a day membership or join one of the Institution’s free guided tours on Wednesday afternoons, providing the perfect excuse to lose an hour or two among the leather-bound books – including some of Austen’s oldest works. Explore Killerton For another dose of history, head to the National Trust’s Killerton, a grand Georgian country house just outside Exeter. Surrounded by thousands of acres of farmland, woodland and orchards, the house is also home to the National Trust’s largest fashion collection – an archive of more than 20,000 items spanning centuries of dress. Think 18th and 19th century clothes – the sort of garments Elinor herself might have worn – alongside pieces belonging to Queen Victoria and 20th-century couture. Not everything is displayed at once, but changing exhibitions offer a fascinating glimpse into the way people have dressed over the centuries. For a heroine known for observing the world around her rather carefully, it feels like a fitting final stop.

item.title: I spent a night in Kenya’s remote bush, and it changed how I think about safaris
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.21
It’s the night of the blood moon in northern Kenya. We sit in a loose semicircle around a crackling bushfire, our canvas chairs settled into the sand of a long-dried riverbed. The flames warm our faces as embers drift up into the starry sky. Gin and tonics sweat in our hands while the bush comes alive at night. Somewhere nearby, hyenas giggle and whoop in the darkness, and a silent group of giraffes glides across the riverbed ahead, their tall silhouettes graceful in the half-light. As the moon slips into the earth’s shadow, soft rhythmic chanting rises from the surrounding manyattas. Samburu women sing, their melodic voices carrying across the plains as part of a ritual to mark the eclipse and guide the moon back to life. We sit quietly, listening as it glows crimson and is slowly reborn. In that moment, caught between moonlight, wildlife, and Samburu tradition, it’s impossible not to feel the captivating pull of Sarara. Sarara sits within the vast Namunyak Conservancy in northern Kenya. It’s more than just a safari destination; it’s a community-led conservation project run with the Samburu people, who have lived here for generations. The project protects over 850,000 acres of wilderness and creates sustainable livelihoods for the local community through tourism, conservation, and cultural programs. The people are at the heart of the experience. Many guides, hosts, and team members come from nearby villages, bringing a deep knowledge of the land, wildlife, and traditions that no guidebook can match. Life beyond the game drive Head out on guided walks and game drives with Samburu trackers, swim in natural rock pools tucked into the hills, or ride on horseback across the open plains. But time here offers a window into life beyond the safari, too. Sarara opens the door to the community behind it, with opportunities to visit the nearby Reteti Elephant Sanctuary — Africa’s first community-owned elephant orphanage — where rescued calves are raised by local keepers before eventually returning to the wild. I fell in love with Long’uro, a baby elephant found trapped in a well, his trunk badly injured after a hyena attack. Seeing him now, with a shortened trunk, gently cared for by the keepers who rescued him, says everything about the sanctuary’s work. There’s also the chance to meet the women behind the Milk Mamas programme, one of the first initiatives in the conservancy to provide women with their own independent income by selling goat milk used to feed the orphaned elephants. One afternoon, I joined a circle of beading mamas, sitting cross-legged together with a translator as we stitched bright beads into ankle bracelets and shared stories about our lives. The conversation was relaxed, curious and open — one of the most memorable experiences of the trip. Spending time in a traditional Samburu manyatta offers a glimpse into daily life within these small homestead communities. Visits to local schools and healthcare projects supported by the conservancy give a deeper understanding of life in this remote region and the work being done to support the community. A handful of hideaways Sarara is a small collection of places to stay scattered across the conservancy. Each offers a slightly different way to experience the landscape, from the privacy of Reteti House to the treetop hideaways of Sarara Treehouses and the remote simplicity of Sarara Wilderness, alongside the original Sarara Camp that first put this remarkable corner of northern Kenya on the safari map. Across them all runs the same design philosophy – open, earthy spaces built from natural materials that blend delicately into the surrounding landscape. Sarara Camp Set on the slopes of the Mathews Mountains, Sarara Camp is the original lodge at the heart of the conservancy, comprising six spacious canvas tents with solar-heated outdoor showers and wide terraces overlooking the valley. At the centre sits a beautiful natural infinity pool overlooking a permanent waterhole. One afternoon, we counted nearly twenty elephants from two different herds gathered there, alongside zebras, giraffes and warthogs, like something out of the opening scene of The Lion King. Wildlife moves easily through camp too; one evening, a zebra grazed quietly outside my window, and most mornings I woke to a giraffe browsing just beyond my tent. Reteti House A short drive from Sarara Camp, Reteti House feels altogether more private, bookable by a single group, meaning the space is entirely your own. It’s a secluded hillside retreat with just four tents and sweeping views across the plains below. The main house is a beautiful gathering space filled with African artefacts and rustic details. A small infinity pool is tucked into the rocks beside it, shaded by trees and looking out across the plains. Down below, a waterhole draws wildlife through the night; more than once, I woke to the unmistakable sound of elephants slurping away in the darkness. Reteti is also known for its resident leopard. My first night alone in the tent was slightly nerve-wracking, but the nerves soon turned to excitement as the distant rasp of the leopard echoed through the cliffs and baboons wailed their alarm calls. Sarara Treehouses Sleeping high in the canopy, Sarara Treehouses is one of the most unique stays in the conservancy. Eight tented suites sit among the branches, linked by wooden walkways that wind through the trees while wildlife moves quietly along the forest floor below. Spending the night in the treetops felt completely magical, something I’d never experienced before, and it brought a surprising sense of luxury to the wilderness. Monkeys chatter constantly overhead, while elephants often wander beneath the decks. The main house is the largest of the camps, its heavy timber beams and striking bar creating a beautiful space for long evenings. Amarula on ice quickly became the drink of choice, best enjoyed while listening for another resident leopard, said to nap in a branch within view from my bed. Sarara Wilderness Sarara Wilderness is the most remote of the camps, reached by a short hop in a small plane with Scenic Air Safaris - an experience in itself. The pilots fly low over the plains, pointing out wildlife and Samburu manyattas below, giving a completely different perspective on the landscape as wildlife moves across the savannah beneath the wings. Landing on the remote airstrip, the sense of isolation becomes immediate. The spacious tents are intentionally temporary, designed to move with the landscape over time, which adds to the feeling of being somewhere truly wild. Days are spent exploring the conservancy with Samburu guides whose knowledge of the land is extraordinary. The wildlife encounters were some of the most memorable of the trip - watching a line of lionesses stride past our vehicle, sitting quietly among an unbothered herd of elephants with a week-old calf and spotting cheetah, leopard and even the rarely seen serval cat. Out here, the wilderness feels closer, wilder, and totally unfiltered. In the end, what defines Sarara is not just the wildlife or the landscapes, but the people. Days quickly turn into friendships with the Samburu guides, hosts and staff who share their knowledge, humour and stories so generously. There’s a genuine sense of connection here, and plenty of opportunities to give back - whether through community projects or simply supporting the people who make this place what it is. It’s that spirit of shared stewardship that makes Sarara feel less like a destination and more like something you become part of, even if only for a little while. Return domestic flights from Nairobi to Namunyak airstrip with Scenic Wilderness start from $600 per person, or alternatively, you can opt for a private air charter with Scenic Air Safaris for up to 9 people at a cost of $3,470 for the aircraft.

item.title: Condé Nast Traveller invites you to A Taste of the Cayman Islands at Wild by Tart this month
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.17
September has long been synonymous with back to school. But in the world of Condé Nast Traveller, it also means making exciting plans for the year ahead – and these typically revolve around the hottest restaurants on the horizon and travel. In the spirit of prolonging the summer sun that is suddenly setting earlier in London, there might be no time more perfect than the turn of the month to join Condé Nast Traveller for an evening celebrating the Cayman Islands at Wild by Tart, Belgravia's chicest coal station-turned-eatery. Set to be hosted by acclaimed Caymanian street food chef Diego Smith, who will be bringing the island's vibrant culinary Caribbean culture to life through an array of cocktails, canapés, and a dinner with wine pairings, we already expect this to be the kind of event where guests will leave happily debating their favourite dish. Not to mention, we'll take any excuse for an evening with a compelling culinary voice from an equally covetable location. Over the course of the evening, Chef Diego Smith will bring the islands to the table via an expertly-curated menu inspired by Cayman’s exceptionally fresh and flavourful produce, all steeped in local traditions and deep sense of place. You can expect anything from mahi ceviche in fresh orange marinade, jerk pork belly on cassava charcoal, grilled chicken papaya salad and traditional Cayman snapper, coconut and breadfruit run-down stew. And if dessert (we won't spoil it) isn't enough to convince you to book a one-way ticket to George Town in your cab home, we don't know what will. From stories behind the kitchen door to the zingy flavours you'd expect straight of a grill on a turquoise water-hemmed beach, we're already counting down the days to this evening that'll be the perfect way to settle back into the bustle of London, all while dreaming for what's ahead. When: Wednesday 30 September from 6.30pm Where: Wild by Tart, 3-4 Eccleston Yards, Belgravia, London, SW1W 9AZ Tickets: From £100 per person, including a cocktail-and-canapé reception and dinner with exceptional wine pairings. Book here.

item.title: The best family-friendly hotels in Sicily, recommended by a parent of three
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.13
The Sicilians are, by and large, remarkably welcoming of bambini, who are embedded in their psyche as a blessing, not an inconvenience. As such, the best family-friendly hotels in Sicily are also some of the island's most lauded. Expect cooing, overly expressive signs of affection and a society that is unabashedly pro-children, being integrated into every facet of life. Even the most elaborate hotels welcome children warmly – perhaps not the sort whose parents turn a blind eye to their darlings smudging pistachio cannoli filling into Zoffany upholstered sofas, but here, first-rate kids' clubs buy parents plenty of off-duty time. Time, that is, to enjoy a sun-dappled terrace framed by crumbling columns and palms, a haze of distant blue ring-fencing the green hills braided in olive groves and vineyards, and the irresistible waft of orange blossom and freshly baked arancini washed down with crisp Etna wines. Sicily is a wildly romantic island, layered in history, wrapped in surreal blue waters, caught in the crosshairs of civilisations, and intensely varied in its landscape, cuisine and culture – depending on which region you pootle a few kilometres over to. Wild spirits can run free on the island’s abundant argiturismos, free of the formalities and precariously balanced 17th-century busts of the high-end hotels. Where you choose to stay depends on your children’s ages, proclivities and really, how you like to holiday. This is our edit of the best family-friendly hotels in Sicily. Editor's picks of the best family-friendly hotels in Sicily: Best for luxury: Villa Sant'Andrea, A Belmond Hotel Best for children at different ages: Veruda Best for teens: Bracciallieri Best kids' club: Veruda Best all-inclusive: Mangia's Costa Ragusa Borgo 5 tips for visiting Sicily with children Prepare for the heat Small children will struggle outdoors in Sicily in peak summer from about 11am-4pm. Unless they’re aligning with Sicilian siesta law or are under a shaded kids’ club, it would be wise to consider shoulder season for pre-schoolers. What’s more, many of the Baroque Sicilian towns and cities’ ancient cobblestones aren’t designed for prams, so remember to bring a good baby carrier, backpack or hop on one of their sweet family train rides that introduces children to grand Baroque architecture, pointing out the best gelato spots, chocolatiers and the gargoyles peering down from atop their palazzi. Pack smart Invest in a wide-brimmed sunhat and long-sleeved, long-legged swimsuits for tinies to save their skin from the fierce Sicilian sun. Always check with your hotel for minimum kids club age, and what time their restaurant opens – what's worse than a 7.45pm restaurant opening time when you’re children are used to eating at 5pm and being tucked up two hours later? Hire a car Unless you’re staying solely in Palermo or Catania (where Sicily’s two airports are based), it’s worth hiring a car to explore, though don’t expect the rental company to procure age-specific carseats (even if this has been agreed). I have experienced this hiccup numerous times and on my last trip, invested in two Cybex foldable Solution G2 carseats for peace of mind. Even if you book a smart transfer with hotels, you really have to emphasise the ages of your children and reconfirm to avoid the booster seat for a six month old scenario. Embrace day trips Older children and teenagers will enjoy exploring Siciliy’s maze-like towns and villages, diving into its Slim Aarons-looking pools and aquamarine swimming spots, and hopping on boat trips for uninhabited islands and caves. The beauty of Sicily is that, no matter where your hotel is located, much of the island can be explored via day trips, though families would be forgiven for indulging a little Dolce Far Niente, poolside or under the shade of the citrus trees. Take your time Having travelled to Sicily as a family multiple times, the best formula for a successful 10 days or two-week break is, unquestionably, combining a family-friendly hotel with a villa stay. Hotels provide parents with all the pampering they’re so desperately in need of (the spa facilities, the elevated dining, the kids’ club or babysitting), then a villa serves up all that precious family time and, crucially, the privacy to let children run wild and the room space to ensure everyone’s banking ample sleep. It works particularly well for multi-generational groups and opens up new areas of the island for everyone to explore. How we choose the best family-friendly hotels in Sicily Every hotel on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveller journalist who knows the destination and has stayed at that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider both luxury properties and boutique and lesser-known boltholes that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination. We’re always looking for beautiful design, a great location and warm service – as well as serious sustainability credentials. We update this list regularly as new hotels open and existing ones evolve. For more information on how we review hotels and restaurants, please look at our About Us page. This is our edit of the best family-friendly hotels in Sicily. For more inspiration on where to stay in Sicily and Italy, visit About the author Rosalyn Wikeley is a regular contributor to Condé Nast Traveller and a ski and Sicily expert. Former Creative Content Editor for the publication, Rosalyn has written for the Financial Times, the Telegraph, The Times, Vogue, House & Garden, the London Standard and consulted on content for leading luxury brands and hotels. She beelines for Sicily's Baroque South East every Autumn to seek out new hotels and arty enclaves, and also writes extensively on Paris, family-friendly stays and skiing.

item.title: New London restaurants to try in September 2026: our editors' honest opinions on the openings everyone's talking about
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.13
We've always got one eye on any new restaurants opening on the London food scene. Our editors are on the ball for the latest openings in each London neighbourhood, from Covent Garden restaurants to Shoreditch hotspots. For the ultimate list of places to eat in the city, check out our definitive guide to London's best restaurants. These are the places that we consider the crème de la crème, from generations-old spots that have stood the test of time and Michelin-starred dining rooms that get better each year to mind-blowing new openings from this list that we decided deserved a spot on the ultimate round-up of the best restaurants in London. For new restaurants opening in London recently, we've seen follow-ups from some of the city's biggest-name chefs and a handful of restaurant openings that have stopped us in our tracks: from London's newfound love for BBQ to a Turkish restaurant that's turning heads. These are our favourite openings of the past six months. How we choose the tastiest new restaurant openings in London The best new restaurants in London are the most exciting places to eat that have just opened in the capital city. Ranging from small affairs with daily changing menus from up-and-coming chefs to Michelin-starred spots with fresh new menus, these are London's new restaurants we've got our eye on right now. Every restaurant on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveller journalist who knows the destination and has eaten at that restaurant. When choosing new restaurants, our editors consider both high-end and affordable eateries that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination. We’re always looking for stand-out dishes, a great location, warm service, and serious sustainability credentials. We update this list regularly as new restaurants open in London. Best new London restaurants in September 2026 Waterhouse Project, Bethnal Green At the start of September, husband-and-wife team Gabriel Waterhouse and Patricia Wakaimba opened the doors to Waterhouse, a much-anticipated restaurant, wine bar and garden set inside a Victorian warehouse on buzzing cobbled Ezra Street, just off Columbia Road Flower Market. Following the closure of The Water House Project in June, their new home is an impeccably designed space, flowing from raised beds outside, where the chefs pick fresh herbs, into a bar area with stainless steel countertops and handcrafted oak furniture, and through to the dining room, which serves 24 covers in an intimate nightly sitting. The food measures up to the space. Chef Gabriel draws on his Northumberland upbringing and the region’s traditional cooking techniques, while adding a playful touch with in-house ingredients such as miso, koji and garums. Start with a punchy, syrupy fig leaf martini at the bar before embarking on the 11-course tasting menu. The ensemble hits a high note immediately with a rich, comforting cep and Madeira tea, before moving into bites that challenge the palate while remaining comforting and, ultimately, delicious. The courses balance refreshing zing, like the oyster with cucumber and sorrel, with familiar but elevated mouthfuls, like the moreish onion crumpet. Larger plates, including a smoked haddock porridge (oyster mushroom for vegetarians), hit a hearty note. The meal ended on singing hinnies, a traditional griddle cake, with boozy-forward lavender and Laphroaig cream. If you manage to have some room left, the seasonal cheese selection isn’t to be missed. This is a savoury, umami-rich tasting menu that has immediately risen to the top of my list for celebratory meals. The team have nailed the difficult task of creating fine-dining plates without a stuffy atmosphere. Gabriel and Patricia’s history of supper clubs, where their journey began, can still be felt in the environment they’ve curated at Waterhouse. Chloe Laws Address: 7A Ezra Street, London, E2 7RH Website: waterhouse.com Bar Blondie, Queen's Park Queen's Park is having a little moment in the limelight of late, preening and showing off as curious eyes turn its way thanks to a slate of clever openings (Don't Tell Dad, where a queue forms for glossy cinnamon buns and plump pains au chocolat every morning; The Salusbury, a smart pub with a dining room that punches above its weight; Naples-inspired joint Casa Felicia) joining some long-standing favourites like Harry and Meghan's favourite Italian Ida and brewery Wolf Pack. Now, everyone's talking about a wine bar that's taking interiors inspiration from Spaghetti Westerns and looking to four imaginary muses – the writer, the actor, the architect and the director – to pull together its cellar book. The Bar Blondie site used to be Milk Beach, an Antipodean all-day restaurant which kickstarted the Queen's Park foodie revolution eight or so years ago. The space is still owned by Aussie Elliot Milne, who's given it a tip-to-toe renovation. Interiors, designed by Macaulay Sinclair (also behind Dishoom's Permit Room and Hawksmoor, among others), are now mid-century sexy with a masculine edge: nutty woods, dark greens, art curated by The Other Art Fair founder Ryan Stanier. The menu looks to France and Italy: delicate grilled artichokes with pecorino di fossa and honey and silky Cantabrian anchovies in puddles of Provençal olive oil are perfect to share, while heartier pastas (we especially liked the paccheri alla vodka with nduja) are the smart choice if you're settling in for the evening. Award-winning sommelier Alexandra Price has curated a wine list that celebrates everything from well-known, beloved estates to emerging producers. I visited earlier in the summer, on opening night, but live close enough to confirm that the buzz has sustained into autumn, too – this is a smart Act II for a cosy neighbourhood joint. Sarah James Address: 19-21 Lonsdale Road, NW6 6RA Website: barblondie.co.uk Best new London restaurants in August 2026 Oudh 1772, Borough Chef Aktar Islam is something of a Brummie legend. He was the first British-born Bangladeshi chef to be awarded a Michelin star in 2019, just one year after opening his debut restaurant, Opheem, in Birmingham's Jewellery Quarter. A few years later, Opheem became the joint-first Indian restaurant to receive two stars, alongside London's Gymkhana, in the 2024 ceremony. Opheem's status as the city's go-to Special Occasion table to book is firmly cemented. So when news of Islam opening in London reached me, a native Brummie, I was naturally a) very proud (how often do chefs find success outside of London and then transplant to Zone 1?) and b) desperate to get through the door. And it is quite the door. Oudh 1772, Islam's Borough restaurant, is set across a Grade-II listed Victorian townhouse, where each storey sits sort of wonkily on top of the next. That's not to say it's not beautiful: designer Polina Sychova collaborated with Islam on the soft, sumptuously layered spaces – all curvy arches and thick drapes, peppered with antiques from Lucknow and even a bespoke hand-painted ceiling in the attic bar. Rather than bouncing across the Indian subcontinent, Islam's menu focuses on the flavours of Awadh, a historic region in the northern state of Uttar Pradesh. Regional street food is a playful place to start: chaat with white peas and potato or gol guppa (better known here, perhaps, as pani puri) are crispy and best eaten with your hands, a perfect way to start any evening. We boldly take on the mutanjan dum biryani with oxtail, a king prawn kebab and the Awadhi monkfish curry – be warned that while this might certainly be a white tablecloth sort of establishment, the portions are hearty. They're also, luckily, all perfectly pitched – perfumed biryani, garlicky prawns, creamy curry.
