Like Opheem before it, this is undoubtedly somewhere for a properly nice supper – prevented from ever becoming too proper by the friendly team and Islam's plucky menu. Add it to the list for your own next Special Occasion. Sarah James Address: 66 Union Street, London SE1 1TD Website: oudh1722.com Kismet, Borough Somewhat unexpectedly located above The Globe Tavern, a buzzy pub on the corner of Borough Market, is Kismet. After passing a throng of pint drinkers, visitors climb a winding staircase and enter a Turkish meyhane – a traditional tavern known for live music and family-style meals. Kismet has captured that atmosphere perfectly: dark, glittering mahogany benches, delicate lace curtains and vintage photographs make the restaurant feel wonderfully homely. Turkish music bubbles away in the background, with live performances on the qanun, a traditional string instrument, even hosted every Thursday evening. The menu follows Turkish meyhane cooking, so come prepared to share. Start with Atom, a thick buffalo milk yoghurt topped with chilli butter; cool and tangy against the gentle heat, it is particularly good scooped up with bread or piled onto Sigara Böreği, a crisp pastry filled with salty white cheese. From the charcoal grill comes Tavuk Şiş, smoky chicken thigh with red pepper, alongside Patates Kizartmasi, fried Cyprus potatoes. Wash it all down with Basketcase, a bottled lager brewed in partnership with Coalition Brewery, or, my personal favourite, a glass of raki. The Turkish anise-flavoured spirit is made for sipping alongside food, its clean, herbal finish acting as a refreshing palate cleanser between bites. The final flourish comes with dessert, when waiters glide between tables carrying silver trays above their heads. Lowered on request, they reveal rows of Turkish tea in delicate tulip-shaped glasses and slices of pistachio baklava drowned in syrup. Kismet is only a year-long residency in the space, so visit while you can. Amelia Dhuga Address: Upstairs at The Globe Tavern, 8 Bedale Street, London, SE1 9AL Website: kismet.london Cue Point, Latimer Road Cue Point is determinedly not a newcomer to the London restaurant scene. For a decade, the hybrid Afghan-Texas BBQ of Kabul-born chef Mursal Saiq and head chef Joshua Moroney has been making a name for itself through pop-ups, residencies and stints at breweries. This summer, they've finally found a permanent home for their low-n-slow, fired-up cooking. Cue Point at The Garden Bar is set inside an unchic West London boozer with, as the name hints, a truly enormous garden out back. Here, meat – Wagyu brisket, oak-smoked lamb shank, black lime pepper chicken bites – is smoked to meltiness, or else cooked over licking flames. Saiq's immaculate Afghan flavours are anything but shy and retiring, and a perfect match for Moroney's expert BBQ techniques. Those chicken bites' gnarly exteriors give way to soft meat – we boldly paired ours with the smoked pimento garlic chilli cheese flatbread to start. Wagyu brisket steak served with fluffy Texas naan and cowboy butter is a non-negotiable, although we'd also recommend ordering the flaky chilli-citrus seabass for something a little (emphasis on the word) lighter. The sticky toffee pudding with Bertotti kulfi was a surprise standout: moreish and sweet, Saiq works with West London gelataria Bertotti to perfect the kulfi. The team serve a special menu on Sundays, when Saiq tells me that people try to sneak in the door; advance reservations are so hard to get. This is West London's opening of the summer, and a must-book for anyone seeking serious flavour. Sarah James Address: Garden Bar Grill & Smokehouse at 41 Bramley Road, Notting Hill, London, W10 6SZ Website: cue-point.co.uk Rosina, Wandsworth It's been 20 years since chef Adam Byatt opened Trinity, which in restaurant years is practically ancient. In that time, the Clapham Old Town spot has not only survived but thrived, earning a Michelin star and cementing itself as a south London favourite – its signature beef tartare is still one of the best dishes I’ve ever had, and I don’t even like beef tartare. So when Byatt opened his latest table, Italian-inspired Rosina, in Wandsworth Common, it was busy from day dot. Busy but effortlessly breezy, with smart couples seated at white linen tables adorned with plates of bread, lemons and olives, and single white candlesticks. Antipasti comes to the table with a vibrant flurry – crimson tuna crudo, smoked sardines on toast, and a heavenly bowl of rainbow Datterini tomatoes with basil, nectarine and buffalo mozzarella. This is the kind of place where everything is confidently simple, and the bread basket is put to good use mopping up every sauce and vinaigrette. For mains, a pillowy turbot is roasted on the bone and swimming in lemon, capers, parsley and wilted spinach. The intriguingly named ‘post-service pasta’ was my favourite; an understated yet masterful bowl of spaghetti with anchovy, chilli, garlic and parsley, essentially the dish Byatt likes to make for himself after a shift in the kitchen. Wonderfully oily and crunchy in equal measure, I ate every tiny crumb and noodle. Pudding is served from the marble trolley that holds court in the centre of the restaurant, with tiramisu rustically served with a generous dollop tableside. If there’s room to try two, the not-too-sweet but cheese-heavy Rosina's torte is a worthy option; the torte and the restaurant are named after Byatt’s daughter Rosie, who also works in the kitchen. Lauren Burvill Address: Rosina, 35 Bellevue Road, London SW17 7EF Website: rosinarestaurant.co.uk All Roads, Brixton I visited All Roads during one of London's many 2026 heatwaves, so it says something about how delicious the food is that I wasn't remotely overwhelmed by the plates of mac and cheese, lamb from the house pot or fried wings that were placed in front of me on one of the hottest days of the year. While the rest of London was digging into light salads, or maybe a barbecue, I was more than happy to get stuck into the hearty dishes from chefs and partners Malika Green and Paschelle Brown, who have finally put down roots in Brixton following three years of sold-out supper clubs. The menu blends Caribbean cuisine with British, European and Southern American influences, resulting in a list of dishes that are hearty, moreish and full of flavour. Split into snacks, smalls, grill and plates (with just two or three dishes to each), it's tempting to order the whole menu – take three friends, and you probably could. Unfortunately for me, I was with just one friend, so we had to be discerning (albeit still rather greedy). Having tried over half of the menu, I truly think it would be difficult to order badly here, but my favourites were undoubtedly the chilli parm clams, served in a sweet and salty tomatoey-soy sauce, with crispy pancetta and topped with parmesan, or the impossibly cheesy baked mac and cheese. We ordered a fresh tomato salad to break up the dishes, and ended with homemade sorrel cheesecake ice cream. In the end, despite the heat, there's nowhere I'd rather have been on a Wednesday evening than here in Brixton Village, soaking up the vibe, flavours and fun of this memorable new spot. Abigail Malbon Address: 44 Atlantic Road, London SW9 8JN Website: allroadsldn.com Hon’s BBQ, Hackney Wick After earning a fiercely loyal following during his two-year residency at All My Friends, chef Man Hon Luk's first bricks-and-mortar restaurant – in the spot formerly occupied by Silo above Crate Brewery – was a natural next step. I never made it to the pop-up, but just knowing that Hon perfected his craft at world-renowned, Michelin-starred Interstellar BBQ was reason enough to clear the diary, hotfoot it over to Hackney Wick and see what all the fuss was about. The space is cool, casual and buzzing – high ceilings, whitewashed walls and simple red wooden tables and chairs let the food do the talking. Hon’s cooking is clearly shaped by his time in Texas, but what lands in front of us is something entirely his own: smoky, low-and-slow meats elevated with Chinese flavours and techniques. Every bite melts in your mouth, with just the right hit of spice and sweetness and the kind of deep caramelised crispy bits you’d fight your fellow diner for. The beef short ribs with Sichuan peppercorn sauce are the star of the show (tender, peppery and sticky) but don’t sleep on the sides; perfectly crunchy green beans with an umami-rich glaze, and a silky mac and cheese with a tangy mustard-laced sauce. Our only regret? Opting to share a bowl of the creamy mango coconut pudding – one each is a must. Sarah Allard Address: First floor, Unit 7, The White Building, Queen's Yard, London E9 5EN Website: honsbbq.com Best new London restaurants in July 2026 Vesper, Exmouth Market When Jackson Boxer opens a new London restaurant, it’s safe to assume it’ll be a smash hit. The chef and restaurateur behind buzzy Brunswick House, Dove and Henri has just opened a new neighbourhood spot on Exmouth Market. Interiors are industrial, with bare brick walls, a metal bar in the centre and curtains hiding candle-lit tables in intimate corners. There’s also plenty of tables that spill onto the sun-drenched street. We dined at Vesper a full month after opening, as tables really are that hard to come by. We made sure to book an early 6pm reservation, as the infamous burger you may have seen plastered all over your Instagram, often quoted as one of the best burgers in London, is ordered off-menu to 10 lucky customers on a first-come, first-served basis. We secured the fourth burger of the evening. The bun is covered in sweet glaze, hugging a hefty slab of seared and torched beef with a rare centre, layered with caramelised onions and oozing gorgonzola sauce. We’d recommend sharing, or you’ll be rolling home without a chance to try any of the other delicious plates. Our favourite dish of the night was the fried potato pizzette: a little circular pizza bread topped with pineapple, stringy stracciatella cheese and mortadella. Other highlights include the green bean salad coated in goat's cheese and gooseberry tahini, the chicken agnolotti – al dente pasta pockets bursting with fragrant chicken liver in a madeira jus. For pudding, order the punchy poached apricot flavoured with ginger and amaretto. Plates were scraped clean, as were our little gimlets, previously filled with the Vesper martini finished with a little squirt of citrus oil. Sophie Knight Address: 8-10 Exmouth Market, London EC1R 4QA Website: vesper.restaurant Langosteria, Whitehall Italian seafood restaurant group Langosteria has a knack for attaching itself to smart addresses in glamorous European locations, from Milan's Design District to St Moritz and the waves at Paraggi near Portofino. So it’s no surprise that the Milanese group’s first UK outpost has made a beeline for Raffles London at The OWO. Whitehall's neoclassical Portland stone grandeur doesn't quite evoke the summery spirit of the Ligurian Riviera, but once you pass through its doors, you're transported to that familiar Langosteria world, with its signature animated wallpaper and matching ambience. Here, everything is bold and impactful with a touch of experimentation – including the bar cocktails. From the concise list, the Pomodoro Mezcal, a smoky take on a Bloody Mary, confused my vodka receptors, but the Spicy Margarita with jalapeño was the unequivocal star. Food-wise, Langosteria casts a wide net in pursuit of freshness and quality, hauling its catch from Italy, Spain, France and Scotland. Locavore advocates will scream, but the quality is undeniable. My Sicilian red prawn starter – butter-soft and topped with wafer-thin slices of pecorino – was beautiful. The mains included Langosteria classics like the King Crab Special Edition 2007 and the Brittany Lobster "Spicy Blue”; I plumped for the crispy-skinned black grouper Chateaubriand, its saltiness offset by tangy-sweet caponata (Sicilian aubergine, olive and caper relish). My langoustine with lobster in a puddle of zingy lemon butter was perfectly al dente, but the Milanese turbot with asparagus and saffron proved somewhat immemorable. I chased it all with a glass of Ferrari Brut from a wine list that features most of the Champagne heavy hitters alongside an impressive, Italian-dominant selection of reds and whites. Portions are generous throughout, and for guests of the Raffles hotel, it's just a short stagger to their rooms upstairs. Noo Saro-Wiwa Address: Langosteria, Whitehall Place at The OWO, London, SW1A 2BD Website: langosteria.com Willet's, Chelsea At the back of The Cadogan, A Belmond Hotel, is an elegant wooden staircase that King Edward VII (when he was the Prince of Wales) ascended to visit his lover, the Victorian actress and socialite Lillie Langtry. It still stands as a testament to the history (and discretion) of this particular 1880s Chelsea townhouse, and today, though less steeped in scandal, it is as regal and luxurious as ever. The Cadogan is also home to Willett’s, a new British bistro that seems set to become a hotspot in its own right, even amongst those not staying upstairs. Studio Shayne Brady, the interiors team behind the renovation, has modernised while remaining true to the hotel's history – bathing the space in calming blues and greens. Executive chef Michael Turner (a Gordon Ramsay alum) is producing à la carte dishes that showcase the very best of British produce in unfussy, delicious dishes. The sourdough crumpets with gentleman’s relish and dressed Dorset crab were the definite showstoppers and are destined to become signature dishes. Mini but mighty, I’d have been more than happy with plates of those alone. Seasonality and locality are buzzwords thrown around quite loosely these days, but Willett’s really does do credit to everything that is brilliant about the produce of the British Isles. I'd also recommend the succulent Beef Wellington and the Colchester oysters. We’ve no doubt that this restaurant will become as legendary as some of the hotel’s historic residents. Cass Farrar Address: 75 Sloane Street, London, SW1X 9SG Website: belmond.com Dante, Mayfair Devotees of all things Stateside were intrigued when one of America's best cocktail bars, New York City's Dante, jumped across the pond in 2025 to pop up at grand dame Claridge’s. Rather than tire and bloat at yet another cross-Atlantic collab, the gourmands kept coming. And so, a year later, the hotel restaurant closed its doors for a facelift any Mayfair resident of a certain age would approve of, led by Bryan O’Sullivan Studio, with a fresh palette of green-and-blue tones and fantastical, botanical murals by Beth Rodway, to welcome Dante as a permanent resident of the neighbourhood's slickest hotel. We follow Billecart-Salmon Champagne with a taster of the Negroni Rosa, a watermelon concoction that tastes like a swig of the summer to come. A host of NYC favourites are now on the menu – we sample delicate caviar tarts and champagne pearls and are taken aback by the gargantuan grilled king prawns, their smoky, chilli-butter scent enveloping our booth. If a dish is preceded by the restaurant’s name, you know it’s one the chef’s hedging their bets on. And so the Dante smash burger arrives: a juicy patty coated in provolone cheese and topped with sweet caramelised onion, beside perfectly crispy chips awaiting their saucy demise. Burger devoured and Parmigiano Reggiano-doused veal Milanese inhaled between us, we call on our second stomachs for pudding with a side of spectacle. An espresso martini arrives, my face staring back at me in cocoa dusting courtesy of the bar’s cocktail-printing sorcery, alongside an uber-indulgent sticky toffee doughnut that illuminates our woozy cheeks with a whiskey flambé. It's a fiery finish to a meal I’ll be dining out on for a long time to come. Connor Sturges Address: Dante Mayfair, Claridge's, Brook Street, London W1K 4HR Website: maybourne.com Best new London restaurants in June 2026 The Sea, The Sea, Chelsea When we walk into Pavilion Road’s The Sea, The Sea – already a familiar name in Chelsea, but now a restaurant serving far more than just drinks and oysters – we don’t know what to expect. Above the ground-floor raw bar, tables are bathed in light, and the design is minimalist, but we quickly learn that all attention is poured into the fare. The menu spotlights lesser-known fish, plus whatever catch is locally abundant from the seafood suppliers they've built trusted relationships with. We start with cold sake and a tin of Imperial (as a caviar enthusiast, I love that the sour cream comes pre-topped with chives), followed by butter-soft Isle of Skye scallops with flowering currant. Often, the raw bar usually outshines everything else to me, but three warm dishes – cuttlefish ragu with green almond, smoked Chalkstream trout on a Jersey royal mash, and a rice vinegar-steeped John Dory with maitake – are impossible to top. The ragu is nothing like we imagine: no pasta, just clean-cut cuttlefish with an unbelievably flavourful squid ink salsify that results in an immediate repeat order. Come dessert, don’t look beyond the potato ice cream with smoked eel. It sounds hard to wrap your head around, and for that reason, you must order it. Tamara Southward Address: 243 Pavilion Road, London SW1X 0AW Website: https://theseathesea.net MA/NA Mayfair A new opening in Mayfair comes with glitzy high expectations, which we immediately felt as we were swept through the doors of MA/NA by a suave-suited doorman. He guided us through the long, winding bar space with a house DJ and down to our table under huge bonsais and gold statement lighting. A martini is poured table-side as we browse the extensive menu divided into small plates, robata (meats from the Japanese grill), sushi, steak cuts and large plates. We ordered to share: rock shrimp tempura in a glazed sticky sauce, juicy chicken thigh skewers from the robata grill, a 12-piece sushi platter with fresh cuts as selected by the chef (which could also pass as a piece of art) and the crunchy duck salad with sweet pomegranate. But, our favourite dish, which – fair warning – comes with a big price tag, was the Japanese A5 Wagyu slices served on a hot Himalayan salt stone, which not only flavours, but sears the meat from its heat. Melt-in-the-mouth slices of the finest beef, packed with flavour. MA/NA is on par, if not tastier than some of London's favourite high-end Japanese spots, with equally flashy guests and interiors. Sophie Knight Address: 30 Upper Grosvenor Street, London, W1K 7PH Website: manarestaurants.com Buvette London, Neal's Yard 14 years since its New York debut, chef Jody Williams has brought Buvette (and with it, the spirit of the West Village) to the cobbled streets of Covent Garden – slap bang in the middle of Neal's Yard. This charmingly chic bistro – complete with curated antiques and a black bicycle parked out front – somehow manages to strike just the right balance between familiar and fancy, with a day-to-night menu focusing on locally-sourced produce. We start with a crisp glass of bubbles as we make our selection, following the house suggestion of sharing three to five dishes between two. Plates are indulgent yet remarkably delicate; a vibrant ratatouille, fresh steak tartare, garlicky escargot, and decadent dauphinois. The standout is, unsurprisingly, Buvette's signature croques; we opted for the forestier, a vegetarian riff on the original, paired with a generous pour of white wine (French, naturally). To end, tarte tatin and a mousse au chocolat, followed by a perfectly chilled martini made just the way you like – a highlight among the well-executed classic cocktails on offer. I can’t wait to visit again, whether for a flaky morning croissant and espresso or another evening encounter with that croque... Drew Burns Address: Buvette London, 2 Neal's Yard, London WC2H 9DP Website: buvette-london.com Ornella, London Fields Foodies and film fanatics flocked to Lupa when it opened its doors in Highbury – an Italian feeding frenzy from restaurateur Ed Templeton and chef Naz Hassan, fuelled by The Gentleman star Theo James’ involvement. The reviews were promising, and bookings soon became hard to come by, so it came as no surprise when the trio announced a follow-up – Ornella. On the corner of a leafy suburban street in London Fields, this new arrival is an edible love letter to Milanese fare that the capital’s food scene has long been crying out for, named in honour of the late singer Ornella Vanoni. Inside, it’s simultaneously cosy and sexy, diners tucked into banquettes and huddled around circular tables illuminated by flickering candlelight. Proceedings start over punchy sbagliato and caffè amaro cocktails – easy on those, mind – before the fluffiest focaccia in town arrives, warm and doused in glittering olive oil, alongside wafer-thin slivers of salty mortadella and coppa. There’s a choice of four starters – shoutout to the sea bream tartare, I hear, from my companion – followed by five ‘primi’ dishes. We slurp on salty onion broth and twirl our forks to catch shavings of cheese in the simple yet moreish butter and Parmesan tagliatelle, all washed down with generous pours of Venetian Manzoni Bianco. Naturally, onto secondi, a satisfyingly crisp chicken Milanese, used mostly to mop up heaps of silky mashed potatoes that likely contain more butter than potatoes (no complaints from us). We saunter into the night, hands in circular motions on our stomachs, remarking on how beige and calorific our spread became. No regrets at all, mind, as we plot our return to get snug in one of Ornella’s corners when the mercury drops, if not before. Connor Sturges Address: Ornella, 51 Wilton Way, London E8 1BG Website: ornella.restaurant Mezzogiorno by Francesco Mazzei It’s no small feat bringing Italian summers to London, so it comes as no surprise to any Italophile that Francesco Mazzei is the one leading this charge for the foodie moment that’s taken root within the grand dame walls of London’s Corinthia Hotel. Designed to transport, its namesake and menu are inspired by the southern regions of Italy, where the sun is the most intense at midday, translated as ‘Mezzogiorno’. Personally more accustomed to London’s shades of grey, I was surprised to enter the opulent Northall bar and find myself in a nonna-esque open kitchen that doubles as a walk-through to the main restaurant. Here, a communal oval table sits opposite the kitchen, where an intimate group sit watching folds of dough being expertly handcrafted into pasta and breadsticks by the chefs in their whites. Inspired by the Baroque palazzos of Southern Italy, the restaurant is adorned with custom-made Murano chandeliers hanging from tall ceilings, held up by dramatic pillars adjoined to a waffled terracotta ceiling, which makes me think of a gelato cone. The scene here on a Tuesday evening is mostly out-of-town pals sharing plates, business comrades and on this occasion, a Hollywood A-lister, but the winning majority here were couples holding hands across tables and huddled in booths. We start by nibbling on the longest breadsticks I’ve ever seen - simple and all unique, the only concern is filling up on them, but they are surprisingly light. Next comes an injection of colour with the Pipi Cruski Limone Di Rocca Mayo, a traditional dish of fire-red peppers that are fried and best enjoyed slovenly dipped into lemon butter. Despite the colour, these aren’t spicy and have the most excellent crunch. Among the tables, we tuck into an antipasti of Orkney scallops, which are tender but fragrant alongside Batutta Di Manzo Inglese, a refreshing mix of chopped beef, salad leaves, pomegranate seeds and large shavings of black truffle. Mouths still full but contentedly chatting, it’s easy to see the inspiration behind this place. With excellent company and ambience, come and come again, but definitely share the hand-made pasta with native blue lobster sauce and T-bone among the table, while you snack on humble traditional Sicilian vegetables and of course, an entire bowl of zucchini sticks. To finish, the showstopping Tiramisu is necessary - presented to the table in a family-style bowl, the friendly server affectionately spoons the dessert onto our plates, like they are welcoming us to the family. Megan Wilkes Address: Whitehall Place, London, SW1A 2BD, United Kingdom Website: corinthia.com/en-gb/london/mezzogiorno/ Kumori, Soho Slap-bang in the heart of Soho, Kumori is a 30-seat handroll bar where most of the action happens at the counter, creating an intimate, immersive feel. Inside, the space feels a little like stepping into a spaceship – all brushed-metal surfaces and iridescent pink and purple lighting. From the plump made-to-order handrolls to the carefully curated soundtrack, everything about Kumori feels cool, fresh and considered. Knees brush as we pore over the tick-box menu, leaving me spiralling as I weigh up how many of the handrolls I can reasonably fit in; there are simply too many good options. The cocktail list is an equally delicious debate, eventually landing on a yuzu mezcal margarita and sitting back to settle in for the show. Behind the counter, chefs move with speed and precision through a menu curated by head chef John Randy De Guzman (formerly Nobu, Tobi Masa and Katsuya). Each roll is served from chef to patron the moment it’s made, turning dinner into a kind of live theatre. Lucy Bruton Address: Kumori, 26 Denman Street, London W1D 7HX Website: kumorirestaurant.com Best new London restaurants in May 2026 Tavern, Shoreditch I’m still thinking about those little melted cheese-filled choux buns that kicked off dinner (the chunion puff), and the dense brown butter muffin that we finished on. But also every course we inhaled in between, which was cooked on open flames from the team behind Michelin-starred Restaurant St Barts in Farringdon. Nest, the high-end tasting-menu restaurant that once sat on this site, is no longer open. The trio behind it, Johnnie Crowe (Co-founder), Brendan Appleby (executive chef), and Kirsty Easterbrook (head chef), have moved away from fine dining, rebranding and reopening as Tavern, a much more casual affair with a nose-to-tail concept using seasonal British produce. I loved the new bistro-style interiors mixed with oldy-worldy pub furnishings. Dark, mismatched wooden chairs, scattered with shaggy sheepskins, are tucked beneath linen-topped tables with flickering candles. Kick things off with a Tavern Pickleback cocktail – a dirty martini infused with pickle juice, served with a cocktail stick of cured meat inside. Small plates (actually on the larger size) are flung out of the kitchen quickly; order the fire bread coated in wild garlic and, obviously, the chunion puff to start. For mains, we loved the asparagus with a dollop of buttery hollandaise and cured egg yolk, the pork and cuttlefish sausage with squid-ink mustard and the huge joint of smoky sirloin with a side of charred leaves, beetroot and horseradish. For dessert, have the black koji custard tart, bitter and sweet at the same time. Sophie Knight Address: Tavern, 374-378 Old Street, London, EC1V 9LT Website: tavernlondon.co.uk The Latimer, North Kensington The Latimer is a true family effort. It's been recently brought to life by Rochelle Canteen co-founder Melanie Arnold, St John and Sessions Arts Club partner Jon Spiteri, and their three children, Lorcan, Fin, and Molly, who have brought their own prowess to London hotspots Caravel and Koya, respectively. Given this resume, I already knew I’d be in good hands when it came to the food, but the clan have also captured a remarkably warm neighbourhood feel. Though it’s been open for just over a week, when we visit, guests here walk around comfortably with a sense of knowing the place. We ordered grilled asparagus in a herb sauce we’d drink by the bowl if we could, confit trout with green beans and new potatoes, and our must-have: unbelievably tender pork belly skewers braised in cider, served with a dollop of applesauce. Grilled-to-perfection sea bream with tiny green and yellow tomatoes in a delectable aioli, and a courgette linguine tossed in stracciatella followed. There are two desserts – an amaretti crumble and a chocolate mousse. Plus, I’m impressed by the drinks here – at £12, they’re decently priced for West London and the chicest thing about the pub. I opt for the Westway, a tequila-and-blood-orange shrub short drink, but mentally bookmark South of the Border, a black coffee-and-reposado tequila drink, for when I’m next here on a weekend. Tamara Southward Address: 274 Latimer Road, London W10 6QW Website: thelatimer.co.uk Bar Etna, Newington Green Does London really need another hype-y pizza joint? Having been left as cold as a next-day margarita by a couple of recent openings, I was sceptical – but having spent the evening being charmed and carbloaded by the team at Bar Etna, I can attest that it absolutely does. Perhaps I shouldn’t have been surprised – this is the dream-team project from Four Legs’ Ed McIlroy (Finsbury Park’s Tollington and The Plimsoll) and Joe Beddia (owner of Philadelphia-based, Bib Gourmand-garlanded Pizzeria Beddia). Their special relationship has resulted in an East Coast pizza bar with mid-century Milanese design and top-notch seasonal British ingredients. The downstairs bar is reserved for walk-ins, while upstairs is (slightly) more formal tables, where we huddle knee-to-knee with strangers in front of an open kitchen from which servers twirl out piping pizzas. The menu is no-fuss: three spritzes plus a special (a tomatini-inspired affair on our visit); negronis or vermouth on tap; an Italian-focused wine list; a couple of snacks; and four thin-crust, Italian-American style pizzas to choose from. Creamy “judion” (butter) beans arrive floating in silky olive oil and liberally doused with salt and lemon zest – perfectly simple and perfectly done, a hint of what’s to come. The must-order tomato pie is a Philly staple of salty, herby tomatoes spread on springy focaccia. My fellow diner deems it “the best, most upscale version of primary school traybake pizza you’ve ever had”. For pizza, we go for a simple Number One (tomato, mozzarella and Neal’s Yard coolea), which elegantly manages the dance between a thin, crispy base and a satisfying amount of flop. The Number Two (cream, cantabrian chillis, greens, coolea) is our favourite, with just the right amount of chilli heat, but the appropriately volcanic Etna Curry Pizza blows my socks off with one bite; it’s not for me, but those made of stronger stuff might enjoy this playful tribute to a curry house saag paneer. A stainless steel coupe of espresso soft serve is tiny and chic and just right to cut through all the carbs. One night after opening, Bar Etna was heaving, with a real house party feel. With plans for late-night pizzas by the slice on Fridays and Saturdays, I can already tell that the pavement outside will be spilling over this summer – and with the recently opened The Gold Tooth (from the pair behind London Fields’ Papi) and existing favourites Cadet and Yield nearby, Newington Green is fast becoming one of the buzziest food spots in this part of town. Olivia Squire Address: 47 Newington Green, London N16 9PX Website: instagram.com/bar.etna.london Idalia at Pillar Hall, Olympia There’s something sparkly happening in West London. Last month saw the opening of Pillar Hall – a landmark new live music venue, 30,000ft restaurant and speakeasy set within a truly magnificent Grade II-listed space, as part of Olympia’s tidy £1.3 billion regeneration. Originally designed in 1886 by architect Henry Edward Coe, it was built for exhibitions, concerts and even the circus. Vivienne Westwood staged her first catwalk show here; Britain hosted one of its earliest film screenings; and now, 140 years on, it’s back with a new outfit for a fresh dose of razzle-dazzle. At its heart sits the sweeping restaurant, Idalia. The name is an alternative moniker for Aphrodite that was rather more in vogue in the 1880s. The vast, gleaming dining room is all verdant glamour, inspired by the nearby gardens of Kensington and Olympia, with space for 300 – so not your quiet Tuesday supper spot. The sparkling wine list is all English and excellent, but do start with one of the cocktails, which are playful, theatrical things served in everything from pink-crusted globes to glass handbags as an homage to Dolce & Gabbana. Of course, it’s a fine dining experience. In the kitchen, Samantha Williams – formerly Angela Hartnett’s executive chef – delivers a modern British menu with the odd Asian interlude. Reasons why, unsure, but why not, I say – and to be fair, the Asian stuff is really good. A bowl of Gochujang chicken thighs are juicy, crispy and drizzled in zesty sriracha mayo, while the whole roasted Turbot, which arrives theatrically and is deboned tableside, comes with a heaping scoop of shichimi togarashi butter oozing atop the skin and some fresh pickled daikon. It’s melty-soft and perfect for sharing, best served with a side of the beef tallow chips – the swankiest fish and chips you’ll eat all year bar none. Finish with the pistachio cheesecake, which is truly humongous and has famously racked up quite a reputation in only the first week of opening. This is a thoroughly grand affair perfect for your next big do – and such a glitzy night deserves a little flourish. Charley Ward Address: Pillar Hall, Olympia Way, London W14 0EY Website: pillarhall.co.uk Fenix, Mayfair I’ll never say no to a Greek salad, but a salad plus endless dips, pittas and charcoal-fired meats and seafood? Count me in. Fenix is a smart Greek-Mediterranean restaurant in the heart of Mayfair (right next to Green Park station), serving sharing plates with a slightly modern twist. The menu is split into spreads, salad, cold dishes, meze, open fire, pasta and rice and sides, and the choice is overwhelming – in the best way. At first glance, I knew I'd have trouble choosing from the vast menu, and there were multiple extra dishes I’d have chosen if I had endless stomach space, but in the end, we went for a little bit of everything. Start with the dips – the spicy feta is creamy with a bit of a kick, but the smoked taramasalata was the real star of the show; full of flavour, a perfect smooth texture and just gorgeous spread across pillowy pita. We saved a little bit of our dips for the meze (the halloumi tempura and caramelised aubergine with tahini miso are must-orders) and added spicy sea bass carpaccio, spicy sweetcorn and orzo with langoustine and feta to finish things off. There wasn’t a dish I regretted, although in hindsight I was probably too stuffed for the crème brûlée – but who can say no to a sweet treat? The space is massive, but it still feels intimate. During our Thursday night dinner, we were catered to by multiple members of staff (all of them friendly and knowledgeable) and our reservation was stretched out for nearly three hours, without ever feeling rushed. The decor is clearly slightly themed towards a taverna (think raffia and wood, plenty of greenery and paved flooring) but avoids being gimmicky thanks to the chic combination of textures and light colour palette. I’d come back here with friends visiting London to show them a cool spot in the city, and for a menu with an endless list of crowd-pleasers. Address: Fenix, Stratton House, 80 Piccadilly, London W1J 8HX Website: fenixrestaurants.com Café Jikoni, Stratford It’s rare for a toastie to be anything more than a rushed, forgettable meal, but at Café Jikoni, that all changed. The Goan aubergine achaar and Mony’s cheddar toastie was one of the best bites I’ve had this year, and without question the finest toastie I’ve ever eaten. The staff insisted we try it, and despite my initial scepticism at choosing a sandwich over something more elaborate, I was quickly proved wrong. It was spicy, oozing, and bright with freshness. To me, the mark of an exceptional chef lies in their ability to elevate the humble. Ravinder Bhogal is a clear master of this, able to refine even the most staple of dishes. Born in Kenya to Indian parents, she is an award-winning food writer, TV presenter, journalist, cook, and restaurateur, and her breadth of experience is evident in every dish. Jikoni Marylebone has long been an essential part of London's dining scene, and now Bhogal has expanded the concept with an all-day café and restaurant housed on the lower ground floor of the new V&A East Museum in Stratford. The striking building feels like a natural home for her food: elevated yet relaxed, inclusive, and creative. Standouts ranged from the nibbles – such as the Shambaa pickles and umami-rich oregano fries – to larger plates like butter beans aglio e olio, topped with irresistibly crunchy pangrattato, and a deeply comforting massaman curry. As someone who eats predominantly plant-based, I found Jikoni sets a high bar for vegetarian cooking, proving it can be just as inventive, flavourful, and satisfying as any meat-based dish. The tofu massaman and butter beans were particularly vibrant and memorable. From the drinks list, the sweet, smoky strawberry margarita and a satisfyingly dry martini are both worth your time. To finish, I watched the sun set over the canal while indulging in an intensely rich Vietnamese coffee brownie, alongside a picture-perfect yuzu, pandan, and strawberry iced bun. Address: Café Jikoni at the V&A East Museum, 107 Carpenters Rd, Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park, Stratford, E20 2AR Website: jikonilondon.com Best new London restaurants in April 2026 Teal by Sally Abé, Hackney Tucked along a leafy Hackney street, Teal by Sally Abé feels immediately at home among neighbourhood pubs, cafés and delis, just a short stroll from London Fields. With its soft green interiors, potted plants and light-filled dining room, the space strikes a balance between relaxed local charm and quietly confident fine dining. This is the latest opening from Sally Abé, whose résumé spans some of London’s most respected kitchens, including Restaurant Gordon Ramsay, The Ledbury and The Harwood Arms. Here, her cooking leans into British produce with a sense of nostalgia, revisiting historic touches such as the £1 “penny lick”, a playful nod to Victorian-era street treats. The menu opens with thoughtful bites, including a standout Locket’s savoury: a salty-sweet mouthful of Stilton on toast, with a fruity finish. Starters showcase the kitchen’s finesse, particularly a delicately balanced asparagus tartlet with Old Winchester, and a Dorset crab royale lifted by peas and lovage. Mains are richer and more robust, from an artichoke and hazelnut vol-au-vent to beef sirloin with wild garlic, Cornish mussels, and a deeply flavoured haunch of deer. Desserts are a highlight. A marmalade ice cream sandwich walks the line between bitter and sweet, while a marshmallow teacake paired with Earl Grey custard offers a playful finish. While traditional British menus can lean heavily towards meat, Teal makes a strong case for its vegetable dishes, which stand confidently alongside their counterparts. The wine list is thoughtfully curated yet accessible, with English options such as Sussex sparkling wines appealing to the local crowd. Service is warm and assured, completing a restaurant that already feels like a natural fixture in the area. Address: Teal by Sally Abé, 52 Wilton Way, London Fields, E8 1BS Website: tealbysallyabe.com Taverna Ermou, Marylebone Taverna Ermou is the closest you’ll feel to being in a Greek taverna in London. Tiled chequered floor, marble tables topped with a little candle, traditional chairs made of wood and straw and lots of framed hand crochet doilies often seen in old-school Greek homes. Staff dressed in white shirts and black aprons run around serving a packed out and very loud restaurant off the already busy James Street in central London. This is the second branch of Ermou, following the original in Athens. It’s warm, welcoming and slightly chaotic – a recipe for a fun evening with friends. The menu is like the interiors: extremely traditional. Expect classics like tzatziki, Greek salad, and super succulent chicken souvlaki. Plates are meant to be shared, served on stainless steel platters and thrown in the middle of the table – we were happy to find there's no skimping on portion sizes either. Every dish was big enough for at least three or four people to share happily. You’ll want to order a bunch of dips, we can’t recommend the deconstructed spanakopita dip enough – a warm spinach and feta paste served with crispy bread. Then order mezze plates, including the Saganaki, which we have seen pop up all over our Instagram: a runny graviera cheese coated in a flaky kataifi phyllo sprinkled with pistachios and spicy honey. A fresh salad and a few bigger plates from the grill and pasta section, such as spiced beef and lamb kebabs, charred octopus and rich creamy crab orzo. We’ve also heard great things about the brunch menu. This all-day dining spot might have just taken the lead as the best Greek restaurant in London. Sophie Knight Address: Taverna Ermou, 38-40 James Street, London W1U 1EU Website: ergonfoods.com Burro, Covent Garden Burro – or butter, in Italian – certainly lives up to its name. Simple ingredients reign supreme here, but in our three-course dinner, we had anchovies with butter and crostini, sole with a butter-and-prosecco sauce, and garlicky Jersey royal potatoes swimming in the good stuff. Personally, I had no complaints (the more butter, the better), but diners should be warned that it’s easy to lean towards heavy dishes… although, isn’t that what lovely Italian dining should be about? It’s very easy to over-order when the menu starts with a selection of antipasti so tempting you could ask for one of each, but I’d certainly recommend the aforementioned anchovies, plus pillowy-fresh foccacia and melty Salumi. When it came to Primi, we misjudged; the fettuccine with duck and porcini ragù was heavy and a little salty; in all honesty, I had hoped for a little more flavour or fun. The sole lifted my spirits a little, but it was dessert – rhubarb granita with vanilla cream – that really left me wanting more. It’s rare for me to skip a tiramisu, but in this case, I was ready for something a little bit lighter, and thank god, because I stumbled upon one of my favourite puddings in a long time. The restaurant is undoubtedly set for big things: its location in Floral Court in Covent Garden is pretty perfect, and comes from a known name in the industry, Conor Gadd, co-owner of much-loved Highbury restaurant Trullo. This is a more suave, grown-up version, where theatre-goers mingle with after-work diners, and the vibe inside is relaxed and fun – helped along by a great team of staff who happily share suggestions. High ceilings, fancy tablecloths, and art dotted across the walls add to the opulence. I'll certainly return to try the constantly changing menu, but I'll be hoping the granita remains. Abigail Malbon Address: Burro, 2, Floral Court, Floral Street, London WC2E 9FB Website: trattoriaburro.com

item.title: Tea Is So Hot Right Now
item.description:
Source: Eater Score: 4.27
In Los Angeles, Tea at Shiloh describes itself as a “late night teahouse.” Here, visitors can reserve slots from 7 to 11 p.m. to sip unlimited amounts of tea — at this hour, all herbal, with blends made by each day’s staff — and sprawl out in nooks of plush cushions, in a warmly lit loft with tall ceilings and exposed brick, while jazz musicians play in a corner. “I was looking for soft spaces in the evening,” says founder Shiloh Enoki, who opened the eponymous teahouse in 2022. Tea Is So Hot Right Now The success of bubble tea and matcha has opened the door for more tea businesses to gain traction Enoki previously worked in the music industry, and her experience with nightlife was often loud and centered on the more performative aspects of dating (“being perceived by guys,” she says). For her new venture, “All I wanted to do was drink tea, listen to jazz, be cozy, and still have the opportunity to meet strangers.” Tea felt like a conduit to an alternative space. While coffee shops tend to encourage a practice of grab and go, or of work or hustle culture, “that’s not the energy of tea,” according to Enoki. “Tea is like, I’m gonna sit here for hours and I’m gonna have a deep conversation with the person sitting across from me, and that’s so rare in our culture.” Despite tea’s astounding popularity globally, the United States has long lagged behind many other countries when it comes to tea consumption, and that conception of tea has mostly been limited to iced black tea. This, however, appears to be changing, with the U.S. importing far more tea — in the hundreds of millions of dollars — this decade than it did 30 years ago, with millennials in particular the most likely to be tea drinkers. Matcha is, obviously, everywhere; according to the New Consumer, it usurped chai as the leading specialty tea drink in cafes. A lot more tea, it seems, is about to follow, as new tea-focused businesses sprout up across the country and as tea sees increased applications as a flavor element in food, desserts, and cocktails in addition to its consumption as a standalone drink. Across the country, teahouses with a similar ethos to Enoki’s are catering to the desire for another kind of space: one that feels slower and more intentional than the average coffee shop, and which offers a different experience than yet another restaurant or high-end cocktail bar. In July, “tea salon” Han Cha opened in Chicago, serving a selection of nine teas from Chicago-based tea company Spirit in the format of British high tea. Over the course of the two-hour-long booking, guests might sip Taiwanese black tea with notes of quince and orange blossom alongside bites of English cheddar and Korean-style quick pickles, or Thai white tea with Japanese curry pimento cheese sandwiches. Heiji Black, who partnered with artist Theaster Gates (in whose Stony Island Arts Bank building the concept is located) on the venture, is compelled by the way tea “makes people slow down and savor the experience.” She cites the teahouses she grew up going to in Korea, which were “really about being social and meeting with people and connecting with them,” as inspiration for Han Cha. At Tea at Shiloh, Enoki also tries to emphasize being in the moment. While the cafe welcomes co-working, especially during the day, she says she wanted to design the experience at night such that people “don’t want to be on their laptop or their phone.” Rather than enforce a hard no-laptop policy, Tea at Shiloh offers other things for people to do with their hands, like games, clay, and watercolors. The dim lighting and communal seating also offer “subtle cues” that the space, at night, isn’t a place for being lost in a screen, she explains. Even teahouses that don’t serve matcha, like Tea at Shiloh, cite its importance in the current teahouse moment. In May, the artist Juno Shen opened Soft Hours, a teahouse in Manhattan’s Chinatown. (A laptop-free space, it draws inspiration from the Song dynasty, which Shen describes as a “culturally rich era” in which scholars “built rituals around slowing down and shifting your attention.”) “Matcha and boba have done something really important in making tea culture relevant to a younger generation, and I think we’re reaching a point where people are asking, What else is there?” Shen says. At Soft Hours, there is no matcha whisked in front of you, poised for a TikTok video. Likewise, “we don’t do boba; we don’t do cold foam. We moved away from all the performance that a trendy tea place would have.” Instead, Shen’s menu hews toward a selection of Chinese teas: streamlined but still showing range. There’s green tea fragrant with jasmine; two kinds of oolong, one oxidized in a way that gives it notes of plum and the other roasted over charcoal until it evokes toasted nuts; black tea with a honey-like body; and a deeply woodsy fermented pu’erh. Perhaps the main concession to trends is that every tea can be ordered as an iced latte as well, which Shen considers a way for people to “softly get introduced” to tea. “I’m not presenting something that’s extremely traditional, so I think I’m just the next step of [people] exploring a little bit more about tea,” Shen says. “I think the next stage of tea culture in America should move beyond individual ingredients becoming trendy [and into] the understanding of tea as this incredibly diverse seasonal category.” Tian Tea House opened in Kansas City, Missouri, in late 2025. Matcha drinks are far and away the most popular, according to co-owner Saranya Hubbard. “I really don’t have to advertise anything that much — it already sells itself,” she says. But similarly to Shen, Hubbard, who grew up in Thailand surrounded by the tea culture in Bangkok’s Chinatown, sees her teahouse as an opportunity to showcase the wider variety of Asian tea culture. Tian brews and offers classes on Chinese gongfu tea and serves lesser-known Thai tea, including one made with hibiscus and bael (a fruit that’s sometimes called golden apple or stone apple). To make the most of the space, the teahouse turns into Moon, a cocktail bar, at night. Tea bridges the gap between the two concepts: There are highballs infused with tea and whisky drinks made with matcha. Further proof of tea’s rising moment can be found in Heytea’s current expansion across the United States. The Chinese chain got global attention when it popularized cheese tea in the late 2010s, but it didn’t enter the U.S. market until 2023, when it opened its first store in NYC; now, it has more than 40 locations nationwide. With drinks like milk tea boba, fruit teas with inclusions, and black teas finished with fluffy toppings, the chain sits at the intersection of the growing cultural fixations on bubble tea, matcha, and highly customized specialty beverages of all kinds, including coffee and dirty soda. The chain describes itself as offering “new-style” tea, which senior PR manager Yinnan Shen explains to mean “experimenting a lot with what tea can become.” Some of its beverages, Shen says, take the approach of crafting a cocktail: What botanics can be added to the drink? What layers of texture and flavor? McDonald’s Sweet Tea this is not. In June, Heytea also opened the first U.S. location of its Teabar offshoot. The concept — which serves dine-in only pots of tea as well as tea ice cream and elaborate beverages like jasmine milk tea topped with a “matcha cloud” — rapidly drew massive crowds. Unlike Heytea shops, which offer a more grab-and-go feel, Teabar was, like some of those independent teahouses, intended to be more of a place to slow down. Together, the interest in Teabar in addition to the original Heytea concept, represent what Shen calls tea’s “continued evolution.” “What Heytea is trying to do is find the most accurate contemporary interpretation of people’s needs around tea,” she says. That seems especially pertinent in the context of the U.S., where the tea culture is nascent compared to China. Now, according to Nethra Rajendran, a beverage experience developer at Oatly, black tea, jasmine, and oolong are starting to “re-emerge in new formats,” particularly in mainstream chains. Instead of boba being the medium for these flavors, they’re increasingly popping up as part of the growing “refresher” category,” she explains. Of course, the interest in tea is no longer limited to the teahouse or tea bar alone. “We can see a very real application of tea beyond a [drink] base in the 2025 resurgence of Earl Grey,” wrote Rajendran, noting the popularity of Earl Grey syrups and creamtops for use in matcha and coffee drinks. Tea is no longer a standalone drink, but, increasingly, a freeform flavor element. When NYC’s ambitious new soft serve shop Unnecessary opened this summer, it launched with a “not-so-plain vanilla,” enriched with osmanthus oolong. Oolong also appears as the grounding basenote of its watermelon-mint flavor, which it developed to be more refreshing than what people might expect from typical milk tea. The argument has been made that we, as modern society, are on a hedonistic hunt for more flavors, our tastebuds “spoiled” by the glut of “maple-matcha-blackberry-thyme-yuzu-miso-caramel everything.” Every drink is involved in a way that only the early days of the Starbucks Frappuccino could have foretold; every dish is a referential mashup of a handful of other dishes or other cultural fascinations. Perhaps tea, with its global breadth barely tapped in the U.S., can provide further flavors to mine. Nearly every culture has a tea to explore, Rajendran adds: the osmanthus and oolong of East Asia, the masala chai and Assam teas of South Asia, the rooibos and kineliba of Africa, the hibiscus in the Caribbean and Latin America, the sweet tea of the American South. Tea has been around for thousands of years, but perhaps we’ve yet to see how far it can continue to go. As Heytea’s Shen says, “Tea is a living culture, and living culture changes.”

item.title: The 12 New Cookbooks We Can’t Wait to Cook From This Fall
item.description:
Source: Eater Score: 2.01
We have reached that time of year again. Every good tomato suddenly prompts the pondering: Will this be the last one for the season? The heat begins to give way to crisper breezes, and we start to crave the comfort of windows fogged up from bubbling pots of soup instead of thinking about how to minimize our time in front of a hot stove. The 12 New Cookbooks We Can’t Wait to Cook From This Fall The season’s exciting new releases include Asian American croissants, divorce cooking, Indian street food, foraged treats, and more Luckily, this season’s cookbooks offer many exciting ways to joyously warm ourselves in the kitchen, whether by baking border-traversing croissants and comforting counter cakes, or keeping the stove simmering with Dutch ovens of borscht, beef noodle soup, or budae jjigae. There are diversions from the standard cookbook on this list, too, like a divorce-inspired reflection (in which the essays are just as essential as the recipes) and a treasure trove of a garden almanac that feels like an escape into another world. I’ve compiled 12 selections from the fall cookbook season that have me especially excited to cook and read this fall and winter. Joyce Tang with Soleil Ho Hardie Grant, out now If you feel like everything is an Asian American bakery now, you’re right. In the Bay Area, Bake Sum — with its Spam-musubi-esque croissants and ube pineapple buns — was an early adopter of the current trend, starting as a pandemic pop-up in 2020 before opening its Oakland location the following year. In her colorful and playful new cookbook, chief baking officer Joyce Tang pulls back the curtain on her cuisine-bending treats, like quiche inspired by chawanmushi, the Japanese savory egg custard, and danishes in the style of okonomiyaki and aloo matar, the Indian dish of spiced potatoes and peas. The bakes involving laminated dough are ambitious, weekend-worthy projects, but the book takes a welcomingly progressive approach, easing in novice bakers via puddings and jellies (its first recipe is a simple, anyone-can-do-it microwave mochi) before exploring more advanced techniques in its chapter on cakes, and then making its way to croissants. This is a book for the person who counts big baking projects among their favorite ways to spend the colder months. Carla Lalli Clarkson Potter, out now Lalli, who won audiences over as Carla Lalli Music during her time at Bon Appétit, has catalogued the dissolution of her 24-year marriage in a cookbook. With its reflections on motherhood, identity, and where a background in restaurants fits into those things, Lalli continues the narrative thread of releases like Tanya Bush’s Will This Make Me Happy and Rebecca May Johnson’s Small Fires. That’s to say that you’re here as much for the essays as for the recipes. The latter, including dishes such as “weeknight lamb chop special, for any number” and “quick beans and rice for when the avocado is ripe,” are delightfully loose and flexible. These are realistic suggestions for weeknights when you’re burnt-out, but also for those glorious instances in which you care more about getting yourself on the sand than fussing about what to make for your beach trip (for those instances: peaches with lime and salt).Many of these ideas were birthed during “separation summer,” when Lalli often found herself eating alone after years of cooking for four. These recipes (and the words that accompany them, like a list of things that “made [Lalli] feel free”) will feel useful on bad days, sick days, and anytime you need to give yourself grace, but also whenever you need to be reminded of how much pleasure life offers. Richard Christiansen Chronicle, September 15 Pleasure Principles is the newest book from Richard Christiansen of Flamingo Estate, the Los Angeles-based lifestyle brand so luxurious and sprawling in its ambitions that even Martha Stewart has described it as “over the top.” Pleasure Principles is predictably maximalist; not specifically a cookbook, it feels like picking up a paper trail while exploring the lush thicket of Christiansen’s secret (if oft-Instagrammed) garden. Stories about the building of Christiansen’s property veer into detours about the history of camellia plants and Coco Chanel, interspersed with archival imagery and photos of flora shot in the style of high-fashion editorial. A primer about the vast range of sage plants gives way to a checklist of garden tasks for January, seasonal project ideas (“help build a bird’s nest” or “make a sage tincture”), and recipes for pasta with sage leaves embedded in the dough and vegetable broth featuring lotus petals and dried skullcap. Pleasure Principles feels like an immersive fantasy world: Open up any random page for a little hit of magic, or an escape into Christiansen’s sparkly, greenery-filled universe. It’s a book that’ll make even winter feel vibrant and full of possibility. Meherwan Irani with Jamie Feldmar Ten Speed Press, September 22 This is a book that will make you want to have a party. That’s partially because recipes like the deep-fried, carb-on-carb vada pav and crisp, thin dosa with coconut chutney will feed six or more (and benefit, process-wise, from the economy of scale). It’s also because it feels raucous and alive, full of bright colors, bold typography, and big proclamations, ready for joyful debate. Is vada pav, as Meherwan Irani writes, “without question, the greatest sandwich of all time”? Is this, indeed, as the title suggests, the best Indian cookbook in the world? This is food that makes you want to crowd around a table, tearing off pieces of seekh kebab with fluffy, still-steaming naan and crushing cold beers. Whether Indian street food is, as Irani audaciously claims, the “best food on the planet” remains up for discussion, but for those of us who can’t get to India or to Irani’s lauded North Carolina restaurants Chai Pani and Botiwalla anytime soon, this book is a good way to test that argument. Alexis Nikole Nelson with Jeanelle Hayner Olson S&S/Simon Element, September 22 Alexis Nikole Nelson, also known as Black Forager, is a bright spot in the doom spiral that social media can often be. Nelson is known (and widely loved, picking up nearly 5 million followers on TikTok alone) for her bubbly disposition, whimsical vibe, and clever creations such as syrup infused with pine cones and color-changing pine-needle cookies. She demystifies the vast array of food that you can forage without even having to go deep into the woods, like acorns and the fruit of the linden trees that are abundant in many parts of the United States, and balances practicality, safety, and play in the process. Her long-awaited cookbook gets its name from the catchphrase that ends her videos: “Happy snacking. Don’t die.” With recipes like pickled magnolia flowers, Japanese knotweed granita, and maitake mushroom “steaks,” this book promises to be a guide to seeing even your suburban neighborhood through new eyes. Dona Murad Quadrille, September 22 New York City’s Librae Bakery draws on its owner Dona Murad’s upbringing in Bahrain with an Indian and Portuguese mother and a Bahraini Persian father; her time spent working in Copenhagen with her husband Andre, who is French Moroccan; and her new life in NYC, where Andre grew up. Naturally, the bakery has embraced the language and perspective of “third-culture” cuisine from the start, serving croissants with pistachio frangipane, scented with rose water; morning buns spread with labneh and za’atar; babka with both lemon curd and loomi (black lime); and more. Much of this book requires getting comfortable with Murad’s “mother dough” recipes — like ones for croissant dough, morning buns, and enriched dough — or working with sourdough starter. For those new to these more involved bakes, Murad provides thorough, nicely documented steps and imagery. If you need something easier than croissants, Murad’s cookies and breads, including cleverly topped sheets of focaccia, provide a more approachable entry point. Another book for bakers who don’t turn down a challenge, Librae is also for anyone who respects traditional pastry techniques but wants to push flavors further. Clara Lee and Eddo Kim Workman, October 6 If it can’t still be summer, at least it’s almost soup season. Here, Clara Lee and Eddo Kim break Korean soups into fundamentals — a chart compares the qualities of guk versus tang versus jjigae versus jeongol; the first section of the book is about making broth, then categorizing those soups into applications. There are quick-cooking soups, soups for slower nights, soups for each season, soups that are especially restorative, and soups for sharing; you could spend the entirety of the coming colder months cooking exclusively through this repertoire. If Lee and Kim’s names are familiar, that’s because they ran the cherished San Francisco superette Queens, which closed in 2023 to transition into a line of pantry staples. The shop has been described as “iconoclastic,” representing the new wave of Korean American cuisine. Consider Korean Soups essential for anyone who loves to be cozy, anyone who’s looking to deepen their understanding of Korean home cooking, or anyone who simply needs more ways to use the gochujang they bought for cookies a while ago. Kay Chun Knopf, October 6 Recipe developers I know cite NYT Cooking contributor Kay Chun among their favorite recipe developers, and it’s easy to see why. Her book starts off with snacks and pickles, Chun adding low-lift but flavor-packed flourishes: She quickly marinates sardines to top toast; her calamari gets a gilda-esque zhuzh, skewered with fried peppers and olives. Gather Around My Table delivers on its promise of simple, weeknight-friendly food that doesn’t feel boring, with dishes such as grilled tofu simmered in soy sauce with aromatics, and then given the ssam and taco treatment with both a perilla leaf and a tortilla. Wakame and a shallot vinaigrette featuring grated tomatoes make her green salad livelier and less run-of-the-mill (her mustard vinaigrette, meanwhile, gets amped up by doenjang). I appreciate that Chun gives tofu an entire chapter, too, coaxing even omnivores to employ it more, as in her pork breakfast sausages with crumbled tofu for added moisture and protein. With Gather Around My Table, Chun consistently offers low-effort ways to make familiar dishes more interesting and rewarding. Eric Sze and Elyse Inamine Hardie Grant, October 13 We’ve come full circle: Fusion is good again, or at least so proclaims chef Eric Sze, known for his New York City restaurant Wenwen and the recently closed 886. His debut cookbook Taiwanese?, emphasis on that question mark, is an ode to letting Taiwanese food be fun, free, and a little freaky: His lu rou fan, also known as lo ba beng, the dish of braised pork over rice, includes the “strange addition of peanut butter,” for example. Why the hell not? Especially when Sze has, as documented in the book (with vivid imagery from star photographer Alex Lau), gone on a bonkers crawl of 60-plus bowls of lu rou fan in a single week; he’s earned the right to experiment. Taiwanese? is not the traditionalist’s guide to the cuisine, but anyone who likes seeing the commonalities between disparate cuisines and playing with the boundaries between them will get a kick out of this book, which includes recipes such as seared zhajiang lasagna with pork and octopus, and beef noodle soup burgers. Suffused throughout is an impish irreverence: Sze calls a soup made with yellow-fat chicken, regular chicken, and goth Silkie chicken “diversity chicken soup”; he’s known, at Wenwen, for the “BDSM chicken” (that incredibly involved recipe’s in here, too). Taiwanese? is a good pick for anyone who’s serious about food but also sees some of the self-imposed rules around it as really not that serious, or for anyone who’s got a great relationship with their local butcher. Caroline Schiff Abrams, October 13 This is, as the name would suggest, a book for the daily-3-p.m.-sweet-treat kind of people. But it’s also a book about making baking less annoying and more chill, a boon for anyone who would love baked goods more often but hates the thought of all the fuss. In her debut cookbook, beloved New York City pastry chef Caroline Schiff, formerly of Gage & Tollner, assures you that sifting is generally unnecessary, and that your baked goods will probably be fine even if you forgot to bring the eggs to room temperature. Her ideas will appeal to the baker without a dishwasher — her giant chocolate chip cookie dirties one bowl and requires no mixer nor hand beater. It’s also for the snacker who wants to reap as many rewards as possible out of a single burst of effort (see: the black and white coconut macaroons and the cardamom counter cake with chocolate ganache, both of which keep for a week). Schiff describes her lifestyle as one in which “there’s always something sweet in [the] kitchen — no special occasion required,” allowing friends to stop by anytime for cake and tea (and that’s both definitions of the latter). Daily Dessert is a call to be less fussy and to enjoy ourselves more, and who isn’t enticed by that? Alissa Timoshkina Quadrille, October 20 The cozy hits continue, and as someone who prefers to eat most food out of the comforting confines of a bowl, I appreciate Alissa Timoshkina’s commitment to a highly specific pursuit: spoonable food. In Lozhka, you’ll find a tour of Eastern Europe through all things slurpable and scoopable. Much of this is soup or stew, as to be expected, but oh, the variety! Here is Slovak and Belarusian mačanka, a mushroom stew infused with sauerkraut brine (and which Timoshkina serves with lokše, crepes made with mashed potato dough); Armenian lentil soup with the tannic touch of both prunes and walnuts; and so many ways to use millet, barley, and beans (on that note, this is a great book for anyone who is trying to eat more fiber). There are filled dumplings and drop dumplings and steamed bread dumplings! I don’t want to hope for a long winter, but with this book to work through, I also wouldn’t mind it quite as much. Lucas Sin Artisan, October 27 Lucas Sin, the chef formerly of New York City’s Junzi, has always been very good at explaining how to cook; his cooking tutorials via Instagram Stories buoyed me through the early pandemic and taught me techniques I still use today. As a cookbook author, he’s a natural. His first cookbook combines his conversational yet helpfully specific instruction style with his clear passion for Hong Kong’s cha chaan tengs, diners where you’ll find set meals of macaroni in soup, luscious scrambled eggs, and toast. The photography here is gorgeous, indulgent, and transportive, each page a rich text: Sin offers a trove of highly readable little insights, like the backstory as to why roast pork belly and tofu skin over rice became known as “A Man’s Romance” (the answer: a viral, anonymous Hong Kong blog post), cast-iron sizzling pan etiquette, his favorite places in Hong Kong to get the dishes mentioned, and more. Sin is in the process of opening his own cha chaan teng in NYC and is testing out his repertoire of dishes in an extremely popular pop-up; especially for those of us who still haven’t gotten a seat, Cha Chaan Teng is the next best thing.

item.title: Chicago: the ultimate insider addresses
item.description:
Source: Food & Drink Score: 4.16
Chicago: the ultimate insider addresses Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter. This article is part of FT Globetrotter’s guide to Chicago When I say Chicago isn’t a celebrity town, that cuts both ways. We have limited tolerance for Instagram culture, we roll our eyes at round-the-block queues and, for most of us, the very notion of $20 trend smoothies triggers an allergic reaction. On the other hand, we can be provincial. At a recent concert at the Jay Pritzker Pavilion in Millennium Park, the Jumbotron cycled through drone footage of American skylines. At the sight of Chicago’s, the crowd exploded. At all others, including a glimmering and handsome New York City? Crickets. Chicagoans have a funny relationship to fame. Seeing a celebrity out and about is not just another Tuesday for us: it’s day-derailing. We’ll ignore the cardinal rule imparted by our peers on the coast and bug the hell out of them, then spend the rest of the day calling our cousins’ cousins. We keep our local celebrities close but feel inordinately stung when they decamp for another city. To better understand this hot-and-cold city, we spoke to eight cultural insiders who know it better than most. Some were forged in Chicago. Others enthusiastically adopted it. And many of them still choose to live here, even when New York and LA beckon. Jump straight to . . . Sandra Cisneros, writer and author of ‘The House on Mango Street’ (born and raised in Chicago; based in San Miguel de Allende, Mexico) Where she’d take someone who already thinks they know Chicago The Aon Center. After going to a concert downtown in Grant Park, we would walk over to what was the Standard Oil Building, now the Aon Center, on East Randolph Street. In the plaza’s sunken garden is the most fabulous treasure: wind sculptures by Harry Bertoia. They look like reeds, and at the dedication ceremony in 1972, the artist climbed inside the installation and “played” them. Bertoia was a furniture designer, too. When his sculptures were displayed at the Art Institute of Chicago in 1975, it was the first and only time I’d seen a sign that said, “Please touch.” I like the idea that he thought about the poetics of these sculptures moving and making these wonderful sounds. Something about Chicago that only other Chicagoans seem to understand Hot dogs. If you haven’t had a Chicago hot dog, you haven’t had a hot dog. You have to have a bun with little poppy seeds on it, it has to be bundled in waxed paper and the french fries have to be good. Now, there are even vegan hot dogs. Recently, my family and I got some at Portillo’s late at night, and they were really good — I was surprised! One more thing I didn’t realise until two years ago that the flowers in Chicago’s public parks were so much a part of the city. To me, lilacs, peonies and lilies of the valley are the quintessential flowers of Chicago. Jeff Tweedy, musician and lead vocalist/guitarist of Wilco (based in Chicago) Where he’d take someone who already thinks they know Chicago The parks. If you want to soak up what the city and culture are really like, I’d pick any of the Chicago Park District parks, like Independence in Irving Park or Gompers in North Park. Have a picnic and see how Chicagoans really recreate. Something about Chicago that only other Chicagoans seem to understand “Dibs”. The concept of saving your parking spot, especially in heavy snow. Technically not legal, but ultimately, pretty fair and moral. If you’re the one who broke your ass shovelling snow, you should get to keep that spot for at least a day or so. What Chicago teaches you When you grow up in a smaller town like I did, there’s a belief that it’s a kinder way to live and that you can’t get that in a city. It’s not true. When I moved to Chicago, I knew more people in my neighbourhood than I did growing up — it’s all about block parties and meeting up with neighbours. Chicago has problems like everywhere else, but it’s a city that facilitates community. Rick Bayless, chef and restaurateur (based in Chicago) Where he’d take someone who already thinks they know Chicago The National Museum of Mexican Art. Rather than establishing the museum downtown, the founders chose Pilsen — a predominantly Latino neighbourhood — and they chose to keep this world-class collection free to all. NMMA is not only one of our city’s best museums but an integral player in this vibrant community. Something about Chicago that only other Chicagoans seem to understand Storefront theatre. Yes, we have grand old theatres that host Broadway touring companies, and yes, we have the internationally acclaimed Steppenwolf, Goodman and Chicago Shakespeare companies. But Chicago is a city of neighbourhoods, and most of them are home to a host of storefront theatres. One of the best is TimeLine Theatre Company, which does historical pieces that have contemporary relevance. Hungry yet? Forty years ago, when we opened Frontera Grill, farmers’ markets hadn’t taken off in Chicago. Today, with local chefs championing local products, there are over 40 and growing. Now communities are hosting “alternative” farmers’ markets that start at 3pm or 4pm and sell until around 7pm on specific weekdays, rather than weekend mornings. Eve L Ewing, author, scholar and co-owner of Build Coffee & Books in Woodlawn (based in Chicago) Where she’d take someone who already thinks they know Chicago The South Shore Nature Sanctuary and Montrose Point Bird Sanctuary. Our city motto is urbs in horto — city in a garden. Away from all the noise and the hubbub, the marshlands and prairie are also part of our identity. Something about Chicago that only other Chicagoans seem to understand Community. The city is famously corrupt, but there’s a more generous way to understand the “you scratch my back and I’ll scratch yours” way we do things, which is that Chicagoans look out for each other and take care of one another. If you’re my neighbour’s cousin’s pick-up basketball buddy, you’re in the circle and I’ve got to take care of you. The hill she’ll die on Everyone likes to share their (mostly ill-informed) opinions on Chicago pizza, but through and through we’re a taco city. Our ratio of great tacos per capita is off the charts. I grew up going to El Cid, a Mexican restaurant in Logan Square, while El Milagro in Pilsen both sells tacos and manufactures the best tortillas and chips. Enrique Mazzola, conductor and music director of the Lyric Opera of Chicago (divides time between Chicago and Paris) Where he’d take someone who already thinks they know Chicago The Driehaus Museum. This small museum just off the Magnificent Mile focuses on the art, architecture and design of the American Gilded Age and the Art Nouveau period. Inside is a magnificent auditorium with interesting and diverse programming. Something about Chicago that only other Chicagoans seem to understand The walks. One of my favourites goes from downtown along the Lakefront Trail to Lincoln Park. Only a true Chicagoan can understand how beautiful this itinerary is. In general, I love walking around the city — I even walk to work at the Lyric Opera of Chicago and enjoy following the Chicago River every day. Bonus recommendation Wander around the boutique shops and cafés in the North Side neighbourhood of Andersonville. You’re still in Chicago but removed from the tourist areas and high-rises of downtown. Isaiah Collier, saxophonist and composer (divides time between Chicago and New York) Where he’d take someone who already thinks they know Chicago 63rd Street Beach. The city has its madness, but it also has its tranquillity, usually by the water. Cats will get together here for drum circles — they’ve been doing it for decades. It’s therapeutic and uniquely ethnic. The overview of the city that you see from down there is kind of mythical, very cinematic. Something about Chicago that only other Chicagoans seem to understand Concerts at Pritzker Pavilion. No matter where you’re from in the city, I think we can all agree there’s something special about being able to witness a proper concert at Pritzker Pavilion. Not amateur stuff, but a full production from start to finish. It’s one hell of a location. A brutal truth We’re the most segregated major city in America. That residual effect has made people feel there are not enough opportunities. It can be disheartening for creatives. Grant Achatz, chef/creative director and co-owner of Chicago’s Alinea restaurant Where he’d take someone who already thinks they know Chicago Primitive on Jefferson Street. It’s a massive showroom packed with rare antiquities from all over the world. I’m into medieval and Egyptian history, so for me it’s a rabbit hole I can lose an afternoon in. Something about Chicago that only other Chicagoans seem to understand The grit. When I showed up in 2001 with this weird, modernist way of cooking, this city embraced the risk and let me build. People here get that ambition runs quiet, that the winters bond everybody together, that nobody’s impressed with you until you’ve put in the work. You can’t feel any of that from a postcard. You’ve got to live here a while. Tasha, singer-songwriter and poet (born and raised in Chicago, based in New York) Where she’d take someone who already thinks they know Chicago Promontory Point. We just call it The Point. I don’t think people who aren’t from Chicago really know the secret, stunning beauty it has, especially on the South Side. There is nothing more romantic than jumping from the rocks at sunset on a sticky, hot summer day, the sky pink behind the city skyline, cicadas buzzing. Something about Chicago that only other Chicagoans seem to understand Being from the city proper. I love the way we bond over that. Not the suburbs. Not the surrounding counties. Definitely not Indiana. A love letter No matter where I end up in the world, Chicago will always be my home, the place I return to, the place that understands me, that holds my whole family and first gave me courage. Chicago forever. What do you love most about Chicago? Tell us in the comments below. And find more of our Chicago guide here Follow us on Instagram at @FTGlobetrotter Cities with the FT FT Globetrotter, our insider guides to some of the world’s greatest cities, offers expert advice on eating and drinking, exercise, art and culture — and much more Find us in Chicago, London, Washington DC, Los Angeles, Tokyo, New York, Paris, Lagos, Rome, Frankfurt, Singapore, Hong Kong, Miami, Toronto, Madrid, Melbourne, Copenhagen, Zürich, Milan, Vancouver, Edinburgh, Venice and Istanbul Comments

item.title: Why pissaladière is the perfect taste of late summer
item.description:
Source: Food & Drink Score: 3.52
Why pissaladière is the perfect taste of late summer Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter.
