item.title: The Famous 1983 Plum Torte Gets a Remix
item.description:
Source: NYT > Dining & Wine Score: 4.66
Advertisement First published in September 1983, Marian Burros’s plum torte has become one of the most popular recipes in the history of The Times, and it’s no mystery why. It’s easy, it’s practically no-fail and it’s endlessly adaptable. Here are five ways to make the 43-year-old recipe your own, drawn directly from readers who have done just that. Recipe: The Original Plum Torte 1. Toss in almost any fruit “Made this for the first time using 4 cups of blueberries and raspberries (mixed). It was perfect!” Apricots, halved and pitted; cranberries or any summer berry work beautifully, as do sliced apples, nectarines, peaches and pears. Canned and frozen fruit can happily stand in for fresh. 2. Experiment with spices, herbs and extracts “I added a teaspoon of finely minced fresh rosemary to the batter. Nice, subtle flavor.” Depending on your mood, add vanilla extract, almond extract, nutmeg, ginger, cardamom, rosemary, orange or lemon zest for a subtle twist. 3. Play with flours “Made this last night after tasting the one made by our daughter. Used raspberries and blackberries, one basket each, instead of plums, and ⅓ cup cornmeal and ⅔ cup flour. Fantastic!!! The cornmeal adds a very sophisticated ‘Italian’ character to it, very slight crunch, and amazing flavor.” For a different texture, consider a half-and-half mixture of almond or cornmeal flour and all-purpose flour. (Melissa Clark made a version with whole-wheat flour.) Or swap in gluten-free flour blends, with excellent results. 4. Change up the pan “Make it in any Pyrex, casserole, anything.” The torte can be baked in any dish provided it’s around 8 to 10 inches in diameter and oven-safe, so spring-form pans, skillets, ceramic casserole dishes will all yield happy results. 5. Double, triple, even quadruple it “Think about making two … one is not enough.” The batter scales up like a dream, and the baked cake freezes well. In 2023, Ms. Burros recounted the time she once made two dozen and asked her friend to store 12 in her freezer. She got 10 back. Follow New York Times Cooking on Instagram, Facebook, YouTube, TikTok and Pinterest. Get regular updates from New York Times Cooking, with recipe suggestions, cooking tips and shopping advice.

item.title: The Quick Sauce That Changed How I Cook Fish
item.description:
Source: NYT > Dining & Wine Score: 2.23
Advertisement Friends often ask me how to cook more fish at home — not salmon, they’ve figured that one out — but the white fish their doctors recommend for its lean protein. They know it cooks quickly and like how it tastes, but worry about preparing it. Recipe: Caramelized Garlic Fish That’s how I felt when I first started cooking professionally, and for myself. It was one thing to learn how to sear flaky white fish on the line in a restaurant, another to make it at home. I was on a tight budget, but even if I hadn’t been, I wouldn’t have been able to find fish as fresh as the kind available at restaurants or the Asian markets of my childhood. Then I made a fish recipe that changed my kitchen life. In her 2001 cookbook, “Pleasures of the Vietnamese Table,” the chef Mai Pham shared her recipe for cá kho tộ and described it as the “one dish that best represents Vietnamese home cooking.” Originally from the south of the country, freshwater snakehead fish (cá lóc) is braised (kho) in a clay pot (tộ) until it becomes deeply savory and a little sticky. Bright with cilantro and black pepper, it begs to be spooned over rice and shoveled. It’s all comfort and still light, punchy but delicate with nuance. And the whole dish comes together in less than 20 minutes. The first time I tried it, I couldn’t believe how easy it was for how good it tasted. I didn’t have a clay pot, but it was, as Ms. Pham promised, “also delicious cooked in a regular pot.” It starts with melting sugar past golden, and then stirring in oil and garlic. As the garlic sizzles and softens, it releases its fragrance into the dark amber caramel. Adding fish sauce and water stops the sugar from going over its bittersweet cliff to burned and turns it into a funky sauce to soak into the fish, and then glaze it with a mahogany shine. This sauce is unbelievable with fish and just as good with tofu, chicken, beef, pork, duck and all kinds of vegetables and seafood. Sometimes known as nước sốt (or kho sauce in English), there are countless variations in Vietnam and its diaspora. Some melt the sugar with oil or vinegar; others add shallots, coconut water or both. As the dish became part of my rotation, I stopped flipping open Ms. Pham’s book and started adjusting it to my taste. I throw in a lot more garlic, splash in less water and skip the scallions in favor of more cilantro. She called for catfish fillets, which are earthy like snakehead fish, but cod, fresh and frozen, is always at my market and its mildness benefits from the big flavors. (Using crosscut fish steaks hews more closely to the dish’s origins, and the bones give the sauce even more body.) It takes only one go to get the rhythm of this sauce. Once you have its pantry ingredients (and stock your freezer with frozen fish fillets), you’ll be able to pull together this one-pot meal any night. item.title: The 100 Best Easy Dinner Ideas for Right Now
item.description:
Source: NYT > Dining & Wine Score: 2.18
The Weeknight 100 is back, with so many fast, delicious dinner ideas for busy times. It’s here: September, and with it arrives the Weeknight 100, New York Times Cooking’s annual list of the dinner recipes you should make in the year ahead. Why publish it in September and not January? It’s back-to-school season, of course, the turning of the dial. It’s that transition from the languid late days of summer, when routine has long ago dissolved into the pool’s chlorine, to the first bell and a newly crammed calendar. Get even more recipes: Sign up for Emily Weinstein’s Five Weeknight Dishes newsletter I’m a summer person, and yet I appreciate the energy and optimism of September. It’s a moment to reset, to block out a new schedule and lay in new habits, to buy clothes, swear that we’ll get to the gym, get a full night of precious sleep or map out a week’s worth of dinners and stick to them. I can’t help you with the gym. But I can help you with dinner. Advertisement I’ve selected the 100 dinner recipes below for you to try. The emphasis is on efficient yet excellent cooking, recipes that are truly delicious and don’t take too much of your time. Everything on this list takes under an hour to make, and a vast majority are much faster than that. I kept kids — those picky, petulant, wonderful beings — in mind when I made this list, and there are many recipes that could work for them, either exactly as written or with simple modifications. But there are also recipes that are more likely to please the adults. Hopefully, whatever your needs are, there’s something here for you. Chicken Chicken and Pesto Rice With Peas A worthy use of a tub of pesto. Sheet-Pan Chicken With Black Beans and Squash Not all sheet-pan recipes are created equal, and this is an especially good one. Tomato Basil Chicken Breasts Take a cue from the blissed-out commenters and make it with the freshest tomatoes you can find (though plump supermarket cherry tomatoes work in a pinch). Keema Palak (Ground Chicken and Spinach Curry) A full pound of baby spinach is wilted into this dish, a quick, very green version of classic keema curries. Honey Ginger Chicken and Carrots The simple honey-ginger-soy marinade is the undisputed star of this stir-fry. Chile Chicken and Bean Guisado Cinnamon-tinged and chile-spiced, this quick stew starts with ground chicken, not rotisserie, for a truer chicken flavor. Creamy Tuscan Chicken A slab of cream cheese melts into this sauce to make it extra bodacious. Rosemary-Garlic Roasted Chicken and Gnocchi Pantry gnocchi subs in for potatoes in this clever sheet-pan recipe. Chicken and Kale Hatch Chile Bowl A can of mild diced green chiles is the key that unlocks this great, simple dinner. Miso-Maple Sheet-Pan Chicken With Brussels Sprouts Sensationally easy, this is the kind of high-reward meal that home cooks rave about. Za’atar Turkey Meatballs With Tahini Yogurt Just imagine these atop a rice bowl instead of falafel, heaped with chopped cucumbers and tomatoes. Greek Chicken With Cucumber-Feta Salad One herbed yogurt sauce, two distinct uses: Half serves as marinade for the chicken, while the other half dresses a briny, crunchy Greek salad. Chicken, Eggplant and Basil Stir-Fry The easy steam-frying technique here gives you eggplant that’s silky, golden and not at all oily. Lemon-Garlic Grilled Chicken Breasts This is it: the only method you need for grilling boneless chicken breasts to juicy perfection. Crispy Cheddar Chicken Tacos These Cheddar-lined tacos are more fun than any quick dinner has a right to be. Quick Harissa Apricot Chicken Intense, beguiling harissa paste is the key ingredient in this speedy recipe; apricot jam brings sweetness to offset any heat. One-Pan Kuku Paka (Chicken in Coconut Curry) Use skin-on chicken thighs in this creamy, richly spiced curry. Chicken With Peas and Mint Sweet peas and fresh mint make an even more pleasing pair when they’re served in a skillet with crisp-skinned chicken thighs. Spicy Paprika Chicken and Potato Stew Like chicken paprikash but in stew form, this recipe swaps out sweet paprika for its spicy cousin. Blackened Chicken Breasts A basic recipe that tastes like anything but, and the leftovers make amazing chicken salad. Stir-Fried Cumin Green Beans and Chicken Even quicker than the typical stir-fry, because you hardly need to do any chopping to prep. Chicken and White Bean Stew This flexible dish is made quickly with boneless breasts poached in broth and made creamy from smashed beans. Pasta, Noodles, Grains Coconut Curry Noodles With Shrimp A weeknight noodle bowl, but make it a luxuriously creamy slurp. Stir-Fried Salt and Pepper Dumplings This recipe convincingly makes the case for stir-frying your freezer dumplings. Ravioli With Roasted Red Pepper Sauce A brilliant and brilliantly simple sauce. Quick Pasta e Fagioli This is a speed-demon version of the classic and is remarkably satisfying for it. Farro With Blistered Tomatoes, Pesto and Spinach The combination of pesto and tomatoes can summon August any time of year. Cream Cheese Ramen In the words of its writer, this nine-minute recipe is a “break glass in case of noodle emergency” dinner, perfect for kids and hospitable to additions like peas. Smoky Chicken and Peppers Penne If fajitas were a pasta dish, it’d be this: sweet, smoky and fun to spear with a fork. Angel Hair Pasta A simple throwback that’s easy to love. Spicy Pork Noodle Soup Ramen is entangled with browned ground pork and thinly sliced veggies in this easy-to-throw-together soup. Salsa Macha Pasta With Shrimp This unique and delicious recipe brings the elements of salsa macha — nuts, seeds, garlic and chiles — into a skillet, where they are tossed with shrimp and spaghetti. Creamy Lemon Asparagus Gnocchi Pasta al limone inspired this pillowy one-pan dinner. Cold Noodles With Steak and Tomatoes This dish is both brawny (from sliced steak) and bright (from fish sauce, lime and juicy tomatoes). Peanut Noodles With Spicy Tofu Chewy, nubby tofu crumbles take this dish to the next level. Cheesy Baked Pasta With Sausage and Ricotta If love were a baked pasta dinner, it would be this one. Soy Sauce and Brown Butter Brussels Sprouts Pasta A surprisingly rich dish, with a soy-butter sauce and tender sliced brussels. Cumin Chicken Fried Rice You can prep all the ingredients ahead for this recipe, including the three-ingredient sauce that knits together all the elements. Tortellini Soup This is screaming, “Make me for dinner!” Creamy Cottage Cheese Basil Pasta We live in the golden age of cottage cheese; in this recipe, it’s blended with spinach and basil to make a silky pasta sauce. One-Pot Orzo and Meatballs This dish may sound Italian Americanish, but it actually has a Spanish streak, with pimentón and fresh chorizo featured in the pot. Kimchi Ramen Silken tofu softens the heat in this customizable soup. One-Pan Dumplings With Greens Just cook that kale right in the pan with your dumplings, drizzle with soy sauce and rice vinegar, and garnish to your heart’s content. Kale Caesar Pasta Salad A hefty, make-ahead pasta for Caesar lovers. Pasta With Tomato-Poached Eggs This is a pantry dish that, against all odds, feels like a luxury. Chilled Sesame Soba and Tofu A light dinner in minutes, substantiated with hunks of firm tofu. Lemony Pasta With Chickpeas and Parsley Use chickpeas to bulk up a simple bowl of pasta. Beef and Pork Beef, Asparagus and Tofu Stir-Fry This clever recipe uses less beef than a typical similar stir-fry without skimping on the protein; it’s better for the planet and more cost-effective, too. Smashed Beef Kebab With Cucumber Yogurt This was our most popular recipe of 2025, and if you make it you’ll see why. Roasted Sausages With Chickpeas and Spinach Keep sausages in your freezer so you can always throw together a dinner like this. Cheeseburger Soup This is the best cheeseburger soup recipe in the land, and yes, kids love it. Kielbasa Coins and Cabbage My favorite touch in this recipe is the apple cider vinegar and Dijon mustard that are stirred into the pan before serving. Sausage, Beans and Greens Soup Sausage is an ingenious base for this satisfying soup, generous with its fat and flavor. Sheet-Pan Charred Meat Pitas Definitely top these delicious pitas with abandon. Sausages With Tangy, Gingery Pineapple Don’t believe the haters: Pork and pineapple belong together. Chile-Garlic Steak and Zucchini A red wine vinegar dressing ties the seared steak and zucchini together. Shake and Bake Pork Chops Definitely serve with applesauce on the side. Sheet-Pan Steak and Pepper Tacos Steak is very satisfying here, but you could use any protein you want (including tofu or tempeh). Skillet Pork Chops With Buttered Corn This is at its best made with peak-season sweet corn, but frozen corn works well, too. Panko-Crusted Pork Tenderloin With Tahini Slaw This method produces utterly juicy pork that is difficult to stop eating. Glazed Chile-Garlic Meatballs Made with soy sauce and maple syrup, this glaze is salty-sweet in just the right way. Charros Corridos (Quick Spicy Bean Soup) Frijoles charros — cowboy beans, studded with sliced hot dogs — are from Northern Mexico, and this recipe lets you have that for dinner in a hurry. Smashed Bean and Sausage Toasts Normalize toasts for dinner, especially when they’re as garlicky and meaty as these; I’d make a green salad to go on the side. Perfect Soy-Grilled Steak Exactly as advertised and very easy to make. Vegetarian Halloumi and Sweet Potato Tacos An unexpected combination that works shockingly well, and a good dinner for kids who don’t eat meat. Skillet Chickpea Parmesan All the saucy, bubbling, dig-in joy of a baked Parmesan dish, but with the pantry-friendly convenience of a few cans of chickpeas. Creamy Butternut Squash and Coconut Noodle Soup An excellent showcase for sweetly familiar butternut squash, inspired by the Thai dish khao soi. Tofu Schnitzel With Buttermilk Slaw Use prepackaged slaw mix as a shortcut here; anything would be great tossed with that creamy, tangy buttermilk dressing. White Bean Shakshuka Heartier than more traditional shakshuka, thanks to those white beans, but no more taxing to make. Chickpea Tomato-Rice Soup The starch from the rice makes this soup creamier than you might imagine. Anda Bhurji (Tomato-Chile Scrambled Eggs) A spicy scramble for nights when it’s eggs for dinner. Buttery Gochujang Tofu and Broccoli You have to stir together only a few ingredients to make the incredible glaze. Charred Broccoli and White Bean Stew Searing the broccoli until it’s golden brown helps build flavor in this pleasingly simple soup. Chile Tofu A vegan take on chile paneer, this recipe soars on the strength of its spicy-sweet sauce. Crispy Tofu and Cheesy Bean Burritos The spiced-and-seared tofu crumbles in this recipe make a killer addition to beany burritos. Ras el Hanout Chickpea and Spinach Stew This is a pretty fabulous way to have chickpeas for dinner. Green Curry Beans and Greens Beans and greens get a bright, hot boost. Hearty Vegetable Tofu Soup Thick with cabbage, carrots and scoops of silken tofu, this gingery soup is a satisfying dinner. Old Bay Tofu Nuggets A gleefully fun vegetarian dinner, especially if you serve it with dipping sauce. Tofu and Sweet Potato Peanut Butter Curry Peanut butter is the heroine of this creamy, sweet-and-salty dish. Soy-Glazed Mushroom Rice Bowl Silky caramelized cabbage adds another layer of flavor; add sardines for protein if you’d like. Seafood Ginger Salmon Lettuce Wraps This great get-your-hands-messy dinner is brought to life by nước chấm, the punchy Vietnamese sauce. Harissa Shrimp With Greens and Feta A genius sheet-pan dinner; the shrimp and greens cook together quickly before they’re topped with feta, avocado and red onion. Spicy Tuna Salad With Crispy Rice A sushi restaurant staple is cleverly remade for home cooks. Salmon and Cherry Tomato Curry You can never go wrong with a coconut-milk curry; this one is flavored with ginger, garlic and the juices of those burst tomatoes. Broiled Wild Salmon and Peppers Running fish and quick-cooking vegetables under the broiler is a weeknight move that reliably delivers. One-Pot Salmon and Dill Rice With Peas The rice, salmon and peas all cook together in this convenient dinner, lightened with yogurt sauce and dill. Crispy Coconut Salmon Bring the tropical, shredded-sweet crunch of fried coconut shrimp to weeknight baked salmon fillets. Shrimp and Bacon Burritas “These were dope,” a commenter wrote. Cod With Caper-Orange Sauce This sauce has the power to make simple cod sing. Baked Salmon Meatballs An excellent use of canned salmon, and a gift from the meal-prep gods. Puttanesca Poached Fish Puttanesca sauce, as bold as can be, is a delicious medium for gently poaching fish. Roasted Cumin Salmon With Carrots A simple recipe that puts earthy cumin front and center (it’s especially nice contrasted with the carrots). Corn and Cod Green Curry This is a heavenly ingredient trio: fish, corn and coconut milk. Crispy Salmon With Lentil Salsa Verde Salsa verde with lentils is more than a sauce; it’s a side dish to this crisp-skinned salmon. Sautéed Shrimp With Lemon-Caper Dressing This is so fancy for how easy it is; serve it with toast, tossed with pasta, over rice or in a salad. Greek Salad With Sardines and Beans A main-course salad that could be made with just about any tinned fish. Sheet-Pan Citrus Salmon With White Beans This recipe is excellent all year round, but save it for the darkest part of winter, when citrus provides some sunshine. Spicy Shrimp Masala Shockingly complex for the speedy cook time, and truly alive with flavor. Tuna Melt This solid rendition of the classic is among the fastest recipes on this list. Follow New York Times Cooking on Instagram, Facebook, YouTube, TikTok and Pinterest. Get regular updates from New York Times Cooking, with recipe suggestions, cooking tips and shopping advice.

item.title: Arc’teryx Wants the Sperro SV to Be the Last Jacket You Ever Buy—Seriously
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 5.01
Engineered for versatility across high-stakes mountain environments, the Sperro SV underwent rigorous testing during ski tours and ice climbing ascents. (Photo: Courtesy of Arc'teryx) Tucked alongside the interior chest pocket of a two-toned magenta Arc’teryx jacket is a laser-etched QR code—but instead of pulling up the menu at your local pub, it prompts you to register your new purchase, immediately kicking off a record of the jacket’s materials, origin, and, eventually, repair history. A QR code seems simple enough—after all, you encounter dozens of them weekly—but a QR code on a mountain-grade hardshell requires a different level of engineering than the laminated square on your bartop. The internal placement makes it near-impossible to destroy or remove; the laser etching, adapted from the electronics industry, underwent multiple trials to ensure it left a permanent mark without degrading the fabric. So why spend so much time, money, and engineering on a single square inch of jacket? For Arc’teryx, that QR code is the entry point into System 0™, a new framework that reimagines how products can be designed, manufactured, used, repaired, and ultimately regenerated. In fact, the QR code is just one of many updates and innovations Arc’teryx built into its first System 0 jacket, the Sperro SV. Among the others: an easily repairable zipper, a nylon face fabric and backer engineered for chemical recyclability, and reinforcement at common failure points. System 0 started as a “what if” conversation between Arc’teryx CEO Stuart Haselden and VP of Advanced Concepts, Alex Plante, brainstorming what circularity would look like for the company. At that point, Arc’teryx’s ReBIRD program already existed, with a solid infrastructure for product repairs, resale, trade-in, and upcycling, but the team knew they were still missing an actual process—a viable, repeatable way to create products that can be used for longer and ultimately regenerated into something new. “We landed on what product we wanted to develop within that [circularity] concept, and then, while we were developing the product, realized that we didn’t have all the pieces of the system,” says Andrew Yip, Senior Director of Materials Innovation at Arc’teryx. That meant building capability as they went, bringing in people like Kyle Wood, Vice President of Strategy, to focus on circularity. They also recruited for other supporting roles, like sourcing manager for raw materials. Throughout the circularity initiative, Yip and his colleagues used one principle as their North Star: Sustainability alone isn’t a reason for a product to exist. Anything they created had to live up to Arc’teryx’s sky-high standards for technical excellence and durability. “Most sustainable materials and products are just less bad than their incumbent,” argues Yip. “If you’re just going to make something less bad from a sustainability perspective but make it worse in terms of performance, then there really isn’t a justification for it to exist.” To that end, Arc’teryx prioritized abrasion resistance on both face fabric and backer, while refusing to compromise on tear and tensile strength, waterproofing, and breathability—all the things that determine whether a jacket becomes a one-season purchase or a mainstay in your gear closet. They also intentionally aligned on nylon 6 as the key material instead of polyester; even though polyester has more recycling opportunities, the team knew that nylon 6 fabric would perform best. To find the exact nylon content ratio—the perfect number that would make the fabric functionally and financially recyclable—Arc’teryx worked closely with Aquafil, the manufacturer of ECONYL® regenerated nylon. According to Aquafil, the textile is known for high wear resistance and impact strength (aka extreme durability). Finding the perfect jacket material was one thing. But that wasn’t the hardest problem the Arc’teryx team had to solve, says Yip. You already know Arc’teryx for its insanely technical, single-purpose shells like the Alpha SV—a scalpel, according to Yip. “It’s really a precision tool, and it was designed for ice climbing,” he explains. “It doesn’t have hand pockets for a reason—you don’t need hand pockets when you’re ice climbing.” On the contrary, the Sperro SV had to be a jacket-of-all-trades, working in a variety of environments and use cases. “With the Sperro SV, we wanted to make something that was multi-environment, multifunctional, and multi-activity,” details Yip. They needed a Swiss Army Knife, not a scalpel—but that Swiss Army Knife couldn’t compromise on durability. To ensure the Sperro SV was worth its mettle, Arc’teryx tested the jacket on ski tours, hiking trips, snowshoeing expeditions, and even ice climbing. They also partnered with the North Shore Search and Rescue, a volunteer-led organization and one of Canada’s oldest search-and-rescue teams, to make sure the jacket performed in high-stakes scenarios. All that engineering ultimately serves one purpose: creating a jacket worthy of what Yip refers to as custodianship, rather than ownership. “Hopefully, the person who’s purchasing this jacket is somebody who cares about their stuff and is going to take care of the garment, bring it in for repair, and extend its lifetime as much as possible,” says Yip. “And only after many, many years and many, many repairs, when something is no longer repairable, only then is when we take it back.” Hence, the QR code. Arc’teryx hopes that by making it as seamless as possible for customers to track the Sperro SV’s lifespan, materials, and repair history, customers will view themselves as custodians with a responsibility to their gear—instead of temporary owners of a disposable item. If all goes according to plan, the Sperro SV might be the last jacket Arc’teryx ever sells you. At a gulp-worthy $1,200 retail price, most customers are probably praying that they never have to buy another jacket again, but it’s not exactly a sound business strategy in an industry that counts on customers to replace old gear. Yip is strangely okay with that. “When we’re developing new products and prototypes, we know we have something when our athletes and field testers don’t want to give it back,” he explains. “Similarly, I think we’re onto something if we have a commercial product that people can buy and they don’t want to replace it. So personally, I would have no problem with that.” When asked to comment on the price, Arc’teryx reps note that the Sperro SV is priced in line with their most advanced hard shells, and the price reflects the design effort and materials that went into this sustainable jacket. “Circularity at this level of performance requires significant investment across materials, manufacturing, certification, and end-of-life infrastructure,” Arc’teryx acknowledges. They believe that the price reflects the value of three years of unlimited repairs, a product they’re backing to last for years, and eventually, an end-of-life offramp. “When you factor in the total life of the jacket, the value calculation looks different than a traditional purchase,” reasons the brand. Whether consumers will find the price a fair trade-off for the total package remains to be seen. The Sperro SV is just the first “statement of intent,” as Yip puts it, for what System 0 can do within the Arc’teryx playbook. With the streamlined processes and internal philosophies Arc’teryx has now aligned on, they’re free to explore further iterations of circular gear. “We started with a hardshell because it’s what we know, what we make, and what we’re known for—so you can imagine that the other things we’re known for and make well are coming down the pipeline,” hints Yip. And for the Arc’teryx loyalists who worry this new iteration of a hardshell won’t live up to their high standards—you’ve got nothing to worry about. “If anyone were to put on the jacket and close their eyes, it really shouldn’t be different at all compared to anything that we’ve made before. And I think that’s the point,” says Yip. “It’s everything else around it that we’re trying to change.”

item.title: A Climber Was Stuck on a Stawamus Chief Cliff. A Flying Drone Delivered a Jacket and a Rope to Save Him.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 4.73
After 10 P.M. on September 10, Squamish Search and Rescue arrived at the Stawamus Chief, specifically on a climbing route known as the Alaska Highway (Photo: Courtesy of Squamish Search and Rescue) A highly specialized search-and-rescue drone team pulled off a bold late-night rescue in Squamish, British Columbia, Canada, after a climber found himself stranded on a cliff. The man was stuck standing on a ten-inch ledge 250 feet above the ground, secured to an anchor but without enough rope to descend. Squamish Search and Rescue sent in two aerial drones, one to light up the wall and provide a bird’s-eye view of the situation, and a second to deliver clothing, lights, and a climbing rope to the stricken climber. The rescue played out on Stawamus Chief, one of the world’s largest granite monoliths that is a hotbed for trad and face climbers. Dustin Wales, 36, is the drone program coordinator for the responding agency, Squamish Search and Rescue. He told Outside that his team spent the last two years preparing for a situation like this, training drone pilots and establishing protocols for any situation across rugged terrain, including this. “We just hadn’t had the opportunity to put this in action,” Wales said. After 10 P.M. on September 10, Squamish Search and Rescue arrived at the Stawamus Chief, where the stuck climber had been attempting a multi-pitch route called Alaska Highway. Between the darkness, rockfall exposure, and scale of the terrain, Wales told Outside that a traditional rope rescue or helicopter evacuation would have been especially difficult. “Both of those options being dangerous and challenging, the managers called up our drone team with a bit of an idea,” Wales said. “We theorized that we could deliver a pilot line to the person stranded on the wall.” The stranded person had been climbing with two other people, who were able to safely scale down the wall. Wales and five other rescuers met them and established communication with the cliffed-out climber, putting a plan in place. “When you’re doing a drone operation, it’s really important to discuss the risks when you have the opportunity to do so,” Wales said. “Through our communication, we were able to ask the climber if he was confident to come down, and also what he needed to come down.” For the first flight, rescuers tethered a pilot line to the drone and flew it up to the climber. Once he had a hold of the line, responders on the ground tied a jacket and headlamp to it, which he then pulled up to himself. He used the gear to stay warm and light the rock. Based on the climber’s information, Wales and his team then used the drone to measure the distance to the ground with lasers and a rangefinder. They then brought in a larger drone with a light, which hovered to spotlight the cliffed-out climber. Rescuers tied a 300-foot pilot line from the smaller drone to a climbing rope, and flew the device to the climber. The rope was a thin-gauge but high-strength Dyneema line, which the team spooled out between a ground operator and the drone. According to Wales, the climber “captured the rope out of the air.” He then tied the line to his climbing harness and an anchor, and rappelled down to safety. Flying drones are becoming common in search and rescue teams worldwide. In recent years, lifesaving officials have used them to spot lost hikers, drop food and water, and take aerial images of huge swaths of backcountry. The Squamish incident shows that drones can also deliver climbing gear to someone in a highly precarious position. “This rescue is a great representation of flight skills, training, management, and practice,” Wales said. “It’s a pretty big win for us. There was a lot of cheering from the ground crew. It was an awesome demonstration of what a lot of effort, training, and facilitation can culminate in.”

item.title: How Skin Tone Affects Wearable Accuracy—and How Tech Giants Are Responding
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 3.87
(Photo: Hill background: Fond, Magnus; Fitness Watch: simplehappyart/Getty; Design: Ayana Underwood/Canva) Wearables have become a near-constant companion for many Americans. According to a 2026 study, nearly 107 million people in the United States own one. People track their steps, workouts, and recovery, and increasingly look to those numbers to tell them how their bodies are doing. But for some—particularly people with darker skin tones—there’s a nagging question: Can I trust what my device is telling me? There’s a good reason to ask. A 2025 review of smartwatch accuracy studies found significant variability in how wearable devices performed across skin tones. According to one study included in the review, a major smartwatch brand measured heart rates within five beats per minute (bpm) across a full spectrum of skin tones. Other devices, however, underestimated heart rate by ten to 15 bpm in darker-skinned users during moderate to vigorous exercise. Researchers also found large discrepancies in heart rate readings during cycling and resistance training in people with dark skin. While heart rate metrics help people gauge workout intensity and how quickly their heart recovers after exercise, heart rate readings can also be lifesaving. An irregular heartbeat may indicate serious cardiovascular issues that can lead to blood clots, stroke, and heart failure, and should be flagged to a doctor. An inaccurate reading could miss these red flags. This issue is not news to wearable companies as getting accurate data from darker skin is a known challenge—one that requires extra effort from wearable makers to ensure the data is reliable. Outside contacted eight major wearable tech companies, including Oura, Apple, WHOOP, Google, and Polar, to find out how they’ve worked to address the wearable skin-tone problem. Here’s why wearables can struggle to get accurate readings on dark skin, and how these companies say they’ve improved their tech to ensure better accuracy across skin tones. Most smartwatches and rings rely on a type of technology called photoplethysmography (PPG), which uses optical sensors. Those sensors detect light to measure blood flow. A typical PPG device shines green light into your skin. (If you take a peek at the underside of your fitness watch, you can probably spot those green flashing lights.) Hemoglobin—a small protein in your blood that carries oxygen from the lungs to the rest of the body—absorbs some of that light, and the rest is reflected back onto the sensor. As blood moves through your vessels, the device measures changes in the reflected light to estimate your heart rate. The catch is that melanin, the pigment that gives skin its color, also absorbs and scatters some of the device’s light. The more melanin in the skin, the more light is absorbed. This makes darker skin tones more vulnerable to data loss compared to lighter skin tones, according to that 2025 review. Categorizing skin tone can be tricky because it’s subjective. But dermatologists often rely on the Fitzpatrick Scale. This scale is the dermatology industry standard classification for skin tone groups, according to a study published in the HCA Healthcare Journal of Medicine in February 2026. The scale is based on people’s self-reported observations of how likely they are to sunburn and tan. That data helped classify skin tone into six categories, from Type I to Type VI. Type I skin is the lightest and burns easily and doesn’t tan; Type VI is the darkest and tans easily and almost never burns. Despite the scale’s widespread use, it’s considered flawed, as that same 2026 study noted that its reliance on self-perception and cultural and societal influences complicates categorization. Even though skin tone can affect watch accuracy, it’s not the only factor that can lead to an inaccurate reading. “Noise is the biggest issue,” Michael Rosenberg, MD, a cardiac electrophysiologist who studies wearables in the division of cardiology at the University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus, told Outside. Noise, Rosenberg said, includes tattoos, body hair, hydration levels, sweat, and residue from lotions or sunscreens. He said that wrist size, skin temperature, and even freckles can impact readings. Improving wearable tech accuracy takes real intention; however, Apple, Oura, WHOOP, Polar, Google, and other wearable companies have made it a priority. Emily Capodilupo, senior vice president of research, algorithms, and data at WHOOP, said they’re intentional about ensuring their studies include people across all six Fitzpatrick values. WHOOP is a wearable company that sells a tiered membership, where customers pay an annual fee that includes their screenless device and access to their app’s metrics and analysis. “When we notice a population—skin tone, gender, age—where we think we’re struggling performance-wise, we overrepresent that group in the data collection efforts, and that’s a very effective technique for improving algorithms,” Capodilupo told Outside. Capodilupo also said WHOOP has specifically designed an algorithm to compensate for how melanin absorbs light. She said that algorithm is constantly validated and updated. The device monitors how much signal it gets back and adjusts the LED brightness accordingly. If the signal is weaker, the LED intensity increases. This approach comes with a trade-off, she explained. More powerful LEDs use more battery. “That’s a trade that we’re willing to make because we want to make sure that we can stand by the data that we provide,” Capodilupo said. Apple’s strategy is similar. The company says that it addresses the issue at the software and hardware level, including by adjusting how much light is transmitted into the skin and how strongly the return signal is amplified. They also said that in every generation of Apple Watch, software and hardware design factors are driven by ensuring users with the darkest skin tones get a strong signal and equivalent performance. At Oura, the company’s smart ring uses the same PPG technology. Senior vice president of science Shyamal Patel, PhD, said the product’s advantage is that the palm side of the finger tends to have more consistent pigmentation than the wrist. The finger, he said, also provides access to larger arteries, which can produce a stronger signal than what you can measure on the wrist with the same kind of hardware setup. That doesn’t solve for everything, though. Patel said the ring’s “smart sensing” capability means there are a number of paths the light can travel through the skin. The device continuously evaluates which path is producing the strongest signal and adjusts accordingly. In a statement via email, Raija Laukkanen, PhD, said that optical heart measurements have improved over the years largely due to better sensor technology, ergonomics and algorithms. Laukkanen is the director of science collaborations at Polar, a wearable tech company that offers watches based on activity types and other products like chest straps. “Optical measurement remains a practical and effective option for continuous heart rate tracking and everyday training. For situations where precision is the priority, electrocardiogram (ECG) remains our recommended approach,” she wrote. Unlike PPG tech, which relies on light sensors to collect heart rate data, ECG or EKG measures electrical heart signals directly through the skin, so it isn’t affected by pigmentation and is considered the gold standard in heart rate testing. The Polar H10 chest strap uses ECG to monitor heart rate during physical activity where real-time data is necessary. (Some Apple Watch, Polar watches, and WHOOP models offer on-demand ECG readings.) Patel said Oura is exploring new ways to characterize skin tones, such as the Monk skin tone scale (MST), which is a ten-tone visual scale that captures a fuller spectrum of darker skin. Patel’s team focuses on improving algorithms to better translate sensor data into useful metrics that can tell users about their overall health and well-being. Patel also said they intentionally collect data in a broad range of locations worldwide to support diversity. “We need to continue expanding the standards and then continue innovating on how we measure and validate the data,” Patel said. Apple also incorporates a spectrophotometer, which helps measure color more objectively. In addition to the standard Fitzpatrick assessment, researchers can use this lab instrument to measure the exact amount of light reflected at different wavelengths. In a statement via email, a Google spokesperson said, “Google Health takes accuracy very seriously and continuously conducts studies to rigorously test the accuracy of our products among diverse groups of users. We also focus on recruiting a diverse testing population from around the globe for wear testing during our development cycles for Google wearables including Fitbit and Pixel Watch devices.” Though wearables provide a wealth of data on users’ health and wellness, Rosenberg said it’s important to remember that wearable devices are still commercial products, not medical ones. So, it’s reasonable to expect occasional inaccuracies, but he said they do detect overall trends pretty well. To get the most accurate readings, the experts contacted for this story said there are a few things that are within your control: keep a snug fit so that the sensor is in contact with the skin, make sure the sensor isn’t sitting directly on a bone, wipe the sensor regularly so it remains free of sweat and residue from lotions, try to keep the sensor away from any tattoos, and install recent device and app updates. If your device isn’t working properly or starts producing strange results, it’s probably best to ditch it for a new one. Wearables aren’t one-size-fits-all. As the technology evolves, continued research and more representative data will be key to ensuring everyone can trust the numbers on their devices. Want more Outside health stories? Sign up for the Bodywork newsletter. And for tips on how to train, fuel, and recover better, sign up for the Sweat Science 101 newsletter.

item.title: The 90/90 Hip-Mobility Exercise Could Help You Run and Hike With Less Pain
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 2.87
(Photo: Woman stretching: shurkin_son/Getty; Design: Ayana Underwood/Canva) As a certified personal trainer, I don’t use social media as my go-to source for reliable fitness info, so I’m always pleasantly surprised when doomscrolling delivers content that’s actually legit. The 90/90 hip stretch—which has been trending lately on TikTok and Instagram—is a prime example of that. The exercise, which takes your hips through both internal and external rotation, is a great way to boost hip mobility. The hip is a ball-and-socket joint, which means it’s designed to work in multiple directions, but mobility restrictions can prevent it from moving as it should. If you’ve got tight hips to begin with, improving mobility of this major joint can help you move more efficiently, better absorb impact, reduce injury risk, and make both everyday life and outdoor adventuring more comfortable. This is especially beneficial when you’re navigating uneven terrain that involves stepping not just forwards but in all planes of motion. More specifically, boosting hip rotation, which is what the 90/90 focuses on, helps stabilize your pelvic floor; it also prevents your knees and back from taking on extra stress. Doing this move regularly can improve your chances of walking, hiking, and trail running without pain or injury. There’s one important caveat: the 90-90 requires a decent amount of mobility to get into, so if your hips are super tight to begin with, it may not be your best starter stretch. (For something a bit easier on the hips, try these easy hip mobility moves.) But if you’re ready to open up your hips, read ahead to get started. Just remember to listen to your body as you try the move. If any pain crops up, back off. Forcing yourself into the stretch can lead to strain or injury. If you need some extra help, follow this fitness coach’s video on how to do it. Final thing: Yes, the 90-90 is beneficial, but it’s just one move and doesn’t target all aspects of hip mobility. If your goal is comprehensive hip mobility, regularly incorporating a variety of hip stretches is a good idea. Here are a few physical therapist-approved moves to consider. item.title: Review: Berghaus Pendower Wind Jacket Review
item.description:
Source: Sectionhiker.com Score: 4.80
The Berghaus Pendower Wind Jacket is a lightweight windbreaker for hiking, trail running, and outdoor activities where you don't need full waterproof protection. Its main strength is its breathability and simplicity: it blocks wind effectively while retaining body heat without the bulk or restriction of a heavier shell jacket. - Gender: Men's (Women's – only available in UK) - Weight: 4.0 oz - Fit: Easy to layer with - Material: Nylon - CFM 1.2 (very windproof) - Fit: true to size The jacket has a clean, understated appearance that works well both on the trail and around town. Its lightweight construction makes it easy to pack into its zippered chest pocket, while the fit leaves enough room for layering. It works especially well over a Polartec Alpha fleece, for example. This creates a warm, highly adaptable system for cool, changeable conditions. The fleece insulates while staying breathable, and the Pendower helps block wind without adding much weight. The Pendower hood is pre-cinched behind the head to keep it snug and has a brim to keep the sun out of your eyes. I have a small hat size, so it's a bit slack on me, but it fills out when worn with a fleece beanie (or if you have a larger head). Fully adjustable windbreaker hoods are pretty rare, especially these days in the race to make the lightest weight gear and clothing. The chest pocket is large enough to hold a Smartphone and has a fabric key fob inside, while the stretch cuffs are wide enough to roll up your arm. The exterior fabric is thin and very quiet, even in gusty wind. These details make the jacket easy to wear and use as a windbreaker. As a windproof outer layer, the Pendower performs well in windy and exposed conditions. It is particularly useful when conditions are too cold and breezy for a fleece alone but not wet enough to justify a heavier waterproof shell, which would retain too much body heat. Breathability is reasonable during gentle to moderate activity. When walking quickly or climbing steep hills, heat can build up, especially when worn over a warm midlayer. This combination is best managed by adjusting layers as activity levels change. Unzipping the central zipper, removing the hood, or rolling up the sleeves all let you dump excess body heat without stopping to remove garments. The low weight is one of the jacket’s biggest advantages. It is easy to carry until needed and takes up little space in a pack. The simple construction also makes it practical for regular use, whether walking, traveling, or wearing around town. Rather than a standalone warm jacket, it works best as part of a layering system. Comparable Wind Jackets | Item | Weight | Price | |---|---|---| | Patagonia Airshed Pro Hoodie | 3.7 oz /105g | $139 | | Patagonia Houdini Jacket | 3.7 oz /105g | $119 | | Enlightened Equipment Copperfield Wind Shirt | 2.05 oz / 58g | $120 | | Mammut Aenergy WB Hooded Jacket | 4.7 oz / 132g | $149 | | Katabatic Gear Crest Windshell | 1.8 oz / 51g | $129 | | Rab Vital Windshell Hoody | 4.6 oz /160g | $100 | | Montbell Hooded Tachyon Jacket | 2.5 oz / 71 g | $130 | | Mountain Hardwear Kor Airshell Hoody | 4.7 oz /133g | $165 | | Arc'teryx Squamish Hoody | 5.3 oz /150g | $200 | | Black Diamond Distance Wind Shell | 3.2 oz/91g | $199 | Recommendation Overall, the Berghaus Pendower Wind Jacket is a dependable and versatile wind layer. It works best over a breathable insulating midlayer such as a fleece or wool pullover in cooler conditions, where it helps turn a lightweight midlayer into a more weather-resistant system. Disclosure: Berghaus donated a jacket for review. SectionHiker never accepts payment for gear reviews or editorial coverage. item.title: Review: Lems Trail Thrasher Pro Shoes
item.description:
Source: Sectionhiker.com Score: 4.64
The Lems Trail Thrasher Pro is a zero-drop shoe with a Vibram Megagrip outsole for people who want a hiking shoe that is more robust than a trail runner but less technical than an approach shoe. With a large toe box, durable Nubuck upper, and waterproof membrane, the Trail Thrasher Pro is a versatile, durable shoe that works well for day hikes, wet-weather walks, travel, and everyday outdoor use. - Gender: Men's (Women's Available) - Weight per shoe: 15.2 oz - Wide sizes: No - Drop: Zero - Stack height: 16mm - Outsole: Vibram Megagrip - Waterproofing: Yes - Upper: Nubuck - Fit: True to Size Fit and Comfort The shoe’s most noticeable feature is its generous toe box, which lets your toes spread and splay naturally. The zero-drop platform lets your foot move more like it would barefoot, reducing fatigue and improving balance on uneven ground. Cushioning is modest but adequate. If you prefer more support or more underfoot padding like a max trail runner, these will feel too minimal. Break-in time is immediate. I could wear them right away without any fit issues. Protection I don't look at my feet when I hike, so I like good toe protection just in case I bash into a rock. Like all serious hikers, I've had my share of broken toes and toenails. The Trail Thrasher scores high in terms of toe and foot protection with hefty front-toe kicks and a nubuck upper that's unlikely to split or get shredded at the corners of the toebox. Waterproofing The waterproof lining helps keep feet dry when worn in wet grass, shallow puddles, and muddy conditions. The tongue and upper also help prevent water and trail debris from entering around the laces. Because this is a low-cut shoe, it cannot protect against water that rises above the collar. Deep puddles and stream crossings will likely leave your feet wet. The waterproof construction can feel warmer than a non-waterproof shoe in hotter weather, but warmer when there's a chill in the air. Nevertheless, for ordinary wet-weather hiking and daily walking, the protection is useful. Traction and Trail Performance The Vibram Megagrip outsole provides solid grip on packed earth, gravel, roots, and rocky inclines. The shoe is stable on maintained trails while remaining comfortable when the route varies between roots and rocks, gravel, or pavement. But the Trail Thrasher is not as flexible a shoe as many zero-drop trail runners and is much sturdier, somewhere in between a trail runner and an approach shoe. That takes a little time to get used to, but it's useful if you want to use them across a wide range of surfaces, from trails to gravel and pavement. Recommendation The Lems Trail Thrasher Pro is a comfortable and versatile choice for day hikers and walkers who prefer a wide, natural zero-drop fit. Its strengths include a zero-drop platform, a spacious toe box, waterproof protection, a grippy Vibram outsole, and durable construction. If it has one weakness, it's the styling. Its plain black look is not the most appealing, even compared with the outlandish color palettes of trail runners and other athletic shoes. Disclosure: Lems donated shoes for review.
