item.title: ‘So big and so close’: spotting endangered bears on a trip to northern Spain
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Score: 4.29
Once upon a time, in the woods outside Pola de Somiedo, lived a family of Cantabrian brown bears. The villagers reported sightings of a mother bear who had lost a leg to a hunter’s trap, her two cubs and two adult males, either of which might have been the father. In those days, at the end of the 1980s, they seemed to be the last of their kind in this part of Asturias. Meanwhile, the wider population dropped to about 60 bears across the surrounding Cantabrian mountain range that gave the species its name. They have since clawed their way back from the edge of extinction here in northern Spain, and nature guide Luis Frechilla believes their numbers may now be upwards of 500 again. “They’re still classed as endangered,” he tells me, until the official count hits 1,000. But relative abundance makes them much easier to see today in Somiedo natural park – one of Spain’s first such protected areas, established in 1988. Setting his scope on a tripod in a steep-angled pasture, Frechilla spots a bear almost as soon as we start looking. A juvenile, apparently, which means the animal is old enough to be foraging alone, but it’s still too small, and too far away, for him to tell if it’s a male or female. Another bear-spotter standing near us seems more willing to take a guess. “Ooh, look at his little ears,” she says delightedly, beaming behind binoculars. No expert myself, I watch that distant fuzzy shape move across the viewfinder and along the sharp ridges opposite, blinking in and out of sight like a cursor on the trend line of a graph. I’m not sure that we are close enough to call this an encounter, but it is an experience. The sun drops behind the peaks; the birds sing a dusk chorus in the birches and oaks; cowbells ring through the valley from the dairy herds that help this region of so-called “Green Spain” look and sound like the Swiss Alps. It gets cold at night up here, and it’s been known to snow in summer, though my own visit in late spring sees the mountaintops looking whiter than anyone around here can remember so deep into May. That weather, and the sheer calorific spend of living and working at a median altitude of 1,300 metres, has made the traditional cuisine much sturdier here than elsewhere in Spain. Down at the village inn, Casa Miño, we share a bottle of regional cider and a cachopo (beef fillet topped with serrano ham, peppers and goat cheese, and pounded into a single solid unit the size of a solar panel). I want fabada, too, the famous Asturian stew of white beans, pork belly and blood sausage. Frechilla says it’s a winter dish, customarily eaten for lunch – too heavy for the body to process later in the day. But I would order fabada at midnight in a heatwave, and keep eating it even while they loaded me into the ambulance. The bears, meanwhile, don’t have much to feed on at the moment. They only woke from hibernation a few weeks ago, explains Alicia Madrid the next day, on a forest trail above the century-old hydroelectric power station at La Malva. A biologist with the conservation group Fundación Oso Pardo, Madrid tells me that Cantabrian bears don’t hibernate as long or deeply as other brown bears and are generally smaller and lighter than American grizzlies. “They’re adapted to this terrain, and they can’t be too heavy because they have to climb a lot,” she says. Their paw prints in the mud look big enough to me, and the bite marks where they chewed clumps of long grasses, and the hairs shed where they scratched their backs against trees. Madrid shows us, too, the hefty rocks they overturned looking for insects. Further into the summer, there’ll be plenty of berries, acorns, chestnuts and maybe some meaty carrion to fatten them up. The foundation has played a major role in the regrowth of bear populations, building bio-corridors with strategic placements of trees and bushes full of all the things they like to eat. Another key factor is the hunting ban, introduced in 1973. The trick now, says Madrid, is coaxing isolated cohorts to breed with other groups and boost genetic diversity. Also: managing the tourists who come to see them, and balancing ecological imperatives against financial incentives. Later, after a long hike through the Valley of the Lake to reach the aptly named Lake of the Valley, I overhear Frechilla fielding the related concerns of two local women. Against a backdrop of blue sky, bright wildflowers and silver waters, the women seem to argue that conservation efforts amount to commercial exploitation. Frechilla gently insists that Somiedo natural park is a model of good practice in Spain. Much of the bears’ territory is closed to the public, and spotting expeditions are only permitted in the company of licensed guides. Nature tourism, he says, keeps villagers in jobs where farming culture cannot, and is proving vastly more sustainable than hunting bears for sport. As for protecting humans, there has been only one bear attack in recent memory, on an elderly lady whose evening stroll led her between a mother and cubs. She survived. For now, at least, most residents seem willing to share the bears with outsiders. That evening, a small crowd gather by the side of a winding back road near Saliencia, some sitting comfortably on camping chairs with spotting scopes in their hands. Everyone is watching a large male bear – so big and so close that they don’t need the viewing equipment – as he lopes across a meadow to take a quick splash in the river. Another male is spotted in the treeline above, and the two circle each other at a distance for a while. There is some speculation that they might fight for this turf, and a man with two leashed greyhounds seems ready to take bets on it. Frechilla shakes his head. “Maybe later in the season, when they’ve gained enough weight.” These bears are doing better now, but it’s still a tough life. The reality of their ongoing baby boom is that only 30% of juveniles will survive on their own, after a year of maternal supervision. This is surely why I find it so moving when we follow reports of another sighting in the twilight: a mother and her two young cubs have been seen climbing a slope called El Diente, or “The Tooth”. It’s getting dark and cold, but we can see them through the scopes, about a mile away from us across the high mountain pass at La Peral. I watch the mother bear waiting and cajoling as needed while the siblings struggle up the vertical planes of rock like toddlers trying to climb a baby gate. On the ridgeline, they turn to silhouettes, play-fighting against a white sky. They disappear over the far side, but then a little one comes back, seeming to wave goodbye with both front paws in the air. I remember a story I read to my daughter once, which put a poignant time limit on the usual fairytale ending: “And they all lived happily together, for as long as they could.” The trip was provided by the Spanish Tourist Office, Turismo Asturias and Casa Miño in Pola de Somiedo. Bear-spotting tours with nature guide Luis Frechilla can be organised through Wild Spain Travel. For more information on the Cantabrian brown bear and related conservation efforts, visit Fundación Oso Pardo Comments (…) Sign in or create your Guardian account to join the discussion

item.title: ‘Fabulous museums and no queues’: five of the best under-the-radar city breaks in Europe
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Score: 3.43
Nantes, France As dilemmas go, it’s an unusual one: saddle up a giant squid or board a submersible for a voyage to the bottom of the ocean. In the end, I find myself drawn to a fierce-looking merhorse and tentatively take the reins. High above, my daughter glides by on a flying fish, metallic fins flapping, while her Dad is battling stormy seas at the helm of a huge conch shell. A ride on the Carrousel des Mondes Marins (marine worlds carousel) – a three-storey steampunk merry-go-round inspired by Jules Verne’s novel Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea – is one of the highlights of a visit to Nantes. A surreal fairground ride, a work of art and a homage to the city’s most famous son. It’s also a lot of fun. On the banks of the Loire, 30 miles from the Atlantic ocean, Nantes is a city whose fortunes were built on the sea. As a young boy growing up near the docks in the 1830s, Verne dreamed of being a ship’s captain, but it wasn’t to be. Instead, he embarked on a series of journeys of the imagination, channelling his wanderlust into novels such as Around the World in 80 Days and Journey to the Centre of the Earth. The last of Nantes’ shipyards closed in the 1980s, but Verne’s unique vision provided the inspiration for a radical art and regeneration project, Les Machines de l’Île, that has breathed life into the abandoned quays and warehouses of the Île de Nantes, the river island that was home to the city’s docks. This is now the stomping ground of the Grand Éléphant, a 12m-high mechanical pachyderm that carries passengers on tours of the island, spraying bystanders with water from its trunk. I’d seen photos but nothing prepares you for the thrill of turning a corner and seeing the real thing lumbering towards you. You can learn about the magic behind the machinery at the nearby Galerie des Machines, where the creators bring a mechanical menagerie of strange creatures to life. The Verne connection also inspired the name of the city’s summer arts festival, Le Voyage à Nantes, which transforms streets, parks and public spaces into an open-air art gallery from July to September. Our visit coincides with the festival’s opening weekend, and the squares and avenues of the elegant Graslin district are busy with DJ sets, food stalls and people checking out the new artworks. In the Place Graslin, a beautiful square built – like much of Nantes – from chalky-white tuffeau stone from the Loire valley, some kind of cataclysmic eruption has been conjured up in front of the opera house. Huge ammonites appear to have been forced up from beneath the earth, engulfing cars in a mountain of rubble, their doors wide open, radios playing, as though abandoned in haste. Just yards away, children are playing in the dancing water fountains of the square, while the white-aproned waiters of art nouveau brasserie La Cigale weave through the pavement tables delivering seafood platters to diners unfazed by the apocalyptic scene before them. Titled Fossil Opera, the artwork is a commentary on consumerism and the fleeting nature of human endeavour, and is one of about a dozen site-specific installations that have appeared in the city, as if by magic. Even outside the summer months, there is plenty to discover in France’s sixth largest city. Each year, a handful of the festival installations are selected to become permanent fixtures, which has resulted in an impressive collection of contemporary public art, from Les Anneaux, a series of 18 giant steel rings on the Quai des Antilles, which frame views of the Loire and light up at night, to Tadashi Kawamata’s Belvédère de l’Hermitage, a viewing platform inspired by a swallow’s nest, which juts over a sheer cliff. All of these cultural highlights, old and new, are linked by the Ligne Verte, a 12-mile (20km) green line painted on the pavement. We follow the trail through the Passage Pommeraye, an exquisite 19th century glass-roofed shopping arcade; past the imposing Château des ducs de Bretagne, a moated 15th-century castle; stop off at the excellent Musée d’arts de Nantes, which houses an impressive collection of international art spanning seven centuries; and finish up at the peaceful Jardin des Plantes, a charming (and free) botanical garden which is home to a handful of modern art installations and a good cafe. From here it’s a short stroll to the Lieu Unique, a cultural space and concert venue in the factory that once produced the city’s beloved buttery LU biscuits. And there’s more to come. The Jardin Extraordinaire is a newly created garden and climbing wall in a disused granite quarry in the Bas‑Chantenay district. The exotic planting, waterfall and paddling pools were inspired by descriptions in Verne’s novel, The Mysterious Island. The nearby Chantenay docks have been colonised by studios, music spaces and the Little Atlantique Brewery, housed in a 19th-century former oil mill. Opposite the quarry, a derelict industrial building is being transformed into a new riverside cultural hub, the Cité des Imaginaires, which will eventually provide a home for an expanded Jules Verne museum. It’s an ambitious project: creative, unconventional and looking to the future. I’m sure Jules Verne would approve. Joanne O’Connor The trip was supported by Le Voyage à Nantes. Oceania Hôtel de France, just off the Place Graslin, has air‑conditioned doubles from €101 room-only Winter’s Journey, a seasonal festival of concerts, temporary light installations, artworks and gastronomic events, runs from 21 November to 3 January. Basel, Switzerland Unless you’re a professional who makes their way to the Art Basel fair every year, chances are Switzerland’s third largest city will have passed you by – or rather you will have passed it by. Basel is one stop before Zurich on the fast train from Paris, but to whiz through would be a mistake. For art and design lovers, it is the perfect city to explore on a long weekend. Basel bills itself as “the city of art and culture on the Rhine”, and it lives up to its boast. Stroll around the charming old town and marvel at the cathedral before enjoying a cold beer at one of the many cafes. If temperatures soar, you might want to join local people with a dip in the Rhine. Once you’ve done all that, you need to engage with the area’s art offerings. Within the city, the Kunstmuseum holds more than 300,000 works spanning eight centuries, with big hitters such as Monet, Van Gogh and Warhol, while Museum Tinguely is home to the work of the idiosyncratic Swiss sculptor Jean Tinguely and his dada-esque machines. But the two real draws are on the outskirts of the city. Fondation Beyeler in the suburb of Riehen is home to an impressive collection of modern and contemporary art, and always has a blockbuster exhibition (currently Pierre Huyghe) to check out. A short bus or train ride across the German border in Weil am Rhein is the Vitra Design Museum, home to one of the world’s largest permanent exhibitions of modern furniture design. Before you admire the furniture collection, take a walk around the campus, where you can marvel at the main museum building designed by Frank Gehry; the Vitra Schaudepot – which houses the furniture collection – designed by Herzog & de Meuron; Zaha Hadid’s former fire station; and Tadao Ando’s conference centre. There is a beautiful garden by the Dutch designer Piet Oudolf, and the recently added Doshi Retreat for a moment of quiet reflection designed by the Indian architect Balkrishna Doshi, his first completed project outside India and the last he worked on before he died in 2023. That’s half the day gone, so time to head inside. In lots of ways, exploring the Schaudepot is like walking through a giant doll’s house, with the rooms filled with instantly recognisable furniture icons from the 19th century to today, including works by Verner Panton, Le Corbusier, Alvar Aalto and Charles and Ray Eames. The museum also puts on temporary exhibitions. And if all of that has exhausted you, head to the VitraHaus Café, which serves a delicious lunch. Max Benato The Volkshaus, a boutique hotel in the old town, has doubles from 152 swiss francs (£138) room-only Lübeck, Germany Unless you’ve read Buddenbrooks, Thomas Mann’s epic family saga, you may not have heard of Lübeck. But in the middle ages, this port city in Germany, 70km north-east of Hamburg, was one of the richest and most powerful places on Earth. Today, despite the best efforts of the RAF to destroy it in 1942, it remains a beautifully intact medieval gem. The old town is a Unesco world heritage site. It sits on an island in the centre of the city, encircled by the rivers Trave and Wakenitz, and the water is a good place to start exploring. My boyfriend and I hired an electric boat (€49 for up to six people) and spent an hour circumnavigating and gazing at its distinctive seven church spires. Back on dry land, we set off on a guided walking tour, starting at the imposing – if wonky – Holsten Gate. We took in the five red brick churches the spires belong to (two have doubles), and climbed one of them, St Petri’s viewing tower, for a panoramic view. We also stopped at the 800-year-old town hall on the marketplace. But just as fascinating was what lies behind the gothic splendour. At one time, there were 180 hidden alleyways and courtyards threaded through the old town, and about 80 remain. These labyrinthine lanes were built behind wealthy merchants’ mansions to house the poor. Today, the restored cottages are sought-after and the flower-filled, cobbled alleys are charming to explore. To better understand Lübeck’s past, we visited the European Hansemuseum in the old castle monastery. It tells the story of the Hanseatic League, the powerful trade network that stretched from England to Russia and gave Lübeck (“the Queen of the League”) its wealth in the middle ages and its status as a free city state right up to 1937. In a nearby palace, the Museum Behnhaus Drägerhaus displays 19th- and early 20th-century German and European art, including work by Edvard Munch, who visited Lübeck and painted its salt warehouses. Just round the corner is the Günter Grass-Haus, where the writer regularly stayed (he died in Lübeck in 2015). We visited in June during the HanseKulturFestival, when the quarter around St Jakob’s church was full of live music stages, food stalls and outdoor bars. The next festival isn’t until 2028, but there are annual museum, theatre and literature nights, and popup live music in the summer. Lübeck has three natural open-air swimming areas, one on the island. And the seaside isn’t far away – we had a day trip to Travemünde, a historic resort town with miles of sandy beach, taking a scenic river ferry there (90 minutes) and a 20-minute train back. In town, the medieval Schiffergesellschaft (Seafarers’ Guild) is now a traditional Hanseatic restaurant, with long communal tables. Alongside North Sea fish and Holstein meat dishes are vegetarian versions of labskaus, a sort of hash. Sadly, we couldn’t visit Buddenbrookhaus, the museum dedicated to the novel, as it is being renovated. It is expected to reopen in 2030 – which gives you plenty of time to read Mann’s 864-page doorstopper. Like Lübeck itself, it is worth the effort. Rachel Dixon The trip was provided by germany.travel and luebeck-tourismus.de. Accommodation was provided by Liho Lübeck, doubles from £73 room-only Parma, Italy Parma is just far enough off Italy’s main travel routes to discourage the huge crowds of tourists that flood the likes of Venice and Florence. Most travellers reach this tranquil Italian gem by flying into Milan or Bologna, followed by an hour’s train ride. It is definitely worth that extra effort, as I discover a city that ticks every box for a weekend getaway: fabulous museums and frescoed churches without long queues or the need to book a timeslot in advance; friendly, affordable trattorie and osterie showcasing a feast of local food and wines; and, if you time it right, the chance to catch an opera composed by locally born Giuseppe Verdi in the intimate Teatro Regio. The historic centre of Parma is small and easily explored on foot, taking me past an array of architectural masterpieces. I kick off at the grand Piazza Duomo, dominated by the imposing 900-year-old romanesque cathedral. Everyone’s eyes are drawn up to the ornate cupola, decorated with a captivating illusionist fresco by local Renaissance artist Antonio da Correggio. Next to the cathedral stands the early gothic Battistero, an octagonal baptistery whose bare, minimalist exterior contrasts with an incredible explosion of colours from the 13th- and 14th-century paintings that cover the interior. Then, tucked away behind the Duomo, I come upon the entrance of the medieval Monastero di San Giovanni Evangelista, whose cloisters and garden are a peaceful oasis. Entry to the monastery and cathedral is free. Parma’s big must-see is the monumental Palazzo della Pilotta, a baroque complex of palatial museums, a library and remarkable 400-year-old theatre, all included in a single €18 entry ticket. Just by the Parma river that slices the city into two, the palazzo was built by the Farnese family, whose patronage created most of the city’s Renaissance monuments. The Teatro Farnese, made almost entirely of wood, is rarely used as a venue today, but a visit remains an incredible experience. I leave most sightseeing time, though, for the Pilotta’s landmark Galleria Nazionale di Parma, a treasure trove of old master paintings. It may not quite rival the collection of the Uffizi, but I enjoy the chance to just turn up without booking in advance and quietly appreciate works by Leonardo da Vinci, Fra Angelico, Canaletto and Tintoretto without being surrounded by crowds. Sightseeing is only part of Parma’s attraction, however, as this is one of Italy’s food capitals. I walk into the rustic, raucous OsteMagno bar, where everyone is tucking into tagliere – wooden boards piled with razor-thin slices of cured ham, the famous prosciutto crudo di Parma, artisan salami and crumbly aged parmigiano reggiano cheese, accompanied by a glass of the local’s favourite tipple, fizzy red Lambrusco wine, which is a lot more drinkable than I expect. This is not a city to seek out chic, gourmet restaurants, but rather one of the many traditional trattorie such as Da Antonia, whose eponymous owner has overseen the cucina for more than 50 years, or the 120-year-old Trattoria Corrieri, serving up generous plates of homemade pasta for less than €15. John Brunton Palazzo Dalla Rosa Prati has doubles from €80 room-only Santander, Spain Often dismissed as little more than a ferry terminal – somewhere to stop overnight if you want to take your dog to Europe or lower your carbon footprint – the port city of Santander is undergoing something of a cultural renaissance. It’s already blessed with a spectacular bay facing the Cantabrian mountains, wide sandy beaches, grand, colonnaded plazas and superb food, but the opening of new art spaces and museums in the coming months will put the Cantabrian capital firmly on the weekend-break map. Leading the way on 8 September is Faro Santander – a new cultural centre in a grand historical building housing a 1,000-piece art collection belonging to Banco Santander, including works by Velázquez, Goya, Titian, Rubens and Picasso. Different parts of the collection will be shown at different times. With its ornate white facade facing the bay, the Pereda building was previously the bank’s headquarters, but has been transformed into a striking, 21st-century museum space by Pritzker prize-winning British architect David Chipperfield. Santander’s moment in the spotlight will extend into 2027 when Madrid’s Reina Sofia Museum opens its first outpost, set in a similarly grand neo-Renaissance building just a few metres away from Faro Santander. The museum will house the Archivo Lafuente, with paintings, sculptures and manuscripts, including major collections on dadaism and the Spanish civil war, as well as art from Spain, North America and Latin America. Faro Santander and Archivo Lafuente will form two points on a kind of “art triangle”, along with architect Renzo Piano’s 2017 Centro Botín contemporary art centre just over the road. With a bijou but impressive permanent collection, including works by Matisse, Juan Gris, Joaquín Sorolla and Mark Rothko, the Centro Botín sits on the waterfront like a giant, stilt-mounted, 60s alarm clock sawn in half. Spaniards cottoned on to Santander’s charms long ago, and the seafront is lined with elegant fin-de-siècle villas built when well-heeled Madrileños discovered that the city’s Atlantic breezes were the perfect respite from the Spanish capital’s infernal summer. More than 100 years later, while Britain was experiencing its own heatwave, I followed their lead. Temperatures were in the balmy high 20s as I ambled past toddlers building sand castles and teenagers frolicking in the surf on El Sardinero beach, just 15 minutes by bus from the city centre. The centre itself is wonderfully walkable and there’s an unhurried, laid-back vibe in the streets, grand plazas and narrow alleys near the gothic cathedral, lined with bars serving pinchos – the Cantabrian equivalent to tapas. After tucking into tender, grilled squid, laced with gutsy garlic and olive oil, at Mesón Rampalay on a leafy square, I spent a fascinating couple of hours at Mupac – the Museum of Prehistory and Archaeology of Cantabria, just a few minutes’ walk away from Faro Santander. The museum, which is home to one of Spain’s most important prehistoric collections, features excellent interactive displays, and in 2027 it is moving to a brand new, multimillion-euro building. By next year, it seems, Santander will be not just the capital of Cantabria, but a capital of culture too. Eddi Fiegel The trip was provided by Faro Santander. Abba Santander, near the Centro Botín, has stylish doubles from €66 room-only

item.title: ‘I never imagined such pleasure could be had from the simple sardine’: readers’ favourite foodie experiences in Europe
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Score: 2.73
Simple sardines in the Algarve Last August, the smoky aroma of grilled sardines drifting over the beach in Portimão woke me up from my sunbathing on the beach. Attracted by the aroma of barbecued fish, we found ourselves in the old port where, for €12, I was served two delicious sandwiches on rustic bread of sardines in garlic and olive oil, with a small cold beer. I sat down, ate and chatted with locals on benches at simple communal tables. The important thing seemed to be to enjoy food together. The next morning, a reenactment of the fishing boats arriving loaded with fish, as they once were, was a real spectacle – complete with guitar playing, drum-banging and excited seagulls whirling and wailing above in the hope of a feast. Later, concerts and dancing animated the town as the party for the sardine festival went on well into the night. Cooking demos and dishes including sardine-based soup and salads, added to the enjoyment. I never imagined such pleasure could be had from the simple sardine. Joe A family dinner in the Faroe Islands My wife and I visited the Faroe Islands a few years ago, where we took part in heimablídni, a concept where traditional Faroese food is served in a home. We found it to be one of the best ways to experience the Faroes and a unique experience to share a meal with a local family. Homecooked dishes showcase ingredients from the surrounding sea and mountains. We were served smoked salmon from the host’s own smoker, lamb, potatoes and traditional specialities, all accompanied with great conversation about Faroese life and traditions. Sitting around a family table makes the experience feel personal and authentic. Mike A vegan feast in Sicily As a vegan who loves trying local cuisine, the combination of warm hospitality and a high proportion of locals with a lactose intolerance makes Sicily the ideal foodie getaway. Having hiked to the top of Monte Pellegrino in 35C heat, we popped into a small nondescript street-food shop (the only place that was open) and were delighted to find panelle – delicious crispy chickpea-flour fritters served in sesame bread. We ate them overlooking Palermo harbour. That evening, we tried Haiku, a vegan restaurant with reimagined classics based on dishes such as carbonara and tiramisu. It was so good we kept ordering more and more courses until we could barely move. Esther Strong spirits and small plates in Greece The city of Volos is famous for its Tsipouradika – tavernas that serve tsipouro, a strong spirit made from pomace, the stems, skins and seeds that are left over from wine making. It comes plain or infused with botanicals and anise, and is served with ice and water. Each glass you order arrives with a different small plate or meze. It could be grilled peppers, sundried octopus, a spicy cheese spread or smoked mackerel. You take pot luck as to what the patron fancies dishing up that day. Barbara The perfect snack to pair with Lithuanian beer In Vilnius, we came across the ultimate food pairing for the fantastic beers available there in the form of kepta duona – deep-fried rye bread with garlic and cheese. Every bar has a slightly different version – raw, roast or confit garlic with cream, melted or simply grated cheese. A heavenly snack that could easily become your main meal. Natalie Vegan delights in the patisseries of Paris Being an unfortunate combination of a foodie and a vegan, I was prepared for a weekend of staring longingly into patisserie windows when heading to Paris earlier this summer. I was not prepared for the unbridled joy awaiting me at the Land & Monkeys boulangeries/patisseries scattered across the capital. It began with an outrageously creamy raspberry petit gateaux from its Montmartre branch, followed by the unbelievable fluff and flake of a croissant aux champignons in the Marais the next day. A parting madeleine for the Eurostar on our last day was the pièce de résistance. Elinor Pasta with pears in Bologna It was in Bologna, Italy’s self-proclaimed food capital, where I sampled the city’s signature dish of tortellini. We stumbled across Rosarose Bistrot, enticed by tables with red-checked cloths set in the middle of a cobblestone road. I enjoyed shells stuffed with tangy gorgonzola cheese and chunks of caramelised pears, a fruit I would usually avoid, but I placed trust in the regional delicacy. The fruit’s sweetness blended harmoniously with the strong cheese flavour; crispy and soft fried bread known as crescentine, was used to soak up the remaining sauce. It was only right to mark this culinary experience with a small tortellini keyring from a nearby gift shop, filled with various merchandise emblazoned with the pasta shell. Caitlin Catalonia’s ultimate slow-food festival Last year, I discovered the ultimate slow-food festival – the Snail Feast of Lleida (L’Aplec del Caragol), 100 miles west of Barcelona. Over a long weekend, there was music, dancing, cooking and feasting, all in celebration of the tiny mollusc. Entrance to the festival is free, and visitors can enjoy traditional snail dishes in tents, local restaurants or simply in the town squares. I had two helpings of snails a la gormanda, cooked in a sauce of spicy paprika and herbs. Since attending the festival, I have been treading carefully in my garden in case I harm what I discovered are delicate and delicious creatures. Helen Heavenly cakes in Slovenia Having travelled by train from Bristol down through the Netherlands, Germany, Switzerland and Italy, we reached our penultimate stop, Lake Bled. We’d been awed by the beautiful Swiss alpine scenery, but Bled took it up a notch. After a day of cycling from Bled to Lake Bohinj and back, we refuelled on the local delicacy, Bled cake, a sumptuously smooth set custard encased in the lightest of mille-feuille pastry and topped with whipped cream. Imagine an English custard slice, only a million times better. It was so welcome after a day in the Slovenian mountain air, we made it a holiday habit. A Bled cake a day until we had to come home! Sara Winning tip: delicious seafood soup in Spain Few meals linger in the memory like a proper Asturian sopa de pescado y marisco (seafood soup). After kayaking 10 miles down the Sella River, my reward in the town of Arriondas wasn’t a humble bowl of soup – it was a whole pan! Every flavour shone through in a broth packed with white fish, prawns and sweet crab claws, so extraordinarily rich it almost brought me to tears. I devoured it all, skipping the rest of the courses without regret. Years later in Gijón, history repeated itself. Even my soup-sceptical husband declared it the best he had ever tasted. In Asturias, fish soup isn’t a starter. It’s an obsession in a pot. Oksana Comments (…) Sign in or create your Guardian account to join the discussion

item.title: 25 years later: Looking back at how 9/11 reshaped the aviation industry
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 5.60
25 years later: Looking back at how 9/11 reshaped the aviation industry It was a day that changed America. The fallout from "9/11" reverberated across the nation, affecting everything from politics and foreign affairs to the economy. But few things changed more for Americans than the way we fly. Even 25 years since 9/11, the day's impact on aviation has been a lasting one. As the attacks unfolded, air traffic controllers and airline personnel scrambled to figure out what was happening, which ultimately culminated in the first (and to this date, only) complete closure of U.S. airspace. But once planes took to the air again, the passenger experience on the ground rapidly evolved. Major security overhaul In the weeks and months that followed 9/11, new security protocols were rolled out at airports nationwide. Gate areas were restricted to ticketed passengers only. No more welcoming loved ones at the gate. As those security perimeters pushed out, a federalized workforce – the Transportation Security Administration – was created to manage secure spaces at U.S. airports and other important travel nodes. This was a major shift from the private companies tasked with securing our skies before 9/11. Of course, it wasn't just the terrorist attacks of that day that brought about changes. The nation's security apparatus continued to evolve as new potential threats emerged. - Dec. 2001: Richard Reid attempted to ignite an explosive device hidden in his shoe, leading to new procedures that required passengers to remove their shoes when proceeding through checkpoints. - Aug. 2006: A foiled plot involving liquid explosives on U.S.-bound flights led to new restrictions on the size of liquids allowed in carry-on luggage, which eventually became the 3-1-1 rule that remains in effect to this day. - Dec. 2009: A Nigerian national gained notoriety when he tried to detonate a device sewn into his underwear, leading to the installation of full-body scanners and more invasive pat-down procedures at airports across the U.S. While this increasingly stringent screening process created plenty of frustration for flyers, the post-9/11 years also saw the emergence of new trusted traveler programs — beginning with Global Entry, which launched as a small pilot program at three airports on June 6, 2008, before becoming a permanent program of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) on March 7, 2012. Applicants undergo a background check, and once approved as "low-risk" travelers, they can enjoy expedited entry into the U.S. after arriving from an international destination. Around that same time, another notable innovation officially launched at Las Vegas' Harry Reid International Airport (LAS) in Dec. 2011: TSA PreCheck. Originally extended for free to frequent flyers on select airlines, the program now offers paid membership for travelers to enjoy quicker, less-intensive screening at U.S. airports. Even Real ID traces its roots back to the attacks, as it was originally passed in 2005 based on recommendations from the 9/11 commission to standardize state-issued identification. That innovation continues today, with new technologies like Touchless ID, Clear and eGates to enable even quicker passenger screening. Financial ramifications Security may have been at the forefront, but 9/11 also helped accelerate the industry's shift from a highly regulated model to the free-market version we know today. The near-immediate collapse in air travel demand dealt the industry a severe financial shock, even with up to $15 billion in federal bailout funds . Planes flew nearly empty in the weeks following 9/11. Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA) remained shut down for weeks, dealing a massive financial blow to US Airways, the largest carrier there (which filed for bankruptcy protection in 2002 and again in 2004 before ultimately merging with America West in 2005). Midway Airlines, a mid-size carrier based in North Carolina that was already teetering financially, abruptly went out of business. Elsewhere, layoffs swelled. Even bigger, established airlines went through bankruptcy-driven restructuring due to losses stemming from 9/11, including United, Delta and Northwest. A series of mergers followed as airlines reorganized to become more powerful by combining with rivals while also streamlining redundant parts of their operations to boost profits. By the end of the 2010s, a dozen major airlines went through a cycle of tie-ups that left four big airlines (American, Delta, United and Southwest) controlling roughly 80% of the U.S. market. Around the same time, airlines began looking for financial lifelines as cash reserves dwindled. They got it from banks willing to buy miles by the millions that they could then dole out to customers holding their cobranded airline credit cards. It's a trend that's grown, hastened further by the financial crisis of 2008-09. Today, airlines make millions of dollars in revenue just from their bank deals on cobranded credit cards. But it wasn't all about dollars and cents. The personal side of the attacks It's impossible to talk about 9/11 without acknowledging the incredible human toll of the attacks. Nearly 3,000 people perished that day, and many more have been impacted with the loss of loved ones — or with lingering health issues from rescue and recovery efforts at Ground Zero. For the aviation industry, the 246 innocent men and women on the four hijacked planes were more than just a number. They were husbands and wives, fathers and mothers, sons and daughters. They were our neighbors, our friends, our coworkers, going about their daily lives when the most mundane of circumstances — a cross-country flight on a Tuesday morning — turned into a tragedy. But those individuals didn't go out quietly. Flight attendants alerted their operations teams from the back of the planes. Passengers called their loved ones. And the 40 brave souls onboard United Flight 93 made the ultimate sacrifice when they stormed the cockpit and forced their aircraft down in rural Pennsylvania, preventing a terrible day from getting even worse. It is these travelers that we honor here today. Twenty-five years ago, 33 airline crew members and 213 passengers took to the skies, not knowing it would be their final flight. Here at The Points Guy, we recognize that travel is a privilege to be cherished. With every trip we take, we make memories that so many no longer can. And we will continue to board those planes, not in spite of what happened that September morning, but because we will not take the gift of travel for granted. We remember them, and we fly on.

item.title: Who's eligible for the Chase Ink Business Cash and Unlimited's $1,000 cash-back welcome offer?
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 5.30
Who's eligible for the Chase Ink Business Cash and Unlimited's $1,000 cash-back welcome offer? If your small business is looking for an affordable way to earn cash back or boost its Ultimate Rewards balance, the Ink Business Cash® Credit Card (see rates and fees) and Ink Business Unlimited® Credit Card (see rates and fees) are two great choices. Currently, both cards are offering their highest-ever welcome bonuses, which could be even more valuable if you have an eligible Ultimate Rewards card that provides access to Chase's transfer partners. It's important to know whether or not you're eligible for a welcome bonus. You don't want to waste a hard pull on your credit just to find out you didn't meet Chase's requirements from the start. Current offers on the Ink Business Cash and Ink Business Unlimited Currently, the Ink Business Cash and Ink Business Unlimited have the same welcome offer: Earn $1,000 bonus cash back after spending $8,000 on purchases in the first four months of account opening. These best-ever offers end on Sept. 17 at 9 a.m. ET, so I recommend applying sooner rather than later. We haven't seen offers this good on either of these cards before. According to TPG's September 2026 valuations, this welcome offer could be worth up to $2,050 if you hold a card that offers access to Chase's transfer partners, such as the Ink Business Preferred® Credit Card (see rates and fees) or the Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business℠ (see rates and fees). That's because you can combine the rewards you earn on your Ink Business Cash or Ink Business Unlimited with that account and redeem them with any of Chase's partners. Am I eligible for the Ink Business Cash or Ink Business Unlimited's welcome bonus? When considering whether you're eligible for a welcome bonus on either card, there are several factors to keep in mind. Chase 5/24 rule Chase's well-known 5/24 rule states that you may not be approved for a new Chase card if you've opened five or more personal credit cards over the past 24 months. While small-business cards like the Ink Business Cash and Ink Business Unlimited don't count toward 5/24, Chase will still take that rule into consideration when deciding whether to approve you. No-annual-fee Ink family rules Chase has gradually tightened its eligibility rules for cards in the same family. For the Ink Cash and Ink Unlimited, you can earn a welcome offer on either card, but not both. That rings true even if you earned a welcome bonus on one of these cards before the rules changed, or if you closed your account years ago. In addition, you likely won't be able to earn a second bonus on the same no-annual-fee Ink card. For example, if you previously earned a welcome bonus on the Ink Unlimited, you probably can't earn another one on that card. Do I need a business to open the Ink Cash or Ink Unlimited? You don't need a traditional business, such as an LLC, to open a small-business card like the Ink Cash or Ink Unlimited. However, you do need a side hustle or similar gig at a minimum. Freelancing, pet sitting, driving for a ride-hailing service and reselling are all examples of work that may qualify you for a small-business card. Related: How to get a business credit card Can I hold both the Ink Cash and Ink Unlimited at the same time? Yes, but remember that you likely won't be able to earn a welcome bonus on both cards. Since both cards have identical welcome offers right now, you don't need to worry about which card offers greater value with its bonus when deciding which to apply for first. If you don't want to hold both cards, your choice will come down to how your business typically spends. Since the Ink Business Cash earns bonus rewards at office supply stores and on common utilities, dining and gas (dining and gas subject to a spending cap), it's a better choice for business owners who frequently make those purchases. The Ink Business Unlimited earns 5% cash back on Lyft (through Sept. 30, 2027) and 1.5% cash back on all other purchases. That makes it an ideal choice for businesses that make a wide variety of purchases or whose spending habits shift regularly. Bottom line It's always important to check whether you're eligible for a card and its welcome bonus before applying. Credit card issuers will almost always perform a hard pull on your credit report when you apply; too many hard pulls on your credit report can lower your credit score. Given that, you don't want to waste a hard pull on a card you more than likely aren't eligible for. That said, if you meet the eligibility requirements for either the Ink Business Cash or Ink Business Unlimited, now is a great time to apply. Both of these cards have a best-ever welcome offer that's ending on Sept. 17 at 9 a.m. ET. To learn more, check out our full reviews of the Ink Business Cash and Ink Business Unlimited. Apply here: Chase Ink Business Cash Apply here: Chase Ink Business Unlimited

item.title: Hilton American Express card offers worth up to 200,000 bonus points
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 5.23
Hilton American Express card offers worth up to 200,000 bonus points Editor's Note If you've been considering a Hilton credit card, you're in the right place. item.title: How to get more out of every all-inclusive vacation with IHG One Rewards
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 4.84
How to get more out of every all-inclusive vacation with IHG One Rewards All-inclusive vacations can simplify trip planning, and IHG Hotels & Resorts makes it easy to discover, compare and book a growing range of participating all-inclusive resorts across destinations worldwide. Booking through IHG can add even more value to the experience. With IHG One Rewards, members can earn and redeem points at participating all-inclusive properties. That means a beach vacation can help fund a future trip or reduce your out-of-pocket cost if you redeem IHG points for your stay. After all, one of the biggest appeals of an all-inclusive vacation is knowing that many of your meals, drinks and activities are included in your stay. But by booking a participating all-inclusive stay through IHG, you may also be able to earn points, work toward elite status and enjoy select IHG One Rewards benefits during your stay. Here's what to know about getting more out of an all-inclusive vacation with IHG One Rewards. IHG has a growing all-inclusive portfolio IHG Hotels & Resorts has expanded its all-inclusive portfolio to give travelers more ways to discover and book resort experiences across a range of brands, destinations and stay types, all through the hotel loyalty program you already know and trust. Iberostar Beachfront Resorts are a key part of IHG's all-inclusive offering, with participating resorts in beach destinations across Mexico, the Caribbean, Europe and Africa. For example, if you're planning an all-inclusive trip to Mexico, you might look at Iberostar Selection Riviera Cancún or JOIA Paraíso by Iberostar. If the Caribbean is calling, Iberostar Selection Bávaro Suites in the Dominican Republic may be worth considering. And if you're thinking about Europe, Iberostar Jardín del Sol Suites in Mallorca might be a good fit. But IHG's all-inclusive options go beyond Iberostar Beachfront Resorts. For example, Holiday Inn Club Vacations Grand Residences All-Inclusive and Holiday Inn Club Vacations The Royal Sands All-Inclusive are notable options in Mexico. And if you're interested in an all-inclusive vacation without leaving the U.S., the voco Sandpiper All-Inclusive Resort in Florida is worth considering. Of course, the best all-inclusive resort for your trip depends on who you are traveling with and what you want from your vacation. Some resorts are better suited for families who want pools, activities and kids clubs. Meanwhile, other resorts are more appealing to couples, friends and multigenerational groups that want to package their stay, dining and activities together. That's one reason it can be useful to start your search on IHG's website or app. You can look for participating all-inclusive resorts by destination and compare options. Plus, booking through IHG ensures your IHG One Rewards number is attached to your reservation. Earn IHG points on all-inclusive stays One of the best reasons to book an all-inclusive stay through IHG is that you can earn IHG points. IHG members earn 10 points per dollar spent on qualifying stays at participating IHG hotels and resorts, including Iberostar Beachfront Resorts and Holiday Inn Club Vacations resorts. Plus, travelers with IHG elite status can earn even more through status bonuses as follows: | IHG elite status tier | Base points on qualifying stays | Status bonus on qualifying stays | Total points earned on qualifying stays | |---|---|---|---| | Member | 10 points per dollar spent | None | 10 points per dollar spent | | Silver Elite | 10 points per dollar spent | 20% | 12 points per dollar spent | | Gold Elite | 10 points per dollar spent | 40% | 14 points per dollar spent | | Platinum Elite | 10 points per dollar spent | 60% | 16 points per dollar spent | | Diamond Elite | 10 points per dollar spent | 100% | 20 points per dollar spent | Earning points can be especially valuable on an all-inclusive stay. Since these stays often cost more than a typical hotel night, a qualifying all-inclusive resort booking could earn you a significant number of IHG points. To earn IHG points on your all-inclusive stay, book through an eligible method such as the IHG website or app and confirm your IHG One Rewards number is attached to your reservation. This is important, as your stay may not qualify for points or IHG One Rewards benefits if you book through another source (including most online travel agencies). Redeem IHG points for all-inclusive stays You can also redeem IHG points for reward nights at all-inclusive properties that participate in the IHG One Rewards program. To redeem IHG points for an all-inclusive stay — including those at Iberostar Beachfront Resorts — go to IHG's website or app, log in to your account and search for your destination, dates and number of guests. Be sure to set your rate preference to "Reward Nights." From there, you can compare properties. On the results page, you'll see the starting nightly award rate and some flags that let you know if the property is all-inclusive or adults only. If you click a specific property, you can see the available room types. Note that some room types may carry a higher nightly award rate. Be sure to click "Reward Nights + All Inclusive" for the room type and rate you select to confirm what's included in the rate. It's important to enter the correct number of guests, including children, when searching for your all-inclusive vacation, as IHG adjusts reward-night pricing based on factors such as guest count and dining plan. For example, a two-night stay at Iberostar Selection Cancun in Mexico might cost 90,000 points per night for two adults but 135,000 points per night for two adults and two children. And at some resorts, such as Iberostar Waves Cristina in Spain, you can choose from breakfast-only, half-board and full all-inclusive award rates, each priced accordingly. If you have an eligible IHG One Rewards credit card, you may be able to get even more value from your points at participating IHG properties. The fourth Reward Night is free when you redeem points for any stay of four or more nights. You'll automatically see the discounted award rates at participating properties if you're logged into your account, have an eligible card and search for a reward stay of four nights or longer. Plus, eligible Cardmembers have an annual Free Night that can be enhanced with points to access hotels above the 40,000-point redemption threshold. Get IHG elite-night credits and benefits on all-inclusive stays Qualifying all-inclusive stays can also help IHG One Rewards members work toward elite status and milestone rewards. Plus, IHG One Rewards members can enjoy select benefits during qualifying all-inclusive stays at participating IHG hotels and resorts and participating Iberostar Beachfront Resorts. Even if you don't have elite status with IHG, you can access member rates, Wi-Fi access and 2 p.m. late checkout, subject to availability at participating hotels. IHG Platinum Elite and Diamond Elite members may be eligible for benefits such as early check-in, room upgrades and a welcome amenity at check-in, subject to availability. And if you have an annual lounge membership that you earned through the milestone rewards program, you can use the Star Prestige facilities when available at participating Iberostar Beachfront Resort properties. All these benefits can be especially useful at a resort. A late checkout can give you a few more hours at the pool before an evening flight, while an early check-in can make a morning arrival less awkward. And a room upgrade can make a special trip feel even more spectacular. Just keep in mind that many elite benefits are subject to availability and may vary by brand, hotel and stay type. Bottom line All-inclusive vacations are appealing because they can make travel simpler, but booking an all-inclusive stay through IHG can add another layer of value. Through IHG Hotels and Resorts, travelers can discover, compare and book all-inclusive resorts in a wide range of vacation destinations. And IHG One Rewards members can earn points on qualifying paid stays, redeem points for all-inclusive stays and enjoy member or elite benefits along the way. Whether you're planning a family beach trip, a couples getaway, a friends trip or a multigenerational vacation, it's worth checking IHG's all-inclusive options before you book.

item.title: Frontier plans first South America service, adds 3 former Spirit routes
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 4.76
Frontier plans first South America service, adds 3 former Spirit routes Frontier Airlines is getting ready to fly to South America for the first time. The Denver-based budget airline on Thursday announced nonstop service to three cities in Colombia. The trio of routes from Orlando International Airport (MCO) will mark the first time Frontier has sent its planes to the continent. It will also be a clear move to pick up routes abandoned by former rival Spirit Airlines, which had a significant presence in Colombia prior to its collapse earlier this year. Among the routes: nonstop service to the Colombian capital city of Bogota, along with new flights to Medellin and Cartagena. Read more: Spirit is gone. Can other budget airlines survive? "We believe there is strong, unmet demand for low-cost travel between Orlando and Colombia, and we look forward to offering affordable flight options between these two magnificent destinations," Tyri Squyres, Frontier's vice president of public and consumer affairs, said in a statement announcing the news. Read more: Frontier wants to be an airline you want to fly. Will first class and new perks do the trick? Frontier's 3 new Colombia routes Here's the full rundown of the new international service Frontier announced: | Route | Launch date | Frequency | |---|---|---| | Orlando to Jose Maria Cordova International Airport (MDE) in Medellin | Dec. 10 | Daily | | Orlando to El Dorado International Airport (BOG) in Bogota | Dec. 14 | Six times per week at the start; daily after March 6, 2027 | | Orlando to Rafael Nunez International Airport (CTG) in Cartagena | Dec. 19 | Weekly | Picking up where Spirit left off All three of those new Frontier flights were routes once served by Spirit. The now-defunct budget airline had been America's top ultra-low-cost carrier in Colombia and in South America. So, Spirit's collapse left a clear void for consumers looking to fly to the region on a budget airline. TPG's Summer Hull: An ode to Spirit Airlines — Yeah, they were all yellow It's worth watching to see whether Frontier makes further moves to acquire former Spirit routes in Latin America. Frontier executives have said the airline would take a more measured approach in picking up service abandoned by its former competitor. At the same time, the airline isn't done adding former Spirit routes to the mix — even though it has been several months since its big yellow planes were grounded. "There are opportunities to pick off markets that they've obviously exited, now, over the coming year or two," Frontier CEO James Dempsey told me in July. Worth noting The reveal of Frontier's first-ever service to South America comes days after the airline confirmed it was fully exiting America's largest market. The carrier plans to bid farewell to New York City's John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) next month. Related reading:

item.title: TPG'S favorite things to do in New York City
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 3.35
TPG'S favorite things to do in New York City There's no place like New York City, and as many of us New Yorkers like to say, "It's New York or nowhere." It's a microcosm of the whole world, but also something so singularly its own. You can hear any language or find any food. You can see the world's next big star play a show in a grimy basement club or see the world's current biggest star play the world's most famous arena. New York City has it all, and then some. But on Sept. 11, 2001, New York City lost a lot: friends, family, colleagues and strangers. What it didn't lose that day 25 years ago was its spirit. If there's ever a place with tenacity, it's New York. So whether you've been dreaming of a trip to "The Big Apple" for years or have been visiting for a long time, our TPG family has shared some of our favorite things to do, see, eat and experience in New York City. Pay your respect at the 9/11 Memorial and Museum Located on the site of the original World Trade Center buildings, the 9/11 Memorial is a breathtaking set of fountains surrounded by the names of those we lost 25 years ago. The memorial itself is moving and profound, but below ground, the museum helps tell "the story of 9/11 through media, narratives, and a collection of monumental and authentic artifacts, presenting visitors with personal stories of loss, recovery, and hope." Note that, in honor of the 25th anniversary, Michael Bloomberg, the former mayor of New York and current chairman of the memorial, will be matching up to $25 million in donations to The Never Forget Fund, which supports operations at the site as well as educational efforts to ensure the memory of 9/11 lives on. Join TPG in donating to The Never Forget Fund today. Catch a Broadway show A trip to New York isn't complete without heading uptown to catch the unique vibe that is Times Square before settling into a powerhouse play or musical on Broadway. There are plenty of ways to get tickets, but many of us New Yorkers use TodayTix for last-minute deals (if you're willing to be flexible on what you see). You could also visit the TKTS booths in Times Square or near Lincoln Center for same-day, discounted tickets to select shows. Otherwise, book in advance to make sure you get a ticket. Right now, it's a great time to see a show because it's Broadway Week, meaning some 2-for-1 tickets are available for a ton of shows between now and Sept. 20. And if you need a suggestion, Rachel Dratch in Richard O'Brien's "The Rocky Horror Picture Show" is truly phenomenal. Go on a food crawl in Flushing, Queens If you visit New York City and only stay in Manhattan, did you really visit? One way to get out to another borough is by popping over to Flushing, Queens, for some of the best food in the country. Home to a large and vibrant Chinese community, the area is stacked with mouthwatering restaurants, food stalls, hole-in-the-wall joints and everything in between. There are a number of companies that offer organized food tours in the area, or search "Flushing Food Crawl" on Instagram and let people's photos guide your stomach. Spend a day museum-hopping New York City is home to some of the best museums in the world, and you've probably heard of some of the major institutions like MoMA (The Museum of Modern Art) and The Met (The Metropolitan Museum of Art). But that's not all. In Queens, the Museum of the Moving Image is a favorite with an incredible exhibition on Jim Henson and the Muppets. In Brooklyn, the Brooklyn Museum has a serious permanent collection alongside a series of rotating exhibitions that always impress. And for a real look at what life was like for many New Yorkers in times past, the Tenement Museum in the Lower East Side that "welcomes you into the historically recreated homes of immigrants, migrants and refugees." Stop for drinks with a view People visiting New York like to go to the tops of buildings (we've got some pretty tall ones). But rather than just go stand in one, why not go drink in one? One great place is Nebeluz by José Andrés at The Ritz-Carlton New York, NoMad. There, you'll want to try the bagel & lox cone and a cocktail of your choice, all while enjoying stunning city views through floor-to-ceiling windows. Need more? Make a reservation at Overystory in FiDi for 64th-floor views and an award-winning cocktail menu. Just go for a walk New York City is so easy to get around, but the way to see it is by lacing up your shoes and setting off on foot. There are a million places we could send you for a dream walk, but I love to wander through the West Village, then up to 14th Street on the west side to reach The High Line, an elevated park that's magical to explore. For incredible views of the city skyline, walk through Williamsburg's Domino Park in Brooklyn, then spend an afternoon shopping on Bedford Avenue. Wherever you go, see if walking can be your first mode of transportation. If not, pop off the subway a stop or two early just to explore. Make the city your own But perhaps the best thing about New York City is that there's no shortage of things to do, places to visit and sights to see. Even as a resident of the city, there's no chance I could ever see or do everything it has to offer. It's one of the reasons visitors keep coming back: there's always something new on the menu. Twenty-five years after the skyline of New York was altered forever, the city is more vibrant than ever. And one of the best ways to honor those we lost on 9/11 is to visit the place they once called home.

item.title: A New York City foodie's secret to saving on restaurants? Blackbird's dining loyalty program
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 2.54
A New York City foodie's secret to saving on restaurants? Blackbird's dining loyalty program New York City has some of the best independent restaurants and coffee shops in the world. It's one of the reasons why I love living here, but it also means dining is easily my largest expense outside of rent each month — and most dining loyalty programs that help you save money at the places you eat at regularly are centered around national chains. Enter Blackbird. Blackbird is a loyalty program and payment app designed for independent restaurants and cafes. A friend introduced me to it earlier this year, and I've since fallen in love with it. You can earn and redeem rewards, access special perks, split and pay your bill and more via the app. The program even has elite status tiers that offer more value. For anyone unfamiliar, I'm breaking down all the program's pros and cons to help you decide if it's worth investing your time and energy. Why Blackbird is a game changer for big-city dining Blackbird allows you to earn Fly rewards points at member restaurants when you check in via the app. The more you check in and spend, the more valuable each visit becomes thanks to the program's loyalty tiers. Those just joining will earn 3 Fly points per dollar spent, but you can earn up to 7 Fly points per dollar spent at the highest Blackbird Club loyalty tier. Right now, Blackbird is available in nine destinations: - New York City (including all boroughs, plus Jersey City and Hoboken, New Jersey) - The Hamptons, New York - Charleston, South Carolina - Los Angeles - San Francisco - Denver - Aspen, Colorado - Vail, Colorado - Breckenridge, Colorado The list of participating restaurants is still growing, but there's a solid number of available spots in New York City currently — from easy weeknight dinner spots like Barn Joo to chains like Tacombi to cocktail bars like The Tusk Bar. I also took a look at available options in Blackbird's other locations. Understandably, New York City has the largest concentration of participating restaurants, but the other major cities on the list have a decent selection of restaurants, too. Checking in is as easy as tapping your phone to the small black Blackbird puck at the host stand, and it's easy to pay your bill (or split it among friends) directly in the app. The best part? You can even stack rewards with your credit card to double up on earning. For example, if you use your American Express® Gold Card to pay your bill through Blackbird, you'll earn Fly points and 4 American Express Membership Rewards points per dollar spent (on up to $50,000 per calendar year, then 1 point per dollar). Related: Best credit cards for dining Blackbird Club tiers If you spend enough with Blackbird throughout the year, you'll get access to higher earning rates and additional benefits via the tiered loyalty program. You get access to higher tiers of the program by spending with Blackbird Pay or preloading money into your Blackbird account to use at checkout (similar to how you can preload money into your Starbucks Rewards account). Here's a quick breakdown of each tier: | Elite status tier | How to qualify | Earning rates | Key benefits | |---|---|---|---| | Member | Spend $500 in a calendar year, or preload $250 to your Blackbird account. | | N/A | | Regular | Spend $5,000 in a calendar year, or preload $2,500 to your Blackbird account. | | | | Friends & Family | Spend $10,000 in a calendar year, or preload $5,000 to your Blackbird account. | | | I wouldn't recommend preloading money into Blackbird to hit any of the elite tiers, as that would limit your ability to double-dip with credit card rewards when paying the bill at the restaurant, but if you do spend enough at Blackbird restaurants throughout the year to gain access to elevated earning rates, priority reservations and concierge help, those are all potentially valuable benefits. The value breakdown Earning and redeeming with Blackbird is surprisingly straightforward. Depending on your status level, you'll earn between 3 and 7 Fly points per dollar spent, and 100 Fly points equals $1 in spending power toward future Blackbird purchases. That means that even at the free level, you're getting a 3% return on spending, which is on par with a lot of credit card earning rates (and remember, you can also earn credit card points or miles on top of your Blackbird earnings). At the highest member tier, you'll get an impressive 7% return on spending. Blackbird also offers opt-in challenges that let you earn additional Fly points (including a first-time user challenge) and a referral bonus, making it really easy to get immediate value from the program even after just one purchase. A concrete example: I spent $45.30 at a Mexican-focused Tacombi location for my first-ever check-in and got 4,095 points total (3 points per dollar spent on the bill, plus a referral bonus and a first-time bonus). Given that points are worth 1 cent each, I had nearly $41 to spend on a future Blackbird Pay bill. The downsides of Blackbird I have laid out many of the pros in this article already, but there are also some downsides to consider. Only nine destinations are currently participating, and within each, only select restaurants are available. In New York City and the other major participating metropolitan areas, like San Francisco and Los Angeles, you'll have plenty of options where you can earn rewards, but even in the Big Apple, the reality is that the majority of restaurants in the city aren't currently on Blackbird. In the Colorado mountain towns where Blackbird operates (Vail, Breckenridge and Aspen), your options for Blackbird are fairly limited. Another con is that the bill split feature doesn't allow you to itemize. If your friend group tends to share food or split things evenly regardless of itemization, that's not an issue. But if you want to itemize, you'll have to do it the old-fashion way: Pick one person to get the full tab, calculate each person's share separately and then settle via Venmo or Cash App. Who will find Blackbird most valuable? Blackbird has the potential to be a really valuable program — but only for the right user. Consider joining if you're: - A foodie who lives where Blackbird operates. Until Blackbird adds more cities, this program is only valuable to those who eat out often in the nine destinations where Blackbird is currently available. - Someone who often eats family-style meals and splits the bill with friends. The ability to split the bill directly in the app is a great benefit for friend groups like mine, where everyone wants to earn credit card points and miles on the meal. We tend to split things evenly instead of itemizing, so it works perfectly for us. - Regularly spending at least $500 on dining a year. Spending $500 per year will get you Member status and an elevated 4 points per dollar spent earning rate. If you also happen to have the Amex Gold, which offers 4 points per dollar spent on dining worldwide (on up to $50,000 per calendar year, then 1 point per dollar), you'll earn a total of 8 points per dollar spent on every qualifying meal. - An adventurous eater who likes trying a variety of restaurants. With Blackbird, you don't have to commit to being loyal to a single restaurant or chain to earn or redeem rewards. Bottom line I love a good travel redemption as much as the next girl, but there's something to be said about an easy way to earn rewards and benefits on an everyday expense like dining. Blackbird is straightforward to use, earns valuable rewards at an array of restaurants and allows me to stack rewards with my credit cards of choice. That's a no-brainer for someone like me who lives in an expensive city like New York and dines out at least once a week with friends. Know, though, that we've seen this movie before with loyalty programs that offer huge sign-up incentives and high earnings without fees. In some ways, this program feels a little too good to be true to me, and, usually, that means it is too good to be true in the long term. (Looking at you, MoviePass.) Still, the current earnings are simply too impressive to ignore, so I'm going to make the most of this program while its points are valuable and its earning rates are high, no matter which status I hold. If you sign up for the program, I'd recommend you do the same.
